Deep Dive · Measure right, reason in powers

Measurement runs quantities (fundamental bases plus derived combinations, SI units fundamental and derived) through dimensions (formulas, analysis, homogeneity checks, conversions) into error control (significant figures, rounding, least counts, accuracy versus precision, absolute-relative-percentage errors with propagation) ending in experiments (vernier, screw gauge techniques). Powers of M-L-T plus error bars underlie every later calculation - measure honestly, compute in dimensions, report with honest precision.
NEET facts:
  • Fundamental SI units number seven (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd).
  • Least count limits precision; percentage errors add in multiplication-division.

Chapter 1 · Topic 1

Physical quantities

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsMeasurements and UnitsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. A physical quantity is a property of a physical object or phenomenon, while a unit is a chosen standard used to express its magnitude. Its numerical value has meaning only when the unit is specified, so a numerical answer without a unit is incomplete. In JEE problems, first identify the quantity and the dimensions of its unit, then perform the required conversion.
Key formula(s). \(\text{numerical value}=\frac{\text{magnitude of the quantity}}{\text{magnitude of the unit}}\); \(1\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}=\frac{10^3\,\mathrm{m}}{3600\,\mathrm{s}}=\frac{5}{18}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); \(1\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}=10^3\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\)
Key points.
  • A correctly stated physical answer has a number, the correct unit, and an appropriate degree of precision.
  • Quantities can be added or subtracted only when they represent the same physical quantity in compatible units.
  • Multiplying a unit by \(10^n\) changes its numerical value by the same factor \(10^{-n}\).
  • A unit is not the same as a dimension: metre and centimetre are different units but have the same length dimension.
  • Products and quotients of units must be treated as products and quotients of the corresponding numerical factors.
Example 1.

The density of a metal is \(7.2\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\). Express it in \(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\).

  1. Convert mass first: \(1\,\mathrm{g}=10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg}\).
  2. Since \(1\,\mathrm{cm}=10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}\), the cubic-centimetre factor is \((10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m})^{-3}=10^6\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\).
  3. Thus \(\rho=7.2\times10^{-3}\times10^6\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\).

Answer: \(\rho=7.2\times10^3\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}=7200\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\).

Example 2.

A car travels \(5400\,\mathrm{km}\) in \(45\,\mathrm{min}\). Express its constant speed in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

  1. Convert the distance: \(5400\,\mathrm{km}=5.4\times10^6\,\mathrm{m}\).
  2. Convert the time: \(45\,\mathrm{min}=45\times60\,\mathrm{s}=2700\,\mathrm{s}\).
  3. Divide distance by time, not the reverse: \(v=(5.4\times10^6)/2700\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Answer: \(v=2.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Writing \(7.2\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) after changing only the mass unit.
  • Omitting the squared or cubed unit factor for area or volume.
  • Reporting \(5400/45\) without converting minutes to seconds.

Chapter 1 · Topic 2

Fundamental quantities

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsMeasurements and UnitsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fundamental quantities (length, mass, time, current, temperature, substance, luminous intensity) are independently defined base units no other quantity derives - seven SI bases chosen by convention. Every measurement expresses through them; dimensional analysis starts here. Memorise the seven with symbols (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd) - dimensions questions assume them cold.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Seven SI bases: length, mass, time, current, temperature, substance, luminous intensity.
  • Independent definitions; all else derives from them.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Which is a fundamental quantity?

Solution: Length is a base quantity; velocity, force and energy all derive.
Key Formulas · Fundamental Quantities
\(\mathrm{m,\,kg,\,s,\,A,\,K,\,mol,\,cd}\) seven SI base units
\(v=[LT^{-1}],\;F=[MLT^{-2}],\;E=[ML^{2}T^{-2}]\) base-built examples

Chapter 1 · Topic 3

Derived quantities

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsMeasurements and UnitsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Fundamental units are chosen independently, whereas derived units are constructed from fundamental units by products, powers, and quotients. The seven SI base units correspond to seven base dimensions, although the radian and steradian are dimensionless SI derived units. In mechanics and electricity, a JEE problem often reduces every quantity to combinations of \(\mathrm{m,\ kg,\ s}\), and sometimes \(\mathrm{A}\), before comparing or calculating.
Key formula(s). \(1\,\mathrm{N}=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}\); \(1\,\mathrm{J}=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}\); \(1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\); \(1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}\); \(1\,\mathrm{C}=1\,\mathrm{A\,s}\)
Key points.
  • A derived unit is chosen so that its defining relation with base units has the numerical factor one.
  • Speed has the derived unit \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), not metre alone or second alone.
  • Force is the product of mass and acceleration, hence \(\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}\).
  • Electric charge is derived from current and time, while electric potential is energy per unit charge.
  • The same physical quantity can have units of different systems, but the seven base units are independent conventions.
Example 1.

A constant net force of \(20\,\mathrm{N}\) acts on a \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) body initially at rest for \(3\,\mathrm{s}\). Determine the body's speed.

  1. The net force has derived unit \(\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}\), so \(F=ma\) gives \(a=F/m\).
  2. Substitute the values: \(a=20/4=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
  3. From rest, \(v=u+at=0+(5)(3)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  4. The final speed is therefore \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Answer: \(v=15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Example 2.

A medium obeys the energy-pressure relation \(U=pV\) and stores \(500\,\mathrm{J}\) uniformly in a volume of \(1.0\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Find the corresponding pressure.

  1. Energy density is energy per unit volume, so its unit is \(\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\).
  2. Energy density and pressure have the same derived unit because \(1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\).
  3. Therefore \(p=u/V=500/1.0\,\mathrm{Pa}\).
  4. No force or length conversion is required once the unit equivalence is used.

Answer: \(p=500\,\mathrm{Pa}=5.0\times10^2\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Calling \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) a fundamental unit.
  • Omitting a power of a unit during multiplication, such as using \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\) for force.
  • Treating joule and newton as interchangeable units.

Chapter 1 · Topic 4

SI units

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsMeasurements and UnitsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. The International System of Units defines seven base units from which a coherent system of measurement is constructed. Choosing one unit of each kind avoids conversion factors among the units used in the basic mechanical and electromagnetic equations. For JEE calculations, recognising derived units such as newton, joule, and watt helps prevent factors of \(10\) from being missed.
Key formula(s). Seven SI base units: \(\mathrm{m,\ kg,\ s,\ A,\ K,\ mol,\ cd}\); \(1\,\mathrm{N}=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}\), \(1\,\mathrm{J}=1\,\mathrm{N\,m}\), \(1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}\); \(1\,\mathrm{C}=1\,\mathrm{A\,s}\), \(1\,\mathrm{V}=1\,\mathrm{W\,A^{-1}}\), \(1\,\mathrm{F}=1\,\mathrm{C\,V^{-1}}\)
Key points.
  • The seven base quantities in the SI are length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, and luminous intensity.
  • Mechanical quantities such as force, work, and power are derived from combinations of the base units \(\mathrm{m,\ kg,\ s}\).
  • A coulomb is derived as \(\mathrm{A\,s}\); the unit symbol \(\mathrm{A}\) denotes ampere, whereas area is written in units such as \(\mathrm{m^2}\) or \(\mathrm{cm^2}\).
  • The kelvin is the thermodynamic unit of temperature; degree Celsius and degree Fahrenheit are non-SI temperature units.
  • The becquerel counts decays, the gray measures absorbed dose, and the sievert measures equivalent biological dose.
Example 1.

A current of \(250\,\mathrm{mA}\) flows for \(4\,\mathrm{min}\). Find the electric charge in coulombs.

  1. Convert current to the SI base unit: \(250\,\mathrm{mA}=0.250\,\mathrm{A}\).
  2. Convert time: \(4\,\mathrm{min}=4\times60\,\mathrm{s}=240\,\mathrm{s}\).
  3. Use the definition of charge, \(Q=It\).
  4. \(Q=0.250\times240=60\,\mathrm{C}\).

Answer: The transferred charge is \(60\,\mathrm{C}\).

Example 2.

A heater consumes \(2.0\,\mathrm{kW}\) for \(30\,\mathrm{min}\). Find the energy consumed in \(\mathrm{kWh}\).

  1. Keep the time in hours because the unit kilowatt-hour pairs power in kilowatts with time in hours.
  2. Convert \(30\,\mathrm{min}\) to \(0.50\,\mathrm{h}\).
  3. Use \(E=Pt\): \(E=(2.0\,\mathrm{kW})(0.50\,\mathrm{h})\).
  4. The numerical product is \(1.0\), and the power unit already supplies the energy unit prefix.

Answer: The energy consumed is \(1.0\,\mathrm{kWh}=3.6\times10^6\,\mathrm{J}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Treating the newton as a base unit rather than \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}\).
  • Confusing electric current in amperes with area in square metres.
  • Writing energy in watt-hours when using \(\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}\).

Chapter 1 · Topic 5

Fundamental SI units

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsMeasurements and UnitsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Fundamental SI units fix the seven bases: metre (length, light-travel definition), kilogram (Planck-constant mass), second (caesium oscillations), ampere (charge flow), kelvin (Boltzmann energy), mole (Avogadro count), candela (luminous intensity). 2019 redefinitions anchor units to constants, not artefacts - the kilogram no longer a Paris cylinder. Definitions plus symbols (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd) are direct one-markers.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela.
  • 2019 redefinition anchors units to physical constants.
Remember
  • Kilogram is now Planck-defined, not artefact-defined.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

SI unit of luminous intensity is

Solution: Candela bases luminous intensity; lux/lumen derive from it.
Key Formulas · Fundamental SI Units
\(1\,\mathrm{m}: c\times(1/299792458)\,\mathrm{s}\) metre from light speed
\(1\,\mathrm{kg}: h/(6.62607015\times10^{-34})\,\mathrm{m^{-2}s}\) kilogram from Planck constant
\(1\,\mathrm{s}: 9192631770\,\mathrm{Cs\,periods}\) second from caesium atom

Chapter 1 · Topic 6

Derived SI units

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsMeasurements and UnitsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Derived SI units combine bases coherently (no conversion factors): newton (kg m/s2 force), joule (energy), watt (power), pascal (pressure), volt, ohm, coulomb, hertz, tesla - each derivable by dimensional multiplication. Special names honour scientists; all reduce to base products. Checking derivations (1 N = 1 kg m/s2) is dimensional-analysis bread and butter.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Newton, joule, watt, pascal, volt - all base-built coherently.
  • Special names honour scientists; dimensions reveal bases.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

One newton equals

Solution: Force dimensions (MLT-2) convert directly to base units.
Key Formulas · Derived SI Units
\(1\,\mathrm{N}=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s^{2}}\) newton
\(1\,\mathrm{J}=1\,\mathrm{N\,m},\;1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J/s}\) joule and watt
\(1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{N/m^{2}},\;1\,\mathrm{Hz}=1\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) pascal and hertz

Chapter 1 · Topic 7

Dimensions

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsDimensionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. The dimensional formula of a quantity expresses its dependence on the fundamental dimensions of mass, length, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, and luminous intensity. Numerical factors, including powers of ten, do not affect dimensions, while the powers of one unit must balance. Dimension notation is essential when testing the consistency of a physical equation and when deriving an unknown dependence.
Key formula(s). \([v]=LT^{-1}\), \([a]=LT^{-2}\), \([F]=MLT^{-2}\), \([W]=ML^2T^{-2}\); \([Q]=IT\), \([V]=ML^2T^{-3}I^{-1}\), \([R]=ML^2T^{-3}I^{-2}\); \([\theta]=1\)
Key points.
  • The commonly used mechanical dimensions are \(M,L,T\), with the independent quantity not appearing in the expression.
  • A dimension in a numerator carries a positive exponent and one in a denominator carries a negative exponent.
  • Powers of a dimension, such as \(L^2\), cannot be written as \(2L\).
  • Radian and steradian are dimensionless because an angle is a ratio of two lengths.
  • Equal dimensions are necessary but not sufficient to prove that two physical quantities are equal.
Example 1.

If the coefficient of dynamic viscosity is defined by \(\eta=\frac{F}{A\,dv/dy}\), determine its dimensional formula.

  1. From \(F=ma\), \([F]=MLT^{-2}\).
  2. Area has dimensions \(A=L^2\).
  3. The velocity gradient has dimensions \([dv/dy]=(LT^{-1})L^{-1}=T^{-1}\).
  4. Hence \([\eta]=MLT^{-2}/(L^2T^{-1})=ML^{-1}T^{-1}\).

Answer: \([\eta]=ML^{-1}T^{-1}\).

Example 2.

From the photon-energy relation \(E=h\nu\), determine the dimensions of Planck's constant.

  1. Energy has dimensions \([E]=ML^2T^{-2}\).
  2. Frequency has dimensions \([\nu]=T^{-1}\).
  3. Since \(E=h\nu\), use \([h]=[E]/[\nu]\).
  4. \([h]=(ML^2T^{-2})/(T^{-1})=ML^2T^{-1}\).

Answer: \([h]=ML^2T^{-1}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Including the dimensionless numerical constant in a dimensional formula.
  • Assigning dimensions to an angle instead of treating it as dimensionless.
  • Equating quantities merely because their dimensional formulas happen to match.

Chapter 1 · Topic 8

Dimensional formula

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsDimensionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Dimensional formula expresses derived quantities as base powers: [MLT-1] momentum, [ML2T-2] energy, [ML-1T-2] pressure - bracketed exponents of M, L, T (plus A, K sometimes). Writing formulas (velocity [LT-1], force [MLT-2]) precedes every homogeneity check and unit conversion. Dimensionless quantities (angles, strain, Reynolds number) carry empty formulas - pure numbers with power.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Bracketed base-power expressions for every quantity.
  • Dimensionless (angle, strain) have empty formulas.
Remember
  • Learn M-L-T exponents for force, energy, power, pressure cold.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Dimensional formula of energy is

Solution: Work (force times distance) squares the length power.
Key Formulas · Dimensional Formula
\([v]=[LT^{-1}],\;[a]=[LT^{-2}]\) motion
\([F]=[MLT^{-2}],\;[E]=[ML^{2}T^{-2}],\;[P]=[ML^{2}T^{-3}]\) force, energy, power
\([\rho]=[ML^{-3}],\;[\eta]=[ML^{-1}T^{-1}]\) density and viscosity

Chapter 1 · Topic 9

Dimensional analysis

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsDimensionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Dimensional analysis tests or derives a physical relation by equating dimensions on all sides of an equation or across a proposed monomial relation. It reduces the unknowns to powers of the basic dimensions, but it cannot determine dimensionless numerical coefficients. The method is most reliable for products and quotients of powers and must not be applied blindly to sums that contain independent additive constants.
Key formula(s). General test: \(\prod_i X_i^{a_i}=\prod_i X_i^{b_i}\Rightarrow\prod_i [X_i]^{a_i-b_i}=1\); for \(Q=\prod_i X_i^{a_i}\), match each basic dimension; dimensionally homogeneous equations contain only dimensionless constants; \(\pi\)-group: \([\Pi]=1\)
Key points.
  • To find unknown powers, express the right side dimensionally and equate the exponents of \(M,L,T\), and any other relevant base dimensions.
  • A dimensionless pure number can never be determined by dimensional analysis.
  • Dimensional analysis can refute a relation quickly, but different relations with identical dimensions may remain possible.
  • Functions such as \(x+x^2\) and the sum \(x+y\) require the homogeneity of every term, not merely of the whole expression.
  • Numerical data can be used after deriving the dimensionless proportionality form to evaluate the remaining constant.
Example 1.

Suppose time is represented as \(t=m^xF^y\), where \(m\) is mass and \(F\) is force. If \(m=2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(F=20\,\mathrm{N}\), and \(t=0.10\,\mathrm{s}\), determine \(x\) and \(y\) and verify the relation.

  1. Write the dimensions as \([m]=M\) and \([F]=MLT^{-2}\).
  2. The proposed relation requires \(T=M^x(MLT^{-2})^y=M^{x+y}L^yT^{-2y}\).
  3. Equating exponents gives \(x+y=0\), \(y=0\), and \(-2y=1\), hence \(x=1\) and \(y=-1\).
  4. Thus \(t=m/F\), and the data give \(2/20=0.10\,\mathrm{s}\).

Answer: \(x=1,\ y=-1,\) and the time is \(0.10\,\mathrm{s}\).

Example 2.

Work is proposed to have the form \(W=p^xV^y\), where \(p\) is pressure and \(V\) is volume. If \(p=2.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\) and \(V=3.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}\), find \(x,y\) and the work.

  1. Use \([p]=ML^{-1}T^{-2}\) and \([V]=L^3\), while \([W]=ML^2T^{-2}\).
  2. The right side has dimensions \((ML^{-1}T^{-2})^xL^{3y}=M^xL^{-x+3y}T^{-2x}\).
  3. Equating exponents gives \(x=1\), \(-1+3y=2\), and \(-2x=-2\), so \(y=1\).
  4. The relation is \(W=pV\); substitution gives \(W=(2.0\times10^5)(3.0\times10^{-3})\,\mathrm{J}\).

Answer: \(x=y=1\) and \(W=6.0\times10^2\,\mathrm{J}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Trying to obtain a pure numerical coefficient by matching dimensions.
  • Checking the dimensions of only the largest term in an equation containing a sum.
  • Claiming a dimensionally correct relation is necessarily the correct physical law.

Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 10

Applications of dimensional analysis

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsDimensionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Dimensional analysis applications: checking equation correctness (homogeneity both sides), converting units across systems (dynes to newtons via M-L-T ratios), deriving relations (pendulum period from length and g up to constants), and spotting impossible formulas ( mismatched dimensions never occur in true laws). Limitations: dimensionless constants invisible, trigonometric/exponential arguments restricted, multi-term correctness unprovable - analysis validates, never fully proves.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Check equations, convert units, derive relations (minus constants).
  • Blind to dimensionless constants and multi-term details.
Uses and limits
PointDetail
CheckingBoth sides same dimensions
ConvertingScale via base ratios
DerivingRelations up to constants
LimitsConstants invisible; trig restricted
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Dimensional analysis CANNOT determine

Solution: Pure numbers escape dimensional reasoning entirely.
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 11

Principle of homogeneity

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsDimensionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. The principle of homogeneity states that every additive term in a correctly stated physical equation must have the same dimensions. It follows because physically meaningful addition requires matching dimensions, and a dimensionally homogeneous relation is also invariant under a consistent change of unit system. In JEE problems, apply this test term by term rather than to an expression containing a hidden offset.
Key formula(s). \(\sum_i a_i X_i=\sum_j b_j Y_j\Rightarrow\sum_i[a_iX_i]=\sum_j[b_jY_j]\); for \(X=C\prod_i Q_i^{n_i}\), \([X]=\prod_i[Q_i]^{n_i}\) and \([C]=1\); \(s=s_0+ut\Rightarrow [u]=LT^{-1}\)
Key points.
  • Every quantity on both sides of an equation must have one common final dimension.
  • All terms inside a parenthesis that are added or subtracted must separately be dimensionally homogeneous.
  • A proportional constant is dimensionless only when the rest of the equation is dimensionally balanced.
  • Terms can differ by a dimensionless factor, but not by dimensions.
  • A dimensionally correct equation is a consistency check, not a complete proof of physical validity.
Example 1.

A force varies as \(F=km^at^b\), where \(k\) is dimensionless. If \(F=20\,\mathrm{N}\), \(m=10\,\mathrm{kg}\), and \(t=5\,\mathrm{s}\), determine \(a,b\) and \(k\).

  1. Using \([F]=MLT^{-2}\), \([m]=M\), and \([t]=T\), the right side has dimensions \(M^aT^b\).
  2. Equating exponents gives \(a=1\) and \(b=-2\), so \(F=km/t^2\).
  3. Since \(k\) is dimensionless, substitute the data into \(k=Ft^2/m\).
  4. \(k=20(5)^2/10=50\), and substitution gives \(F=50(10)/(5)^2=20\,\mathrm{N}\).

Answer: \(a=1,\ b=-2,\) and \(k=50\).

Example 2.

A fluid drag is proposed to obey \(F=br^2v\). If \(b=2.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N\,s\,m^{-3}}\), \(r=0.50\,\mathrm{m}\), and \(v=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), check homogeneity and find \(F\).

  1. The known constant has dimensions \([b]=(MLT^{-2})/(L^3T^{-1})=ML^{-2}T^{-1}\).
  2. The right side has dimensions \((ML^{-2}T^{-1})L^2(LT^{-1})=MLT^{-2}\).
  3. This equals the dimension of force, so the relation is homogeneous.
  4. Substitute the values: \(F=(2.0\times10^{-3})(0.50)^2(10)\,\mathrm{N}\).

Answer: \(F=5.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Testing only the dimensions of the sum of terms rather than each term.
  • Assigning dimensions to a proportionality constant before the proposed relation has been balanced.
  • Assuming a dimensionally correct equation must be experimentally valid.
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 12

Unit conversion

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsDimensionsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Unit conversion changes the representation of a physical quantity without changing the quantity itself. Every conversion factor is raised to the same power as the unit involved: one for length, two for area, and three for volume. JEE problems combine decimal and binary prefixes, so the safest method is to convert first to a common base unit and then into the requested unit.
Key formula(s). \(1\,\mathrm{km}=10^3\,\mathrm{m}\), \(1\,\mathrm{cm}=10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}\), \(1\,\mathrm{m^2}=10^4\,\mathrm{cm^2}\); \(1\,\mathrm{m^3}=10^6\,\mathrm{cm^3}\), \(1\,\mathrm{L}=10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}\); \(1\,\mathrm{N}=10^5\,\mathrm{dyne}\), \(1\,\mathrm{J}=10^7\,\mathrm{erg}\), \(1\,\mathrm{cal}=4.184\,\mathrm{J}\)
Key points.
  • A prefix changes the numerical factor by a power of ten, not by a fixed additive amount.
  • Length conversion is linear, but area and volume factors acquire powers of two and three.
  • \(1\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}=10^3\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), while \(1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}=10^{-3}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\).
  • The litre is accepted for ordinary use but is not an SI base unit of volume.
  • Compound units convert factor by factor, and every factor must be included.
Example 1.

Express an energy of \(2.4\times10^{15}\,\mathrm{erg}\) in joules and kilojoules.

  1. Use the exact relation \(1\,\mathrm{erg}=10^{-7}\,\mathrm{J}\).
  2. Convert to joules: \(2.4\times10^{15}\times10^{-7}=2.4\times10^8\,\mathrm{J}\).
  3. Since \(1\,\mathrm{kJ}=10^3\,\mathrm{J}\), divide the joule value by \(10^3\).
  4. This gives \(2.4\times10^5\,\mathrm{kJ}\), equivalently \(240\,\mathrm{MJ}\).

Answer: The energy is \(2.4\times10^8\,\mathrm{J}=2.4\times10^5\,\mathrm{kJ}\).

Example 2.

A pressure is \(2.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Express it in atmosphere and millimetres of mercury, given \(1\,\mathrm{atm}=1.013\times10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\) and \(1\,\mathrm{atm}=760\,\mathrm{mm\,Hg}\).

  1. Divide by pascals per atmosphere: \(p=(2.0\times10^5)/(1.013\times10^5)\,\mathrm{atm}\).
  2. This gives \(p=1.97\,\mathrm{atm}\).
  3. Convert atmospheres to millimetres of mercury by multiplying by \(760\,\mathrm{mm\,Hg\,atm^{-1}}\).
  4. \(p=1.97\times760=1.50\times10^3\,\mathrm{mm\,Hg}\).

Answer: \(p\approx1.97\,\mathrm{atm}=1.50\times10^3\,\mathrm{mm\,Hg}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Applying \(10^{-2}\) to an area instead of \(10^{-4}\).
  • Converting the numerator but leaving the denominator in the original unit.
  • Treating the Celsius or Fahrenheit temperature scale as a simple power-of-ten unit.
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 13

Significant figures

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Significant figures are all reliable digits in a measured number plus the first uncertain digit. They convey measurement precision, whereas the position of the decimal point alone does not establish reliability. A reported result should normally have the same order of precision as the data that produced it, so counting significant figures is part of numerical correctness in JEE numerical problems.
Key formula(s). Count significant digits from the first nonzero digit through the last known digit; \(\text{relative uncertainty}\approx\frac{\Delta x}{|x|}\); for \(x=n\times10^k\), \(k=\lfloor\log_{10}|x|\rfloor+1\) and \(1\leq|n|<10\)
Key points.
  • All nonzero digits in a measured number are significant.
  • Zeros between nonzero digits are significant, as in \(4.007\,\mathrm{m}\).
  • Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant, so \(12.30\,\mathrm{m}\) has four significant figures.
  • A trailing zero in an integer may or may not be significant unless a decimal point or precision statement resolves the ambiguity.
  • Exact defined counts, such as exactly \(12\) trials, do not restrict significant figures.
  • A calculated answer should not carry more precision than the measurements justify.
Example 1.

Report the measured length \(12.734\,\mathrm{cm}\) to three significant figures.

  1. Significant digits are counted from the first nonzero digit, so the first three are \(1,2,7\).
  2. The first discarded digit is \(3\), which is less than \(5\).
  3. No upward rounding is needed, and the last retained digit is in the tenths place.

Answer: \(12.7\,\mathrm{cm}\) (three significant figures).

Example 2.

Two independent readings of a length are \(1.234\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(1.236\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find their mean with the precision supported by the measurements.

  1. Add the two readings: \(1.234+1.236=2.470\,\mathrm{cm}\).
  2. Divide by the exact count: \(\bar{x}=2.470/2=1.235\,\mathrm{cm}\).
  3. The divisor \(2\) is exact, so it does not impose a significant-figure limit.
  4. Both readings contain four significant figures, so the mean is reported to four.

Answer: The mean length is \(1.235\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Counting every zero in \(100\,\mathrm{m}\) without knowing whether trailing zeros were measured.
  • Preserving extra digits in a final answer beyond the least precise input.
  • Applying the addition decimal-place rule to a single rounded measurement.
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 14

Rules of significant figures

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Significant-figure rules depend on the operation: addition and subtraction require matching decimal-place precision, whereas multiplication, division, and powers use the fewest significant figures among the operands. Intermediate results should retain at least one guard digit to avoid premature rounding. A common JEE trap is to use the multiplication rule for a sum or the addition rule for a product.
Key formula(s). For \(z=x+y\) or \(z=x-y\), retain the fewest decimal places present; for \(z=xy\) or \(z=x/y\), retain the fewest significant figures; for \(z=xy\), \(\frac{\Delta z}{z}=\frac{\Delta x}{x}+\frac{\Delta y}{y}\); for \(z=x/y\), \(\frac{\Delta z}{z}=\frac{\Delta x}{x}+\frac{\Delta y}{y}\); \(\Delta(a^n)\approx n|a|^{n-1}\Delta a\)
Key points.
  • Addition compares place value, not significant-figure count: \(12.3+0.456\) is reported to the tenths place.
  • Multiplication and division are controlled by the operand with the fewest significant figures.
  • Powers and roots have the same number of significant figures as the original value.
  • Keep guard digits through intermediate calculations, but round the final result only once.
  • For logarithms, the number of decimal places in the mantissa equals the number of significant figures in the original number.
  • The characteristic of a logarithm and any integer exponent are not restricted by the mantissa rule.
Example 1.

Add \(14.26\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(3.178\,\mathrm{m}\), reporting the result with justified precision.

  1. The first measurement is precise to \(0.01\,\mathrm{m}\), while the second is precise to \(0.001\,\mathrm{m}\).
  2. Addition requires the result to be rounded to \(0.01\,\mathrm{m}\).
  3. The raw sum is \(17.438\,\mathrm{m}\).
  4. The hundredths digit is \(3\), and the next digit is \(8\), so increase it to \(4\).

Answer: \(14.26+3.178=17.44\,\mathrm{m}\).

Example 2.

Calculate \(z=\frac{(4.80)(2.15)}{1.032}\) to the correct number of significant figures.

  1. All three input numbers have three significant figures, so the final result needs three.
  2. Retain the product as \(4.80\times2.15=10.32\), with extra digits as guard digits.
  3. Divide without rounding the guard digits: \(z=10.320/1.032=10.0\).
  4. The three-significant-figure form of the result is \(10.0\), not \(10\) or \(10.000\).

Answer: \(z=10.0\) (three significant figures).

Common mistakes.
  • Applying the fewest-significant-figures rule to addition or subtraction.
  • Rounding an intermediate product before the final division.
  • Writing \(10\) for a three-significant-figure result near \(10\).
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 15

Rounding off

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Rounding off follows the 5-rule: digits below 5 drop, above 5 round up, exactly 5 rounds even digit up (banker convention in precise work; school rule rounds 5 up always). Rounding preserves significant figures after calculations - results never exceed least-precise input precision. Premature rounding compounds errors; round only final answers. Calculator ten-digit displays must round to input precision.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Below 5 drop, above 5 raise, exactly 5 to even (precise work).
  • Round final answers only, to least-precise input.
Remember
  • Never report ten calculator digits from three-digit inputs.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

2.745 rounded to three significant figures (5-rule) is

Solution: Exactly-5 rounds even digit up: 4 becomes 5? no - 2.74 even stays? School rule rounds up to 2.75.
Key Formulas · Rounding Off
\(x<5\Rightarrow\mathrm{drop},\;x>5\Rightarrow\mathrm{raise}\) below 5 drop, above 5 raise
\(=5\Rightarrow\mathrm{even\,digit\,rule}\) exactly 5 goes to even (precise work)
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 16

Least count

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Least count is the smallest change in a measured value that an instrument can resolve directly. It is fixed by the scale divisions and, for screw gauges, by the pitch and number of circular divisions. The least count sets reading resolution and an associated maximum error, but calibration accuracy and zero error must be considered separately when judging the quality of a measurement.
Key formula(s). Vernier least count: \(\mathrm{LC}=1\,\mathrm{MSD}-1\,\mathrm{VSD}\); if \(V\) vernier divisions equal \(v\) main-scale divisions, \(\mathrm{LC}=(1-v/V)\mathrm{MSD}\); screw-gauge least count: \(\mathrm{LC}=\frac{\text{pitch}}{N}\); analog reading error \(=\mathrm{LC}/2\)
Key points.
  • The smallest numerical least count generally corresponds to the greatest instrument resolution.
  • Least count is a fixed property of the scale configuration, not a value to be averaged over readings.
  • A vernier is designed so that one vernier division is slightly shorter than one main-scale division.
  • A digital display may be read to the last shown digit, but its accuracy can still be poorer than its resolution.
  • Halving the least count halves the resolution contribution to maximum error, not necessarily the total experimental error.
  • An instrument with high resolution but large zero error can produce precise-looking readings that are inaccurate.
Example 1.

A vernier caliper has \(1\,\mathrm{MSD}=1\,\mathrm{mm}\), and \(50\) vernier divisions equal \(49\) main-scale divisions. Find its least count and the maximum resolution error.

  1. One vernier division is \(49/50=0.98\,\mathrm{mm}\).
  2. The least count is \(1.00-0.98=0.02\,\mathrm{mm}\).
  3. For a nearest-division reading, the maximum resolution error is half this value.
  4. Hence \(\Delta x_{\max}=0.02/2=0.01\,\mathrm{mm}\).

Answer: \(\mathrm{LC}=0.02\,\mathrm{mm}\), with maximum resolution error \(0.01\,\mathrm{mm}\).

Example 2.

An analog ammeter has a range of \(0\) to \(10\,\mathrm{mA}\) and \(100\) equal scale divisions. It reads \(6.3\,\mathrm{mA}\). Find its least count and maximum resolution error.

  1. The value represented by one division is \(10/100=0.1\,\mathrm{mA}\).
  2. Therefore the least count is \(0.1\,\mathrm{mA}\).
  3. Half a division gives the maximum resolution error, \(0.05\,\mathrm{mA}\).
  4. The reading can be represented as \(6.3\pm0.05\,\mathrm{mA}\) from resolution alone.

Answer: \(\mathrm{LC}=0.1\,\mathrm{mA}\) and \(\Delta I_{\max}=0.05\,\mathrm{mA}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Finding the difference of the two scales without ensuring that it is positive.
  • Confusing instrument resolution with calibration accuracy.
  • Reporting a maximum error equal to the full least count for a nearest-division reading.
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 17

Accuracy

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Accuracy (closeness to true value) reflects calibration plus technique - accurate darts cluster at bullseye. Systematic errors (faulty zero, bent scale) destroy accuracy correctably; random errors scatter correctably by averaging. Accurate instruments need traceable standards (NPL calibrations). High accuracy with low precision is rare (bias-free but shaky); low accuracy with high precision is common (miscalibrated consistents).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Closeness to true value; killed by systematic errors.
  • Calibration against standards restores accuracy.
Remember
  • Accurate means true-centred; precise means tightly grouped.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Systematic errors mainly affect measurement

Solution: Biases shift means from truth; averaging cannot remove them.
Key Formulas · Accuracy
\(\Delta a=|a_{m}-a_{t}|\) absolute error vs true value
\(\mathrm{accuracy\uparrow\iff\Delta a\to0}\) closer to truth means more accurate
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 18

Precision

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Precision (repeatability, closeness among readings) reflects instrument resolution plus steadiness - precise darts cluster tightly (possibly off-bullseye). Least count sets precision ceilings (vernier 0.01 cm beats metre-scale 0.1 cm); random errors scatter precision improvable by averaging. Precise-but-inaccurate instruments mislead confidently - calibration converts precision into accuracy.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Repeatability among readings; least count ceilings it.
  • Averaging improves precision, never accuracy.
Remember
  • Precise off-target darts are consistent yet wrong.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Precision of measurement is limited mainly by instrument

Solution: Finer least counts resolve repeat readings more tightly.
Key Formulas · Precision
\(\mathrm{LC}=\frac{1\,\mathrm{MSD}}{N_{div}}\) least count sets resolution
\(\bar{a}=\frac{1}{n}\sum a_{i}\) mean tightens precision by averaging
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 19

Errors in measurement

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Measurement error is the difference between a measured value and the true value of the quantity. Systematic errors shift results consistently because of calibration, zero error, or an incorrect method, while random errors vary unpredictably between repetitions. Accuracy means closeness to the true value, whereas precision means closeness among repeated readings, so a highly precise instrument can still be inaccurate if miscalibrated.
Key formula(s). \(\text{measured value}=\text{true value}+\text{error}\); signed error \(e=x_m-x_t\); absolute error \(\Delta x=|x_m-x_t|\); corrected value \(=x_m-e\); \(\bar{x}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_i\)
Key points.
  • Absolute error uses a magnitude and has the same unit as the measurement; relative and percentage errors are dimensionless.
  • Systematic errors cannot be reduced merely by taking more readings; they require calibration or correcting the method.
  • Random uncertainty generally decreases when the number of independent readings is increased.
  • Precision concerns the spread of repeated readings and does not establish that the mean is close to the true value.
  • Accuracy improves only when systematic bias is removed and random uncertainty is sufficiently small.
  • Every instrument reading should be recorded with a precision consistent with its resolution and calibration.
Example 1.

A spring balance reads \(0.50\,\mathrm{N}\) when unloaded. When an object of unknown true weight is placed on it, the reading becomes \(75.40\,\mathrm{N}\). Apply the zero correction and classify the error.

  1. Closing or unloading the balance identifies a positive zero error of \(+0.50\,\mathrm{N}\).
  2. This offset repeats for a given instrument setting, so it is systematic rather than random.
  3. The zero-corrected indicated weight is obtained by subtracting the signed zero error.
  4. \(W_{\mathrm{true}}=75.40-0.50\,\mathrm{N}\).

Answer: The corrected weight is \(74.90\,\mathrm{N}\); the error is a systematic positive zero error.

Example 2.

Repeated readings of a nominally \(5.00\,\mathrm{N}\) force are \(4.99,\ 5.01,\ 5.00,\ 5.02\,\mathrm{N}\). Find the mean and the maximum deviation from it.

  1. The sum is \(20.02\,\mathrm{N}\), so the mean is \(20.02/4=5.005\,\mathrm{N}\).
  2. The absolute deviations from the unrounded mean are \(0.015,\ 0.005,\ 0.005,\ 0.015\,\mathrm{N}\).
  3. The largest deviation is therefore \(0.015\,\mathrm{N}\), which is characteristic of random scatter.
  4. Reported to the supported \(0.01\,\mathrm{N}\) resolution, the mean is \(5.01\,\mathrm{N}\).

Answer: Mean \(=5.01\,\mathrm{N}\); maximum absolute deviation \(=0.015\,\mathrm{N}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Calling small random scatter evidence of accuracy when the zero is unknown.
  • Reducing a calibration error by averaging many repeated readings.
  • Reporting a mean with more reliable precision than the original instrument readings.
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 20

Absolute error

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Absolute error is the magnitude of the difference between a measured value and the true or accepted value of a quantity. It carries the same unit as the measurement and is never negative. Resolution sets the smallest available interval of an instrument; for an analog scale modeled as continuously variable, the maximum reading error is commonly assigned as half one scale division in JEE calculations.
Key formula(s). \(\Delta x_i=|x_i-x_{\mathrm{true}}|\); mean absolute error \(\Delta\bar{x}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta x_i\); for least count \(c\), \(\Delta x_{\max}=c/2\); measured range \(x_{\mathrm{true}}\in[x_m-\Delta x_{\max},x_m+\Delta x_{\max}]\)
Key points.
  • Absolute error has units; relative and percentage errors do not.
  • The largest of several reported absolute errors determines the conservative absolute error of their sum.
  • A change in the least count changes the possible resolution but does not automatically remove zero or calibration error.
  • For an analog scale, reading to the nearest scale division is usually modeled by a maximum error of half a division.
  • The sign of an error describes bias, whereas absolute error discards that sign.
  • A claimed range should contain every value compatible with the stated instrument uncertainty.
Example 1.

An analog voltmeter has a least count of \(0.1\,\mathrm{V}\) and reads \(12.3\,\mathrm{V}\). State the reading with its maximum possible error.

  1. Half the least count is \(0.1/2=0.05\,\mathrm{V}\).
  2. With a positive zero, the possible true voltage may be \(0.05\,\mathrm{V}\) below the observation.
  3. It may also be \(0.05\,\mathrm{V}\) above the observation.
  4. Hence the uncertainty interval is \(12.25\leq V\leq12.35\,\mathrm{V}\).

Answer: \(V=(12.30\pm0.05)\,\mathrm{V}\).

Example 2.

A stopwatch has a least count of \(0.01\,\mathrm{s}\). The first observer starts it at \(12.34\,\mathrm{s}\) and the second stops it at \(44.56\,\mathrm{s}\). Find the elapsed time and its maximum instrumental error.

  1. Subtract the stopwatch readings: \(t=44.56-12.34=32.22\,\mathrm{s}\).
  2. Each timing has a maximum error of \(0.01/2=0.005\,\mathrm{s}\).
  3. The two endpoint errors act in opposite directions in the difference, so their magnitudes add: \(\Delta t=0.005+0.005=0.01\,\mathrm{s}\).
  4. The possible interval is therefore \(32.21\leq t\leq32.23\,\mathrm{s}\).

Answer: \(t=(32.22\pm0.01)\,\mathrm{s}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Equating a least count with the maximum absolute error.
  • Using a negative absolute error in a final uncertainty interval.
  • Ignoring that subtraction of two timings adds the magnitudes of their endpoint uncertainties.
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 21

Relative error

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Relative error is the absolute error divided by the magnitude of the measured or true value, making it a dimensionless measure of precision. It is the appropriate quantity for comparing instruments that measure quantities of different sizes or units. A smaller relative error indicates greater relative precision, even if the absolute error of the measurement is numerically larger.
Key formula(s). \(\epsilon_x=\frac{\Delta x}{|x|}\); percentage error \(=100\epsilon_x\); if \(Q=\prod_i x_i^{n_i}\), \(\frac{\Delta Q}{|Q|}\leq\sum_i|n_i|\frac{\Delta x_i}{|x_i|}\); for \(Q=x^m/y^n\), \(\frac{\Delta Q}{|Q|}\leq|m|\frac{\Delta x}{|x|}+|n|\frac{\Delta y}{|y|}\)
Key points.
  • Relative error has no unit and is often written as a fraction or percentage.
  • Two absolute errors cannot be compared directly unless they refer to the same measured quantity.
  • Measurements expressed in different units have unchanged physical errors but identical relative errors after consistent conversion.
  • A small absolute error on a small quantity can produce a large relative error.
  • Relative errors add in magnitude for products and quotients under maximum-error estimation.
  • Relative precision is not a measure of systematic bias or proximity to a certified true value.
Example 1.

A length is measured as \(25.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) with an absolute error of \(0.5\,\mathrm{cm}\). Find the relative error and percentage error.

  1. Write the absolute error as a positive magnitude: \(\Delta x=0.5\,\mathrm{cm}\).
  2. Divide it by the measured length: \(\epsilon_x=0.5/25.0=0.020\).
  3. Confirm that numerator and denominator use the same unit, so the result is dimensionless.
  4. Multiply by \(100\) to obtain the percentage error, \(2.0\%\).

Answer: Relative error \(=0.020\), and percentage error \(=2.0\%\).

Example 2.

Compare the relative precision of \(L_1=(1.200\pm0.006)\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(L_2=(500\pm5)\,\mathrm{mm}\).

  1. For \(L_1\), the relative error is \(0.006/1.200=0.0050=0.50\%\).
  2. For \(L_2\), the relative error is \(5/500=0.010=1.0\%\).
  3. Both values are stated as numbers with units, so their units do not affect the comparison.
  4. Since \(0.50\%<1.0\%\), the first measurement has the smaller relative uncertainty.

Answer: \(L_1\) is more precise; the relative errors are \(0.50\%\) and \(1.0\%\), respectively.

Common mistakes.
  • Comparing absolute errors from measurements of different sizes.
  • Omitting the factor \(100\) when the result is requested as percentage error.
  • Treating a dimensionless relative error as having the unit of the measured quantity.
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 22

Percentage error

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Percentage error expresses relative error as a percentage and provides a quick measure of the reliability of a reported value. It is independent of the units provided the numerator and denominator use the same units. The percentage error of a final result should be propagated from all measured quantities that influence it, rather than inferred merely from the final displayed digits.
Key formula(s). \(\text{percentage error}=100\frac{\Delta x}{|x|}\); if \(Q=x^m y^n\), \(\%\text{ error in }Q\leq |m|\frac{\Delta x}{|x|}\times100+|n|\frac{\Delta y}{|y|}\times100\); acceptable match criterion \(\Delta x<x_{\mathrm{measured}}\)
Key points.
  • A percentage error of \(5\%\) means an error of five units per hundred units of the measured value.
  • Percentage error is dimensionless even though absolute error carries the measurement unit.
  • Relative error can exceed \(100\%\) when the uncertainty is larger than the measured value.
  • In propagation by the maximum-error rule, fractional errors add in magnitude.
  • Experimental agreement is often judged by comparing predicted and observed values using their fractional separation.
  • A large percentage error indicates poor relative reliability but says nothing by itself about systematic direction.
Example 1.

A measured length is \(9.96\,\mathrm{m}\pm0.02\,\mathrm{m}\). Calculate its percentage error.

  1. Use the magnitude of the uncertainty: \(\Delta x=0.02\,\mathrm{m}\).
  2. Form the relative error: \(0.02/9.96\approx0.002008\).
  3. Multiply by \(100\): percentage error \(\approx0.2008\%\).
  4. Round according to the precision of the error, which is about one significant figure.

Answer: The percentage error is approximately \(0.2\%\).

Example 2.

The density of a liquid is \(2.70\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\) with absolute error \(0.01\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\), and a speed is \(90\pm3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Which measurement is relatively more precise?

  1. The density error is \((0.01/2.70)\times100=0.370\%\).
  2. The speed error is \((3/90)\times100=3.33\%\).
  3. Relative precision is judged by percentage error, not absolute error.
  4. Since \(0.370\%<3.33\%\), the density has the smaller fractional uncertainty.

Answer: The density measurement is more precise; its percentage error is about \(0.37\%\).

Common mistakes.
  • Multiplying by \(100\) twice when first writing a percentage error.
  • Treating a percentage error above \(100\%\) as impossible.
  • Selecting the measurement with the smaller absolute error without checking its scale.
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 23

Error propagation

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Errors combine according to the operation used to calculate a physical quantity. For sums and differences, absolute errors add in magnitude; for products, quotients, and powers, fractional errors add in magnitude. This is the maximum-error rule used in school laboratory calculations, and it gives a conservative uncertainty range even when several errors point in the same direction.
Key formula(s). \(Q=x+y\Rightarrow\Delta Q\leq\Delta x+\Delta y\), \(Q=x-y\Rightarrow\Delta Q\leq\Delta x+\Delta y\); \(Q=xy\Rightarrow\frac{\Delta Q}{|Q|}=\frac{\Delta x}{|x|}+\frac{\Delta y}{|y|}\); \(Q=x/y\Rightarrow\frac{\Delta Q}{|Q|}=\frac{\Delta x}{|x|}+\frac{\Delta y}{|y|}\); \(Q=x^n\Rightarrow\frac{\Delta Q}{|Q|}=|n|\frac{\Delta x}{|x|}\)
Key points.
  • Add absolute errors for addition and subtraction because one plus one minus one gives one.
  • Add fractional errors for multiplication and division after first reducing each error to a fraction.
  • Powers multiply the fractional error by the absolute value of the power.
  • The maximum-error method adds magnitudes, not signed errors, so it is conservative.
  • Exact count factors and defined conversion factors do not contribute uncertainty.
  • For independent random uncertainties, root-sum-square propagation is a separate statistical rule and should not be silently substituted for the JEE maximum-error rule.
Example 1.

If \(x=(12.3\pm0.2)\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(y=(4.56\pm0.05)\,\mathrm{cm}\), determine their sum with maximum error.

  1. Add the central values: \(x+y=12.3+4.56=16.86\,\mathrm{cm}\).
  2. For a sum, add the absolute uncertainties: \(\Delta(x+y)=0.2+0.05=0.25\,\mathrm{cm}\).
  3. To match the uncertainty precision, quote the result as \(16.9\pm0.3\,\mathrm{cm}\).
  4. The unrounded bookkeeping form is \(16.86\pm0.25\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Answer: \(x+y=(16.9\pm0.3)\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Example 2.

If \(p=(8.0\pm0.1)\), \(q=(5.00\pm0.02)\), and \(r=(2.00\pm0.01)\), find the maximum percentage error in \(z=pq/r\).

  1. The central value is \(z=(8.0\times5.00)/2.00=20.0\).
  2. The maximum relative error is \(\Delta z/z=\Delta p/p+\Delta q/q+\Delta r/r\).
  3. Substitute: \(\Delta z/z=0.1/8.0+0.02/5.00+0.01/2.00=0.0215\).
  4. The percentage error is \(2.15\%\), and the maximum absolute error is \(0.0215\times20.0=0.43\).

Answer: The percentage error in \(z\) is \(2.15\%\), so \(z=20.0\pm0.43\).

Common mistakes.
  • Adding absolute errors when calculating a product.
  • Cancelling errors in a quotient because one quantity is in the denominator.
  • Using the error rule meant for addition on a multiplication of measured quantities.
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 1 · Topic 24

Experimental measurements

Physics and MeasurementMechanicsErrors and MeasurementStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Experimental measurements must connect instrument choice, data handling, and uncertainty to the physical quantity being measured. Random scatter is reduced by repeated independent readings and usually by a suitable mean, whereas systematic bias is reduced by zero correction, calibration, and a sound method. A trustworthy result states the value, its uncertainty, the units, and enough precision to reproduce the measurement.
Key formula(s). \(\bar{x}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_i\); sample standard deviation \(s=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^2}{N-1}}\); standard error of mean \(s_{\bar{x}}=s/\sqrt{N}\); \(\%\text{ uncertainty}=100s_{\bar{x}}/\bar{x}\)
Key points.
  • Select an instrument whose range includes the value and whose least count is fine enough for the required precision.
  • Average independent repeated readings to reduce random error, not systematic error.
  • A zero check performed under the same conditions as the measurement helps identify instrumental bias.
  • The sample standard deviation requires division by \(N-1\) for an unbiased estimate from a sample.
  • More digits are not more accurate; the reported uncertainty should be comparable in precision to the mean.
  • Use a measurement procedure that isolates the desired effect and minimizes other influences.
Example 1.

Five independent readings of a pendulum period are \(1.98,\ 2.02,\ 2.00,\ 2.04,\ 1.96\,\mathrm{s}\). Find the mean, sample standard deviation, and standard error of the mean.

  1. Their sum is \(10.00\,\mathrm{s}\), giving \(\bar{t}=10.00/5=2.00\,\mathrm{s}\).
  2. Squared deviations from the mean are \(0.0004,\ 0.0004,\ 0,\ 0.0016,\ 0.0016\,\mathrm{s^2}\), with sum \(0.0040\,\mathrm{s^2}\).
  3. The sample variance is \(0.0040/(5-1)=0.0010\,\mathrm{s^2}\).
  4. Thus \(s=\sqrt{0.0010}=0.0316\,\mathrm{s}\) and \(s_{\bar{x}}=0.0316/\sqrt{5}=0.0141\,\mathrm{s}\).

Answer: Mean \(=2.000\,\mathrm{s}\), \(s=0.032\,\mathrm{s}\), and standard error \(=0.014\,\mathrm{s}\).

Example 2.

A solid cube has side \(12.0\pm0.1\,\mathrm{cm}\) and mass \(216\pm2\,\mathrm{g}\). Find its density and the maximum percentage uncertainty.

  1. Its volume is \((12.0)^3=1728\,\mathrm{cm^3}\).
  2. The density is \(\rho=M/V=216/1728=0.125\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\).
  3. For \(\rho=M/a^3\), the maximum fractional error is \(\Delta\rho/\rho=\Delta M/M+3\Delta a/a\).
  4. Substitution gives \(2/216+3(0.1)/12.0=0.03426\), or \(3.43\%\).
  5. The corresponding absolute uncertainty is \(0.125(0.03426)=0.00428\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\).

Answer: \(\rho=(0.125\pm0.004)\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\), with a \(3.4\%\) maximum uncertainty.

Common mistakes.
  • Averaging repeated readings to cure a constant zero error.
  • Reporting the sample standard deviation as the uncertainty of the mean.
  • Ignoring the factor three when propagating side-length error into cube volume.

Index / Mechanics
Chapter 2 · Topic 1

Motion in One Dimension

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. One-dimensional motion is described completely by a single coordinate \(x(t)\) together with time, since all relevant vectors lie along one axis and become signed scalars. Every quantity in this chapter (position, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration) is then a function of \(t\) alone, and differentiation or integration of \(x(t)\) yields the rest. The JEE skill being tested is the disciplined setting of an origin and a positive direction, after which all questions reduce to a single algebraic function.
Key formula(s). \[x = x(t)\] ; \[v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}\] ; \[a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}\] ; \[\Delta x = x_2 - x_1,\quad s = \int |dx|\] ; \[v_{\rm av} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t},\quad u_{\rm av} = \dfrac{s}{\Delta t}\]
Key points.
  • Fixing the origin arbitrarily changes only the numbers, never the physical conclusions; the choice of positive direction is free but must be stated.
  • In one dimension every vector is collinear, so the sign of the quantity is the only extra information a vector would carry.
  • Differentiate \(x(t)\) to get velocity and differentiate again for acceleration; integrate acceleration with proper initial conditions to invert the process.
  • Turning points are where \(v = 0\); they are found by differentiating, and at such instants the acceleration is generally not zero.
  • JEE problems that give \(x(t)\) in polynomial or trigonometric form are always solved by this differentiate-integrate route.
  • A motion described completely needs \(x_0\), \(v_0\) and the law of variation of acceleration; anything less leaves the motion undetermined.
Example 1.

A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis so that its position varies as \(x = (3t^2 - 6t + 5)\ \mathrm{m}\). Find its position at \(t = 0\), the instant at which it reverses its direction with the corresponding position, and its total distance travelled in the interval \(0 \leq t \leq 4\ \mathrm{s}\).

  1. Position at \(t = 0\): \(x(0) = 5\ \mathrm{m}\), so the particle starts 5 m from the origin on the positive side.
  2. Velocity: \(v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = (6t - 6)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); direction changes where \(v = 0\), i.e. at \(t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\).
  3. Position at that instant: \(x(1) = 3 - 6 + 5 = 2\ \mathrm{m}\), so the turning point is 2 m from the origin.
  4. Acceleration \(a = 6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) is positive throughout, so the particle moves in \(-x\) for \(0 < t < 1\ \mathrm{s}\) and in \(+x\) for \(t > 1\ \mathrm{s}\).
  5. Position at \(t = 4\ \mathrm{s}\): \(x(4) = 3(16) - 6(4) + 5 = 48 - 24 + 5 = 29\ \mathrm{m}\).
  6. Distance \(= |5 - 2| + |29 - 2| = 3 + 27 = 30\ \mathrm{m}\), whereas the magnitude of displacement is only \(29 - 5 = 24\ \mathrm{m}\).

Answer: Starts at \(x = 5\ \mathrm{m}\), reverses at \(t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\) at \(x = 2\ \mathrm{m}\), and covers \(30\ \mathrm{m}\) of path in \(0 \leq t \leq 4\ \mathrm{s}\) (net displacement \(24\ \mathrm{m}\)).

Example 2.

A car travels \(30\ \mathrm{km}\) at a uniform \(30\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\), then \(30\ \mathrm{km}\) at \(60\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\), and finally \(30\ \mathrm{km}\) at \(90\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\). Find the average speed of the whole trip and state the speeds at which the car would have to travel uniformly to cover the same total distance in the same total time.

  1. Times for the three legs: \(t_1 = 30/30 = 1\ \mathrm{h}\), \(t_2 = 30/60 = 0.5\ \mathrm{h}\), \(t_3 = 30/90 = 0.333\ \mathrm{h}\).
  2. Total distance \(= 90\ \mathrm{km}\), total time \(= 1 + 0.5 + 0.333 = 1.833\ \mathrm{h} = 11/6\ \mathrm{h}\).
  3. Average speed \(= 90/(11/6) = 540/11 = 49.1\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\), which lies between the slowest and fastest leg speeds as it must.
  4. The equivalent uniform speed over the whole trip is precisely this average speed, \(49.1\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\), since equal distances (not equal times) are lumped.
  5. Note the time saved by the faster legs: if all \(90\ \mathrm{km}\) had been covered at \(30\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) the time would have been \(3\ \mathrm{h}\), i.e. \(1.167\ \mathrm{h}\) more.

Answer: Average speed \(= 49.1\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\), and the equivalent uniform speed for the whole trip is also \(49.1\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Averaging the speeds directly (\((30+60+90)/3 = 60\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\)), which is valid only for equal times, not equal distances.
  • Dividing total distance by total displacement or using distance where displacement is asked.
  • Assuming a particle at rest has zero acceleration; at a turning point the velocity vanishes but the acceleration does not.
  • Ignoring the sign of \(dx/dt\) when computing distance, so that a reversal is not detected and the path length comes out too small.

Chapter 2 · Topic 2

Frame of reference

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Frame of reference (coordinate system plus clock from which motion is described) decides motion descriptions - same car moves relative to roadside observers, rests relative to passengers. Inertial frames (unaccelerated: Newton laws hold directly) versus non-inertial (accelerating: pseudo forces appear). Ground frames serve most problems; centre-of-mass frames simplify collisions. Motion has no meaning without stated frames - always anchor observations.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Coordinate-plus-clock viewpoint defining motion descriptions.
  • Inertial frames obey Newton directly; accelerating frames add pseudo forces.
Remember
  • Passengers see fellow riders at rest - frames decide motion.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Pseudo forces appear in frames that are

Solution: Accelerating viewpoints need fictitious forces to explain observations.
Key Formulas · Frame of Reference
\(x^{\prime}=x-vt,\;t^{\prime}=t\) Galilean transform between frames
\(\vec F_{pseudo}=-m\vec a_{frame}\) pseudo force in accelerating frames

Index / Mechanics
Chapter 2 · Topic 3

Position

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Position is the coordinate specifying where a particle is at a given instant, measured from a chosen origin along a fixed axis, and it is a signed quantity in one-dimensional motion. A complete description of position as a function of time, \(x = x(t)\), is the starting point of all kinematics because velocity and acceleration are its time derivatives. JEE problems that hand you \(x(t)\) expect you to read off positions, turning points and the sign of motion directly from that function.
Key formula(s). \[x = x(t)\] ; \[x_2 - x_1 = \Delta x\] ; \[v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}\] ; \[\text{turning points: } \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 0\] ; \[\left|\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right|_{t_1}^{t_2} \text{ gives the distance in that interval}\]
Key points.
  • Position is a signed coordinate; two points can have the same distance from the origin and different positions.
  • The instantaneous position is a point on the number line, while the displacement between two instants is a difference of positions.
  • A negative value of \(x(t)\) simply means the particle is on the negative side of the chosen origin; nothing is unphysical about it.
  • Where \(dx/dt = 0\) the particle is momentarily at rest and reverses or pauses; this is how turning points are located in JEE graphs.
  • The position function must be differentiable for velocity to exist; a corner in a graph means velocity is not defined at that instant.
  • On a straight road with fixed markings, the odometer reads path length while the position coordinate reads displacement from a datum.
Example 1.

A particle moves on the \(x\)-axis with \(x = (4t^2 - 2t)\ \mathrm{m}\), with \(t\) in seconds. Find the position at \(t = 0\), \(0.5\ \mathrm{s}\), \(1\ \mathrm{s}\) and \(2\ \mathrm{s}\), and state the intervals in which the particle moves in the positive and negative directions.

  1. Evaluate the position function: \(x(0) = 0\ \mathrm{m}\) (starts at the origin).
  2. \(x(0.5) = 4(0.25) - 2(0.5) = 1 - 1 = 0\ \mathrm{m}\), so at \(0.5\ \mathrm{s}\) the particle is again at the origin.
  3. \(x(1) = 4 - 2 = 2\ \mathrm{m}\) and \(x(2) = 16 - 4 = 12\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Velocity \(v = 8t - 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); it vanishes at \(t = 0.25\ \mathrm{s}\).
  5. For \(t < 0.25\ \mathrm{s}\), \(v < 0\), so the particle moves in \(-x\); for \(t > 0.25\ \mathrm{s}\), \(v > 0\), so it moves in \(+x\).
  6. The graph is a parabola of minimum value \(x = 4(0.0625) - 2(0.25) = 0.25 - 0.5 = -0.25\ \mathrm{m}\) at \(t = 0.25\ \mathrm{s}\).

Answer: Positions are \(0,\ 0,\ 2,\ 12\ \mathrm{m}\) at \(t = 0,\ 0.5,\ 1,\ 2\ \mathrm{s}\); the particle moves in \(-x\) for \(t < 0.25\ \mathrm{s}\) and in \(+x\) after that.

Example 2.

A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis with \(x = 2t\) metres for \(0 \leq t \leq 2\ \mathrm{s}\), and then with \(x = 4 - t/2\) metres for \(2 \leq t \leq 6\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the position and time at which the particle reverses, the total distance travelled, the displacement in \(6\ \mathrm{s}\), and the average speed.

  1. In the first interval \(v = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) (constant), so at \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\) the position is \(x = 4\ \mathrm{m}\).
  2. In the second interval \(v = -t/2\) derivative, i.e. \(v = -0.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) (constant), so the velocity changes sign at the junction: the particle reverses at \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\), \(x = 4\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. Final position: \(x(6) = 4 - 3 = 1\ \mathrm{m}\), so the displacement in \(6\ \mathrm{s}\) is \(1 - 0 = 1\ \mathrm{m}\) in \(+x\).
  4. Distance: first leg \(4\ \mathrm{m}\) (from \(0\) to \(4\ \mathrm{m}\)), second leg \(|4 - 1| = 3\ \mathrm{m}\), so total distance \(= 4 + 3 = 7\ \mathrm{m}\).
  5. Since the velocity never vanishes for finite time, the particle never truly stops; average speed \(= 7/6 = 1.17\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and average velocity \(= 1/6 = 0.167\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  6. The \(x\)-\(t\) graph is a straight line of slope \(+2\) up to \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\) and a straight line of slope \(-0.5\) after it: a sharp corner at the junction.

Answer: Reversal at \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\) at \(x = 4\ \mathrm{m}\); total distance \(7\ \mathrm{m}\), displacement \(1\ \mathrm{m}\), average speed \(1.17\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Reading a position off the \(y\)-axis of an \(x\)-\(t\) graph or confusing the slope of the graph with the position.
  • Concluding that the particle is at rest for an interval because two positions are equal; equal positions at two instants mean it returned, not that it waited.
  • Treating a negative position as an error; the origin choice is arbitrary and negative values are perfectly meaningful.
  • Computing distance by taking \(x(6) - x(0)\) when the particle has reversed direction.

Explanation

Concept. The position vector of a point is the vector drawn from the chosen origin to that point, written \(\vec r = x\hat i + y\hat j + z\hat k\). It is the vector form of the scalar position coordinate, and choosing a different origin changes \(\vec r\) by a constant vector without changing velocity or acceleration. In JEE projectile and orbital problems the position vector at time \(t\) is obtained by integrating the velocity, or directly from the equation of motion.
Key formula(s). \[\vec r = x\hat i + y\hat j + z\hat k,\quad |\vec r| = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\] ; \[\vec v = \frac{d\vec r}{dt},\quad \vec a = \frac{d^2\vec r}{dt^2}\] ; \[\vec s = \vec r_2 - \vec r_1\] ; \[\vec r(t) = \vec r_0 + \vec u\,t + \tfrac12\vec a\,t^2\] ; \[\vec r_{\rm proj} = (u\cos\theta)\,t\,\hat i + \left[(u\sin\theta)t - \tfrac12 g t^2\right]\hat j\]
Key points.
  • \(\vec r\) is measured from the origin, so the answer changes if the origin is shifted by a constant vector \(\vec r_0\); velocities and accelerations are unaffected.
  • The distance of the point from the origin is \(|\vec r|\), while the distance from any other point \(P\) is \(|\vec r - \vec r_P|\).
  • For a particle in free fall from rest at height \(h\), \(\vec r = -\tfrac12 g t^2\hat j\) measured from the release point.
  • Differentiating the position vector gives velocity and differentiating again gives acceleration, componentwise, since \(\hat i, \hat j, \hat k\) are constants.
  • For uniform circular motion \(|\vec r| = R\) is constant even though the vector \(\vec r\) changes; constant distance does not mean the position vector is constant.
  • The displacement between two points is independent of the path but, like \(\vec r\), it is not a position; it is a difference of two position vectors.
Example 1.

A particle moves such that at \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\) its position vector is \(\vec r = (4\hat i + 3\hat j)\ \mathrm{m}\). Find the distance of the particle from the origin, the unit vector from the origin to the particle, and the direction of the position vector.

  1. Distance from the origin: \(r = |\vec r| = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5\ \mathrm{m}\).
  2. Unit vector along the position vector: \(\hat r = (4\hat i + 3\hat j)/5\).
  3. The direction is found from \(\tan\theta = y/x = 3/4\), so \(\theta = 36.87^\circ\) with the positive \(x\)-axis in the \(xy\) plane.
  4. The vector is perpendicular to the line through the origin with slope \(-4/3\), which is a common auxiliary construction in JEE problems.
  5. The \(z\)-component is zero, so the motion described lies entirely in the \(xy\) plane.

Answer: Distance \(5\ \mathrm{m}\), unit position vector \((4\hat i + 3\hat j)/5\), direction \(36.9^\circ\) above the \(x\)-axis.

Example 2.

A stone is projected horizontally with \(35\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) from the top of a cliff of height \(140\ \mathrm{m}\), with \(g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Take the origin at the foot of the cliff. Find the position vector after \(3\ \mathrm{s}\) and the distance of the stone from the foot at that instant.

  1. With the origin at the foot, the initial position is \(\vec r_0 = 140\hat j\ \mathrm{m}\) and the initial velocity is \(\vec u = 35\hat i\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  2. The acceleration is \(\vec a = -10\hat j\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), so using \(\vec r = \vec r_0 + \vec u t + \tfrac12\vec a t^2\):
  3. \(\vec r(3) = 140\hat j + 35(3)\hat i + \tfrac12(-10)(9)\hat j = 105\hat i + (140 - 45)\hat j = 105\hat i + 95\hat j\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Distance from the foot: \(r = \sqrt{105^2 + 95^2} = \sqrt{11025 + 9025} = \sqrt{20050} = 141.6\ \mathrm{m}\).
  5. The direction of the position vector from the foot is \(\tan^{-1}(95/105) = 42.1^\circ\) below the horizontal, along which the stone actually fell.

Answer: \(\vec r(3) = (105\hat i + 95\hat j)\ \mathrm{m}\) and the distance from the foot of the cliff is \(141.6\ \mathrm{m}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Forgetting the constant offset \(\vec r_0\) when the origin is not at the point of launch; then the computed position is a displacement, not a position vector.
  • Assuming \(|\vec r|\) is constant implies the particle is at rest; in circular motion the position vector rotates with constant length.
  • Differentiating the magnitude \(|\vec r|\) instead of the components when finding velocity in a general (non-radial) motion.
  • Using a vector formula with a scalar result, e.g. writing \(\vec r = ut + \tfrac12 at^2\) for a horizontal projectile; the components must be handled separately.

Chapter 2 · Topic 4

Distance

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Distance is the total length of the path actually traversed by the particle, irrespective of direction; it is a scalar, always non-negative, and can only increase or stay constant with time. It is obtained by summing the magnitudes of the successive displacements, or by integrating the speed, \(s = \int |v|\,dt\). The essential JEE point is that distance and magnitude of displacement are equal only for motion in a single direction with no reversal.
Key formula(s). \[s = s_1 + s_2 + s_3 + \cdots\] ; \[s = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} |v|\,dt = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \left|\frac{dx}{dt}\right|dt\] ; \[\left|\Delta x\right| = |x_2 - x_1| \leq s\] ; \[\text{equal only if the path is a straight line traversed once}\]
Key points.
  • Distance has no sign and no direction; two opposite motions of the same size give zero displacement but twice the distance.
  • Distance is a monotonically increasing function of time for any real motion.
  • On a straight line, distance equals \(|x_2 - x_1|\) only if the particle never reverses direction between the two instants.
  • For a body completing one full circle, distance is the circumference \(2\pi R\) while displacement is zero.
  • Distance is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement, a useful check on any numerical answer.
  • The odometer of a vehicle measures distance, while the trip meter measures displacement; the ratio is a common JEE conceptual question.
Example 1.

A body moves \(4\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(+x\) direction, then \(3\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(-x\) direction, and finally \(5\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(-x\) direction. Find the total distance travelled, the displacement, and the ratio of distance to magnitude of displacement.

  1. Distance is the sum of the magnitudes of the three legs: \(s = 4 + 3 + 5 = 12\ \mathrm{m}\).
  2. Net displacement: \(+4 - 3 - 5 = -4\ \mathrm{m}\), i.e. \(4\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(-x\) direction.
  3. Magnitude of displacement \(= 4\ \mathrm{m}\), so the ratio \(s/|\Delta x| = 12/4 = 3\).
  4. The inequality \(|\Delta x| \leq s\) is satisfied with equality nowhere, which confirms that a reversal has occurred.
  5. The final position is \(4\ \mathrm{m}\) on the negative side of the origin, reached by travelling \(12\ \mathrm{m}\).

Answer: Distance \(= 12\ \mathrm{m}\), displacement \(= -4\ \mathrm{m}\) (that is, \(4\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(-x\) direction), and the ratio is \(3:1\).

Example 2.

A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis with position \(x = (t^3 - 3t^2)\ \mathrm{m}\) for \(0 \leq t \leq 3\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the total distance travelled in this interval and comment on the motion.

  1. Velocity \(v = 3t^2 - 6t = 3t(t - 2)\), which is zero at \(t = 0\) and \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\); this is the only reversal.
  2. Positions: \(x(0) = 0\), \(x(2) = 8 - 12 = -4\ \mathrm{m}\), \(x(3) = 27 - 27 = 0\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. On \(0 < t < 2\ \mathrm{s}\), \(v < 0\), so the particle moves from \(0\ \mathrm{m}\) to \(-4\ \mathrm{m}\), covering \(4\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. On \(2 < t < 3\ \mathrm{s}\), \(v > 0\), so it returns from \(-4\ \mathrm{m}\) to \(0\ \mathrm{m}\), covering another \(4\ \mathrm{m}\).
  5. Total distance \(= 4 + 4 = 8\ \mathrm{m}\), while the displacement over the whole interval is \(x(3) - x(0) = 0\).
  6. Acceleration \(a = 6t - 6\) is negative up to \(t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\) and positive after, so the speed first decreases to zero and then increases.

Answer: Total distance \(= 8\ \mathrm{m}\) (with a reversal at \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\)), while the net displacement is zero.

Common mistakes.
  • Adding displacements with their signs to get the distance; signed addition gives displacement, not distance.
  • Assuming distance equals magnitude of displacement in a problem where the particle reverses or takes a curved path.
  • Forgetting to add the leg before the reversal, which is the most common loss of marks in distance questions.
  • Reporting distance with a sign, or saying distance is zero for a closed path when it is the circumference.

Chapter 2 · Topic 5

Displacement

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Displacement is the change in position, \(\Delta x = x_2 - x_1\), the straight-line vector from the initial to the final point; it depends only on the endpoints and never on the path followed. In one dimension it is a signed quantity, positive or negative according to whether the final position is to the right or left of the initial one, and it may be zero even when a great deal of motion has occurred. JEE tests the pair (displacement, distance) and their ratio, and the equality \(|\Delta x| = s\) holds only for unidirectional straight-line motion.
Key formula(s). \[\Delta x = x_2 - x_1\] ; \[|\Delta x| \leq s\] ; \[\vec s = \vec r_2 - \vec r_1\] ; \[\Delta x = 0 \text{ if } x_2 = x_1\] ; \[\text{half circle: } |\Delta x| = 2R\]
Key points.
  • Displacement is a vector, so in multi-dimensional motion it is the difference of position vectors, not the sum of path pieces.
  • It can be positive, negative or zero; a return to the starting point gives exactly zero displacement.
  • Only the endpoints matter: two paths between the same points have identical displacement but very different distances.
  • The maximum possible displacement in a given time is the total distance covered, and it equals it only for unidirectional motion.
  • For a body on a circular track completing one full round, the displacement is zero; for half a round it is the diameter \(2R\).
  • The average velocity is the rate of change of displacement, so a zero net displacement always implies zero average velocity.
Example 1.

A body moves \(10\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(+x\) direction and then \(6\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(-x\) direction. Find the displacement, the distance travelled, and state whether \(|\Delta x| = s\).

  1. Displacement: \(\Delta x = 10 + (-6) = 4\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(+x\) direction.
  2. Distance: \(s = 10 + 6 = 16\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. Since \(|\Delta x| = 4\ \mathrm{m} \neq 16\ \mathrm{m}\), the body reversed direction once during the motion.
  4. Final position relative to the start is \(4\ \mathrm{m}\) ahead; the return leg of \(6\ \mathrm{m}\) exceeded the earlier \(10\ \mathrm{m}\) leg only in part.
  5. The ratio \(s/|\Delta x| = 4\), which is the number of times the body effectively retraced its steps in aggregate.

Answer: Displacement \(= 4\ \mathrm{m}\) along \(+x\), distance \(= 16\ \mathrm{m}\), and they are not equal because of the reversal.

Example 2.

An athlete completes one and a half rounds of a circular track of radius \(35\ \mathrm{m}\) in \(45\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the magnitude of the displacement, the distance covered, the average velocity and the average speed.

  1. One and a half rounds means the final point is diametrically opposite the start, so the displacement is the diameter: \(|\Delta \vec s| = 2R = 70\ \mathrm{m}\).
  2. The displacement is directed along the diameter, from the start to the diametrically opposite point, which is all that the magnitude formula needs.
  3. Distance covered \(= 1.5 \times 2\pi R = 1.5 \times 2\pi \times 35 = 329.9\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Average velocity \(= |\Delta \vec s|/t = 70/45 = 1.56\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) directed along the diameter from start to finish.
  5. Average speed \(= s/t = 329.9/45 = 7.33\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which is the larger quantity as expected.
  6. The ratio of average speed to average velocity is \(329.9/70 = 4.71\), reflecting the extra half round retraced.

Answer: Displacement magnitude \(70\ \mathrm{m}\) (along the diameter), distance \(330\ \mathrm{m}\), average velocity \(1.56\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), average speed \(7.33\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Adding the path lengths to obtain displacement; that gives distance.
  • Assuming displacement is always positive and reporting a magnitude when the sign matters.
  • Using the radius instead of the diameter for the displacement after half a revolution.
  • Reporting the magnitude of the displacement after a partial revolution; only a full round trip gives zero, while half a round trip gives the diameter \(2R\).
