Chapter 2 · Topic 6

Speed

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Speed is the rate at which the path length is covered, \(\text{speed} = ds/dt\), a scalar that can never be negative and carries no information about direction. In one dimension, speed equals the magnitude of velocity, so the two differ only in sign information; in higher dimensions the distinction becomes physical. The average speed is total distance divided by total time, and for unidirectional motion it coincides with the magnitude of the average velocity.
Key formula(s). \[\text{speed} = \left|\frac{dx}{dt}\right| = |v|\] ; \[\text{average speed} = \frac{s}{\Delta t}\] ; \[\text{maximum speed} = \max |v|\] ; \[\mathrm{unit} = \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \text{ or } \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}},\ 1\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}} = \tfrac{5}{18}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\]
Key points.
  • Speed is a scalar and its instantaneous value is \(|v|\); it never carries a sign even when the motion reverses.
  • Average speed is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of the average velocity, with equality only for unidirectional motion.
  • The instantaneous speed may be zero at an instant (turning point) without the body being at rest for any finite time.
  • Speed in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) are related by a factor of \(18/5\); a frequent source of numerical error in JEE papers.
  • A body can have constant speed (uniform circular motion) and still have a continuously changing velocity, because the direction changes.
  • When a graph of speed is given, the distance is the area under the speed-time graph.
Example 1.

A car covers \(90\ \mathrm{m}\) in \(6\ \mathrm{s}\), stops for \(4\ \mathrm{s}\), and then covers \(150\ \mathrm{m}\) in \(10\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the total distance, the total time, the average speed, and the speed during the stationary interval.

  1. Total distance \(= 90 + 150 = 240\ \mathrm{m}\); the stationary interval contributes no distance.
  2. Total time \(= 6 + 4 + 10 = 20\ \mathrm{s}\), and the stopping time must be included in the total, which is the trap in this question.
  3. Average speed \(= 240/20 = 12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  4. During the \(4\ \mathrm{s}\) stop the speed is \(0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and its average over that interval is also zero.
  5. The speeds during the moving intervals were \(90/6 = 15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(150/10 = 15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so the motion speed was uniform while moving.
  6. Since both moving legs had the same speed, the average over the moving \(16\ \mathrm{s}\) is also \(15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); including the stop drags it down to \(12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Answer: Total distance \(240\ \mathrm{m}\) in \(20\ \mathrm{s}\), so the average speed is \(12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) (speed during the stop is \(0\)).

Example 2.

A particle has position \(x = (2t^3 - 9t^2)\ \mathrm{m}\) for \(0 \leq t \leq 6\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the total distance travelled, the displacement, the average speed and the average velocity.

  1. Velocity \(v = 6t^2 - 18t = 6t(t-3)\), zero at \(t = 0\) and \(t = 3\ \mathrm{s}\), so there is one reversal.
  2. Positions: \(x(0) = 0\); \(x(3) = 2(27) - 9(9) = 54 - 81 = -27\ \mathrm{m}\); \(x(6) = 2(216) - 9(36) = 432 - 324 = 108\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. First leg (0 to 3 s): distance \(= |0 - (-27)| = 27\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(-x\) direction.
  4. Second leg (3 to 6 s): distance \(= |108 - (-27)| = 135\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(+x\) direction.
  5. Total distance \(= 27 + 135 = 162\ \mathrm{m}\), whereas the displacement \(= 108 - 0 = 108\ \mathrm{m}\).
  6. Average speed \(= 162/6 = 27\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); average velocity \(= 108/6 = 18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and indeed \(27 \geq 18\) as required.

Answer: Distance \(162\ \mathrm{m}\), displacement \(108\ \mathrm{m}\), average speed \(27\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), average velocity \(18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Excluding the time spent at rest from the total time when computing average speed.
  • Using signed velocity where speed is asked, producing a negative value for a scalar.
  • Forgetting to add the two legs separated by a reversal when summing the distance.
  • Mixing up the conversion factors: \(1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = 3.6\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) and \(1\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}} = 5/18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Chapter 2 · Topic 7

Average speed

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Average speed is the total distance covered divided by the total time elapsed, \(\bar{u} = s/\Delta t\), a scalar that can never be negative and always lies between the minimum and maximum instantaneous speeds. When equal times (not equal distances) are spent at different speeds, the correct operation is the arithmetic mean; when equal distances are covered at different speeds, a harmonic-type mean is required. This single distinction decides the answer in most JEE average-speed questions.
Key formula(s). \[\text{average speed} = \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}} = \frac{s_1+s_2+\cdots}{t_1+t_2+\cdots}\] ; \[\text{equal distances } d:\ \bar u = \frac{2d}{d/v_1 + d/v_2} = \frac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}\] ; \[\text{equal times } t:\ \bar u = \frac{v_1 + v_2}{2}\] ; \[\bar u \geq |\bar v|,\quad \frac{v_{\min} + v_{\max}}{2} \text{ for uniform } a\]
Key points.
  • For equal distances at speeds \(v_1, v_2\), the average speed is the harmonic mean \(2v_1v_2/(v_1+v_2)\), never the arithmetic mean.
  • For equal times at speeds \(v_1, v_2\), the average speed is the arithmetic mean \((v_1+v_2)/2\).
  • For equal distances on a round trip, the average speed is independent of the total distance and equals \(2v_1v_2/(v_1+v_2)\).
  • For uniformly accelerated motion, average speed is \((u+v)/2 = u + at/2\), which is also the velocity at the mid-time.
  • Average speed always lies between the slowest and fastest speeds used, and never below the magnitude of the average velocity.
  • A stoppage must be included in the total time; omitting it inflates the average speed.
Example 1.

A car travels the first \(60\ \mathrm{km}\) at \(20\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) and the next \(60\ \mathrm{km}\) at \(60\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\). Find the average speed of the whole journey and the uniform speed at which the same journey would have to be driven to take the same time.

  1. Times: \(t_1 = 60/20 = 3\ \mathrm{h}\) and \(t_2 = 60/60 = 1\ \mathrm{h}\).
  2. Total distance \(= 120\ \mathrm{km}\), total time \(= 4\ \mathrm{h}\).
  3. Average speed \(= 120/4 = 30\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\).
  4. As a check, the equal-distance formula gives \(\bar u = 2(20)(60)/(20+60) = 2400/80 = 30\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\), the harmonic mean.
  5. The arithmetic mean \((20+60)/2 = 40\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) would be correct only if the car had spent equal times at the two speeds, which it did not.
  6. The answer lies between 20 and 60 as required, and is closer to the lower value because more time was spent at it.

Answer: Average speed \(= 30\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\), and a uniform speed of \(30\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) covers the same \(120\ \mathrm{km}\) in the same \(4\ \mathrm{h}\).

Example 2.

A car moves from town A to town B at \(60\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) and returns over the same road at \(40\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\). Find the average speed for the whole trip, the magnitude of the average velocity, and comment on why the two differ.

  1. Let the one-way distance be \(d\) km; the answer must not depend on \(d\), so leave it symbolic.
  2. Total time \(= d/60 + d/40 = d(2/120 + 3/120) = 5d/120 = d/24\) hours.
  3. Total distance for the round trip \(= 2d\), so the average speed \(= 2d/(d/24) = 48\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\).
  4. As a check, the harmonic mean of 60 and 40 is \(2(60)(40)/(60+40) = 4800/100 = 48\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\), correct.
  5. The body returns to A, so the displacement is zero and the average velocity is zero.
  6. The average speed is non-zero because \(330\ \mathrm{km}\) of road was actually covered in the same time; average speed measures effort, average velocity measures change of position.
  7. Hence \(\bar u \geq |\bar v|\) with a very large gap: \(48\) versus \(0\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\).

Answer: Average speed \(48\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) while the average velocity is zero, since the car ends where it started.

Common mistakes.
  • Taking the arithmetic mean of the speeds when the distances are equal; that gives \(50\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) in the second example and is wrong.
  • Excluding rest or stoppage time from the total time.
  • Reporting zero average speed for a round trip because the displacement is zero; that is the average velocity, not the average speed.
  • Assuming the average speed is independent of the distances involved; it is not when the legs are unequal.

Chapter 2 · Topic 8

Instantaneous speed

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Instantaneous speed (ds/dt magnitude at an instant - speedometer readings) differs from average (total path over total time) whenever pace varies. Speed (scalar, path rate) versus velocity (vector, displacement rate) split on direction - circular uniforme motion holds constant speed with changing velocity. Speedometer plus odometer pair instantaneous versus average readings daily.
NEET Snapshot:
  • ds/dt magnitude now; speedometer shows it live.
  • Speed scalar ignores direction; velocity vectors it.
Remember
  • Odometer totals path; speedometer reports instant rate.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Speedometer of a vehicle measures

Solution: Live dial readings report ds/dt at each instant.
Key Formulas · Instantaneous Speed
\(v=\frac{ds}{dt}=|\vec v|\) rate of path length, speedometer reading
\(v_{av}=\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}\) average over intervals differs when pace varies

Chapter 2 · Topic 9

Velocity

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Velocity is the rate of change of displacement (equivalently of position), \(v = dx/dt\), and in one dimension it is a signed scalar whose sign states the direction of motion. The average velocity \(\Delta x/\Delta t\) is a single number for a whole interval, whereas the instantaneous velocity describes one instant and equals the slope of the \(x\)-\(t\) graph. The key JEE distinction is that average velocity can vanish while the body has certainly moved.
Key formula(s). \[v_{\rm av} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}\] ; \[v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}\] ; \[v = \text{slope of the } x\text{-}t \text{ graph}\] ; \[\text{sign of } v \text{ gives the direction: } +x \text{ or } -x\]
Key points.
  • Velocity is a vector; in 1D its sign is the only directional information, and it is zero only at instants of rest.
  • Average velocity over an interval is the chord slope of the \(x\)-\(t\) graph; instantaneous velocity is the tangent slope at that point.
  • Average velocity can be zero (return to start) or smaller than the average speed; it can never exceed the average speed in magnitude.
  • If the body moves in one direction throughout, average velocity equals the average speed.
  • Velocity is not uniform unless the position varies linearly with time; a constant velocity means zero acceleration.
  • For several successive intervals, use the time-weighted mean: \(\bar v = \sum \Delta x_i / \sum \Delta t_i\), not the arithmetic mean of the interval velocities.
Example 1.

A particle's position is \(x = t^3\ \mathrm{m}\) with \(t\) in seconds. Find its velocity in the interval \(1\ \mathrm{s}\) to \(2\ \mathrm{s}\), its average velocity in that interval, and its instantaneous velocity at \(t = 1.5\ \mathrm{s}\).

  1. Positions: \(x(1) = 1\ \mathrm{m}\), \(x(2) = 8\ \mathrm{m}\), so \(\Delta x = 7\ \mathrm{m}\) in \(\Delta t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\).
  2. Average velocity in the interval: \(v_{\rm av} = 7/1 = 7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along \(+x\).
  3. Instantaneous velocity: \(v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3t^2\), so \(v(1.5) = 3(2.25) = 6.75\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  4. The average velocity of a non-uniform motion lies between the velocities at the endpoints: \(v(1) = 3\) and \(v(2) = 12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and \(6.75\) and \(7\) both lie in that range, as they must.
  5. Acceleration \(a = 6t = 9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) at \(1.5\ \mathrm{s}\), positive, so the speed is increasing.
  6. Note that the chord slope \(7\) exceeds the tangent slope \(6.75\) at the midpoint because the graph is convex (accelerating).

Answer: Average velocity over \(1\) s to \(2\) s is \(7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 1.5\ \mathrm{s}\) is \(6.75\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), both along \(+x\).

Example 2.

A particle moves with \(x = (6t - 3t^2)\ \mathrm{m}\). Find its average velocity in the interval \(0 \leq t \leq 2\ \mathrm{s}\), its instantaneous velocity at \(t = 0.5\ \mathrm{s}\), the instant at which its velocity is zero, and its position then.

  1. Positions: \(x(0) = 0\) and \(x(2) = 12 - 12 = 0\ \mathrm{m}\), so the particle returns to the origin at \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\).
  2. Average velocity over \(0 \to 2\ \mathrm{s}\): \(v_{\rm av} = (0 - 0)/2 = 0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), although the body certainly moved.
  3. Instantaneous velocity: \(v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 6 - 6t\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so \(v(0.5) = 6 - 3 = 3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  4. Velocity vanishes at \(6 - 6t = 0\), i.e. at \(t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\).
  5. Position at that instant: \(x(1) = 6 - 3 = 3\ \mathrm{m}\), the maximum position reached; the motion is symmetric about \(t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\).
  6. Distance travelled: from \(0\) to \(3\ \mathrm{m}\) and back to \(0\ \mathrm{m}\), so \(s = 6\ \mathrm{m}\); average speed \(= 6/2 = 3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) while average velocity is zero.

Answer: Average velocity over \(0\) to \(2\ \mathrm{s}\) is \(0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), instantaneous velocity at \(0.5\ \mathrm{s}\) is \(3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the velocity is zero at \(t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\) when \(x = 3\ \mathrm{m}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Equating average velocity with the arithmetic mean of the endpoint velocities; valid only for uniform acceleration.
  • Reporting zero velocity and concluding the body did not move; the average over the interval was zero because it returned to its start.
  • Taking the average of the velocities of several legs without weighting by the time spent in each leg.
  • Sign errors when differentiating, e.g. writing \(v = 3t^2 + 6t\) for \(x = t^3 + 3t^2\).

Chapter 2 · Topic 10

Average velocity

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Average velocity is the displacement divided by the elapsed time, \(\bar v = \Delta x/\Delta t = \vec s/\Delta t\), and it is a vector whose value lies between the minimum and maximum velocities of the interval. It depends only on the two instants chosen, not on how the particle got from one to the other, and it can be zero even when the particle has travelled far. The classic JEE contrast is a round trip, where the average velocity vanishes but the average speed is large.
Key formula(s). \[\bar v = \frac{\Delta \vec r}{\Delta t} = \frac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}\] ; \[\text{several legs: } \bar v = \frac{\sum \Delta x_i}{\sum \Delta t_i}\] ; \[|\bar v| \le \frac{1}{\Delta t}\int |v| dt = \text{average speed}\] ; \[\bar v = 0 \text{ for a round trip}\]
Key points.
  • Only the initial and final positions enter the formula; the path in between is irrelevant.
  • For successive legs, add the displacements algebraically and the times arithmetically, then form one ratio; never average the leg velocities directly.
  • The average velocity is the chord slope of the \(x\)-\(t\) graph, which is a very fast way to read it in JEE graph questions.
  • It is zero whenever the initial and final positions coincide, and also when positive and negative displacements cancel exactly.
  • Its magnitude never exceeds the average speed; equality only holds for unidirectional motion.
  • For uniformly accelerated motion, \(\bar v = (u+v)/2\), the velocity at the mid-point of the time interval.
Example 1.

A body moves \(10\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(+x\) direction in the first \(2\ \mathrm{s}\), then \(10\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(-x\) direction in the next \(2\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the displacement, the average velocity and the average speed.

  1. Displacement: \(+10 + (-10) = 0\ \mathrm{m}\); the body returns to its starting point.
  2. Total time \(= 4\ \mathrm{s}\), so the average velocity \(= 0/4 = 0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  3. Distance \(= 10 + 10 = 20\ \mathrm{m}\), so the average speed \(= 20/4 = 5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  4. The individual velocities were \(+5\) and \(-5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); their arithmetic mean is zero, which coincides with the correct answer only because the times are equal.
  5. If the second leg had taken \(5\ \mathrm{s}\) instead, the average velocity would have been \((10-10)/7 = 0\) still, but the leg velocities \(+5\) and \(-2\) would average to \(+1.5\), which is wrong.
  6. This is why the correct procedure is always total displacement over total time.

Answer: Displacement \(0\), average velocity \(0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and average speed \(5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Example 2.

A particle moves with velocity \(+10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for \(4\ \mathrm{s}\), then \(-20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for \(3\ \mathrm{s}\), and finally \(+5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for \(5\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the total displacement, the total distance, the average velocity and the average speed.

  1. First leg: \(\Delta x_1 = 10 \times 4 = 40\ \mathrm{m}\) in \(+x\).
  2. Second leg: \(\Delta x_2 = -20 \times 3 = -60\ \mathrm{m}\), so the body returns past its starting point.
  3. Third leg: \(\Delta x_3 = 5 \times 5 = 25\ \mathrm{m}\) in \(+x\).
  4. Total displacement \(= 40 - 60 + 25 = 5\ \mathrm{m}\) along \(+x\); total time \(= 4 + 3 + 5 = 12\ \mathrm{s}\).
  5. Average velocity \(= 5/12 = 0.417\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along \(+x\).
  6. Total distance \(= 40 + 60 + 25 = 125\ \mathrm{m}\), so the average speed \(= 125/12 = 10.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  7. The huge gap between the two averages is because the body retraced its path; the average velocity is not an average of the leg velocities, which would give \((10 - 20 + 5)/3 = -1.67\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), a wrong answer.

Answer: Total displacement \(5\ \mathrm{m}\), total distance \(125\ \mathrm{m}\), average velocity \(0.417\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along \(+x\), average speed \(10.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Taking the arithmetic mean of the velocities of the legs instead of total displacement over total time.
  • Reporting a magnitude for average velocity when the direction matters; a small positive value is not the same as zero.
  • Using average velocity where the problem asks for average speed on a return journey.
  • Ignoring the initial position and computing displacement from the origin when the body started at \(x_0 \ne 0\).

Index / Mechanics
Chapter 2 · Topic 11

Instantaneous velocity

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Instantaneous velocity is the limit of the average velocity as the averaging interval shrinks to zero, \(v = dx/dt\), and it is the derivative of the position function with respect to time. Geometrically it is the slope of the tangent to the \(x\)-\(t\) graph at that instant, which is the standard JEE interpretation of every tangent drawn on such a graph. It is a signed quantity in one dimension, zero at a turning point, and may differ from the average velocity over any finite interval.
Key formula(s). \[v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{x(t+\Delta t) - x(t)}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}\] ; \[v = \text{slope of the tangent to the } x\text{-}t \text{ curve}\] ; \[v = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{x(t+h) - x(t)}{h}\] ; \[\bar v_{\rm finite\ interval} \ne v_{\rm instantaneous}\ \text{unless the motion is uniform}\]
Key points.
  • Instantaneous velocity is the tangent slope, while average velocity is the chord slope; for a curved graph they differ.
  • Where the tangent is horizontal, \(v = 0\): the body is momentarily at rest and the position function has an extremum.
  • A negative slope means the position coordinate is decreasing, i.e. the body moves in the \(-x\) direction.
  • For uniform velocity the position-time graph is a straight line and the tangent slope equals the chord slope everywhere.
  • The velocity of a graph can be estimated by a central difference \((x(t+h) - x(t-h))/(2h)\), which is exact for uniform acceleration.
  • Velocity is undefined where the graph has a corner, since the derivative does not exist there.
Example 1.

A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis with \(x = (2t^2 - 4t + 3)\ \mathrm{m}\). Find the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 1.5\ \mathrm{s}\), the instant at which the velocity is zero, the acceleration, and the position at the turning point.

  1. Differentiate: \(v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 4t - 4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  2. At \(t = 1.5\ \mathrm{s}\): \(v = 4(1.5) - 4 = 6 - 4 = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), positive, so the body moves in \(+x\).
  3. Velocity zero: \(4t - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\).
  4. Acceleration: \(a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = 4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), positive, so the turning point is a minimum position.
  5. Position at the turning point: \(x(1) = 2 - 4 + 3 = 1\ \mathrm{m}\).
  6. The graph is a parabola of minimum value \(1\ \mathrm{m}\) at \(t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\); the tangent is horizontal there and the body reverses direction.
  7. Average velocity over \(0 \to 2\ \mathrm{s}\) is \((x(2)-x(0))/2 = (8-8+3-3)/2 = 0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), unlike the instantaneous value at \(1.5\ \mathrm{s}\).

Answer: \(v(1.5\ \mathrm{s}) = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along \(+x\), velocity is zero at \(t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\) where \(x = 1\ \mathrm{m}\), and \(a = 4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Example 2.

The positions of a particle along the \(x\)-axis at \(t = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8\ \mathrm{s}\) are \(0, 10, 28, 54, 88\ \mathrm{m}\). (i) Find the average velocity in the first \(8\ \mathrm{s}\). (ii) Estimate the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 4\ \mathrm{s}\). (iii) Is the motion uniformly accelerated?

  1. Average velocity over \(0 \to 8\ \mathrm{s}\): \(\bar v = (88 - 0)/8 = 11\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along \(+x\).
  2. First differences over successive \(2\ \mathrm{s}\) intervals: \(10, 18, 26, 34\ \mathrm{m}\), so the average speeds in those intervals are \(5, 9, 13, 17\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  3. Second differences are constant: \(8, 8, 8\ \mathrm{m}\), so the acceleration is uniform with \(a = 8/2^2 = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
  4. Fitting the data gives \(x = t^2 + 3t\), hence \(v = 2t + 3\) and \(a = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), consistent with the differences above.
  5. Instantaneous velocity at \(t = 4\ \mathrm{s}\): \(v = 2(4) + 3 = 11\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); the central difference gives \((54 - 10)/(6 - 2) = 44/4 = 11\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), the same value.
  6. For uniform acceleration the average velocity over a symmetric interval equals the instantaneous velocity at the mid-point, which is why all three figures are \(11\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Answer: Average velocity \(= 11\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), instantaneous velocity at \(t = 4\ \mathrm{s} = 11\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the motion is uniformly accelerated with \(a = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Reading the chord slope as the instantaneous velocity in a curved \(x\)-\(t\) graph.
  • Saying the velocity is zero over an interval because the graph is horizontal over a range; horizontal tangent means zero velocity at that instant only.
  • Using the velocity at the end of the interval as the average velocity for non-uniform motion.
  • Ignoring the sign of the slope and reporting a positive speed when the body moves in the \(-x\) direction.

Chapter 2 · Topic 12

Acceleration

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Acceleration is the time rate of change of velocity, \(a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2\), a vector quantity that measures how quickly the velocity changes. In one dimension a positive acceleration does not necessarily mean speeding up; the sign of \(a\) compared with the sign of \(v\) decides whether the speed increases or decreases. JEE problems constantly separate these two ideas, especially in vertical motion where a rising body slows although its acceleration is downward.
Key formula(s). \[a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}\] ; \[v = u + at\] ; \[a = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{t_2 - t_1}\] ; \[a = 0 \Rightarrow v = \text{const}\] ; \[|a| = \frac{\text{change in speed}}{\text{time}} \text{ for unidirectional 1D motion}\]
Key points.
  • Acceleration is zero for uniform velocity, not for uniform speed in general; a body on a circular track at constant speed has centripetal acceleration.
  • Sign convention: if \(a\) and \(v\) have the same sign the speed increases; if opposite signs the speed decreases (retardation).
  • Retardation is the magnitude of acceleration opposing the motion, so it is reported as a positive number.
  • From \(x(t)\), the number of differentiations gives the quantity: \(x \to v \to a \to\) jerk.
  • For vertical motion under gravity take upward positive, then \(a = -g = -10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) always, whatever the direction of motion.
  • A body at a turning point has \(v = 0\) but generally non-zero \(a\); only uniform velocity implies \(a = 0\).
Example 1.

A car travelling at \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) applies its brakes and comes to rest in \(8\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the retardation, the distance covered during braking, and the average speed during that interval.

  1. Take the direction of motion as positive: \(u = 20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(v = 0\), \(t = 8\ \mathrm{s}\).
  2. Retardation magnitude: \(|a| = (u - v)/t = 20/8 = 2.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), so \(a = -2.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) in the chosen positive direction.
  3. Distance: \(s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2 = 20(8) + \tfrac12(-2.5)(64) = 160 - 80 = 80\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Cross-check with the average-velocity form: \(s = \tfrac12 (u + v) t = \tfrac12 (20)(8) = 80\ \mathrm{m}\), correct.
  5. Average speed during braking \(= s/t = 80/8 = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), exactly half the initial speed because the speed falls linearly.
  6. The body has negative acceleration throughout, so its speed decreases continuously to zero at \(t = 8\ \mathrm{s}\).

Answer: Retardation \(2.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), braking distance \(80\ \mathrm{m}\), and average speed during braking \(10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Example 2.

The velocity of a particle is \(v = (2t^2 - 8t + 6)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for \(0 \leq t \leq 4\ \mathrm{s}\), measured along the \(x\)-axis. Find the instants at which the particle stops, the acceleration at those instants, the total distance covered in \(4\ \mathrm{s}\), and the average velocity in that time.

  1. Setting \(v = 0\): \(2t^2 - 8t + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow t^2 - 4t + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow (t-1)(t-3) = 0\), so the particle stops at \(t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\) and \(t = 3\ \mathrm{s}\).
  2. Acceleration: \(a = 4t - 8\), hence \(a(1) = -4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(a(3) = +4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\); both stops are momentary, not permanent.
  3. Integrate for position: \(x = \tfrac23 t^3 - 4t^2 + 6t\), so \(x(0) = 0\), \(x(1) = 2.67\ \mathrm{m}\), \(x(3) = 18 - 36 + 18 = 0\ \mathrm{m}\), \(x(4) = 42.67 - 64 + 24 = 2.67\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. The body moves \(0 \to 2.67\ \mathrm{m}\), back to \(0\ \mathrm{m}\), then out to \(2.67\ \mathrm{m}\) again, so the total distance is \(2.67 + 2.67 + 2.67 = 8.0\ \mathrm{m}\).
  5. Displacement \(= 2.67 - 0 = 2.67\ \mathrm{m}\), so the average velocity \(= 2.67/4 = 0.67\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the average speed \(= 8/4 = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  6. The particle passes through the origin twice with non-zero acceleration, showing that position and rest are unrelated quantities.

Answer: It stops momentarily at \(t = 1\ \mathrm{s}\) and \(t = 3\ \mathrm{s}\) with accelerations \(-4\) and \(+4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\); total distance \(8\ \mathrm{m}\) and average velocity \(0.67\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Concluding that positive acceleration always means increasing speed; the sign of \(v\) must also be considered.
  • Writing the retardation as a negative number and then using it as a distance in the equation of motion.
  • Forgetting that \(a = 0\) does not mean \(v = 0\); uniform motion has non-zero velocity with zero acceleration.
  • Computing distance as \(x(4) - x(0) = 2.67\ \mathrm{m}\) when the body has reversed twice, losing \(5.33\ \mathrm{m}\) of path.

Chapter 2 · Topic 13

Uniform motion

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Uniform motion is motion in which the velocity does not change with time, so the acceleration is zero and the position varies linearly, \(x = x_0 + vt\). The body covers equal distances in equal intervals of time in the same direction, making the \(x\)-\(t\) graph a straight line and the \(v\)-\(t\) graph a horizontal line. Uniform motion is the reference case: any deviation in the \(x\)-\(t\) slope, however small, marks the beginning of non-uniform motion.
Key formula(s). \[a = 0,\quad v = \text{constant},\quad x = x_0 + vt\] ; \[s = |v|\,t\] ; \[s_{t_1 \to t_2} = |v|(t_2 - t_1)\] ; \[x = x_1 + \frac{s_2}{s_1}(x_2 - x_1)\ \text{for equal times}\]
Key points.
  • Uniform motion requires constant velocity, not merely constant speed; in one dimension the two are equivalent.
  • In uniform motion the average velocity equals the instantaneous velocity at every instant, and both equal the average speed.
  • The \(x\)-\(t\) graph is a straight line and the \(v\)-\(t\) graph is a horizontal line at height \(v\).
  • Equal distances are covered in equal times: a \(1\ \mathrm{km}\) marker spacing passes at a constant rate, so the ratio of successive segments is fixed.
  • For a train of length \(L\) at speed \(v\), the time to pass a pole is \(L/v\) and to pass a platform of length \(P\) is \((L+P)/v\).
  • Uniform motion for a finite interval does not imply uniform motion for all time; the graph may bend at the boundaries.
Example 1.

A train \(150\ \mathrm{m}\) long moves at a uniform speed of \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). (i) How long does it take to pass a pole? (ii) How long to pass a platform \(250\ \mathrm{m}\) long? (iii) How far does it travel in the first \(5\ \mathrm{s}\) and in the \(8\)th second?

  1. Passing a pole requires the train to cover its own length, so \(t = L/v = 150/20 = 7.5\ \mathrm{s}\).
  2. Passing a platform requires covering the train length plus the platform length, so \(t = (150+250)/20 = 400/20 = 20\ \mathrm{s}\).
  3. In the first \(5\ \mathrm{s}\) the distance is \(s = vt = 20 \times 5 = 100\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Distance in the \(n\)th second equals \(v\) for uniform motion: the \(8\)th second (from \(7\) to \(8\ \mathrm{s}\)) covers \(v \times 1 = 20\ \mathrm{m}\).
  5. Consistency check: distance in \(8\ \mathrm{s}\) is \(160\ \mathrm{m}\) and in \(7\ \mathrm{s}\) is \(140\ \mathrm{m}\), the difference being \(20\ \mathrm{m}\).
  6. The average speed over any interval is \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the acceleration is zero throughout.

Answer: (i) \(7.5\ \mathrm{s}\) to pass a pole, (ii) \(20\ \mathrm{s}\) to pass the platform, (iii) \(100\ \mathrm{m}\) in the first \(5\ \mathrm{s}\) and \(20\ \mathrm{m}\) in the \(8\)th second.

Example 2.

A body moves on a straight track. In case (i) it moves at \(5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for the first half of a total time of \(12\ \mathrm{s}\) and at \(15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for the second half. In case (ii) it covers the first half of a total distance of \(120\ \mathrm{m}\) at \(5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the second half at \(15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the average speed in each case and the total time in each case.

  1. Case (i): each half of the time is \(6\ \mathrm{s}\), so the distances are \(5 \times 6 = 30\ \mathrm{m}\) and \(15 \times 6 = 90\ \mathrm{m}\).
  2. Total distance in case (i) \(= 30 + 90 = 120\ \mathrm{m}\) in \(12\ \mathrm{s}\), so the average speed \(= 120/12 = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), the arithmetic mean of the two speeds.
  3. Case (ii): each half of the distance is \(60\ \mathrm{m}\), so the times are \(60/5 = 12\ \mathrm{s}\) and \(60/15 = 4\ \mathrm{s}\).
  4. Total time in case (ii) \(= 12 + 4 = 16\ \mathrm{s}\), so the average speed \(= 120/16 = 7.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), the harmonic mean of the speeds.
  5. The two averages differ (\(10\) versus \(7.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)) even though the same two speeds and the same totals appear, because the fractions of the total differ.
  6. In case (i) the body spends more time at the higher speed, so more distance is covered at \(15\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which pulls the average up; the average always lies between 5 and 15.

Answer: Case (i) average speed \(10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) in \(12\ \mathrm{s}\); case (ii) average speed \(7.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) in \(16\ \mathrm{s}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Using the train's own length only when asked for the time to cross a platform; the platform length must be added.
  • Computing distance in the \(n\)th second as \(vn\) instead of \(v\); \(vn\) is the distance in the first \(n\) seconds.
  • Averaging two speeds for equal distances (arithmetic mean) and getting \(10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) where \(7.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) is correct.
  • Assuming uniform motion continues indefinitely; the statement usually applies to the stated interval only.

Chapter 2 · Topic 14

Non-uniform motion

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Non-uniform motion is any motion in which the velocity changes with time, either in magnitude, in direction, or in both, so that the acceleration is not identically zero. It includes uniformly accelerated motion, uniformly decelerated motion, and even constant-speed circular motion where only the direction changes. JEE problems handle it by splitting the journey into segments of constant acceleration and then adding the distances and times of the segments.
Key formula(s). \[\text{segment: } v = u+at,\ s = ut+\tfrac12 at^2,\ v^2 = u^2+2as\] ; \[\text{overall: } v_{\rm av} = \frac{\sum s_i}{\sum t_i}\] ; \[\text{curvilinear motion at constant } v:\ a = \frac{v^2}{R}\] ; \[\text{speed changes: } \left|\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\right| = |a|\]
Key points.
  • Any change of velocity, including a change of direction alone, makes the motion non-uniform; \(a \ne 0\) is the test.
  • Split the motion at every change of acceleration and at every reversal, then treat each segment independently.
  • Uniformly circular motion has constant speed but non-zero acceleration, so it is non-uniform motion.
  • Distance in each segment is obtained from the segment's own initial and final velocity using \(s = \frac{v_i^2 - v_f^2}{2a}\) or the mean-velocity form.
  • The overall average speed is total distance over total time, not the mean of the segment averages.
  • The slope of the \(v\)-\(t\) graph is the acceleration, so a bend in the graph marks a change of phase such as a stop or a reversal.
Example 1.

A cyclist starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at \(2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) for \(10\ \mathrm{s}\), then coasts at the constant speed attained for \(20\ \mathrm{s}\), and finally decelerates uniformly at \(4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) until rest. Find the total time, the total distance, the average speed and the maximum speed.

  1. Phase 1: \(v_1 = 0 + 2(10) = 20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), distance \(s_1 = \tfrac12 (0+20)(10) = 100\ \mathrm{m}\).
  2. Phase 2: constant speed \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for \(20\ \mathrm{s}\), so \(s_2 = 400\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. Phase 3: \(0 = 20 - 4t \Rightarrow t_3 = 5\ \mathrm{s}\), and \(s_3 = \tfrac12(20+0)(5) = 50\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Total time \(= 10 + 20 + 5 = 35\ \mathrm{s}\); total distance \(= 100 + 400 + 50 = 550\ \mathrm{m}\).
  5. Average speed \(= 550/35 = 15.7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which lies between 0 and the maximum speed \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) as it must.
  6. The average speed is not \(10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) (half the maximum) because the coasting phase occupies more than half the total time.

Answer: Total time \(35\ \mathrm{s}\), total distance \(550\ \mathrm{m}\), average speed \(15.7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and maximum speed \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Example 2.

A car travels the first \(600\ \mathrm{m}\) at a constant \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), then accelerates uniformly to \(40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) over the next \(20\ \mathrm{s}\), maintains \(40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for \(60\ \mathrm{s}\), and finally decelerates uniformly to rest in \(10\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the total time, the total distance, the average speed, and the time interval during which the speed is maximum.

  1. Phase 1: \(t_1 = 600/20 = 30\ \mathrm{s}\) at \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  2. Phase 2: uniform acceleration from 20 to 40 m/s in 20 s, so \(a_2 = 1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(s_2 = \tfrac12(20+40)(20) = 600\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. Phase 3: \(s_3 = 40 \times 60 = 2400\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Phase 4: uniform deceleration from 40 m/s to rest in 10 s, so \(a_4 = -4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(s_4 = \tfrac12(40+0)(10) = 200\ \mathrm{m}\).
  5. Total time \(= 30 + 20 + 60 + 10 = 120\ \mathrm{s}\); total distance \(= 600 + 600 + 2400 + 200 = 3800\ \mathrm{m}\).
  6. Average speed \(= 3800/120 = 31.7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), comfortably between \(20\) and \(40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  7. The maximum speed \(40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) persists from \(t = 50\ \mathrm{s}\) to \(t = 110\ \mathrm{s}\), a duration of \(60\ \mathrm{s}\), which dominates the total distance.

Answer: Total time \(120\ \mathrm{s}\), total distance \(3800\ \mathrm{m}\), average speed \(31.7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the speed is maximum (\(40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)) from \(50\ \mathrm{s}\) to \(110\ \mathrm{s}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Using one uniform-acceleration formula for the entire journey when the acceleration changes between phases.
  • Averaging the phase speeds instead of dividing total distance by total time.
  • Forgetting that in the uniform phase the speed reached at the end of phase 1 is the initial speed of phase 2, so no time is lost at the junction.
  • Assuming constant speed implies zero acceleration in a circular path; the direction change gives centripetal acceleration.

Chapter 2 · Topic 15

Uniform acceleration

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Uniform acceleration (constant a: free fall g ignoring air, inclined frictionless slides) unlocks the three motion equations (v=u+at, s=ut+1/2at2, v2=u2+2as) - variable acceleration needs calculus (integrate a(t) twice). Graphs straighten (v-t linear, s-t parabolic). Galileo inclined planes proved uniform g; Atwood machines measure it. Constant-a assumption gates equation use - check uniformity first.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Constant acceleration enables v=u+at family equations.
  • Free fall and smooth inclines approximate uniform a.
Remember
  • Equations apply only when acceleration stays constant.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

First equation of motion v=u+at needs acceleration

Solution: Constant-a integration yields linear velocity growth.
Key Formulas · Uniform Acceleration
\(v=u+at\) velocity grows linearly
\(s=ut+\frac12at^{2},\;v^{2}=u^{2}+2as\) position and velocity-position relations

Chapter 2 · Topic 16

Equations of motion

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. The three equations of kinematic motion, valid only for constant acceleration, relate initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, displacement and time in any order, so that whatever three quantities are given the remaining two can be found. Choosing the right equation is the main skill: use \(v = u+at\) when time is given, \(v^2 = u^2+2as\) when time is not, and \(x = ut+\tfrac12 at^2\) when velocity is not. The sequence \(s_n = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)\) handles questions about a single second.
Key formula(s). \[v = u + at\] ; \[x = s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2\] ; \[v^2 = u^2 + 2as\] ; \[x_{\rm nth\ second} = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)\] ; \[x_n = \left[u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)\right]n\] ; \[s = \tfrac{u+v}{2}\,t\]
Key points.
  • All three equations require constant acceleration; for variable acceleration only \(v = \int a\,dt\) and \(x = \int v\,dt\) are valid.
  • The time in \(v = u+at\) and \(x = ut+\tfrac12 at^2\) must be the same interval as \(u\) and \(v\), measured from the start of that interval.
  • If time is not involved use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\); if the velocity is not involved use \(x = ut+\tfrac12 at^2\).
  • For uniform acceleration, average velocity \((u+v)/2\) is exact, which gives \(x = (u+v)t/2\) as a quick fourth route.
  • The distance covered in the \(n\)th second is \(u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)\), and the distance in the first \(n\) seconds is the sum of these terms, \(n\left[u + \tfrac{a}{2}n\right]\).
  • In vertical motion with upward positive, \(a = -g\); writing the sign inside the equation prevents the classic error of a body never returning to the ground.
Example 1.

A body starts from rest with a uniform acceleration of \(2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its velocity after \(5\ \mathrm{s}\), the distance covered in \(5\ \mathrm{s}\), the distance covered in the \(5\)th second, and the velocity after covering \(45\ \mathrm{m}\).

  1. With \(u = 0\), \(a = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), \(t = 5\ \mathrm{s}\): \(v = 0 + 2(5) = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  2. Distance in \(5\ \mathrm{s}\): \(s = 0 + \tfrac12 (2)(25) = 25\ \mathrm{m}\), which also equals \(\tfrac12 v t = 25\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. Distance in the \(5\)th second: \(s_5 = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1) = 0 + 1 \times (9) = 9\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Check: \(s_4 = \tfrac12 (2)(16) = 16\ \mathrm{m}\), so \(s(5\ \mathrm{s}) - s(4\ \mathrm{s}) = 25 - 16 = 9\ \mathrm{m}\), agreeing with the formula.
  5. Velocity after \(45\ \mathrm{m}\): use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 0 + 2(2)(45) = 180\), so \(v = \sqrt{180} = 13.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  6. Time for \(45\ \mathrm{m}\) would be \(s = \tfrac12 at^2 \Rightarrow t^2 = 45 \Rightarrow t = 6.7\ \mathrm{s}\), and \(v = at = 13.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), consistent.

Answer: \(v(5\ \mathrm{s}) = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), distance in \(5\ \mathrm{s}\) \(= 25\ \mathrm{m}\), distance in the \(5\)th second \(= 9\ \mathrm{m}\), and \(v = 13.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) after \(45\ \mathrm{m}\).

Example 2.

A car moving at \(30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) applies its brakes and stops uniformly in \(15\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the retardation, the braking distance, the distance covered in the \(5\)th second of braking, and then the distance and speed after it accelerates uniformly at \(4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) for \(10\ \mathrm{s}\) from rest.

  1. Retardation: \(0 = 30 - |a|(15)\), so \(|a| = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(a = -2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
  2. Braking distance: \(s = \tfrac12 (u+v)t = \tfrac12 (30)(15) = 225\ \mathrm{m}\); cross-check with \(v^2 = u^2+2as \Rightarrow 0 = 900 - 4s \Rightarrow s = 225\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. Distance in the \(5\)th second of braking: \(s_5 = u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1) = 30 - (1)(9) = 21\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Now the car starts from rest with \(a = +4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) for \(10\ \mathrm{s}\): \(v = 4(10) = 40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(s = \tfrac12 (4)(100) = 200\ \mathrm{m}\).
  5. Total distance over both phases \(= 225 + 200 = 425\ \mathrm{m}\) in total time \(15 + 10 = 25\ \mathrm{s}\).
  6. Average speed for the whole trip \(= 425/25 = 17\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), while the maximum speed \(40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) is reached at the very end.

Answer: Retardation \(2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), braking distance \(225\ \mathrm{m}\), distance in the \(5\)th second of braking \(21\ \mathrm{m}\); after the \(10\ \mathrm{s}\) acceleration the car has covered \(200\ \mathrm{m}\) more and moves at \(40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Applying the equations when the acceleration is not constant; the results then look plausible but are wrong.
  • Using \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) for the distance in the \(n\)th second, which needs the \(u + \tfrac{a}{2}(2n-1)\) form.
  • Taking \(s = ut + \tfrac12 at^2\) as the distance in the \(n\)th second rather than in \(n\) seconds.
  • Omitting the sign of \(a\) in vertical motion, so the body appears to accelerate upward indefinitely.

Chapter 2 · Topic 17

Position-time graph

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. The position-time (or displacement-time) graph displays position along one axis as a function of time, and its slope at any instant is the velocity of the body. A straight line therefore means uniform velocity, a parabola means uniform acceleration, and a curve whose slope decreases means slowing down. In JEE, the two decisive readings from an \(x\)-\(t\) graph are the slope (velocity) and the area under it, which is not defined, so all distance information must come from slopes.
Key formula(s). \[v = \text{slope of } x\text{-}t\] ; \[\bar v = \text{slope of the chord}\] ; \[\text{parabola} \Rightarrow a = \text{constant},\ a = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}\] ; \[x = x_0 + vt\ \text{(straight line)},\quad x = x_0 + ut + \tfrac12 at^2\ \text{(parabola)}\]
Key points.
  • Slope of the \(x\)-\(t\) graph equals velocity; a horizontal tangent means the instantaneous velocity is zero.
  • Straight line means uniform velocity and zero acceleration; its slope is the velocity and its intercept is the initial position.
  • An upward-opening parabola means positive acceleration; a downward-opening one means negative acceleration; a symmetric parabola has zero velocity at its vertex.
  • The sign of the slope gives the direction of motion, so a decreasing position with time means motion along \(-x\).
  • The chord joining two points gives the average velocity over that interval, which generally differs from the tangent slope.
  • The area under an \(x\)-\(t\) graph has no physical meaning; distance and displacement must be obtained by examining the slope sign and adding segments.
Example 1.

The \(x\)-\(t\) graph of a particle is a straight line from \((0, 0)\) to \((4\ \mathrm{s}, 20\ \mathrm{m})\), followed by a parabola that starts at \((4\ \mathrm{s}, 20\ \mathrm{m})\) with a horizontal tangent and passes through \((8\ \mathrm{s}, 36\ \mathrm{m})\). Find the velocity in each phase, the acceleration in the second phase, the velocity at \(t = 6\ \mathrm{s}\), the distance travelled and the average velocity over \(8\ \mathrm{s}\).

  1. Phase 1 (straight line): the slope is constant, \(v = 20/4 = 5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so the acceleration is zero and the motion is uniform.
  2. Phase 2 (parabola with zero slope at \(t = 4\ \mathrm{s}\)): write \(x = 20 + \tfrac12 a(t-4)^2\), and the point \((8, 36)\) gives \(36 = 20 + \tfrac12 a (16)\), so \(a = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
  3. Velocity in phase 2 is \(v = a(t-4) = 2(t-4)\), which is zero at the junction and grows linearly thereafter.
  4. At \(t = 6\ \mathrm{s}\): \(v = 2(2) = 4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), positive, so the body still moves in \(+x\).
  5. The slope is never negative, so there is no reversal: distance \(= x(8) - x(0) = 36\ \mathrm{m}\).
  6. Average velocity over \(0 \to 8\ \mathrm{s}\): \(36/8 = 4.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which is larger than the instantaneous velocity at \(6\ \mathrm{s}\) because the body went faster earlier.

Answer: \(v = 5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) uniformly in the first phase, then \(a = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) with \(v = 4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(t = 6\ \mathrm{s}\); distance \(36\ \mathrm{m}\) and average velocity \(4.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Example 2.

A particle's \(x\)-\(t\) graph is a straight line joining \((0\ \mathrm{s}, 10\ \mathrm{m})\) to \((6\ \mathrm{s}, -10\ \mathrm{m})\). After \(t = 6\ \mathrm{s}\) the particle reverses and comes to rest at \(x = 10\ \mathrm{m}\) at \(t = 8\ \mathrm{s}\). Find the velocity in each phase, the instants at which \(x = 0\), the total displacement, the total distance, the average velocity and the average speed over \(8\ \mathrm{s}\).

  1. Phase 1: slope \(= (-10 - 10)/6 = -20/6 = -3.33\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), constant, so the motion is uniform with negative velocity.
  2. Phase 2: from \(-10\ \mathrm{m}\) back to \(+10\ \mathrm{m}\) in \(2\ \mathrm{s}\), the velocity is \(+20/2 = +10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) (uniform in this idealised description).
  3. The particle crosses \(x = 0\) where \(10 - 3.33t = 0\), i.e. at \(t = 3\ \mathrm{s}\), and it is again at \(x = 0\) at \(t = 7\ \mathrm{s}\) while returning.
  4. Total displacement over \(8\ \mathrm{s}\) \(= 10 - 10 = 0\ \mathrm{m}\), so the average velocity is zero.
  5. Total distance \(= |{-10} - 10| + |10 - (-10)| = 20 + 20 = 40\ \mathrm{m}\), i.e. \(20\ \mathrm{m}\) in phase 1 and \(20\ \mathrm{m}\) in phase 2.
  6. Average speed \(= 40/8 = 5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) while the average velocity is \(0\), because the body ends where it started.

Answer: Velocities are \(-3.33\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) then \(+10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); the particle is at \(x = 0\) at \(t = 3\ \mathrm{s}\) and \(t = 7\ \mathrm{s}\); total displacement \(0\), total distance \(40\ \mathrm{m}\), average velocity \(0\) and average speed \(5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Reading the ordinate of the graph as the velocity instead of its slope.
  • Using the area under an \(x\)-\(t\) graph as a distance; only the slope carries kinematic information.
  • Assuming a horizontal \(x\)-\(t\) graph means the body is at rest forever; it is at rest at that instant and reverses if the curve bends.
  • Taking the chord slope as the instantaneous velocity in a curved region of the graph.

Chapter 2 · Topic 18

Velocity-time graph

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. The velocity-time graph shows how the velocity of a body varies, and its area over any interval equals the displacement in that interval, while its slope gives the acceleration. Every geometric feature has a kinematic meaning: the area gives displacement, the sign of the area gives direction, the slope gives acceleration, and crossings of the time axis mark reversals of motion. In JEE, relative-motion questions about two objects are solved entirely by comparing the heights and areas of their \(v\)-\(t\) graphs.
Key formula(s). \[\text{area} = \text{displacement},\quad \text{slope} = \text{acceleration}\] ; \[\text{triangle: } \tfrac12 th,\quad \text{trapezium: } \tfrac12 (v_1+v_2)t\] ; \[v_{\rm av} = \frac{\text{total area}}{T},\quad \text{speed}_{\rm av} = \frac{\text{total area magnitude}}{T}\] ; \[t_{\rm meet} : x_A(t) = x_B(t)\]
Key points.
  • Displacement equals the area under the \(v\)-\(t\) graph counted with sign; the total distance is the sum of the areas regardless of sign.
  • The average velocity is the mean height of the graph, that is the total area divided by the total time.
  • The slope of the graph is the acceleration; a horizontal segment means zero acceleration and constant velocity.
  • Two objects have equal displacement when the areas under their graphs are equal up to that instant, and their separation is the difference of the areas.
  • Relative speed between two objects is the vertical gap between the two curves at that instant; the separation is maximum when that gap is zero.
  • For a body returning to rest, the area under the graph during the outward and return legs gives the maximum displacement reached.
Example 1.

A body's \(v\)-\(t\) graph is a straight line rising from \((0\ \mathrm{s}, 0)\) to \((10\ \mathrm{s}, 20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})\), then a straight line falling from \((10\ \mathrm{s}, 20)\) to \((15\ \mathrm{s}, 0)\). Find the displacement, the distance, the average velocity, the average speed, the maximum velocity, the maximum displacement and the accelerations in the two phases.

  1. Rising phase: triangle of area \(\tfrac12 \times 10 \times 20 = 100\ \mathrm{m}\), giving a displacement of \(100\ \mathrm{m}\) in the first \(10\ \mathrm{s}\).
  2. Falling phase: triangle of area \(\tfrac12 \times 5 \times 20 = 50\ \mathrm{m}\), adding another \(50\ \mathrm{m}\) in the last \(5\ \mathrm{s}\).
  3. Total displacement \(= 100 + 50 = 150\ \mathrm{m}\); the graph is entirely above the axis so the distance is also \(150\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Average velocity \(= 150/15 = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the average speed is the same, \(10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), since the velocity never becomes negative.
  5. Maximum velocity is \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at the single instant \(t = 10\ \mathrm{s}\), where the graph changes slope.
  6. Maximum displacement is \(150\ \mathrm{m}\), reached at \(t = 15\ \mathrm{s}\) when the velocity (and hence the displacement) first becomes zero.
  7. Accelerations: rising phase \(a_1 = 20/10 = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), falling phase \(a_2 = (0-20)/5 = -4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Answer: Displacement \(= 150\ \mathrm{m}\), distance \(= 150\ \mathrm{m}\), average velocity \(= 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), maximum velocity \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(10\ \mathrm{s}\), maximum displacement \(150\ \mathrm{m}\), with accelerations \(+2\) and \(-4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Example 2.

Particle A moves with a constant velocity of \(6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) from the origin, while particle B starts from rest at the same point and instant with a constant acceleration of \(4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Using the \(v\)-\(t\) graphs, find (i) when they next meet, (ii) when their velocities are equal, (iii) the maximum separation and when it occurs, and (iv) the separation at \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\).

  1. The graph of A is a horizontal line at \(6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); the graph of B is a straight line of slope \(4\) starting from the origin, crossing A's line at \(4t = 6\).
  2. (ii) Equal velocities at \(t = 6/4 = 1.5\ \mathrm{s}\), at which instant both have travelled \(x = 6(1.5) = 9\ \mathrm{m}\) and B has covered \(\tfrac12 (4)(2.25) = 4.5\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. (i) They meet when the areas are equal: \(6t = \tfrac12 (4)t^2 \Rightarrow t = 3\ \mathrm{s}\), at a common position \(x = 18\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. (iii) The separation is the difference of the areas, \(S(t) = 6t - 2t^2\), a downward parabola with its maximum where \(dS/dt = 6 - 4t = 0\), i.e. at \(t = 1.5\ \mathrm{s}\).
  5. Maximum separation \(S(1.5) = 9 - 4.5 = 4.5\ \mathrm{m}\); the separation is zero at \(t = 0\) and again at \(t = 3\ \mathrm{s}\).
  6. (iv) At \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\): A has covered \(12\ \mathrm{m}\) and B has covered \(\tfrac12 (4)(4) = 8\ \mathrm{m}\), so the separation is \(12 - 8 = 4\ \mathrm{m}\).
  7. At that instant B's speed is \(4(2) = 8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} > 6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so B is already the faster body and is closing the gap, which is why the separation is now shrinking.

Answer: They meet again at \(t = 3\ \mathrm{s}\) at \(x = 18\ \mathrm{m}\); their velocities are equal at \(t = 1.5\ \mathrm{s}\); the maximum separation is \(4.5\ \mathrm{m}\) at \(t = 1.5\ \mathrm{s}\); the separation at \(t = 2\ \mathrm{s}\) is \(4\ \mathrm{m}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Taking the area as the distance and forgetting that the part below the time axis contributes negatively to displacement.
  • Reading the maximum of the graph as the maximum distance; the maximum displacement is where the velocity first reaches zero.
  • Finding the meeting time from equal velocities instead of equal areas; the velocities are equal at the point of maximum separation, not at the meeting.
  • Computing the separation as the vertical gap of the graphs instead of the difference of the areas enclosed up to that instant.

Chapter 2 · Topic 19

Acceleration-time graph

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. The acceleration-time graph describes how the velocity of a particle changes, with \(a=\frac{dv}{dt}\), rather than describing the force producing that change. The signed area under an \(a-t\) graph gives the change in velocity, whereas displacement is the signed area under a \(v-t\) graph. For JEE problems, first identify the relevant graph and then interpret its ordinate, area, slope, or intercept physically.
Key formula(s). \[a=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}=\frac{dv}{dt}, \quad \Delta v=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}a(t)\,dt\]; \[s=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}v(t)\,dt,\quad v=u+\int_{t_1}^{t_2}a(t)\,dt,\quad [a]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\]
Key points.
  • The slope of an \(a-t\) graph equals the rate of change of acceleration, known as jerk, not the acceleration itself.
  • An area above the time axis is positive velocity change and area below it is negative velocity change.
  • If a particle reverses direction, distance is the sum of absolute areas under the \(v-t\) graph, whereas displacement is their signed sum.
  • Zero acceleration means constant velocity, including the case of rest; it does not mean zero velocity.
  • When \(a>0\), a positive velocity grows and a negative velocity becomes less negative; when \(a<0\), the trend reverses. A negative slope of the \(a-t\) graph alone does not determine the sign of velocity.
Example 1.

A particle moves according to \(v=6-2t\) metres per second for \(0\le t\le5\,\mathrm{s}\). Take the positive direction along its initial motion and find its acceleration, displacement, and total distance travelled.

  1. The constant acceleration is \(a=\frac{dv}{dt}=-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
  2. The velocity vanishes at \(6-2t=0\), so the reversal time is \(t=3\,\mathrm{s}\).
  3. Displacement is the signed area \(\frac12(3)(6)-\frac12(2)(4)=9-4=5\,\mathrm{m}\).
  4. Distance is the sum of the two positive geometric areas, \(9+4=13\,\mathrm{m}\).

Answer: Acceleration is \(-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), displacement is \(5\,\mathrm{m}\), and distance travelled is \(13\,\mathrm{m}\).

Example 2.

A particle has \(v=6t-2t^2\) during \(0\le t\le4\,\mathrm{s}\). Determine its displacement, average acceleration, and instantaneous acceleration at \(t=4\,\mathrm{s}\).

  1. The displacement is \(\int_0^4(6t-2t^2)\,dt=[3t^2-\frac23t^3]_0^4=\frac{16}{3}\,\mathrm{m}\).
  2. The endpoint velocities are \(v(0)=0\) and \(v(4)=-8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  3. Average acceleration is \(\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}=\frac{-8-0}{4}=-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
  4. Instantaneous acceleration is \(a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}=6-4t\), so \(a(4)=-10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
  5. The velocity and acceleration are both negative at the endpoint, so the particle is speeding up in the negative direction.

Answer: Displacement is \(\frac{16}{3}\,\mathrm{m}\), average acceleration is \(-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), and \(a(4)=-10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Treating the area under an \(a-t\) graph as displacement instead of velocity change.
  • Ignoring the interval where velocity changes sign when calculating distance.
  • Equating average acceleration with \(\frac{dv}{dt}\) evaluated at the final time.

Chapter 2 · Topic 20

Graph interpretation

KinematicsMechanicsMotion in One DimensionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Kinematic graphs display the variation of position, velocity or acceleration with time and are converted into one another by differentiation and integration. The slope of the \(x\)-\(t\) graph is velocity, the slope of the \(v\)-\(t\) graph is acceleration, the area under the \(v\)-\(t\) graph is displacement and the area under the \(a\)-\(t\) graph is the change in velocity. Every JEE graph question is answered by these two rules, and total distance is the sum of the absolute areas.
Key formula(s). \[\text{slope of } x\text{-}t = v,\quad \text{slope of } v\text{-}t = a\] ; \[\text{area under } v\text{-}t = \Delta x,\quad \text{area under } a\text{-}t = \Delta v\] ; \[\text{distance} = \int |v| dt = \text{sum of absolute areas}\] ; \[v_{\rm av} = \frac{\text{area under } v\text{-}t}{T}\] ; \[x = \int v\,dt,\quad v = \int a\,dt\]
Key points.
  • On a \(v\)-\(t\) graph, area above the time axis is positive displacement and area below it is negative displacement; total distance is the sum of the absolute values.
  • A horizontal \(v\)-\(t\) line means constant velocity and zero acceleration; a horizontal \(x\)-\(t\) line means the body is at rest.
  • A \(v\)-\(t\) graph crossing the time axis signals a reversal of direction, and a tangent parallel to the axis signals a turning point of the \(x\)-\(t\) graph.
  • The maximum of a \(v\)-\(t\) graph (horizontal tangent) is where acceleration is zero, not where velocity is zero.
  • For a parabola on the \(v\)-\(t\) graph the acceleration is linear in time and the \(x\)-\(t\) graph is cubic.
  • The area under an \(a\)-\(t\) graph gives the change in velocity, so a graph that returns to zero net area leaves the velocity unchanged.
Example 1.

A body starts from rest and accelerates at \(2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) for \(10\ \mathrm{s}\), then moves with constant velocity for \(10\ \mathrm{s}\), and finally decelerates at \(2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) until it stops. Sketch the \(v\)-\(t\) graph, and from it find the displacement, the distance, the average velocity, the maximum velocity and the total time.

  1. The \(v\)-\(t\) graph is a straight line of slope \(+2\) from \((0,0)\) to \((10\ \mathrm{s}, 20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})\), then a horizontal line at \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) from \(10\) to \(20\ \mathrm{s}\), then a straight line of slope \(-2\) from \((20\ \mathrm{s}, 20)\) to \((30\ \mathrm{s}, 0)\).
  2. The first region is a triangle of area \(\tfrac12 \times 10 \times 20 = 100\ \mathrm{m}\), the middle region a rectangle of area \(10 \times 20 = 200\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. The last region is another triangle of area \(\tfrac12 \times 10 \times 20 = 100\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Total displacement \(= 100 + 200 + 100 = 400\ \mathrm{m}\); the graph never goes below the time axis, so the distance equals the displacement, \(400\ \mathrm{m}\).
  5. Average velocity \(= 400/30 = 13.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) (the mean height of the graph), with the total time \(30\ \mathrm{s}\).
  6. Maximum velocity is \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), attained over the whole interval \(10 \leq t \leq 20\ \mathrm{s}\), where the graph is horizontal and the acceleration is zero.

Answer: Displacement \(= 400\ \mathrm{m}\), distance \(= 400\ \mathrm{m}\), average velocity \(= 13.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), maximum velocity \(20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for \(10\) s to \(20\ \mathrm{s}\), total time \(30\ \mathrm{s}\).

Example 2.

The \(v\)-\(t\) graph of a particle is a straight line from \((0\ \mathrm{s}, 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})\) to \((6\ \mathrm{s}, 0)\) and then continues as a straight line to \((10\ \mathrm{s}, -10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})\). Find the total displacement, the total distance, the average velocity, the average speed and the accelerations in the two segments.

  1. First segment: the area is a triangle above the axis, \(\tfrac12 \times 6 \times 10 = 30\ \mathrm{m}\), so the displacement is \(+30\ \mathrm{m}\).
  2. Second segment: the graph is below the axis from \(0\) to \(-10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) over \(4\ \mathrm{s}\), a trapezium of signed area \(\tfrac12 (0 + (-10))(4) = -20\ \mathrm{m}\).
  3. Total displacement \(= 30 - 20 = 10\ \mathrm{m}\); total distance \(= 30 + 20 = 50\ \mathrm{m}\).
  4. Average velocity \(= 10/10 = 1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); average speed \(= 50/10 = 5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  5. Accelerations: first segment \(a_1 = (0 - 10)/6 = -1.67\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), second segment \(a_2 = (-10 - 0)/4 = -2.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
  6. The particle reverses at \(t = 6\ \mathrm{s}\), reaching a maximum position of \(30\ \mathrm{m}\) and returning to \(10\ \mathrm{m}\) by \(t = 10\ \mathrm{s}\).

Answer: Total displacement \(10\ \mathrm{m}\), total distance \(50\ \mathrm{m}\), average velocity \(1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), average speed \(5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), with accelerations \(-1.67\) and \(-2.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Adding the areas algebraically to obtain distance; the signed area gives displacement, and distance needs absolute values.
  • Reading the maximum of a \(v\)-\(t\) graph as the place where the velocity is zero; the maximum velocity occurs where the curve is horizontal.
  • Interpreting a horizontal line on a \(v\)-\(t\) graph as the body being at rest; it means constant velocity.
  • Skipping the trapezium area formula and using a triangle when the graph does not reach zero at the end of the interval.

\(\hat A=\vec A/|\vec A|\) unit vector along A

Chapter 2 · Topic 22

Scalar quantities

KinematicsMechanicsVectorsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Scalar quantities (magnitude only: distance, speed, mass, temperature, energy, time) add algebraically - 5 kg plus 3 kg always 8 kg regardless of arrangement. No direction, no components, no cross products - arithmetic suffices. Temperature, though directional in gradients, remains scalar (magnitude at points). Scalars combine simply; vectors demand geometry - quantity type decides mathematics.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Magnitude only; algebraic addition always.
  • Distance, speed, mass, energy, time are scalars.
Remember
  • Scalars add like bills; vectors add like journeys.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Which is a scalar quantity?

Solution: Speed magnitudes motion without direction; velocity vectors it.
Key Formulas · Scalar Quantities
\(s=\int|v|dt=\mathrm{path\,length}\) distance accumulates path
\(W=\int\vec F\cdot d\vec s\) work-type scalars need dot products
Back to Index
Index / Mechanics
Chapter 2 · Topic 23

Vector quantities

KinematicsMechanicsVectorsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. A scalar has magnitude only and is combined by ordinary algebra, whereas a vector has both magnitude and direction and obeys vector addition. Speed, distance, mass, and time interval are scalars, while displacement, velocity, acceleration, and weight are vectors. In JEE geometry and kinematics, identifying the direction of each quantity before adding is often the decisive step.
Key formula(s). \(\text{distance}=s\), \(\text{displacement}=|\Delta\mathbf r|\); \(\text{speed}=\frac{ds}{dt}\), \(\mathbf v=\frac{d\mathbf r}{dt}\); \(\mathbf a=\frac{d\mathbf v}{dt}\); \(\mathbf F=m\mathbf a\)
Key points.
  • Scalars are added directly, but vectors must be resolved in common directions before adding components.
  • Two vectors are equal only if both magnitude and direction agree.
  • Displacement can be smaller than, equal to, or never greater than the path length for a given motion.
  • Constant speed does not imply zero acceleration because the direction of velocity may change.
  • Mass is an intrinsic scalar, while weight is the gravitational force and is a vector.
  • Two vectors of equal magnitude need not be equal, just as two equal scalars have no direction to compare.
Example 1.

A person walks \(4\,\mathrm{km}\) east and then \(3\,\mathrm{km}\) north. Find the distance travelled and the displacement, including its direction.

  1. The total distance is the scalar sum of path segments: \(4+3=7\,\mathrm{km}\).
  2. East and north are perpendicular, so the displacement magnitude is \(\sqrt{4^2+3^2}\,\mathrm{km}\).
  3. Its component ratio gives \(\tan\theta=3/4\), where \(\theta\) is measured north of east.
  4. Since the ratio is \(3:4:5\), \(\sin\theta=3/5\) and \(\theta=36.9^\circ\).

Answer: Distance \(=7\,\mathrm{km}\); displacement \(=5\,\mathrm{km}\) at \(36.9^\circ\) north of east.

Example 2.

A car travels east at \(60\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) for \(30\,\mathrm{min}\), then west at \(90\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) for \(20\,\mathrm{min}\). Find the total distance and net displacement.

  1. The eastward distance is \(60(0.50)=30\,\mathrm{km}\).
  2. The westward distance is \(90(1/3)=30\,\mathrm{km}\).
  3. Total distance is \(30+30=60\,\mathrm{km}\).
  4. Taking east as positive, net displacement is \(+30-30=0\,\mathrm{km}\).

Answer: Total distance \(=60\,\mathrm{km}\), and net displacement \(=0\).

Common mistakes.
  • Treating the magnitude of the displacement as the distance travelled.
  • Assuming equal magnitudes imply that two velocity vectors are equal.
  • Calling a curved path of fixed length a uniform vector velocity.

Explanation

Concept. Vectors are classified according to equality, direction, coplanarity, initial point, and magnitude. Collinear vectors are parallel or antiparallel, and any two nonzero vectors lie in at least one common plane, but three vectors may or may not be coplanar. Dot and cross products provide quick tests of angle and spatial orientation in JEE problems.
Key formula(s). \(\mathbf A=\mathbf B\) only if magnitudes and directions agree; collinearity: \(\mathbf A\times\mathbf B=\mathbf 0\) for parallel vectors; perpendicularity: \(\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf B=0\) when both are nonzero; \(\mathbf A\parallel\mathbf B\iff A_yB_z-A_zB_y=0\), \(A_zB_x-A_xB_z=0\), \(A_xB_y-A_yB_x=0\); \(\hat{\mathbf A}=\mathbf A/|\mathbf A|\)
Key points.
  • Equal vectors have equal magnitude and the same direction; equal magnitude alone is not enough.
  • Parallel vectors may be in the same or opposite directions, while antiparallel vectors point exactly opposite.
  • Coplanar vectors lie in one plane, not necessarily along one straight line.
  • Two nonzero perpendicular vectors are necessarily coplanar even in three-dimensional space.
  • A zero vector has no defined direction and cannot uniquely be called parallel or antiparallel.
  • Concurrent vectors act through a common point, whereas initial-point-free vectors can be translated without changing their physical effect.
Example 1.

Let \(\mathbf A=2\hat{\mathbf i}+3\hat{\mathbf j}\), \(\mathbf B=-4\hat{\mathbf i}-6\hat{\mathbf j}\), and \(\mathbf C=\hat{\mathbf i}-\hat{\mathbf j}\). Classify the relations among them and determine whether all three lie in one plane.

  1. Since \(\mathbf B=-2\mathbf A\), vectors \(\mathbf A\) and \(\mathbf B\) are collinear, antiparallel, and unequal in magnitude.
  2. Their scalar product is \(\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf C=2(1)+3(-1)=-1\), so they are not perpendicular.
  3. All three vectors have zero \(z\)-component.
  4. Therefore all three lie in the \(xy\)-plane.
  5. Compute \(\mathbf A\times\mathbf B=5\hat{\mathbf i}+15\hat{\mathbf j}+20\hat{\mathbf k}\,\mathrm{N^2}\).

Answer: \(\mathbf A\) and \(\mathbf B\) are antiparallel and unequal, \(\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf C=-1\), and all three are coplanar.

Example 2.

For \(\mathbf A=6\hat{\mathbf i}+2\hat{\mathbf j}-3\hat{\mathbf k}\,\mathrm{N}\), \(\mathbf B=-\hat{\mathbf i}+3\hat{\mathbf j}-2\hat{\mathbf k}\,\mathrm{N}\), and \(\mathbf C=\hat{\mathbf i}\,\mathrm{N}\), test coplanarity and find the angle between \(\mathbf A\) and \(\mathbf B\).

  1. Since this cross product is nonzero, the three vectors \(\mathbf A,\mathbf B,\mathbf C\) are not coplanar.
  2. The dot product is \(\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf B=-6+6+6=6\,\mathrm{N^2}\).
  3. Their magnitudes are \(|\mathbf A|=7\,\mathrm{N}\) and \(|\mathbf B|=\sqrt{14}\,\mathrm{N}\).
  4. Hence \(\cos\theta=6/(7\sqrt{14})\), so \(\theta=\cos^{-1}(6/(7\sqrt{14}))\).

Answer: The three vectors are noncoplanar, while \(\mathbf A\) and \(\mathbf B\) make an angle \(\theta\approx76.8^\circ\).

Common mistakes.
  • Calling vectors equal because their magnitudes agree.
  • Assuming nonzero vectors in three dimensions are automatically noncoplanar.
  • Using the zero vector to define a unique direction.

Chapter 2 · Topic 24

Vector representation

KinematicsMechanicsVectorsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. A vector can be represented geometrically by an arrow directed from a tail to a head or analytically by ordered Cartesian components. A position vector depends on the origin, while a displacement vector between two points is independent of the choice of origin. Magnitude follows from the sum of squared Cartesian components, and a unit vector is obtained by dividing a vector by that magnitude.
Key formula(s). \(\overrightarrow{AB}=(x_B-x_A)\hat{\mathbf i}+(y_B-y_A)\hat{\mathbf j}+(z_B-z_A)\hat{\mathbf k}\); \(|\mathbf r|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\); \(\hat{\mathbf r}=\mathbf r/|\mathbf r|\); \(\mathbf r=\frac12(\mathbf r_1+\mathbf r_2)\)
Key points.
  • An arrow's length represents magnitude and its arrowhead represents the direction of the vector.
  • Cartesian components are scalars and may be positive, negative, or zero.
  • A three-dimensional vector has three components, and its magnitude uses the Euclidean distance formula.
  • \(\overrightarrow{AB}=-\overrightarrow{BA}\).
  • Translating a free vector without rotating it does not change the vector.
  • Dividing by the magnitude produces a unit vector with the same direction and magnitude one.
Example 1.

Point \(A\) has coordinates \((2,-1,3)\) and point \(B\) has coordinates \((-2,4,-1)\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and its magnitude.

  1. Subtract the coordinates of \(A\) from those of \(B\): \(\Delta x=-2-2=-4\), \(\Delta y=4-(-1)=5\), and \(\Delta z=-1-3=-4\).
  2. Therefore \(\overrightarrow{AB}=-4\hat{\mathbf i}+5\hat{\mathbf j}-4\hat{\mathbf k}\).
  3. Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{(-4)^2+5^2+(-4)^2}=\sqrt{57}\).
  4. Numerically, \(\sqrt{57}\approx7.55\).

Answer: \(\overrightarrow{AB}=(-4,5,-4)\), with magnitude \(7.55\).

Example 2.

A vector has components \(\mathbf r=2\hat{\mathbf i}-3\hat{\mathbf j}+6\hat{\mathbf k}\). Find its magnitude and unit vector.

  1. Compute \(|\mathbf r|=\sqrt{2^2+(-3)^2+6^2}=\sqrt{49}=7\).
  2. Divide every Cartesian component by the magnitude \(7\).
  3. Thus \(\hat{\mathbf r}=(2/7)\hat{\mathbf i}-(3/7)\hat{\mathbf j}+(6/7)\hat{\mathbf k}\).
  4. Its components satisfy \(4/49+9/49+36/49=1\), confirming unit magnitude.

Answer: \(|\mathbf r|=7\) and \(\hat{\mathbf r}=\frac{1}{7}(2\hat{\mathbf i}-3\hat{\mathbf j}+6\hat{\mathbf k})\).

Common mistakes.
  • Forming \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) by subtracting \(B\) from \(A\).
  • Replacing absolute values while finding a vector's magnitude.
  • Normalising only one component rather than the entire vector.

Chapter 2 · Topic 25

Unit vector

KinematicsMechanicsVectorsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. A unit vector is a vector of magnitude one that only serves to specify a direction; it is written as a hat over a symbol such as \(\hat i, \hat j, \hat k\). Every vector in physics is a magnitude times a unit vector, so the unit vector carries the direction information while the scalar carries the size. JEE problems constantly test the right-hand rule needed to fix the sense of the standard unit vectors and of cross products.
Key formula(s). \[\hat i\times\hat i = \hat j\times\hat j = \hat k\times\hat k = \vec 0\]; \[\hat i\times\hat j = \hat k,\quad \hat j\times\hat k = \hat i,\quad \hat k\times\hat i = \hat j\]; \[\hat n = \frac{\vec A}{|\vec A|},\ |\hat n| = 1\]; \[\vec A\cdot\vec A = |\vec A|^2,\quad \hat n\cdot\hat n = 1\]
Key points.
  • \(\hat i, \hat j, \hat k\) form a right-handed mutually perpendicular triad: \(\hat i\times\hat j = \hat k\) in a right-handed Cartesian frame.
  • Reversing any two of \(\hat i, \hat j, \hat k\) flips the handedness and hence flips the sign of every cross product; this is why \(\hat j\times\hat i = -\hat k\).
  • The unit vector of a sum of collinear vectors is that of the resultant with its own sign, so a negative scalar is what produces an antiparallel unit vector.
  • Since \(|\hat n|^2 = \hat n\cdot\hat n = 1\), projecting a vector on a unit vector returns a scalar length, while projecting on a general vector does not.
  • Orthogonal unit vectors form a complete basis of 3-space: any vector is a unique sum \(A_x\hat i + A_y\hat j + A_z\hat k\).
  • In a right-handed system \(\hat i \times (\hat j\times\hat k) = \hat i \times \hat i = \vec 0\), a quick consistency check often asked in JEE.
Example 1.

A vector is \(\vec A = 3\hat i - 4\hat j + 12\hat k\) units. Find the magnitude of \(\vec A\), the unit vector along it, and the projection of \(\vec A\) on the \(y\)-axis.

  1. Magnitude: \(|\vec A| = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13\) units.
  2. Divide through by the magnitude: \(\hat n = (3\hat i - 4\hat j + 12\hat k)/13\), and \(|\hat n| = 13/13 = 1\).
  3. The projection on the \(y\)-axis is the scalar component \(A_y = \vec A\cdot\hat j = -4\) units, i.e. \(4\) units in the \(-\hat j\) direction.
  4. The vector projection on the \(y\)-axis is \(A_y\hat j = -4\hat j\); the distinction between scalar and vector projection is a common JEE test.
  5. The angle with the \(y\)-axis obeys \(\cos\theta_y = -4/13 = -0.3077\), so \(\theta_y = 107.9^\circ\).

Answer: \(|\vec A| = 13\) units, \(\hat n = (3\hat i - 4\hat j + 12\hat k)/13\), and the projection on the \(y\)-axis is \(-4\) units (that is \(4\) units along \(-\hat j\)).

Example 2.

A cube of edge \(4\ \mathrm{cm}\) has one vertex at the origin \(O = (0,0,0)\) and the opposite vertex at \(C = (4,4,4)\). Find the unit vector from \(O\) to \(C\), the angle it makes with the \(x\)-axis, and the length of the body diagonal.

  1. The position vector of the far corner is \(\vec r = 4\hat i + 4\hat j + 4\hat k\ \mathrm{cm}\).
  2. Its magnitude is the body diagonal: \(|\vec r| = \sqrt{16 + 16 + 16} = \sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt 3 = 6.93\ \mathrm{cm}\).
  3. Unit vector along the body diagonal: \(\hat n = (4\hat i + 4\hat j + 4\hat k)/(4\sqrt 3) = (\hat i + \hat j + \hat k)/\sqrt 3\).
  4. The angle with the \(x\)-axis satisfies \(\cos\theta = \hat n\cdot\hat i = 1/\sqrt 3 = 0.5774\), giving \(\theta = 54.7^\circ\).
  5. As a check, the direction cosines are \(1/\sqrt3, 1/\sqrt3, 1/\sqrt3\) and their squares sum to \(3(1/3) = 1\), as required.

Answer: \(\hat n = (\hat i + \hat j + \hat k)/\sqrt 3\), the angle with the \(x\)-axis is \(54.7^\circ\), and the body diagonal is \(4\sqrt 3 \approx 6.93\ \mathrm{cm}\).

Common mistakes.
  • Treating \(\hat i \times \hat i\) as \(\hat j\) or \(\hat k\); a vector crossed with itself (or with a parallel vector) is zero.
  • Using a left-handed cyclic order such as \(\hat j\times\hat k = -\hat i\); the standard triad is right-handed.
  • Confusing the unit vector \(\hat n = \vec A/|\vec A|\) with the original vector, thereby losing the magnitude.
  • Reporting the projection of a vector on an axis as a vector when the question asks for a scalar, or forgetting that projections carry a sign.
