    Chapter 2 · Topic 40

    Relative velocity

    KinematicsMechanicsMotion in Two DimensionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Relative velocity is the rate at which one object's position changes as observed from another object, and it is obtained by vector subtraction. Its magnitude is the relative speed, while its direction indicates how the relative position changes. In JEE problems, clearly assign the numerator object and use components in a common frame before applying relative-motion formulas.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec v_{A/B}=\frac{d\vec r_A}{dt}-\frac{d\vec r_B}{dt}=\vec v_A-\vec v_B,\quad v_{A/B}=|\vec v_{A/B}|\]; \[\vec r_{A/B}=\vec r_A-\vec r_B,\quad \vec a_{A/B}=\vec a_A-\vec a_B\]
    Key points.
    • Relative velocity is a vector; subtracting the two speed magnitudes is valid only for collinear velocities with a carefully chosen sign.
    • Reversing the order gives the opposite vector, so \(\vec v_{B/A}=-\vec v_{A/B}\).
    • The relative position derivative gives relative velocity only when both positions are written in the same coordinate frame.
    • A relative speed equal to zero means two objects have identical velocity, not necessarily zero speed.
    • For perpendicular velocities \(\vec u\perp\vec v\), the relative speed is \(\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\), not \(|u-v|\) or \(u+v\).
    Example 1.

    Car A moves east at \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), while car B moves north at \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the velocity of A relative to B, its magnitude, and its direction.

    1. Take east as \(+\hat i\) and north as \(+\hat j\).
    2. The velocity vectors are \(\vec v_A=20\hat i\) and \(\vec v_B=15\hat j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Hence \(\vec v_{A/B}=20\hat i-15\hat j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{20^2+15^2}=25\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. Its direction is south of east, with \(\tan\alpha=\frac{15}{20}=\frac34\).

    Answer: A has velocity \((20\hat i-15\hat j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) relative to B, of magnitude \(25\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and direction \(\tan^{-1}(3/4)\) south of east.

    Example 2.

    Two cars leave the same intersection on perpendicular roads at the same instant. Car A travels east at \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and car B travels north at \(30\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find their relative speed and the displacement of B relative to A after \(5\,\mathrm{s}\).

    1. Taking east as \(\hat i\) and north as \(\hat j\), \(\vec v_{A/B}=20\hat i-30\hat j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. The relative speed is \(|\vec v_{A/B}|=\sqrt{400+900}=10\sqrt{13}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. After \(5\,\mathrm{s}\), A has displacement \(100\hat i\,\mathrm{m}\) and B has displacement \(150\hat j\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. Therefore \(\vec r_{B/A}=\vec r_B-\vec r_A=-100\hat i+150\hat j\,\mathrm{m}\).
    5. The magnitude of this relative displacement is \(50\sqrt{13}\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The relative speed is \(10\sqrt{13}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and B's displacement relative to A after \(5\,\mathrm{s}\) is \((-100\hat i+150\hat j)\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Subtracting speed magnitudes for velocities at right angles.
    • Using \(\vec v_A-\vec v_B\) while calling it the velocity of B relative to A.
    • Confusing relative velocity with the time rate of change of relative position measured in different frames.

    Explanation

    Concept. Relative motion in one dimension is described by subtracting the position, velocity, or acceleration of one object from that of another measured in the same frame. For \(\Delta x=x_A-x_B\), \(d\Delta x/dt<0\) means the gap is closing, while \(d\Delta x/dt>0\) means it is increasing. Applying these relations to a chosen moving origin eliminates unneeded common motion and exposes the physically relevant encounter or overtake condition.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec r_{A/B}=\vec r_A-\vec r_B,\quad \vec v_{A/B}=\vec v_A-\vec v_B=\frac{d\vec r_{A/B}}{dt},\quad \vec a_{A/B}=\vec a_A-\vec a_B\]; \[\Delta x(t)=\Delta x_0+v_{A/B}t+\frac12a_{A/B}t^2\]
    Key points.
    • Both relative quantities must be expressed along the same axis; reversing the order changes both vector and signed scalar results.
    • For collinear motion, relative speed is the magnitude of the signed velocity difference: \(|u_1-u_2|\) for the same direction and \(u_1+u_2\) for opposite directions.
    • An overtake requires the relative position to be zero and usually a nonzero closing relative velocity.
    • A relative velocity can be zero even when neither object is at rest in the ground frame.
    • In an inertial frame, a constant relative acceleration produces the standard one-dimensional kinematic equations.
    Example 1.

    Car A starts from \(x=0\) and moves with constant velocity \(+20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Car B starts from \(x=100\,\mathrm{m}\) and moves with velocity \(-10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). When and where do they meet?

    1. In A's frame, \(v_{A/B}=20-(-10)=30\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. The initial relative position is \(r_{A/B}(0)=0-100=-100\,\mathrm{m}\).
    3. Since the relative acceleration is zero, \(0=-100+30t\), giving \(t=\frac{10}{3}\,\mathrm{s}\).
    4. Using the ground frame, \(x_A=20\left(\frac{10}{3}\right)=\frac{200}{3}\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: They meet after \(\frac{10}{3}\,\mathrm{s}\) at \(x=\frac{200}{3}\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Example 2.

    For \(0\le t\le12\,\mathrm{s}\), two particles have positions \(x_A=6t^2\) and \(x_B=60t\), with \(t\) in seconds and positions in metres. Find their maximum separation and the time when A overtakes B.

    1. The relative position is \(r_{A/B}=6t^2-60t\).
    2. The relative velocity is \(v_{A/B}=12t-60\), which vanishes at \(t=5\,\mathrm{s}\).
    3. At that instant, \(r_{A/B}=6(25)-60(5)=-150\,\mathrm{m}\), so the separation is \(150\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. For an overtake, \(6t^2-60t=0\), giving the physical solution \(t=10\,\mathrm{s}\).
    5. The meeting position is \(x_A=6(10)^2=600\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The maximum separation is \(150\,\mathrm{m}\) at \(t=5\,\mathrm{s}\); A overtakes B at \(t=10\,\mathrm{s}\) and \(x=600\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding velocities for two objects travelling in the same direction.
    • Using a relative position with the opposite order from the stated relative velocity.
    • Accepting the root \(t=0\) as a later physical overtake in a relative-position quadratic.

    Explanation

    Concept. River navigation is a frame-relative velocity problem in which the ground velocity of a boat is the vector sum of its velocity relative to water and the water velocity relative to bank. Shortest time and shortest distance generally require different aiming directions. For JEE solutions, draw the velocity triangle and remember that a downstream or upstream component of water changes the resultant speed.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec v_{B/G}=\vec v_{B/W}+\vec v_{W/G}\]; \[v_{\rm ground}=\sqrt{(u\sin\phi\pm v)^2+(u\cos\phi)^2}\]; \[t_{\rm crossing}=\frac{\text{bank width}}{u\cos\phi}\]
    Key points.
    • In the speed formula, \(\phi\) is the boat's water-relative angle from the perpendicular to the bank, and the \(+\) sign denotes a downstream current component.
    • For minimum time across a river, the boat's velocity relative to water is perpendicular to the bank; the current then causes drift.
    • For minimum crossing distance, aim the along-bank component of the boat's velocity against the current so the net along-bank ground velocity is zero.
    • A perpendicular path in the water frame is not a perpendicular path on the ground.
    • Upstream speed for a direct upstream crossing is \(u-v\), while downstream speed is \(u+v\), provided \(u>v\).
    • The boat's speed relative to water remains constant in the ideal model and need not equal its speed relative to ground.
    Example 1.

    A river \(800\,\mathrm{m}\) wide flows downstream at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). A boat of speed \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) relative to water points directly across the river. Find the crossing time, downstream drift, and velocity relative to bank.

    1. The boat's across-river component is \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so the crossing time is \(t=\frac{800}{8}=100\,\mathrm{s}\).
    2. The downstream component is the current speed \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Therefore the downstream drift is \(4(100)=400\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. The ground velocity is \(\vec v_{B/G}=4\hat i+8\hat j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. Its magnitude is \(4\sqrt5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the path is not perpendicular to the bank.

    Answer: The crossing time is \(100\,\mathrm{s}\), the downstream drift is \(400\,\mathrm{m}\), and the velocity relative to bank is \((4\hat i+8\hat j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(400\,\mathrm{m}\) wide river flows at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). A boat can move at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) relative to water. Find the minimum crossing time and the length of the ground path followed during that minimum-time crossing.

    1. Minimum time requires the boat to point perpendicular to the bank, so its across-river speed remains \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. Thus \(t_{\min}=\frac{400}{5}=80\,\mathrm{s}\).
    3. During this time, the current carries the boat downstream by \(3(80)=240\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. The ground-frame displacement is \(240\hat i+400\hat j\,\mathrm{m}\).
    5. Its length is \(\sqrt{240^2+400^2}=560\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The minimum crossing time is \(80\,\mathrm{s}\), and the path length in that crossing is \(560\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Assuming the boat's speed relative to bank is always equal to its speed in still water.
    • Using the shortest-path direction when the question asks for minimum time.
    • Failing to account for downstream or upstream signs in the velocity triangle.

    Explanation

    Concept. A rain-man problem compares the velocity of rain with that of an observer using relative motion. The apparent rain velocity is \(\vec v_{R/M}=\vec v_{R/G}-\vec v_{M/G}\), so reversing this relation recovers the actual rain velocity from its observed direction. The direction in which rain appears to move is therefore set by relative velocity, not generally by the actual vertical rainfall direction.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec v_{R/M}=\vec v_{R/G}-\vec v_{M/G},\quad \vec v_{R/G}=\vec v_{R/M}+\vec v_{M/G}\]; \[\text{if rain is vertical:}\quad v_{R/M}=\sqrt{v_R^2+v_M^2},\quad \tan\alpha=\frac{v_M}{v_R}\]
    Key points.
    • If the man moves horizontally and the rain falls vertically, the apparent rain has both a backward horizontal component and a downward component.
    • To move in a direction free of rain, the man's relative velocity must be opposite to \(\vec v_{R/M}\).
    • Observed rain direction is an apparent direction; the actual rain must be found by adding the man's velocity.
    • A larger observer speed does not necessarily produce a more tilted apparent direction if the actual rain speed also changes.
    • In three dimensions, include the along-track and across-track components of both velocities.
    Example 1.

    Rain falls vertically at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and a man walks east at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the velocity of rain relative to the man, its speed, and the apparent direction of the rain.

    1. Take east as \(+\hat i\) and upward as \(+\hat j\).
    2. The ground velocities are \(\vec v_{R/G}=-10\hat j\) and \(\vec v_{M/G}=6\hat i\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Hence \(\vec v_{R/M}=-6\hat i-10\hat j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The apparent speed is \(\sqrt{6^2+10^2}=2\sqrt{34}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. The apparent rain velocity points downward and west, with \(\tan\alpha=\frac{6}{10}=\frac35\) from the downward vertical.

    Answer: The relative rain velocity is \((-6\hat i-10\hat j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), its speed is \(2\sqrt{34}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and it appears directed \(\tan^{-1}(3/5)\) west of downward vertical.

    Example 2.

    A man walking east at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) observes rain of relative speed \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) directed \(37^\circ\) from the downward vertical toward the west. Using \(\sin37^\circ=\frac35\) and \(\cos37^\circ=\frac45\), find the actual rain velocity, its speed, and the angle of its ground-frame direction from vertical.

    1. The westward component of apparent rain is \(-10\sin37^\circ=-6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. Its downward component is \(-10\cos37^\circ=-8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Thus \(\vec v_{R/M}=-6\hat i-8\hat j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. Adding the man's velocity gives \(\vec v_{R/G}=(-6+4)\hat i-8\hat j=-2\hat i-8\hat j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. Its speed is \(\sqrt{4+64}=2\sqrt{17}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), directed west of vertical with \(\tan\beta=\frac28=\frac14\).

    Answer: The actual rain velocity is \((-2\hat i-8\hat j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), with speed \(2\sqrt{17}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and direction \(\tan^{-1}(1/4)\) west of downward vertical.

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating the observed rain direction as the actual direction in the ground frame.
    • Using the man's velocity with the wrong sign in \(\vec v_{R/G}=\vec v_{R/M}+\vec v_{M/G}\).
    • Finding only an angle without its reference line, such as horizontal or vertical.

    Explanation

    Concept. A wind problem is a relative-motion problem between a projectile or aircraft and the moving air. Constant wind without a vertical component changes the horizontal ground-frame motion but not the vertical acceleration caused by gravity. The path relative to air follows the usual projectile or straight-line equations, while adding the wind velocity shifts or alters the ground-frame trajectory.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec v_{P/G}=\vec v_{P/A}+\vec v_{A/G},\quad a_{\rm vertical}=-g,\quad a_{\rm horizontal}=0\ \text{relative to air}\]; \[x=(u\cos\theta+w_x)t,\quad y=(u\sin\theta+w_y)t-\frac12gt^2\]
    Key points.
    • A constant horizontal wind leaves the time to reach any height and the maximum height unchanged, but it changes the horizontal distance.
    • The air-relative launch angle and speed are not generally equal to the ground-relative values.
    • A headwind or tailwind changes ground range, while a crosswind changes the horizontal displacement and the position of the trajectory's apex.
    • If the wind is constant, subtracting its velocity produces the standard projectile motion in the air frame.
    • A vertical wind component would alter the vertical motion and require that component in the time-of-flight equation.
    Example 1.

    A projectile is fired with air-relative speed \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(30^\circ\) to the horizontal in a wind blowing east at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and it lands at its launch level. With \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), find the time of flight, maximum height, and ground range.

    1. The horizontal ground velocity is \(20\cos30^\circ+10=10\sqrt3+10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. The vertical ground velocity is \(20\sin30^\circ=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Since the wind has no vertical component, \(T=\frac{2(10)}{10}=2\,\mathrm{s}\).
    4. The maximum height is \(H=\frac{10^2}{2(10)}=5\,\mathrm{m}\).
    5. The ground range is \((10\sqrt3+10)(2)=20(\sqrt3+1)\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The time of flight is \(2\,\mathrm{s}\), the maximum height is \(5\,\mathrm{m}\), and the ground range is \(20(\sqrt3+1)\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Example 2.

    An aircraft has airspeed \(200\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) directed \(30^\circ\) west of north. A wind blows at \(50\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) toward the east. Find the aircraft's ground velocity and its ground direction.

    1. Take east as \(+\hat i\) and north as \(+\hat j\).
    2. The air-relative velocity is \(-200\sin30^\circ\hat i+200\cos30^\circ\hat j=(-100\hat i+100\sqrt3\hat j)\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\).
    3. Adding the wind velocity \(50\hat i\) gives \(\vec v_G=-50\hat i+100\sqrt3\hat j\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\).
    4. The westward resultant component means the ground track is west of north.
    5. If \(\beta\) is measured west of north, \(\tan\beta=\frac{50}{100\sqrt3}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}\).

    Answer: The ground velocity is \((-50\hat i+100\sqrt3\hat j)\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\), directed \(\tan^{-1}(1/(2\sqrt3))\) west of north.

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding wind speed instead of wind velocity to the air-relative velocity.
    • Claiming a horizontal wind changes maximum projectile height.
    • Mixing the direction of the wind with the direction in which it is coming from.

    Chapter 2 · Topic 41

    Uniform circular motion

    KinematicsMechanicsMotion in Two DimensionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Uniform circular motion (constant speed around circles: satellites, electrons, merry-go-rounds) accelerates centripetally (v2/r toward centre) despite steady speed - direction changes continuously. Period (2πr/v), frequency, angular velocity (ω=v/r) describe timing; centripetal force (mv2/r) provides turning (tension, gravity, friction, normal components). No tangential acceleration (speed constant); radial acceleration rules.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Constant speed, changing direction, centre-seeking acceleration.
    • Satellites and electrons run on centripetal provision.
    Remember
    • Speed steady yet accelerated - direction change accelerates.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    In uniform circular motion, acceleration is directed

    Solution: Centripetal v2/r turns velocity continuously centreward.
    Key Formulas · Uniform Circular Motion
    \(v=\omega r,\;T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}\) speed-period link
    \(a_{c}=\frac{v^{2}}{r}=\omega^{2}r\) centre-seeking acceleration
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 2 · Topic 42

    Angular velocity

    KinematicsMechanicsMotion in Two DimensionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Angular velocity (ω=dθ/dt, rad/s) links rotation to translation (v=rω, a=rα tangential plus ω2r centripetal) - gears, pulleys and orbits share ω across radii while speeds scale. Direction follows right-hand rule along axes; rpm converts (×2π/60 to rad/s). Uniform circular motion holds ω constant; angular acceleration (α=dω/dt) changes it. Rotation angle, rate and change mirror displacement-velocity-acceleration linearly.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Rotation rate (rad/s); v=rω links to linear speed.
    • Right-hand rule points ω along rotation axes.
    Remember
    • Same ω, different v across radii - gears share rate.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Linear speed v relates to angular velocity ω by

    Solution: Outer radii sweep faster at shared rotation rates.
    Key Formulas · Angular Velocity
    \(\omega=\frac{d\theta}{dt}=\frac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi f\) rate of angle
    \(v=r\omega,\;a_{t}=r\alpha\) linear links via radius

    Centripetal acceleration

    KinematicsMechanicsMotion in Two DimensionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Centripetal acceleration (a=v2/r=ω2r toward centre) turns velocity without changing speed - tension (string whirls), gravity (orbits), friction (level curves), normal components (banked roads) supply it. Centrifugal force is the rotating-frame pseudo counterpart (real inertia misread). Loop-the-loop needs v2/r exceeding g at top (normal stays positive); skidding starts when required exceeds available friction.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • v2/r centre-seeking; supplied by tension, gravity, friction.
    • Loop tops need speed keeping normal positive.

    Force

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Force (push or pull changing motion: F=ma when mass constant) is a vector needing direction - net (resultant) force alone accelerates; balanced forces maintain rest or uniform motion. Units newton (SI) and dyne (CGS, 10^5 dynes per newton); dimensions [MLT-2]. Contact (friction, normal, tension, spring) versus field forces (gravity, electric, magnetic) classify origins. First law defines force qualitatively; second quantifies it.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Net unbalanced force accelerates (F=ma); balanced maintains state.
    • Newton SI; dyne CGS; dimensions MLT-2.
    Remember
    • Only net force matters - balanced forces cancel out.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 2

    Inertia

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Inertia is the body's tendency to resist a change in its state of rest or uniform motion. Translational inertia is measured by mass, so the same resultant force gives a smaller acceleration to a body of larger mass. The property itself is not a force and must be connected to acceleration through Newton's second law.
    Key formula(s). \[a=\frac{F_{\rm net}}{m},\quad m=\frac{F_{\rm net}}{a},\quad [m]=\mathrm{kg}\]; \[F_{\rm net}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad a=0\]
    Key points.
    • Inertia is present in a body at rest as well as in a body in motion.
    • Inertia depends on mass and is a scalar property, unlike weight, which equals \(mg\) and depends on the gravitational field.
    • A body with greater mass does not necessarily experience a greater external force; it responds more weakly to the same resultant force.
    • A force can change only the direction of velocity without changing its magnitude, so acceleration need not imply a speed change.
    • Rotational inertia is represented by moment of inertia and is not the same as translational mass, although both characterize resistance to change of motion.
    Example 1.

    The same resultant force of \(10\,\mathrm{N}\) acts on two bodies of masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Compare their accelerations and the mass that has greater translational inertia.

    1. For the \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body, \(a_1=\frac{10}{2}=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    2. For the \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) body, \(a_2=\frac{10}{5}=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    3. Hence \(a_1:a_2=5:2\) under equal resultant forces.
    4. The \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) body has greater translational inertia because it has greater mass.

    Answer: The accelerations are \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), respectively, and the \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) body has greater inertia.

    Example 2.

    A \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) body is initially at rest. It is acted on by a constant net force of \(12\,\mathrm{N}\) for \(5\,\mathrm{s}\). Find the impulse, final momentum, and change in speed.

    1. The acceleration is \(a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{12}{3}=4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), illustrating the weaker response of a larger mass to the same resultant force.
    2. The final velocity is \(v=at=4(5)=20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. The change in momentum is \(\Delta p=mv=3(20)=60\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The constant force gives impulse \(J=Ft=12(5)=60\,\mathrm{N\,s}\), agreeing with \(\Delta p\).
    5. Since the force acts in the direction of motion, the change in speed is also \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The impulse is \(60\,\mathrm{N\,s}\), the final momentum is \(60\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), and the speed changes by \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating inertia as a force that always opposes motion.
    • Confusing mass with weight and writing weight as the universal measure of inertia.
    • Assuming a larger mass means a larger acceleration under the same force.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 3

    Newton's First Law

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Newton's first law states that an object continues in its state of rest or of uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a nonzero resultant external force. It identifies inertial frames, in which the laws of mechanics have their usual form. The key JEE tool is \(\sum\vec F_{\rm ext}=m\vec a=0\): zero net force implies constant velocity, but not necessarily zero velocity.
    Key formula(s). \[\sum\vec F_{\rm ext}=m\vec a=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{d\vec v}{dt}=0\]; \[\vec v=\vec u,\quad \vec r(t)=\vec r_0+\vec u t\quad\text{for a constant velocity}\]
    Key points.
    • Zero resultant force implies constant velocity, while a changing velocity requires a nonzero resultant force.
    • A body at rest can be subject to balanced nonzero forces, such as weight and normal reaction.
    • Equal and opposite forces cancel only if they act on the same body and have the same line of action when rotational equilibrium is involved.
    • Newton's first law does not say that a moving body must eventually stop; ideal motion continues without a net force.
    • An elevator moving with constant velocity is an inertial frame, but one accelerating vertically is not.
    Example 1.

    A \(60\,\mathrm{kg}\) passenger stands on the floor of a lift moving upward with constant velocity \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and find the acceleration, net force on the passenger, and normal reaction.

    1. Constant velocity means \(\vec a=0\), regardless of the direction of motion.
    2. Therefore the net force on the passenger is \(m\vec a=0\).
    3. Vertically, the only forces are upward normal reaction \(N\) and downward weight \(mg\).
    4. Equilibrium requires \(N=mg=60(10)=600\,\mathrm{N}\).
    5. The passenger's apparent weight is unchanged because the lift has no acceleration.

    Answer: The acceleration and net force are zero, and the normal reaction is \(600\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Example 2.

    Three constant forces act on a \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle: \(10\,\mathrm{N}\) east, \(8\,\mathrm{N}\) north, and \(6\,\mathrm{N}\) west. Find the resultant force, acceleration, and direction of motion from rest.

    1. Taking east and north as positive, the resultant components are \(F_x=10-6=4\,\mathrm{N}\) and \(F_y=8\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. The resultant magnitude is \(\sqrt{4^2+8^2}=4\sqrt5\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. Newton's second law gives \(\vec a=\frac{\vec F}{m}=2\hat i+4\hat j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    4. The acceleration direction has \(\tan\alpha=\frac{4}{2}=2\), measured north of east.
    5. Since the particle starts from rest, its initial motion follows the resultant force direction.

    Answer: The resultant force is \((4\hat i+8\hat j)\,\mathrm{N}\), the acceleration is \((2\hat i+4\hat j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), and the motion is along a line with \(\tan\alpha=2\) north of east.

    Common mistakes.
    • Interpreting zero net force as zero velocity.
    • Treating the normal reaction as always equal to \(mg\) regardless of vertical acceleration.
    • Cancelling forces that act on different objects rather than on the chosen free body.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 4

    Newton's Second Law

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Newton's second law states that the resultant external force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum, and for constant mass this becomes \(\vec F_{\rm ext}=m\vec a\). The law relates the chosen free body's net force to its acceleration, not automatically to any single applied force. In JEE problems, write scalar or vector component equations, especially when force or mass varies with time.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec F_{\rm ext}=\frac{d\vec p}{dt},\quad \vec p=m\vec v,\quad \vec F_{\rm ext}=m\vec a\quad(m\text{ constant})\]; \[\vec v_f-\vec v_i=\frac{1}{m}\int_{t_i}^{t_f}\vec F_{\rm ext}\,dt,\quad [F]=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}=\mathrm{N}\quad(m\text{ constant})\]
    Key points.
    • For a variable-mass system, include the momentum carried by entering or leaving mass in a momentum balance; \(d\vec P_{\rm sys}/dt=\vec F_{\rm ext}\) is safest for a chosen closed system.
    • The SI unit of force is one newton, equal to \(1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}\).
    • Newton's second law applies independently along each direction and does not require the acceleration to point along a particular individual force.
    • A zero resultant force implies zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity or momentum.
    • If \(F=ma\) appears to fail, first check the frame, the selected system, and any omitted force such as friction, gravity, or normal reaction.
    Example 1.

    A net force of \(20\,\mathrm{N}\) acts east on a \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) block for \(4\,\mathrm{s}\). The block starts from rest, and the force is constant. Find its acceleration, final velocity, and displacement.

    1. The acceleration is \(a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{20}{5}=4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) east.
    2. With initial velocity zero, \(v=at=4(4)=16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) east.
    3. The displacement is \(x=ut+\frac12at^2=0+\frac12(4)(4^2)=32\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. All three quantities are in the direction of the resultant force.

    Answer: Acceleration \(=4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) east, final velocity \(=16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) east, and displacement \(=32\,\mathrm{m}\) east.

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle starts from rest and is acted on by \(\vec F=(4-2t)\hat i+3\hat j\,\mathrm{N}\) from \(t=0\) to \(5\,\mathrm{s}\). Find the impulse, final momentum, and final velocity.

    1. The impulse is \(\vec J=\int_0^5\vec F\,dt=[4t-t^2]_0^5\hat i+[3t]_0^5\hat j=-5\hat i+15\hat j\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    2. Since the particle starts from rest, \(\vec p_f=\vec J=-5\hat i+15\hat j\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Divide by the mass to obtain \(\vec v_f=-2.5\hat i+7.5\hat j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The speed is \(\sqrt{(-2.5)^2+7.5^2}=\frac{5\sqrt{10}}2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. The acceleration is not constant because the x-component of force decreases with time.

    Answer: The impulse is \((-5\hat i+15\hat j)\,\mathrm{N\,s}\), the final momentum is the same vector in \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), and the final velocity is \((-2.5\hat i+7.5\hat j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Equating the resultant force with just the driving force and omitting opposing forces.
    • Treating \(F=mv\) as a valid general kinematic formula.
    • Ignoring the time dependence of force when using constant-acceleration equations.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 5

    Newton's Third Law

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Newton's third law states that two bodies exert equal-magnitude, opposite-direction forces on each other simultaneously. These action-reaction forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel in the free-body diagram of either body by themselves. For JEE problems, first isolate one object and include every external interaction acting on it; only then identify the corresponding force on the other object.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec F_{A\text{ on }B}=-\vec F_{B\text{ on }A},\quad |\vec F_{A\text{ on }B}|=|\vec F_{B\text{ on }A}|\]
    Key points.
    • The two forces act on different objects and generally have different lines of action in an extended system.
    • Newton's third-law forces arise from the same interaction and are simultaneous; they are not one force and its reaction separated in time.
    • Weight and normal reaction are not a third-law pair because both act on the same body.
    • A rocket accelerates because exhaust is continuously expelled, so the thrust is not balanced by an equal forward force on the rocket.
    • The law holds in all inertial frames, though the numerical values of other forces may change between frames.
    Example 1.

    A car of mass \(1000\,\mathrm{kg}\) accelerates horizontally at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the force exerted by the road on the car and the corresponding force exerted by the car on the road.

    1. The road's static friction is the only horizontal external force on the car in the simplified model.
    2. Newton's second law gives \(F_{\rm road\to car}=ma=1000(2)=2000\,\mathrm{N}\) forward.
    3. By Newton's third law, the car exerts an equal force of \(2000\,\mathrm{N}\) backward on the road.
    4. The two forces act on different bodies and do not cancel the car's forward motion.

    Answer: The road exerts \(2000\,\mathrm{N}\) forward on the car, and the car exerts \(2000\,\mathrm{N}\) backward on the road.

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block accelerates vertically upward at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) while in contact with a horizontal floor. Taking \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), find the normal force on the block and the corresponding force of the block on the floor.

    1. For the block's free body, \(N-mg=ma\) vertically upward.
    2. Thus \(N=m(g+a)=2(10+4)=28\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. The floor exerts \(28\,\mathrm{N}\) upward on the block.
    4. The block exerts \(28\,\mathrm{N}\) downward on the floor by Newton's third law.
    5. These forces are an action-reaction pair, not the balanced vertical forces on the block.

    Answer: The normal force on the block is \(28\,\mathrm{N}\), and the block exerts an equal \(28\,\mathrm{N}\) force downward on the floor.

    Common mistakes.
    • Placing action and reaction forces in the same free-body diagram and cancelling them.
    • Pairing the weight of a body with the normal reaction on that same body.
    • Using \(N=mg\) in a problem where the body has vertical acceleration.

    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 3 · Topic 6

    Momentum

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Linear momentum is defined by \(\vec p=m\vec v\), the product of scalar mass and the velocity vector. It is a vector quantity and is conserved for a system only when the net external impulse is zero. Momentum is distinct from kinetic energy: a system can have zero total momentum while still possessing kinetic energy.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec p=m\vec v=p_x\hat i+p_y\hat j,\quad |\vec p|=m\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}\]; \[\frac{d\vec p}{dt}=\vec F_{\rm ext},\quad K=\frac{|\vec p|^2}{2m}\]
    Key points.
    • Momentum and velocity point in the same direction for positive mass.
    • Zero total momentum does not imply that every particle is at rest; momenta in opposite directions may cancel.
    • Doubling both mass and velocity multiplies momentum by four, whereas doubling only speed doubles momentum.
    • Momentum is conserved in a collision only for the complete system over the collision interval, not for each colliding body separately.
    • At the same kinetic energy, a larger mass has smaller momentum magnitude because \(p=\sqrt{2mK}\).
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle has velocity \(\vec v=(3\hat i+4\hat j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its momentum vector, momentum magnitude, direction, and kinetic energy.

    1. The momentum vector is \(\vec p=m\vec v=2(3\hat i+4\hat j)=6\hat i+8\hat j\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. Its magnitude is \(|\vec p|=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. The direction satisfies \(\tan\alpha=\frac{p_y}{p_x}=\frac{8}{6}=\frac43\), measured above the positive x-axis.
    4. Since the speed is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(K=\frac12(2)(5^2)=25\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. This also equals \(\frac{p^2}{2m}=\frac{100}{4}=25\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The momentum is \((6\hat i+8\hat j)\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), has magnitude \(10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), and points at \(\tan^{-1}(4/3)\) above the x-axis; the kinetic energy is \(25\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(0.2\,\mathrm{kg}\) ball moving east at \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) strikes a \(0.3\,\mathrm{kg}\) block initially at rest and sticks to it. Find the common velocity and the loss of kinetic energy.

    1. The initial momentum of the ball-block system is \(0.2(20)\hat i=4\hat i\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. During the short collision, external impulse is neglected, so \(4=(0.2+0.3)v\).
    3. Therefore \(v=8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) east.
    4. The initial kinetic energy is \(\frac12(0.2)(20^2)=40\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. The final kinetic energy is \(\frac12(0.5)(8^2)=16\,\mathrm{J}\), so the loss is \(24\,\mathrm{J}\).
    6. Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic collision.

    Answer: The common velocity is \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) east, and \(24\,\mathrm{J}\) of kinetic energy is lost.

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding masses as vectors or adding momentum magnitudes without resolving directions.
    • Claiming that conservation of momentum requires total kinetic energy to remain constant.
    • Using mass alone instead of mass times velocity to represent momentum.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 7

    Impulse

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Impulse is the integral of force over time and equals the change in momentum of the object. A constant-force graph is a rectangle and a variable-force graph is an area under the \(F-t\) curve. In JEE problems, impulse is especially useful for collisions and for intervals in which the force changes rapidly but momentum remains easy to evaluate.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec J=\int_{t_i}^{t_f}\vec F\,dt=\Delta\vec p=\vec p_f-\vec p_i,\quad \vec F_{\rm avg}=\frac{\vec J}{\Delta t}\]; \[J=F\Delta t\quad\text{for constant force},\quad [J]=\mathrm{N\,s}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\]
    Key points.
    • Impulse is a vector; opposite forces acting for different durations can give different net impulses.
    • A smaller force over a longer time can produce the same impulse as a larger force over a shorter time.
    • The net impulse determines momentum change, not necessarily the change in kinetic energy.
    • Internal action-reaction impulses in a collision cancel when considering the complete system.
    • A force pulse with a large peak but very short duration may have a smaller impulse than a sustained moderate force.
    Example 1.

    A constant force of \(20\,\mathrm{N}\) acts on a \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body for \(0.5\,\mathrm{s}\), initially at rest. Find the impulse, final momentum, and final speed.

    1. The impulse has magnitude \(J=F\Delta t=20(0.5)=10\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    2. Since the body starts from rest, the final momentum has magnitude \(10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\) in the force direction.
    3. Dividing by the mass gives \(v_f=\frac{10}{2}=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. This also follows from acceleration \(a=F/m=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(v=a\Delta t=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The impulse is \(10\,\mathrm{N\,s}\), the final momentum is \(10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), and the final speed is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A force \(F(t)=6t\,\mathrm{N}\) acts on a \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body initially at rest over \(0\le t\le4\,\mathrm{s}\). Find the impulse, average force, final momentum, and final speed.

    1. The impulse is \(J=\int_0^4 6t\,dt=[3t^2]_0^4=48\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    2. The average force is \(F_{\rm avg}=\frac{48}{4}=12\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. Initial momentum is zero, so the final momentum is \(48\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The final speed is \(v_f=\frac{48}{2}=24\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. The instantaneous force at the end is not the average force, illustrating why the area under the curve is required.

    Answer: The impulse is \(48\,\mathrm{N\,s}\), the average force is \(12\,\mathrm{N}\), the final momentum is \(48\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), and the final speed is \(24\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the instantaneous final force as the average force over the interval.
    • Confusing impulse with force and omitting the time factor or area.
    • Adding impulses as unsigned magnitudes when their directions differ.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 3 · Topic 8

    Conservation of linear momentum

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Conservation of linear momentum states that the vector sum of momenta of an isolated system remains constant when the net external impulse is zero. Internal action-reaction forces cancel by Newton's third law, even though they need not cancel individually on either body. This principle is the primary tool for one-dimensional and two-dimensional collision problems, including perfectly inelastic collisions.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec p_{\rm initial}=\vec p_{\rm final},\quad \sum_{\rm initial}m_i\vec v_i=\sum_{\rm final}m_f\vec v_f\quad\text{if }\vec J_{\rm ext}=0\]; \[1\mathrm{D}:\quad m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2\]
    Key points.
    • Momentum is a vector, so horizontal and vertical components must be conserved separately.
    • The system may be isolated during a collision even when kinetic energy is not conserved.
    • In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies have a common final velocity and mechanical energy is converted into other forms.
    • External impulses can be negligible over a short collision even if they are not literally zero.
    • The condition concerns total momentum of the system, not conservation of each body's momentum.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body moving east at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) collides with a \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) body initially at rest. Immediately after the collision, the \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body moves east at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the final velocity of the \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) body.

    1. Take east as positive. The initial total momentum is \(2(6)+1(0)=12\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. The final momentum is \(2(2)+1v=4+v\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Neglecting external impulse, \(12=4+v\), so \(v=8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The final total momentum is \(4+8=12\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), confirming conservation.

    Answer: The \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) body moves east at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle with velocity \((3\hat i+4\hat j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) collides perfectly inelastically with a \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle initially at rest. Find the common velocity and speed after collision.

    1. The initial total momentum is \(2(3\hat i+4\hat j)=6\hat i+8\hat j\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. After sticking, the total mass is \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    3. Thus \(3\vec V=6\hat i+8\hat j\), giving \(\vec V=2\hat i+\frac83\hat j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The common speed is \(\sqrt{2^2+(\frac83)^2}=\frac{5\sqrt5}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. The x and y momentum components are conserved separately.

    Answer: The common velocity is \((2\hat i+\frac83\hat j)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), with speed \(\frac{5\sqrt5}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Conserving kinetic energy as if every collision were elastic.
    • Forgetting that sticking gives one common final velocity.
    • Adding one-dimensional momentum equations without assigning signs to opposing directions.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 9

    Applications of momentum conservation

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Momentum conservation applications: recoil guns (gun backward as bullet forward), rocket propulsion (exhaust momentum down, rocket up - variable-mass equation), explosions (fragments momenta vector-sum zero), collisions (airbags extend impact time cutting force), jumping (bend knees lengthening stopping time). All exploit zero-external-impulse constancy - internal redistribution keeping vector sums fixed. Space travel runs purely on recoil physics.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Recoil guns, rockets, airbags, landings - conservation at work.
    • Extend impact time to cut impact force (impulse same).
    Remember
    • Bend knees landing - time stretches force shrinks.

    Rocket propulsion works on conservation of

    Solution: Backward exhaust momentum balances forward rocket momentum.
    Key Formulas · Momentum Applications
    \(M\vec V+m\vec v=0\) recoil: gun back, bullet forward
    \(F=v_{ex}\frac{dm}{dt}\) rocket thrust from exhaust rate

    Chapter 3 · Topic 10

    Equilibrium of concurrent forces

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Equilibrium of concurrent forces (vector sum zero: Lami theorem - each force proportional to sine of opposite angle for three forces; closed triangle/polygon of forces) holds bodies at rest or uniform motion. Static structures (bridges, ladders with friction), hanging masses (tension components balancing weight), and inclined blocks (resolved components cancelling) all satisfy zero net force plus zero net torque. Non-inertial frames add pseudo forces before balancing.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Zero vector sum (plus zero torque) defines equilibrium.
    • Lami theorem proportions three-force balances.
    Remember
    • Closed force triangle proves three-force balance.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Lami theorem applies to bodies in equilibrium under forces numbering

    Solution: Each force proportional to sine of opposite angle.

    Explanation

    Concept. A pseudo-force is the inertial force introduced when Newton's laws are used in a frame accelerating translationally. For a frame accelerating at \(\vec a_0\), it acts on a mass as \(\vec F_{\mathrm{pseudo}}=-m\vec a_0\), even though no physical source exerts this force. It is a bookkeeping device that makes the equations in the accelerating frame match the observed motion.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec F_{\mathrm{pseudo}}=-m\vec a_0\] ; \[\sum\vec F_{\mathrm{real}}+\vec F_{\mathrm{pseudo}}=m\vec a_{\mathrm{relative}}\] ; \[g_{\mathrm{eff}}=g-a\quad\text{for a lift accelerating downward}\] ; \[\tan\theta=\frac{a}{g+a}\quad\text{for a pendulum in an upward-accelerating lift}\]
    Key points.
    • Pseudo-force has units of force but is not an interaction and should not appear in a ground-frame free-body diagram.
    • A frame accelerating upward produces a downward pseudo-force, just like a gravity-like contribution.
    • The mass of the object does not affect its acceleration caused solely by pseudo-force.
    • Do not add both a pseudo-force and a real force that already represents frame acceleration in the same calculation.
    • Rotating-frame pseudo-forces require additional terms beyond \(-m\vec a_0\).
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block rests on the frictionless floor of a cart accelerating horizontally at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the block's acceleration in the ground frame and the horizontal force required to produce this motion. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. In the cart frame, the block experiences a horizontal pseudo-force \(ma_0=2(3)=6\,\mathrm{N}\) toward the left.
    2. Since there is no horizontal real force or friction, its relative acceleration would be \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) leftward if released freely.
    3. While it remains fixed relative to the cart, a real horizontal force of \(6\,\mathrm{N}\) rightward is required.
    4. The resulting ground-frame acceleration is \(F/m=3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) rightward.

    Answer: The block accelerates at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) rightward, and the required real force is \(6\,\mathrm{N}\) rightward.

    Example 2.

    A simple pendulum is in equilibrium relative to a lift accelerating upward at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the angle its string makes with the vertical. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. In the lift frame, the bob experiences gravity \(mg\) and a downward pseudo-force \(ma\), both vertically downward.
    2. Their effective downward acceleration is \(g+a=13\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    3. If the string makes angle \(\theta\) with the vertical, horizontal and vertical balance gives \(\tan\theta=T\sin\theta/(T\cos\theta+mg)\), or directly \(\tan\theta=ma/[m(g+a)]\).
    4. Thus \(\tan\theta=3/13\), so \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(3/13)\).

    Answer: \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(3/13)\approx13.0^\circ\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating pseudo-force as a real force in the ground frame.
    • Omitting the mass while retaining the symbol \(m\) in \(\tan\theta=ma/(g+a)\).
    • Forgetting that an upward-accelerating lift increases the effective gravity, rather than decreasing it.

    Explanation

    Concept. A non-inertial frame is one that is accelerating or rotating relative to an inertial frame, so Newton's first and second laws do not hold unchanged in it. For a translating frame, one adds the appropriate pseudo-force and uses relative acceleration; for a rotating frame, centrifugal, Coriolis, and Euler terms may also be required. A sound JEE solution either includes all relevant terms or works entirely in the ground frame.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec a_P=\vec a_O+\vec a_{P/O}\quad\text{with the same time derivative}\] ; \[\vec F_{\mathrm{pseudo,O}}=-m\vec a_O\] ; \[\vec F_{\mathrm{centrifugal}}=-m\vec\Omega\times(\vec\Omega\times\vec r)\] ; \[\vec F_{\mathrm{Coriolis}}=-2m\vec\Omega\times\vec v_{\mathrm{rel}}\]
    Key points.
    • Relative acceleration is zero for an object fixed in a translating frame, but the object can still have a large ground-frame acceleration.
    • Fictitious forces depend on the chosen frame; a real contact force such as friction must be used consistently in all frames.
    • The freely falling lift frame is non-inertial, yet gravity and the upward pseudo-force cancel for every body.
    • A rotating frame at constant angular speed has no Euler term, but centrifugal and Coriolis terms can remain.
    • When a block slips in a truck frame, its relative and ground-frame accelerations differ by the truck's acceleration.
    Example 1.

    A ball is released inside a freely falling lift whose acceleration is \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) downward. Describe its acceleration relative to the lift and its normal reaction from the floor.

    1. In the ground frame, the only force before contact is gravity, so the ball accelerates downward at \(g\).
    2. The lift also accelerates downward at \(g\), so \(\vec a_{\mathrm{rel}}=\vec a_{\mathrm{ball}}-\vec a_{\mathrm{lift}}=0\).
    3. In the lift frame, gravity \(mg\) downward and pseudo-force \(mg\) upward cancel.
    4. Hence the ball remains stationary relative to the lift and the floor normal is zero.

    Answer: The ball has zero acceleration relative to the lift and \(N=0\).

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block initially rests on the rough floor of a truck accelerating right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). If \(\mu_s=0.4\) and \(\mu_k=0.2\), find its acceleration relative to the truck after slipping. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. Static friction required for rest relative to the truck is \(ma_0=10\,\mathrm{N}\) rightward.
    2. Its maximum value is \(\mu_smg=0.4(2)(10)=8\,\mathrm{N}\), so the block slips backward relative to the truck.
    3. In the truck frame, the leftward pseudo-force is \(ma_0=10\,\mathrm{N}\), while kinetic friction acts rightward with \(f_k=0.2(2)(10)=4\,\mathrm{N}\).
    4. Therefore the relative acceleration is \(a_{\mathrm{rel}}=(10-4)/2=3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) toward the rear of the truck.
    5. For comparison, \(a_{\mathrm{ground}}=5-3=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) rightward.

    Answer: The block's acceleration relative to the truck is \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) toward the rear.

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding a pseudo-force while also defining acceleration as ground-frame acceleration.
    • Omitting the opposite pseudo-force in the equivalent non-inertial treatment.
    • Concluding that a body fixed relative to an accelerating frame is inertial.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 11

    Free-body diagrams

    Laws of MotionMechanicsForce and LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A free-body diagram is an isolated representation of one chosen object showing every real external force acting on it, with no internal forces or force pairs included. Forces are drawn at their points or lines of application and resolved only after selecting axes. Correct FBDs are the foundation of Newton's-law problems because a missing force changes the net force, while an invented interaction makes the solution unphysical.
    Key formula(s). \[\sum\vec F_{\rm ext}=m\vec a,\quad \sum F_x=ma_x,\quad \sum F_y=ma_y\]; \[\text{constraint example: }\sum F_{\perp\ \mathrm{surface}}=0\quad\text{when there is no normal acceleration}\]
    Key points.
    • Draw only forces exerted by objects outside the chosen system; internal forces cancel for the system analysis.
    • Never place an action-reaction pair from Newton's third law in the same free-body diagram.
    • Weight, normal reaction, tension, friction, applied force, and air resistance must be included when relevant.
    • An FBD does not show motion, velocity, or the direction of acceleration unless these are separately labelled.
    • Resolve forces into components only along convenient axes; do not add forces geometrically before choosing a sign convention.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block rests on a horizontal floor with no other horizontal force. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Identify the forces on the block, the net force, and the normal reaction.

    1. The block's free body has downward weight \(mg=20\,\mathrm{N}\) and upward normal reaction \(N\).
    2. There is no horizontal force, so the horizontal net force is zero.
    3. Since the block has no vertical acceleration, \(N-mg=0\).
    4. Therefore \(N=20\,\mathrm{N}\) and \(\vec F_{\rm net}=0\).

    Answer: The forces are weight \(20\,\mathrm{N}\) downward and normal reaction \(20\,\mathrm{N}\) upward; the net force is zero and \(N=20\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(1000\,\mathrm{kg}\) car on a horizontal road experiences a \(3000\,\mathrm{N}\) forward driving force and \(500\,\mathrm{N}\) backward resistance. Find the net force and acceleration, and state the correct horizontal FBD forces.

    1. The horizontal FBD contains the forward driving force and the backward resistance, with weight and normal canceling vertically.
    2. The net horizontal force is \(3000-500=2500\,\mathrm{N}\) forward.
    3. Newton's second law gives \(a=\frac{2500}{1000}=2.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) forward.
    4. Only these two horizontal forces enter the horizontal equation; the force exerted by the car on the road is not an additional force on the car.

    Answer: The car has a net forward force of \(2500\,\mathrm{N}\) and acceleration \(2.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\); its FBD contains the driving and resistance forces, not the force exerted by the car on the road.

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding an internal force or a Newton's-third-law partner to the chosen FBD.
    • Omitting friction, air resistance, or a normal reaction.
    • Drawing motion or velocity as an additional force.

    Explanation

    Concept. The normal reaction is the contact force exerted by a surface perpendicular to the contact surface, subject to the presence of other contact and applied forces. It adjusts to prevent interpenetration and is therefore not automatically equal to \(mg\). Vertical equilibrium or vertical acceleration determines the normal force, with sign conventions handled carefully.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec N\perp\text{contact surface},\quad N\ge0\]; \[\text{vertical upward acceleration }a:\quad N-mg=ma\quad\Rightarrow\quad N=m(g+a)\]; \[\text{vertical downward acceleration of magnitude }a:\quad mg-N=ma\quad\Rightarrow\quad N=m(g-a)\]
    Key points.
    • On a frictionless horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration, \(N=mg\); this is a consequence, not a universal law.
    • A horizontal push or pull on a vertical wall changes \(N\), while gravity acts along the wall and is not balanced by it unless another force acts.
    • The normal force can be zero when contact is just lost or only impending, and it cannot be negative for a passive surface.
    • A block on an accelerating lift has \(N=m(g+a)\) for upward acceleration and \(N=m(g-a)\) for downward acceleration.
    • Friction is parallel to the surface and should not be confused with the normal force.
    Example 1.

    A \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) person stands in a lift accelerating upward at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and find the normal reaction on the person.

    1. On the person, the upward normal reaction \(N\) balances weight while supplying upward acceleration.
    2. The vertical equation is \(N-mg=ma\).
    3. Substituting gives \(N-50=5(2)\).
    4. Hence \(N=60\,\mathrm{N}\).
    5. The normal force is greater than the weight because the lift accelerates upward.

    Answer: The normal reaction on the person is \(60\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) block is held against a smooth vertical wall by a horizontal force of \(40\,\mathrm{N}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and find the normal reaction and the block's acceleration.

    1. The horizontal wall force is the only horizontal force, so it determines the normal reaction: \(N=40\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. The weight is \(mg=50\,\mathrm{N}\) downward, and the smooth wall provides no vertical force.
    3. Thus the net vertical force is \(50\,\mathrm{N}\) downward.
    4. The acceleration is \(a=g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) downward.
    5. The normal force here is not equal to \(mg\) because the contact geometry is vertical.

    Answer: The normal reaction is \(40\,\mathrm{N}\), and the block accelerates vertically downward at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Setting \(N=mg\) before considering orientation and vertical acceleration.
    • Treating the normal force as a reaction to the body's weight on the same contact.
    • Allowing \(N<0\) in a result, which indicates loss of contact rather than a physical pulling normal force.

    Explanation

    Concept. Tension is the force transmitted along an ideal massless, inextensible string, and an ideal string can pull but cannot push. A massless string has uniform tension, while a massive string may have different tensions along its length. JEE problems require an FBD of each object and the string constraints, rather than assuming that tension always equals weight.
    Key formula(s). \[T_{\rm massless\ string}=\text{constant along the string}\]; \[T=mg\quad\text{for a mass at rest},\quad T-mg=ma\quad\text{for upward acceleration}\]; \[T=m_1(g+a_1)\quad\text{for a mass accelerating upward on an ideal pulley}\]
    Key points.
    • A string transmits tension through its length, but a string going slack has zero tension and cannot transmit compression.
    • A massless string has no finite weight, so uniform tension follows from force balance on each infinitesimal segment.
    • Two strings meeting at a massless ring pull the ring in two directions; the ring's equilibrium determines the magnitudes.
    • In an ideal pulley, the two string tensions are equal, but this is not generally true for a massive pulley or one with axle friction.
    • A tension value can be less than, equal to, or greater than \(mg\), depending on acceleration and direction.
    Example 1.

    A \(10\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass hangs at rest from a vertical massless string. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and find the tension in the string.

    1. The forces on the mass are its weight \(mg=100\,\mathrm{N}\) downward and tension \(T\) upward.
    2. Since the mass is at rest, its acceleration is zero.
    3. The vertical force equation is \(T-mg=0\).
    4. Therefore \(T=100\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Answer: The string tension is \(100\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(50\,\mathrm{kg}\) monkey and a \(20\,\mathrm{kg}\) lift are connected by a massless string passing over a fixed ideal pulley. The lift accelerates upward at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and find the tension and the upward acceleration of the monkey.

    1. The tension is the same in both segments of the ideal massless string and ideal pulley.
    2. For the monkey, \(T-mg=ma_m\), so \(T=m(g+a_m)\).
    3. The string constraint gives the same acceleration magnitude for the monkey and lift, with the monkey accelerating upward when the lift does.
    4. Thus \(a_m=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) upward and \(T=50(10+2)=600\,\mathrm{N}\).
    5. For the lift, \(T-Mg=Ma\) gives \(600-20(10)=20(2)\), confirming the result.

    Answer: The tension is \(600\,\mathrm{N}\), and the monkey accelerates upward at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Assuming tension is always \(mg\) for every suspended object.
    • Applying equal tension to a string with appreciable mass or a frictional pulley.
    • Treating a string as capable of pushing when the required tension would be negative.

    Explanation

    Concept. Connected bodies are linked by a taut inextensible string, so their displacements or accelerations along the string are constrained. Two bodies connected directly over a pulley usually have equal acceleration magnitudes, while their tensions need not be equal if pulley inertia or string mass cannot be neglected. The standard JEE method is to isolate each body and form coupled equations from \(\sum F=ma\).
    Key formula(s). \[a_1=-a_2\quad\text{for a direct two-body constraint}\] ; \[\sum F_{1}=m_1a,\qquad \sum F_{2}=m_2a\] ; \[a=\frac{m_2g-\mu_km_1g}{m_1+m_2}\quad\text{for a block pulled by a hanging mass}\]
    Key points.
    • A string constrains distance, not the individual speeds of different bodies; tension can differ along a massive string.
    • For an ideal massless string over an ideal pulley, the tension is the same on both sides.
    • The equations must assign opposite positive directions to bodies pulled toward opposite ends.
    • Friction acts on each body with the appropriate normal reaction, and the two frictional forces need not be equal.
    • A movable pulley changes the displacement or force ratio even when every rope has the same tension.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block on a rough horizontal table is connected over a smooth pulley to a \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) hanging block. The coefficient of kinetic friction is \(0.10\). Find the acceleration and tension. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. For the table block, \(N=m_1g=20\,\mathrm{N}\) and \(f_k=0.1(20)=2\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. Taking the hanging block downward and the table block toward the pulley as positive, \(m_2g-f_k=(m_1+m_2)a\).
    3. Thus \(30-2=5a\), so \(a=5.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    4. For the table block, \(T-2=2(5.6)\), giving \(T=13.2\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Answer: \(a=5.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(T=13.2\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Example 2.

    Three blocks of masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), and \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) are connected in sequence by two light strings over smooth fixed pulleys. Constant horizontal forces \(30\,\mathrm{N}\) and \(40\,\mathrm{N}\) pull the \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) blocks respectively to the right. Find the common acceleration and the tension in the middle string.

    1. All three blocks have the same acceleration magnitude \(a\) to the right; let the two string tensions be \(T_1\) and \(T_2\).
    2. For the \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block, \(30-T_1=2a\), so \(T_1=30-2a\).
    3. For the middle \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) block, \(T_2-T_1=3a\).
    4. For the \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) block, \(40-T_2=4a\), so \(T_2=40-4a\).
    5. Substituting into the middle equation gives \(40-4a-(30-2a)=3a\), hence \(a=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    6. The middle-string tension is \(T_2=40-4(2)=32\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Answer: \(a=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) to the right and \(T_2=32\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Assuming every string has the same tension without checking for string mass or pulley inertia.
    • Giving connected bodies the same signed acceleration when their chosen positive directions are opposite.
    • Omitting friction from only one of the bodies in a system.

    Explanation

    Concept. A pulley system transmits force through one or more ropes, and the correct kinematic constraint depends on which rope ends move. For an ideal rope, the tension is uniform, but a movable pulley is supported by two tension segments. JEE problems are efficiently solved by combining the correct length or acceleration constraint with the force balance for every moving pulley and mass.
    Key formula(s). \[L=2y_{\rm movable}-y_{\rm free}=\text{constant}\quad\text{when both rope ends are above the pulley}\] ; \[2v_{\rm movable}-v_{\rm free}=0,\qquad 2a_{\rm movable}-a_{\rm free}=0\] ; \[R=2T\quad\text{for one movable pulley with two rope segments}\] ; \[a=\frac{|m_1-m_2|}{m_1+m_2}g\quad\text{for an ideal Atwood machine}\]
    Key points.
    • An ideal massless rope has one tension, and an ideal pulley has no net torque from unequal tensions.
    • A fixed pulley only changes direction; a movable pulley can halve the required applied force.
    • With one fixed end above the pulley and the free end also above it, downward coordinates give \(2y_{\rm movable}-y_{\rm free}=\text{constant}\).
    • If the pulley is massive or the axle has friction, the two tensions need not be equal.
    • Never assign a common acceleration to all bodies before deriving the actual string constraint.
    Example 1.

    Two masses of \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) hang from an ideal Atwood machine. Find their acceleration magnitude and the tension. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The two masses have equal acceleration magnitudes in opposite directions.
    2. Writing \(3g-T=3a\) for the heavier mass gives \(30-T=3a\).
    3. Writing \(T-2g=2a\) for the lighter mass gives \(T-20=2a\).
    4. Adding the equations yields \(10=5a\), so \(a=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), and \(T=24\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Answer: \(a=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(T=24\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Example 2.

    One end of an ideal rope is fixed to the ceiling. The rope passes around a movable pulley of mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\), and its free end is above the pulley and pulled upward with a constant force \(50\,\mathrm{N}\). Find the acceleration of the movable pulley and the free end. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The massless rope has tension \(T=50\,\mathrm{N}\), and its two segments exert a total upward force \(2T=100\,\mathrm{N}\) on the movable pulley.
    2. The pulley therefore has net force \(100-4(10)=60\,\mathrm{N}\) upward and acceleration \(60/4=15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) upward, so \(a_{\rm movable}=-15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) with downward coordinates.
    3. The rope constraint is \(2a_{\rm movable}-a_{\rm free}=0\).
    4. Hence \(a_{\rm free}=2(-15)=-30\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) in the downward coordinate, so the free end accelerates \(30\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) upward.

    Answer: The movable pulley accelerates \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) upward, and the free end accelerates \(30\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) upward.

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating the two supporting segments of a movable pulley as one segment.
    • Using \(a_{\rm pulley}=a_{\rm free}\) instead of the factor-of-two relation imposed by the two supporting segments.
    • Assuming equal tensions when pulley mass or friction is not negligible.

    Explanation

    Concept. A wedge problem is solved by isolating the block and the wedge, resolving each force parallel and perpendicular to the inclined surface, and using the acceleration of the wedge. The normal reaction is not generally \(mg\cos\theta\) when the wedge or block has a horizontal acceleration. A relative-acceleration or non-inertial-frame condition is often cleaner than finding all ground-frame accelerations.
    Key formula(s). \[N=m(g\cos\theta-a_w\sin\theta)\quad\text{with positive }a_w\text{ to the right}\] ; \[a_{\rm rel,\parallel}=g\sin\theta+a_w\cos\theta\quad\text{toward the lower end}\] ; \[\text{no sliding relative to wedge}\Rightarrow a_w=-g\tan\theta\] ; \[a_{\rm block}=N\sin\theta/m\quad\text{toward the left in this geometry}\]
    Key points.
    • Always draw separate free-body diagrams for the wedge and each block.
    • Contact acceleration need not be purely along or perpendicular to the incline in the ground frame.
    • For a horizontal force toward the upper end of a fixed incline, \(N=mg\cos\theta+F\sin\theta\), with \(\theta\) measured from the horizontal.
    • The condition for no relative sliding follows from the component of pseudo-force along the plane.
    • If the calculated normal reaction is nonpositive in magnitude, the assumed contact has failed and the block separates.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block rests on a smooth fixed wedge inclined at \(37^\circ\). A horizontal force \(30\,\mathrm{N}\) acts on the block toward the upper end of the incline. Find the normal reaction and the acceleration along the incline. Take \(\sin37^\circ=3/5\), \(\cos37^\circ=4/5\), and \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. Perpendicular to the incline, the applied force presses into the surface with component \(F\sin37^\circ=18\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. The weight contributes \(mg\cos37^\circ=16\,\mathrm{N}\) into the surface, so \(N=18+16=34\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. Along the plane, the driving force is \(F\cos37^\circ=30(4/5)=24\,\mathrm{N}\), while the opposing component is \(mg\sin37^\circ=12\,\mathrm{N}\).
    4. Therefore \(ma=24-12=12\,\mathrm{N}\), so \(a=6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) up the incline.

    Answer: \(N=34\,\mathrm{N}\) and \(a=6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) up the incline.

    Example 2.

    A smooth wedge has an incline rising at \(30^\circ\) to the horizontal and is accelerated horizontally to the left. A block remains fixed relative to the wedge. Find the required wedge acceleration. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. In the wedge frame, apply a pseudo-force \(mA\) horizontally to the right on the block.
    2. Gravity acts down the plane, while the pseudo-force has upslope component \(mA\cos30^\circ\); the normal reaction is perpendicular to the plane.
    3. Relative equilibrium along the incline requires \(mg\sin30^\circ=mA\cos30^\circ\).
    4. Therefore \(A=g\tan30^\circ=10/\sqrt3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    Answer: The wedge must accelerate leftward at \(\frac{10}{\sqrt3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(N=mg\cos\theta\) when the wedge is horizontally accelerated.
    • Omitting the pseudo-force or the block's ground-frame acceleration in a moving-wedge analysis.
    • Using \(A=g\tan\theta\) without checking which horizontal wedge acceleration keeps the block fixed.

    Explanation

    Concept. In a vertically accelerating elevator, a scale reads the normal reaction, which is the occupant's apparent weight and need not equal \(mg\). For upward acceleration, the normal reaction exceeds the true weight; for downward acceleration, it is smaller. The actual gravitational force remains \(mg\) in every inertial frame.
    Key formula(s). \[N=m(g+a)\quad\text{when acceleration is upward}\] ; \[N=m(g-a)\quad\text{when acceleration is downward}\] ; \[N=mg\quad\text{when acceleration is zero}\] ; \[\text{downward free fall}\Rightarrow N=0\quad(a=g)\]
    Key points.
    • "Moving upward" does not imply an upward acceleration; velocity and acceleration are independent.
    • A spring scale measures the support force, not the true gravitational force directly.
    • A downward acceleration greater than \(g\) requires a downward support force and changes the type of contact.
    • The same equations apply to a block on a scale, a lift cable force, or an elevator wall when the chosen direction is stated.
    • Constant velocity is equivalent to zero acceleration for apparent-weight calculations.
    Example 1.

    A \(50\,\mathrm{kg}\) person stands on a weighing machine in an elevator accelerating upward at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). What does the machine read? Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. Taking upward as positive, the forces on the person are \(N\) upward and \(mg\) downward.
    2. Newton's second law gives \(N-mg=ma\).
    3. Thus \(N=m(g+a)=50(10+2)\).
    4. The reading is therefore \(N=520\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Answer: The machine reads \(520\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Example 2.

    An \(800\,\mathrm{kg}\) lift is moving upward at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and slows uniformly at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the tension in its cable, neglecting pulley mass. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. Since the lift is moving upward but slowing, its acceleration is \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) downward.
    2. With upward positive, \(T-mg=m(-2)\).
    3. Therefore \(T=m(g-2)=800(8)\).
    4. The cable tension is \(T=6400\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Answer: The cable tension is \(6400\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Taking apparent weight equal to \(mg\) whenever the lift has nonzero velocity.
    • Inferring acceleration direction solely from the direction of motion.
    • Applying \(N=m(g-a)\) when the lift is actually accelerating upward.
