    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 3 · Topic 12

    Friction

    Laws of MotionMechanicsFrictionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Friction is a contact force parallel to a surface that opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion between surfaces. Static friction adjusts continuously up to a maximum value and does not generally equal \(\mu_sN\), while kinetic friction is usually modeled as \(f_k=\mu_kN\). The direction is set by relative slipping at the contact, not simply by whether the object is moving in the laboratory frame.
    Key formula(s). \[0\le f_s\le f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN,\quad f_k=\mu_kN\quad\text{during sliding}\]; \[\vec N\perp\text{surface},\quad a=\frac{F_{\rm applied}-f_{\rm friction}}{m}\]
    Key points.
    • On an inclined plane, the limiting static-friction condition is \(\mu_s\ge\tan\theta\), assuming no other forces along the plane.
    • If sliding begins, use \(\mu_k\), not \(\mu_s\), in the subsequent acceleration calculation.
    • Friction can act up a slope on an object sliding down it, and it can also act on a stationary object that tends to slip.
    • The normal force changes on an incline: for a frictionless plane \(N=mg\cos\theta\), and applied forces can modify it.
    • A coefficient of friction is dimensionless, while the friction force has the unit \(\mathrm{N}\).
    Example 1.

    A \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) block on a horizontal floor has coefficients \(\mu_s=0.4\) and \(\mu_k=0.3\). A horizontal force of \(18\,\mathrm{N}\), and then \(21\,\mathrm{N}\), is applied. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and state the motion in each case.

    1. The normal reaction is \(N=mg=50\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. The maximum static friction is \(\mu_sN=0.4(50)=20\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. For an applied force of \(18\,\mathrm{N}\), static friction can equal \(18\,\mathrm{N}\), so the block remains at rest.
    4. For an applied force of \(21\,\mathrm{N}\), the static limit is exceeded and the block slides forward.
    5. While sliding, \(f_k=0.3(50)=15\,\mathrm{N}\), so \(a=\frac{21-15}{5}=1.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) forward.

    Answer: The block remains at rest under \(18\,\mathrm{N}\); under \(21\,\mathrm{N}\), it accelerates forward at \(1.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) block is placed on a rough incline with \(\sin\theta=\frac35\), \(\cos\theta=\frac45\), \(\mu_s=0.5\), and \(\mu_k=0.3\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and determine whether it stays at rest and, if it slides, find its acceleration.

    1. The component down the incline is \(mg\sin\theta=5(10)\frac35=30\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. The normal reaction is \(mg\cos\theta=5(10)\frac45=40\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. The maximum static friction is \(0.5(40)=20\,\mathrm{N}\), less than the downslope component, so the block begins sliding.
    4. The kinetic friction is \(0.3(40)=12\,\mathrm{N}\) up the incline.
    5. The net force down the incline is \(30-12=18\,\mathrm{N}\), hence \(a=18/5=3.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    Answer: The block cannot remain at rest; it slides down the incline with acceleration \(3.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Setting static friction equal to \(\mu_sN\) even when the applied force is smaller.
    • Using \(\mu_k\) for a block that is still at rest.
    • Choosing the friction direction opposite to motion without checking the direction of relative slipping.

    Explanation

    Concept. The angle of friction is the angle between the resultant contact reaction and the normal reaction when limiting friction acts. If the normal and friction components are \(N\) and \(f_L\), then \(\tan\phi=f_L/N=\mu_s\). The possible directions of the resultant reaction form a friction cone of semi-angle \(\phi\).
    Key formula(s). \[\tan\phi=\frac{f_L}{N}=\mu_s\] ; \[\vec R=\vec N+\vec f_L,\qquad R=\sqrt{N^2+f_L^2}\] ; \[\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{f_s}{N}\right)\le\phi\]
    Key points.
    • The angle of friction is associated with the pair of surfaces and is independent of the normal load in the Coulomb model.
    • Its usual range is \(0^\circ\le\phi<90^\circ\), since \(0\le\mu_s<\infty\).
    • The resultant reaction lies inside the friction cone for no sliding and on its boundary at impending sliding.
    • The angle between \(R\) and \(N\) is not the angle between the applied force and the surface.
    • A smaller actual resultant angle indicates that static friction is below its limiting value.
    Example 1.

    The coefficient of static friction between a steel block and a fixed incline is \(0.60\). Find the angle of friction.

    1. Let \(\phi\) be the angle between the resultant contact reaction and the normal at limiting friction.
    2. By definition, \(\tan\phi=\mu_s=0.60\).
    3. Therefore \(\phi=\tan^{-1}(0.60)\).
    4. Evaluating the inverse tangent gives \(\phi\approx30.96^\circ\).

    Answer: The angle of friction is approximately \(30.96^\circ\).

    Example 2.

    A \(50\,\mathrm{kg}\) box is pressed against a rough vertical wall by a horizontal force \(P\). The coefficient of static friction is \(0.40\). Find the minimum \(P\) that can prevent the box from sliding down. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The wall's normal reaction is \(N=P\).
    2. At the threshold of downward motion, the upward limiting friction is \(f_L=0.40P\).
    3. Force balance requires \(f_L=mg=50(10)=500\,\mathrm{N}\).
    4. Hence \(0.40P=500\), giving \(P_{\min}=1250\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Answer: \(P_{\min}=1250\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Writing \(\tan\phi=\mu_k\) for the usual angle of friction.
    • Treating the angle of friction as the actual angle of every resultant reaction.
    • Forgetting that \(N=P\) in a horizontal wall-press problem.

    Explanation

    Concept. The angle of repose is the maximum angle that an inclined surface can make with the horizontal before a body placed on it just begins to slide. For a rough plane and a simple block, it equals the angle of friction because both conditions involve impending relative motion. In JEE problems, it is often used to determine a limiting coefficient of static friction.
    Key formula(s). \[\theta_R=\phi=\tan^{-1}\mu_s\] ; \[\mu_s=\tan\theta_R\] ; \[\tan\theta_R=\frac{\text{downslope force}}{\text{normal force}}\text{ at limiting equilibrium}\]
    Key points.
    • The angle of repose is a static-equilibrium concept and does not describe motion after sliding starts.
    • For a block on a stationary plane, \(\tan\theta_R=\mu_s\) regardless of the block's mass.
    • A real surface may show a range between the angle of first motion and complete motion because of irregularity.
    • The condition \(\theta\le\theta_R\) allows rest, while \(\theta>\theta_R\) generally causes sliding.
    • Added forces can alter the effective downslope and normal components, thereby changing the limiting condition.
    Example 1.

    A block just begins to slide down a rough incline when the incline is at \(30^\circ\) to the horizontal. Find the coefficient of static friction between the block and the incline.

    1. At the angle of repose, \(mg\sin30^\circ=f_{s,\max}\).
    2. The normal reaction is \(N=mg\cos30^\circ\).
    3. Dividing the limiting equation by \(N\) gives \(\mu_s=\tan30^\circ\).
    4. Since \(\tan30^\circ=1/\sqrt3\), \(\mu_s=1/\sqrt3\).

    Answer: \(\mu_s=\frac1{\sqrt3}\approx0.577\).

    Example 2.

    Dry sand forms a conical heap whose surface makes an angle \(30^\circ\) with the horizontal. Assuming grains on the surface are just prevented from sliding, find the required minimum coefficient of static friction.

    1. Resolve the weight of a surface grain into components normal to and down the local inclined surface.
    2. The normal component is \(mg\cos30^\circ\), while the downslope component is \(mg\sin30^\circ\).
    3. At limiting rest, \(mg\sin30^\circ=\mu_smg\cos30^\circ\).
    4. Thus \(\mu_{s,\min}=\tan30^\circ=1/\sqrt3\).

    Answer: The required coefficient is \(\mu_s=\frac1{\sqrt3}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the dynamic coefficient in the angle-of-repose relation.
    • Confusing the angle of repose with the angle the moving block actually makes after release.
    • Comparing angles without first checking that the force directions are consistent.

    Explanation

    Concept. Motion on an inclined plane is analyzed by resolving forces parallel and perpendicular to the plane, because the acceleration need not be along the chosen global vertical. A frictionless incline leaves \(N=mg\cos\theta\) and gives \(a=g\sin\theta\) down the plane. With kinetic friction, the downslope acceleration becomes \(a=g(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta)\) for a block sliding downward.
    Key formula(s). \[N=mg\cos\theta\] ; \[a_{\parallel}=g\sin\theta\quad\text{on a smooth incline}\] ; \[a=g(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta)\quad\text{downward slide}\] ; \[a=g(\sin\theta+\mu_k\cos\theta)\quad\text{upward deceleration}\] ; \[v^2=u^2+2as\]
    Key points.
    • Resolve along the incline, not along the floor, when applying Newton's second law.
    • Static friction must be checked before kinetic friction is used for a block released from rest.
    • A block can remain at rest when \(\tan\theta\le\mu_s\), even though the smooth-plane result would predict motion.
    • The normal reaction is reduced to zero in an ideal vertical free fall or when contact is lost.
    • For upward motion, both gravity and kinetic friction point down the plane, so the stopping distance is shortened.
    Example 1.

    A \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) block is released from rest on a rough incline of angle \(30^\circ\) and slips immediately. If \(\mu_k=0.2\), find its acceleration and speed after \(2\,\mathrm{s}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The normal reaction is \(N=4(10)\cos30^\circ=20\sqrt3\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. The kinetic friction is \(f_k=0.2(20\sqrt3)=4\sqrt3\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. The net force down the plane is \(ma=20-4\sqrt3\), hence \(a=5-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    4. Since it starts from rest, \(v=a(2)=10-2\sqrt3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(a=5-\sqrt3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(v=10-2\sqrt3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), down the incline.

    Example 2.

    A block is projected up a rough incline of angle \(30^\circ\) with speed \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). If \(\mu_k=0.2\), find its stopping time and the distance travelled before it reverses. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. While moving upward, gravity and friction both act down the plane.
    2. The acceleration magnitude is \(g(\sin30^\circ+\mu_k\cos30^\circ)=5+\sqrt3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    3. From \(0=100-2(5+\sqrt3)t\), \(t=\frac{50}{5+\sqrt3}\,\mathrm{s}\).
    4. Equivalently, \(s=\frac{u^2}{2(5+\sqrt3)}=\frac{50}{5+\sqrt3}\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The stopping time is \(\frac{50}{5+\sqrt3}\,\mathrm{s}\), and the stopping distance is \(\frac{50}{5+\sqrt3}\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Writing the normal reaction as \(mg\) for a nonhorizontal plane.
    • Using the downward-slide formula while the block is moving upward.
    • Applying kinetic friction without first establishing that sliding occurs.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 13

    Static friction

    Laws of MotionMechanicsFrictionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Static friction is the self-adjusting frictional force that prevents relative sliding between two surfaces in contact. Its magnitude is determined by the force required for equilibrium, not automatically by \(\mu_sN\); equality is made only when slipping is just about to begin. In JEE problems, first isolate the body and use equilibrium to find the required friction, then compare it with the limiting value.
    Key formula(s). \[0\le f_s\le \mu_sN\] ; \[f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN\] ; \[\vec f_s\text{ opposes the tendency of relative motion}\]
    Key points.
    • Static friction may be zero, for example on a frictionless-looking contact when no tangential force is required.
    • The coefficient of static friction \(\mu_s\) is a dimensionless material-pair property under standard surface conditions.
    • The normal reaction is found from force balance perpendicular to the contact surface, not from the weight alone.
    • The inequality \(f_s\le\mu_sN\) is a test for equilibrium; equality alone does not mean the body is moving.
    • In multi-body problems, the direction of the tendency of motion must be identified before assigning the friction direction.
    Example 1.

    A \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) block rests on a rough horizontal surface and is pulled horizontally by an \(18\,\mathrm{N}\) force. If \(\mu_s=0.6\), find the friction force and state whether the block moves. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The vertical forces give \(N=mg=4(10)=40\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. The maximum static friction is \(f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN=0.6(40)=24\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. The applied force tends to move the block right, so equilibrium requires \(f_s=18\,\mathrm{N}\) toward the left.
    4. Since \(18<24\), the block remains at rest and static friction does not reach its limiting value.

    Answer: The friction force is \(18\,\mathrm{N}\) toward the left, and the block does not move.

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block is placed on a rough incline of angle \(30^\circ\). Find the minimum coefficient of static friction for which it remains at rest. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The normal reaction is \(N=mg\cos30^\circ=20(\sqrt3/2)=10\sqrt3\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. The component of weight down the plane is \(mg\sin30^\circ=20(1/2)=10\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. At the minimum coefficient, \(mg\sin30^\circ=\mu_sN\).
    4. Therefore \(\mu_{s,\min}=\frac{10}{10\sqrt3}=\frac1{\sqrt3}\).

    Answer: \(\mu_{s,\min}=\frac1{\sqrt3}\approx0.577\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Setting \(f_s=\mu_sN\) in every static-equilibrium problem.
    • Applying \(N=mg\) on an incline or when another force has a normal component.
    • Assigning friction opposite displacement when the body is actually at rest.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 14

    Limiting friction

    Laws of MotionMechanicsFrictionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Limiting friction is the greatest static friction that can occur while contact is maintained, reached when relative sliding is impending. It equals \(\mu_sN\), where \(N\) is the instantaneous normal reaction. Once sliding begins, the friction generally drops to \(\mu_kN\), so an acceleration can appear suddenly.
    Key formula(s). \[f_{L}=\mu_sN\] ; \[f_k=\mu_kN<\mu_sN\] ; \[\sum F_{\parallel}=ma\quad\text{after sliding begins}\]
    Key points.
    • Impending motion is a condition of maximum static friction, not actual nonzero velocity.
    • For a body at rest, required friction below the limiting value is permitted to remain static.
    • On a stationary incline, \(N=mg\cos\theta\) and the limiting condition is \(mg\sin\theta=\mu_smg\cos\theta\).
    • The coefficient of limiting friction is commonly denoted \(\mu_s\), and the limiting-friction angle is \(\phi=\tan^{-1}\mu_s\).
    • An external force can change \(N\), so the limiting friction need not remain fixed as the force changes.
    Example 1.

    A \(50\,\mathrm{kg}\) crate on rough horizontal ground is lifted vertically by a constant rope force of \(500\,\mathrm{N}\). If \(\mu_s=0.6\) and \(\mu_k=0.4\), find its acceleration just after lifting starts. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The limiting friction is \(0.6(50)(10)=300\,\mathrm{N}\), so the \(500\,\mathrm{N}\) lift exceeds it and upward motion begins.
    2. After sliding starts, the upward friction on the crate is \(f_k=0.4(50)(10)=200\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. Newton's second law gives \(500-500-200=50a\).
    4. Therefore \(a=4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) upward.

    Answer: The crate accelerates upward at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) block lies on a rough incline with \(\sin37^\circ=3/5\) and \(\cos37^\circ=4/5\). It is pulled up the plane by \(100\,\mathrm{N}\). If \(\mu_s=0.5\) and \(\mu_k=0.4\), find its acceleration after it starts moving. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The normal reaction is \(N=5(10)(4/5)=40\,\mathrm{N}\), so \(f_{s,\max}=20\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. The downslope weight is \(30\,\mathrm{N}\); the \(100\,\mathrm{N}\) pull exceeds the opposing limit, so the block moves upward.
    3. After motion begins, \(f_k=0.4(40)=16\,\mathrm{N}\) down the plane.
    4. Thus \(100-30-16=5a\), giving \(a=10.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) up the plane.

    Answer: \(a=10.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) up the incline.

    Common mistakes.
    • Calling limiting friction the friction during all motion.
    • Assuming friction is always \(\mu_sN\) even when the required value is smaller.
    • Failing to change from \(\mu_s\) to \(\mu_k\) after impending sliding.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 3 · Topic 15

    Kinetic friction

    Laws of MotionMechanicsFrictionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Kinetic friction acts when there is relative sliding between rough surfaces. Unlike static friction, its magnitude is fixed at \(f_k=\mu_kN\) and normally \(\mu_k<\mu_s\). Its direction opposes the actual relative velocity, and it usually produces mechanical-energy loss.
    Key formula(s). \[f_k=\mu_kN\] ; \[f_k=\mu_kmg\quad\text{on a horizontal surface}\] ; \[a=\frac{F_{\parallel}-f_k}{m}\] ; \[W_f=-f_kd\] ; \[0=u^2+2as\quad\Rightarrow\quad s=\frac{u^2}{2\mu_k g}\text{ when stopped}\]
    Key points.
    • Kinetic friction is nearly independent of sliding speed in the standard school model.
    • Its SI unit is newton and the coefficient \(\mu_k\) is dimensionless.
    • On a horizontal surface, \(N=mg\) only if no vertical acceleration or other vertical force exists.
    • During slipping, the force required for equilibrium no longer applies; use \(\sum F=ma\).
    • A block cannot slide up a rough plane indefinitely without an external force because kinetic friction dissipates energy.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block starting from rest on a rough horizontal floor is pulled horizontally by a constant \(14\,\mathrm{N}\) force. If \(\mu_k=0.2\), find its acceleration and the work done by friction in the first \(3\,\mathrm{s}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The normal reaction is \(N=2(10)=20\,\mathrm{N}\), so \(f_k=0.2(20)=4\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. The net force to the right is \(14-4=10\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. Hence \(a=\frac{10}{2}=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), giving \(s=\frac12at^2=22.5\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. Since friction opposes the displacement, \(W_f=-f_ks=-4(22.5)=-90\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(a=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(W_f=-90\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) block moving at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) on a rough horizontal floor has coefficient of kinetic friction \(0.25\). Find the stopping time and stopping distance. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The friction force is \(f_k=0.25(4)(10)=10\,\mathrm{N}\) opposite the motion.
    2. The acceleration is \(a=-\frac{10}{4}=-2.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    3. From \(0=25-2(2.5)t\), the stopping time is \(t=2\,\mathrm{s}\).
    4. The stopping distance is \(s=\frac{u^2}{2\mu_kg}=\frac{25}{5}=5\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The block stops after \(2\,\mathrm{s}\) after travelling \(5\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(\mu_sN\) after the body has started sliding.
    • Forgetting the negative sign in the work done by friction.
    • Treating \(s=ut\) when the block is decelerating to rest.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 16

    Laws of friction

    Laws of MotionMechanicsFrictionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Laws of friction (Coulomb-Amontons): proportional to normal reaction (F=μN), independent of contact area, opposes relative motion (static adjusts up to limiting μsN; kinetic stays ~constant μkN, usually less than static), and direction always against slip. Microscopic welds (cold junctions) plus roughness explain origins; lubrication (fluid films), polishing and ball bearings cut friction; non-confirming cases (adhesion, high speeds) limit laws.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Proportional to normal force; area-independent; opposes slip.
    • Static adjusts to limiting; kinetic stays lower constant.
    Remember
    • Static is adjustable; kinetic is (nearly) constant.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Friction force is independent of

    Solution: Amontons law: area cancels, normal reaction rules.
    Key Formulas · Laws of Friction
    \(F\le\mu_{s}N,\;F_{k}=\mu_{k}N\) static adjusts, kinetic stays
    \(\mu_{s}>\mu_{k}\;\mathrm{usually}\) breakaway exceeds sliding
    Back to Index

    Chapter 3 · Topic 17

    Coefficient of friction

    Laws of MotionMechanicsFrictionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Coefficient of friction (μ=F/N ratio: static μs for impending motion, kinetic μk for sliding; μs exceeds μk usually) measures surface pair grip - rubber-concrete ~1, ice-steel ~0.03, lubricated joints ~0.001. Angle of friction (resultant-reaction angle, tan=μ) plus angle of repose (slip-start incline angle equals friction angle) geometrise μ. Anti-lock brakes (rolling grip beats skidding) exploit μs-over-μk superiority.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • μ=F/N grip ratio; static exceeds kinetic usually.
    • Angle of friction/repose geometrise μ directly.
    Remember
    • Rubber grips (~1); ice slips (~0.03) - pair property.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Angle of repose equals

    Solution: Slip-start incline angle matches friction angle exactly.
    Key Formulas · Coefficient of Friction
    \(\mu=F/N\) grip ratio of surface pair
    \(\tan\theta_{f}=\mu,\;\theta_{repose}=\theta_{f}\) friction and repose angles
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 3 · Topic 18

    Rolling friction

    Laws of MotionMechanicsFrictionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Rolling friction (deformation losses at rolling contacts) runs far below sliding friction (steel wheels ~0.001 vs sliding ~0.5) - ball bearings convert sliding to rolling, tyres balance grip versus rolling resistance (tread patterns, pressure tuning), trains exploit steel-steel lowness. Deflated tyres waste fuel (hysteresis losses); over-inflation sacrifices grip. Rolling resistance still dissipates - free motion remains ideal fiction.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Rolling beats sliding friction hundred-fold.
    • Bearings, tyres and rails exploit rolling lowness.
    Remember
    • Ball bearings turn sliding into rolling contacts.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Rolling friction compared to sliding friction is

    Solution: Deformation losses trail far below sliding shear.
    Key Formulas · Rolling Friction
    \(F_{roll}\ll F_{slide}\) rolling beats sliding hundred-fold
    \(v_{cm}=\omega R\;\mathrm{(no\,slip)}\) rolling-without-slipping link
    Back to Index

    Chapter 3 · Topic 19

    Circular motion

    Laws of MotionMechanicsCircular MotionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Circular motion is motion in which the direction of velocity changes continuously, producing acceleration even when the speed is constant. In uniform circular motion, the acceleration has constant magnitude \(v^2/r\), points toward the centre, and is perpendicular to velocity. For nonuniform circular motion, an additional tangential acceleration changes the speed.
    Key formula(s). \[a_c=\frac{v^2}{r}=\omega^2r=\frac{4\pi^2r}{T^2}\] ; \[\omega=\frac{v}{r}=\frac{2\pi}{T}\] ; \[a_t=\frac{dv}{dt}\quad\text{for speed to change}\] ; \[\vec v_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\vec r_f-\vec r_i}{\Delta t},\qquad v_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\text{distance}}{\Delta t}\]
    Key points.
    • Centripetal acceleration is a radial acceleration description, not an additional force acting on the particle.
    • For uniform circular motion, tangential acceleration is zero but the total acceleration is not zero.
    • Average speed uses path length, whereas average velocity uses displacement.
    • Angular speed and linear speed obey \(v=r\omega\) for rigid rotation or instantaneous circular motion.
    • Over a full revolution, displacement and average velocity are zero even though path length and average speed are nonzero.
    Example 1.

    A particle moves in a circle of radius \(7\,\mathrm{m}\) with constant speed \(14\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its centripetal acceleration and period of revolution.

    1. The centripetal acceleration is \(a_c=v^2/r=14^2/7=28\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    2. The distance travelled in one revolution is \(2\pi r=14\pi\,\mathrm{m}\).
    3. Since speed is constant, \(T=2\pi r/v=14\pi/14=\pi\,\mathrm{s}\).
    4. The acceleration points toward the centre throughout the motion.

    Answer: \(a_c=28\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(T=\pi\,\mathrm{s}\).

    Example 2.

    A particle traverses a semicircle of radius \(10\,\mathrm{m}\) at constant speed \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its average speed and the magnitude of its average velocity.

    1. The path length is \(\pi r=10\pi\,\mathrm{m}\).
    2. The elapsed time is \(t=(\pi r)/v=10\pi/5=2\pi\,\mathrm{s}\).
    3. Average speed is therefore \(\frac{10\pi}{2\pi}=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), equal to the constant speed.
    4. The displacement across the diameter has magnitude \(2r=20\,\mathrm{m}\).
    5. The average-velocity magnitude is \(20/(2\pi)=10/\pi\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), directed along the diameter.

    Answer: Average speed is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and average-velocity magnitude is \(10/\pi\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Setting the total acceleration to zero because the speed is constant.
    • Confusing distance travelled with displacement for a curved path.
    • Using \(v=2\pi r/T\) with a wrong sign or as an average relation for nonuniform motion.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 3 · Topic 20

    Centripetal force

    Laws of MotionMechanicsCircular MotionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Centripetal force is the name for the net inward force required to keep an object moving in a circular path of instantaneous radius \(r\). It is not a new interaction; gravity, tension, normal reaction, friction, or their components must together provide the inward resultant. Its magnitude is \(mv^2/r\) only for the inward component of the net force.
    Key formula(s). \[F_c=ma_c=\frac{mv^2}{r}=m\omega^2r\] ; \[\sum F_{\mathrm{inward}}=\frac{mv^2}{r}\] ; \[\text{vertical loop at top}:\quad mg+N=\frac{mv_{\mathrm{top}}^2}{r}\] ; \[\text{vertical loop minimum contact}:\quad N_{\mathrm{top}}=0\Rightarrow v_{\mathrm{top,min}}=\sqrt{gr}\]
    Key points.
    • No physical "centrifugal force" acts outward in the inertial frame; the net force points inward.
    • For a banked road, the horizontal and vertical components of the normal reaction together provide centripetal force.
    • At the top of a vertical loop, the inward direction is downward, so both weight and normal reaction may contribute.
    • The minimum-speed contact condition requires \(N\ge0\), not merely enough total force.
    • If attached by a string, the tension equation must be resolved along the inward radial direction at the chosen point.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass moves at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along a horizontal circle of radius \(20\,\mathrm{m}\). Find the net inward force required.

    1. The required centripetal force is \(F_c=mv^2/r\).
    2. Substituting gives \(F_c=2(10)^2/20=10\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. Its direction is toward the centre of the circle at every instant.
    4. The net inward force may be supplied by several real-force components acting together.

    Answer: The required net inward force is \(10\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Example 2.

    A small block moves inside a fixed vertical circular track of radius \(5\,\mathrm{m}\). Find its minimum speed at the top for which the block can remain in contact. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. At the top, both weight \(mg\) and normal reaction \(N\) point toward the centre.
    2. The radial equation is \(mg+N=mv^2/r\).
    3. The smallest permitted normal reaction is \(N=0\), because a track cannot pull the block inward.
    4. Thus \(mg=mv_{\min}^2/r\), so \(v_{\min}=\sqrt{gr}=\sqrt{50}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(v_{\min}=5\sqrt2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx7.07\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding an extra outward force to the forces already producing centripetal acceleration.
    • Equating \(mv^2/r\) with only one force when another force has an inward component.
    • Setting the top-of-loop normal force to a negative value instead of checking the contact condition.

    Explanation

    Concept. A conical pendulum consists of a bob moving in a horizontal circle while the string makes a constant angle \(\theta\) with the vertical. The vertical component of tension balances weight, while its horizontal component provides centripetal force. The radius of the circular path is \(r=L\sin\theta\), so the speed, tension, and period all depend on the angle as well as the string length.
    Key formula(s). \[r=L\sin\theta\] ; \[T\cos\theta=mg\] ; \[T\sin\theta=\frac{mv^2}{r}\] ; \[v=\sqrt{gr\tan\theta}=\sqrt{\frac{gL\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta}}\] ; \[T=\frac{mg}{\cos\theta},\qquad \tau=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L\cos\theta}{g}}\]
    Key points.
    • The string does not remain vertical because the bob must execute circular motion.
    • The centripetal force is the horizontal component \(T\sin\theta\), not the full tension.
    • The mass cancels from the speed and period for fixed \(L\) and \(\theta\).
    • Small-angle approximations are not assumed; the exact circle radius is \(L\sin\theta\).
    • The vertical force balance makes \(T>mg\), so tension must always be resolved before writing the radial equation.
    Example 1.

    A \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) bob is attached to a \(1\,\mathrm{m}\) string and moves as a conical pendulum with the string at \(37^\circ\) to the vertical. Find the circular radius, speed, and tension. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. With \(\sin37^\circ=3/5\) and \(\cos37^\circ=4/5\), the radius is \(r=L\sin37^\circ=3/5\,\mathrm{m}\).
    2. Vertical balance gives \(T=mg/\cos37^\circ=4(10)/(4/5)=50\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. From \(v^2=gr\tan37^\circ\), \(v^2=(10)(3/5)(3/4)=4.5\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\).
    4. Hence \(v=\sqrt{4.5}=3/\sqrt2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(r=0.60\,\mathrm{m}\), \(v=\frac{3}{\sqrt2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and \(T=50\,\mathrm{N}\).

    Example 2.

    A conical-pendulum bob is attached by a light string of length \(2\,\mathrm{m}\), and the string is at \(30^\circ\) to the vertical. Find its period of revolution, independent of the bob's mass. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The period follows from \(\tau=2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\theta/g}\).
    2. Substituting \(L=2\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(\theta=30^\circ\) gives \(\tau=2\pi\sqrt{2(\sqrt3/2)/10}\).
    3. Thus \(\tau=2\pi\sqrt{\sqrt3/10}\,\mathrm{s}\).
    4. The mass is absent because both the balancing and radial forces are proportional to it.

    Answer: \(\tau=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\sqrt3}{10}}\,\mathrm{s}\approx2.61\,\mathrm{s}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(L\cos\theta\) instead of \(L\sin\theta\) as the circle radius.
    • Equating the full tension with centripetal force.
    • Claiming the period depends on bob mass for fixed string length and angle.

    Chapter 3 · Topic 21

    Vehicle on level road

    Laws of MotionMechanicsCircular MotionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Level-road turning relies purely on static friction (mv2/r ≤ μsN) - speed limits (v ≤ √(μsrg)) beyond which skidding starts outward. Banking adds normal-component help (tanθ=v2/rg ideal, zero friction needed at design speed); wider tyres (area-independent grip) don't raise limits - friction depends on μN, not contact patch. Wet roads (μ crashes) demand slower curves - friction budgets shrink dangerously.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Friction alone turns level curves (v limit √(μrg)).
    • Banking adds normal help; area never matters.
    Remember
    • Wet μ crashes demand slower curve speeds.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Maximum safe speed on unbanked curve radius r is about

    Solution: Friction-provided centripetal force caps cornering speed.
    Key Formulas · Vehicle on Level Road
    \(\frac{mv^{2}}{r}\le\mu_{s}N\) friction supplies turning
    \(v_{max}=\sqrt{\mu_{s}rg}\) safe-speed cap on flat curves

    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 3 · Topic 22

    Vehicle on banked road

    Laws of MotionMechanicsCircular MotionStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A banked road is inclined so that the normal reaction alone has an inward horizontal component and an upward vertical component. For a frictionless banked curve at constant speed, \(N\sin\theta\) provides centripetal force and \(N\cos\theta\) balances weight. Friction must be included when the design speed differs from the speed at which no lateral friction is required.
    Key formula(s). \[\frac{v^2}{rg}=\tan\theta\quad\text{frictionless bank}\] ; \[v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}\] ; \[N\sin\theta+f\cos\theta=\frac{mv^2}{r}\] ; \[N\cos\theta-f\sin\theta=mg\quad\text{with friction down the slope}\] ; \[\frac{v^2}{rg}=\frac{\sin\theta+\mu\cos\theta}{\cos\theta-\mu\sin\theta}\]
    Key points.
    • A frictionless bank works without friction only at the design speed \(\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}\).
    • At speeds above the design value, the tendency is to slide up the slope, so friction acts down the slope.
    • On an unbanked road, lateral friction supplies all the centripetal force and gives \(v_{\max}=\sqrt{\mu rg}\).
    • Banking reduces reliance on friction and allows a higher safe speed.
    • The required friction must satisfy \(|f|\le\mu N\); otherwise the vehicle loses lateral grip.
    Example 1.

    A frictionless road is banked at \(30^\circ\) and has radius of curvature \(50\,\mathrm{m}\). Find the safe constant speed for a vehicle. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. For the frictionless bank, \(\tan\theta=v^2/(rg)\).
    2. Rearranging gives \(v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}\).
    3. Substituting \(r=50\,\mathrm{m}\), \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), and \(\tan30^\circ=1/\sqrt3\) gives \(v=\sqrt{500/\sqrt3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The normal reaction balances the weight vertically and supplies the inward horizontal component.

    Answer: \(v=\sqrt{\frac{500}{\sqrt3}}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx17.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A road is banked at \(30^\circ\) with radius \(50\,\mathrm{m}\). The coefficient of friction between tyre and road is \(0.20\). Find the maximum safe speed. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. At maximum speed, the vehicle tends to slide up the bank, so friction \(f=\mu N\) acts down the slope.
    2. Resolve the forces to obtain \(\frac{v^2}{rg}=\frac{\sin30^\circ+\mu\cos30^\circ}{\cos30^\circ-\mu\sin30^\circ}\).
    3. With \(\mu=0.2\), the ratio is approximately \(\frac{0.5+0.2(0.866)}{0.866-0.2(0.5)}\approx0.879\).
    4. Therefore \(v^2=0.879(10)(50)\approx439.5\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\).
    5. Taking the square root gives the maximum speed.

    Answer: \(v_{\max}\approx21.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), or \(75.5\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the frictionless bank relation for every speed when friction is available.
    • Directing friction up the bank at maximum speed.
    • Treating the normal reaction as horizontal and omitting its vertical balance equation.

    Deep Dive · Work in, energy around, power out

    Work-energy story: work (force-dot-displacement, positive-negative-zero by angle, constant versus variable force integrals) converts to kinetic energy (work-energy theorem: net work equals ΔK) and potential stores (gravitational mgh, spring ½kx², elastic extras) under conservation (mechanical constancy with conservative forces; non-conservative friction dissipates); power (work rate, average versus instantaneous) paces delivery; collisions (elastic kinetic-conserved, inelastic merged with restitution and 1D-2D analysis) test conservation; vertical circles (tension-gravity varying speeds, √(gr) loop-top critical) combine everything.
    NEET facts:
    • Net work equals kinetic change (work-energy theorem).
    • Elastic conserves kinetic too; perfectly inelastic merges with maximum loss.
    Fig: Kinetic converts to potential with frictional heat leaking.

    1

    Work-energy theorem states net work equals change in

    Solution: Net force-displacement integral accumulates as ΔK exactly.

    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 1

    Work

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsWorkStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Work is the scalar transfer of energy caused by a force acting through a displacement and is defined by the dot product \(\vec F\cdot d\vec r\). A force perpendicular to the instantaneous displacement does no work, while a force opposing displacement does negative work. For a general force field, the work may depend on the specified path, so the direction of motion must be tracked throughout the process.
    Key formula(s). \[dW=\vec F\cdot d\vec r=F\,ds\cos\theta\] ; \[W=\int\vec F\cdot d\vec r\] ; \[W=F s\cos\theta\quad\text{for a constant force and constant angle}\] ; \[W=\vec F\cdot\vec s\quad\text{for a constant force}\]
    Key points.
    • Work is a scalar measured in joule, with \(1\,\mathrm{J}=1\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
    • Only the component of force parallel to the instantaneous displacement contributes.
    • A perpendicular force may change the path without doing work on that segment.
    • Negative work means the force removes kinetic energy or increases potential energy.
    • Zero net work does not necessarily mean zero work by every individual force.
    Example 1.

    A constant force of \(10\,\mathrm{N}\) acts at \(60^\circ\) to the direction of motion while a particle moves \(2\,\mathrm{m}\). Find the work done.

    1. The work is \(W=\int\vec F\cdot d\vec r\), so only the parallel component matters.
    2. The parallel force component is \(F\cos60^\circ=5\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. Thus \(W=(F\cos60^\circ)s=5(2)=10\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. The positive sign is consistent with the force having a component along the displacement.

    Answer: The work done is \(10\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A constant force has Cartesian components \(F_x=5\,\mathrm{N}\) and \(F_y=3\,\mathrm{N}\). A particle undergoes displacement \(\Delta x=2.4\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(\Delta y=3.2\,\mathrm{m}\). Find the work done by the force.

    1. For constant components, \(W=F_x\Delta x+F_y\Delta y\).
    2. The first contribution is \(5(2.4)=12\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. The second contribution is \(3(3.2)=9.6\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. Therefore \(W=12+9.6=21.6\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(W=21.6\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Writing \(W=Fs\) without checking whether the force is parallel to the displacement.
    • Adding the magnitudes of work done by different forces before determining their signs.
    • Treating work as a vector and using the law of vector addition.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 2

    Positive work

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsWorkStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Positive work (force component along displacement: pushing crates forward, gravity pulling falling bodies) adds energy - cosθ positive for acute angles, maximum at θ=0 (W=Fs). Muscles, engines and falling weights do positive work routinely. Sign convention (positive adds, negative removes) tracks energy flow direction precisely - work-energy theorem balances the books.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Force along motion adds energy (acute angles).
    • Pushing forward, falling down do positive work.
    Remember
    • θ=0 maximises; acute angles stay positive.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Work is positive when force-displacement angle is

    Solution: Forward components add energy to bodies.
    Key Formulas · Positive Work
    \(W=Fs\cos\theta>0\;(\theta<90^{\circ})\) forward components add energy
    \(W_{max}=Fs\;(\theta=0)\) aligned push pays most
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 3

    Negative work

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsWorkStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Negative work (force opposing displacement: friction braking slides, gravity lifting loads, brakes stopping cars) removes energy - cosθ negative for obtuse angles, most negative at 180 degrees (W=-Fs). Muscles absorb (downhill walking thighs), brakes heat (kinetic to thermal), gravity taxes climbs. Negative work never destroys energy - it transfers to heat, sound or potential stores.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Opposing force removes energy (obtuse angles).
    • Friction, brakes and gravity climbs do negative work.
    Remember
    • Brakes convert kinetic to heat negatively.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Friction does work on sliding bodies that is

    Solution: Opposing displacement removes kinetic energy as heat.
    Key Formulas · Negative Work
    \(W=Fs\cos\theta<0\;(\theta>90^{\circ})\) opposing components remove energy
    \(W_{fric}=-\mu_{k}Nd\) friction billing by distance

    Chapter 4 · Topic 4

    Zero work

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsWorkStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Zero work happens three ways: zero force (inertia coasting), zero displacement (pushing walls, holding loads - muscles tire without physics work), or perpendicular force-displacement (circular motion centripetal force, satellites orbiting, charges in magnetic fields - cos90°=0). Weightlifters holding barbells do zero physics work despite effort - force without displacement moves no energy.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • No force, no displacement, or perpendicular - all give zero.
    • Circular centripetal force never works (always perpendicular).
    Remember
    • Holding loads tires muscles yet does zero physics work.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Work done by centripetal force in uniform circular motion is

    Solution: Perpendicular force-motion pairs transfer no energy.
    Key Formulas · Zero Work
    \(W=0\;\mathrm{if\;}F=0,\,s=0,\,\theta=90^{\circ}\) three routes to nothing
    \(W_{centripetal}=0\;\mathrm{always}\) perpendicular force never pays
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 5

    Constant force

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsWorkStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The work done by a constant force depends only on the force vector and the net displacement, because the integration limits are fixed and the force components do not change. Equivalently, it is \(Fs\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the force and displacement. This constant-force result can be used even when the actual path is curved.
    Key formula(s). \[W=\vec F\cdot(\vec r_f-\vec r_i)=Fs\cos\theta\] ; \[W=F_x\Delta x+F_y\Delta y+F_z\Delta z\] ; \[W_g=mg(y_i-y_f)\quad\text{for a uniform gravitational field}\]
    Key points.
    • A curved path does not affect the work of a constant force.
    • The angle is measured between the force and total displacement, not between the force and every path segment.
    • If either the force or displacement is zero, the work is zero.
    • Work by gravity is the weight multiplied by the net vertical drop, independent of the route.
    • For several constant forces, total work is the algebraic sum of their individual dot products.
    Example 1.

    A constant force of \(20\,\mathrm{N}\) acts on a block that moves \(10\,\mathrm{m}\) along a path whose net displacement makes an angle \(30^\circ\) with the force. Find the work done by the force.

    1. The net displacement has magnitude \(10\,\mathrm{m}\), even if the path is curved.
    2. Apply \(W=\vec F\cdot\Delta\vec r=Fs\cos30^\circ\).
    3. Substitution gives \(W=20(10)(\sqrt3/2)\).
    4. Therefore \(W=100\sqrt3\,\mathrm{J}\), which is positive.

    Answer: \(W=100\sqrt3\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A constant force has components \(\vec F=(8\hat i+6\hat j)\,\mathrm{N}\). A particle moves through displacement \(\Delta\vec r=(-3\hat i+4\hat j)\,\mathrm{m}\). Find the work done.

    1. Use the component form \(W=F_x\Delta x+F_y\Delta y\).
    2. The \(x\)-contribution is \(8(-3)=-24\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. The \(y\)-contribution is \(6(4)=24\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. Since the contributions cancel, the total work is zero.

    Answer: \(W=0\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Taking the angle between force and the initial tangent of a curved path.
    • Adding \(F_x\Delta x\) and \(F_y\Delta y\) without their algebraic signs.
    • Assuming zero work means the force is zero; it may be perpendicular to the displacement.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 6

    Variable force

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsWorkStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. When force or its direction varies, work is the path integral \(W=\int\vec F\cdot d\vec r\), not a single product of final values. In one dimension this becomes an area under the force-position graph. A linear force law can be integrated using the average of its initial and final values.
    Key formula(s). \[W=\int_{x_i}^{x_f}F(x)\,dx\] ; \[W=\int_{x_i}^{x_f}[F_x(x,y)\,dx+F_y(x,y)\,dy]\] ; \[F=F_i+k(x-x_i)\Rightarrow W=\frac{F_i+F_f}{2}(x_f-x_i)\] ; \[dW=\text{signed area under the }F\text{-}x\text{ graph}\]
    Key points.
    • A large graph area means large work magnitude, while the sign is determined by whether the force assists displacement.
    • A constant force is a special case of a variable-force integral.
    • The average-force shortcut is exact only when the force varies linearly with position.
    • If force depends on time as well as position, the actual position and velocity history must be used in \(F(x)\).
    • For radial work, write \(dW=F_r\,dr\) after choosing the radial direction consistently.
    Example 1.

    A particle moves along the positive \(x\)-axis from \(x=0\) to \(x=4\,\mathrm{m}\) under the variable force \(F(x)=5+2x\) newtons. Find the work done.

    1. Since the motion is one-dimensional, \(W=\int_0^4F(x)\,dx\).
    2. Substitute the force law to obtain \(W=\int_0^4(5+2x)\,dx\).
    3. Integrating gives \(W=[5x+x^2]_0^4=20+16\).
    4. The positive result is consistent with the force acting along the positive displacement.

    Answer: \(W=36\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A force field is \(\vec F=(3+x)\hat i+4\hat j\,\mathrm{N}\). A particle follows the path \(y=x^2/10\) from \((0,0)\) to \((10,5)\,\mathrm{m}\). Find the work done.

    1. The work is \(W=\int[(3+x)\,dx+4\,dy]\) between the endpoints.
    2. Along the path, \(\int_0^{10}(3+x)\,dx=[3x+x^2/2]_0^{10}=30+50=80\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. The vertical part contributes \(\int4\,dy=4(5-0)=20\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. Adding the signed contributions gives \(W=80+20=100\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(W=100\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Multiplying the final force by displacement in a variable-force problem.
    • Using the average-force formula for a non-linear \(F(x)\).
    • Interpreting area under the graph as always positive and ignoring the displacement direction.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 7

    Work-energy theorem

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsWorkStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a particle equals the change in its kinetic energy. It is a direct consequence of Newton's second law and avoids tracking time when a problem asks about speed. The theorem remains valid for any net force, provided the same inertial frame is used throughout.
    Key formula(s). \[W_{\mathrm{net}}=\Delta K=K_f-K_i\] ; \[\Delta K=\frac12m(v_f^2-v_i^2)\] ; \[W_{\mathrm{net}}=\int\vec F_{\mathrm{net}}\cdot d\vec r\] ; \[F_{\mathrm{net}}s=\frac12mv^2\quad\text{from rest, constant force along motion}\]
    Key points.
    • The theorem concerns the work of the resultant force, not the work of one chosen force in isolation.
    • In the absence of a net force, kinetic energy is constant in an inertial frame.
    • Nonzero net work can change only speed; it cannot directly change the direction of velocity.
    • A one-line energy calculation can replace kinematics when the net force is known.
    • Pseudo-forces may be used in a non-inertial frame only if the theorem is written for relative kinetic energy with the correct effective force balance.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block starts with speed \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). A constant net force of \(10\,\mathrm{N}\) acts along its displacement through \(5\,\mathrm{m}\). Find its final speed. Take the force to do positive work.

    1. The initial kinetic energy is \(K_i=\frac12(2)(4^2)=16\,\mathrm{J}\).
    2. The net work is \(W_{\mathrm{net}}=10(5)=50\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. By the work-energy theorem, \(K_f=16+50=66\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. Since \(K_f=\frac12(2)v_f^2=v_f^2\), \(v_f=\sqrt{66}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(v_f=\sqrt{66}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) block starts from rest and slides \(5\,\mathrm{m}\) down a rough incline with \(\sin37^\circ=3/5\), \(\cos37^\circ=4/5\), and \(\mu_k=0.2\). Find its speed at the end. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The work done by gravity is \(mg\sin37^\circ\,s=4(10)(3/5)(5)=120\,\mathrm{J}\).
    2. The normal reaction does no work, and friction does \(W_f=-\mu_kmg\cos37^\circ\,s=-0.2(40)(4/5)(5)=-40\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. Thus \(W_{\mathrm{net}}=120-40=80\,\mathrm{J}\), which equals the gain in kinetic energy.
    4. Therefore \(\frac12(4)v^2=80\), so \(v=\sqrt{40}=2\sqrt{10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(v=2\sqrt{10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the work of only gravity as the net work on a rough surface.
    • Setting final kinetic energy equal to net work even when initial kinetic energy is nonzero.
    • Including normal-reaction work without checking whether the normal is perpendicular to the path.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 8

    Kinetic energy

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsEnergyStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Kinetic energy is the energy associated with a particle's motion in a chosen inertial frame and is \(K=\frac12mv^2\). It is always nonnegative and depends on the square of speed, not its direction. The work-energy theorem identifies kinetic-energy change with net work, making it a central quantity in collision, projection, and force problems.
    Key formula(s). \[K=\frac12mv^2\] ; \[\Delta K=\frac12m(v_f^2-v_i^2)=W_{\mathrm{net}}\] ; \[K=\frac{p^2}{2m}\quad\text{in one dimension}\] ; \[K_{\mathrm{rel}}=\frac12\mu v_{\mathrm{rel}}^2,\qquad \mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}\]
    Key points.
    • Kinetic energy is frame dependent, unlike total energy conservation in a closed system.
    • For orthogonal velocity components, \(v^2=v_x^2+v_y^2\) and hence \(K=\frac12m(v_x^2+v_y^2)\).
    • A doubled speed gives four times the kinetic energy.
    • The zero of kinetic energy is defined by zero speed and is physically unambiguous.
    • For a moving centre of mass, total kinetic energy splits into translational and relative parts.
    Example 1.

    Find the kinetic energy of a \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle moving at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and state its value if the speed is doubled without changing direction.

    1. The kinetic energy is \(K=\frac12mv^2\).
    2. Substitution gives \(K=\frac12(4)(5^2)=50\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. Doubling the speed to \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) multiplies \(v^2\), and hence \(K\), by four.
    4. The new kinetic energy is \(4(50)=200\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The original kinetic energy is \(50\,\mathrm{J}\), and at twice the speed it is \(200\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle initially moves at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along the \(x\)-axis. Its final velocity has magnitude \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along the \(y\)-axis. Find the net work done on it.

    1. The initial kinetic energy is \(\frac12(2)(3^2)=9\,\mathrm{J}\).
    2. The final kinetic energy is \(\frac12(2)(5^2)=25\,\mathrm{J}\); the perpendicular direction does not alter the speed-squared formula.
    3. By the work-energy theorem, \(W_{\mathrm{net}}=K_f-K_i\).
    4. Therefore \(W_{\mathrm{net}}=25-9=16\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The net work is \(16\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding signed velocity components when finding \(v^2\).
    • Assuming kinetic energy determines the direction of motion.
    • Forgetting that the work-energy theorem uses net work.

    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 9

    Potential energy

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsEnergyStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Potential energy is position-dependent energy associated with a conservative interaction and is defined so that the work done by that interaction changes it in the opposite sense. Only a difference in potential energy is physically meaningful, since its additive constant is arbitrary. In one dimension, a conservative force obeys \(F=-dU/dx\).
    Key formula(s). \[\vec F=-\nabla U\] ; \[\Delta U=U_f-U_i=-\int_i^f\vec F\cdot d\vec r\] ; \[W_{\mathrm{cons}}=U_i-U_f\] ; \[U(x_2)-U(x_1)=-\int_{x_1}^{x_2}F(x)\,dx\]
    Key points.
    • A value of potential energy at one point is arbitrary, but differences are frame and reference independent.
    • Zero potential energy is not necessarily the point where the force is zero.
    • Potential energy can be positive or negative; kinetic energy cannot be negative.
    • If other forces also act, total kinetic-energy change is governed by the work of all forces, not by potential energy alone.
    • Units of \(U\) and work are joule, and for one-dimensional potentials \(F\) is minus the slope of the \(U\)-versus-position graph.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) ball falls vertically from rest through a height \(5\,\mathrm{m}\) in a uniform gravitational field. Find the change in gravitational potential energy and the work done by gravity. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. Taking upward as positive, a downward displacement has \(\Delta y=-5\,\mathrm{m}\).
    2. The potential-energy change is \(\Delta U=mg\Delta y=2(10)(-5)\).
    3. Thus \(\Delta U=-100\,\mathrm{J}\), meaning potential energy decreases.
    4. The work by gravity is \(W_g=-\Delta U=+100\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(\Delta U=-100\,\mathrm{J}\) and \(W_g=100\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    In a conservative one-dimensional field, \(U(x)=2x^2-8x+4\) when \(x\) is in metres and \(U\) is in joules. A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle starts at \(x=0\) with speed \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and moves in the positive \(x\)-direction. Find its first turning point.

    1. At \(x=0\), \(U_i=4\,\mathrm{J}\) and \(K_i=\frac12(2)(2^2)=4\,\mathrm{J}\).
    2. The force is \(-dU/dx=8-4x\), so it points right at \(x=0\); the particle initially moves in the positive direction.
    3. Total mechanical energy is \(E=4+4=8\,\mathrm{J}\), and is conserved because the force is conservative.
    4. At a turning point \(K=0\), so \(2x^2-8x+4=8\).
    5. This gives \(2x^2-8x-4=0\), or \(x=2\pm\sqrt6\).

    Answer: The first turning point reached while moving right is \(x=2+\sqrt6\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating the numerical value of \(U\) at a point as reference-independent.
    • Using \(W=\Delta U\) instead of \(W_{\mathrm{cons}}=-\Delta U\).
    • Confusing a point where \(U=0\) with a point where \(F=0\).

    Chapter 4 · Topic 10

    Gravitational potential energy

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsEnergyStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is \(mgy\), where \(y\) is measured from a chosen horizontal reference level. Only the change in height matters for a uniform field, and the work done by gravity equals the loss in gravitational potential energy. For planetary-scale height changes, \(g\) must be treated as variable and universal-gravitational potential energy is used.
    Key formula(s). \[U_g=mgy\quad\text{for uniform }g\] ; \[\Delta U_g=mg(y_f-y_i)\] ; \[W_g=mg(y_i-y_f)=-mg\Delta y\] ; \[U_g=-\frac{GMm}{r},\qquad \Delta U_g=GMm\left(\frac1{r_f}-\frac1{r_i}\right)\] ; \[W_g=\int_{y_i}^{y_f}-mg(y)\,dy\]
    Key points.
    • The zero of \(mgy\) changes when the reference level changes, but \(\Delta U_g\) does not.
    • On a frictionless track, loss of gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy.
    • A body can have zero gravitational potential energy yet nonzero total mechanical energy.
    • For constant \(g\), a lower final height always means a negative change in \(U_g\).
    • The approximation \(U=mgy\) is local; it is not valid for very large changes in distance from Earth.
    Example 1.

    A \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) body is lowered vertically through \(4\,\mathrm{m}\) in a uniform gravitational field. Find the change in its gravitational potential energy and the work done by gravity. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The vertical displacement is \(\Delta y=-4\,\mathrm{m}\).
    2. The potential-energy change is \(\Delta U_g=mg\Delta y=3(10)(-4)\).
    3. Therefore \(\Delta U_g=-120\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. Gravity does positive work equal in magnitude to this loss: \(W_g=-\Delta U_g=120\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(\Delta U_g=-120\,\mathrm{J}\) and \(W_g=120\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) body rises \(200\,\mathrm{m}\) where \(g\) decreases approximately linearly from \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) at the lower level to \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) at the upper level. Find the change in gravitational potential energy.

    1. For linearly varying \(g\), its average value over the height interval is \((10+8)/2=9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    2. The gravitational work is \(W_g=-m\bar g\Delta h=-5(9)(200)\).
    3. Thus the potential-energy increase is \(-\!W_g=9000\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. No other energy change is needed; the problem asks only for the gravitational potential difference.

    Answer: \(\Delta U_g=9.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Keeping \(g\) constant over a very large planetary height change.
    • Using the work done by an external lift as automatically equal to the potential-energy change if there is acceleration.
    • Reporting a unique absolute value of \(U_g\) without specifying a reference level.

    Chapter 4 · Topic 11

    Spring potential energy

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsEnergyStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. An ideal spring exerts the restoring force \(F=-kx\), where \(x\) is displacement from the spring's natural length. The corresponding spring potential energy is \(\frac12kx^2\), measured so that it is zero at the natural length. Energy methods reveal the maximum extension, equilibrium position, and speed at equilibrium without time-based kinematics.
    Key formula(s). \[F_s=-kx,\qquad k=-\frac{F}{x}\] ; \[U_s=\frac12kx^2\] ; \[k=\frac{F}{x}\quad\text{in magnitude for Hooke's law}\] ; \[x_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{mg}{k}\quad\text{for a vertical mass-spring system}\] ; \[x_{\max}=\frac{2mg}{k}\quad\text{when released from the natural length}\]
    Key points.
    • The restoring force is zero at the natural length but generally nonzero at the static equilibrium position.
    • A spring stores energy for both compression and extension because \(x\) enters quadratically.
    • The graph of spring potential energy versus position is a parabola.
    • Hooke's law is valid only within the spring's elastic range.
    • With no damping, total mechanical energy is conserved while contact and the elastic limit remain satisfied.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block on a smooth horizontal surface compresses a spring of constant \(100\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\) by \(0.60\,\mathrm{m}\) and is released from rest. Find its maximum speed when the spring returns to its natural length.

    1. With no friction or external force, mechanical energy is conserved.
    2. The initial spring energy is \(\frac12kx_0^2=\frac12(100)(0.60^2)=18\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. At maximum speed the spring is at its natural length, so all this energy is kinetic.
    4. Therefore \(\frac12(2)v_{\max}^2=18\), giving \(v_{\max}=3\sqrt2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(v_{\max}=3\sqrt2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block is attached to a vertical spring of constant \(100\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\), initially unstretched. It is released from rest and reaches a first maximum downward extension. Find that extension. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The spring is unstretched initially, so the initial mechanical energy can be set to zero.
    2. At maximum extension the speed is zero, while the gravitational potential-energy loss is \(mgx\).
    3. Conservation gives \(mgx=\frac12kx^2\).
    4. For the nonzero solution, \(x=2mg/k=2(2)(10)/100=0.40\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The first maximum extension is \(0.40\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Setting the maximum extension equal to the static-equilibrium extension \(mg/k\).
    • Giving spring potential energy a negative sign for extension in the usual convention.
    • Assuming the spring force is constant instead of proportional to deformation.

    Chapter 4 · Topic 12

    Elastic potential energy

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsEnergyStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Elastic potential energy (½kx2 stored in stretched springs, bent bows, drawn catapults) powers toys, clocks and pole vaults - spring constant k times square extension. Conservative (full recovery minus losses); combined with gravity in vertical oscillations (effective potentials add). Rubber bands heat on stretching (entropy elasticity) unlike metal springs - polymer versus crystal storage physics differ.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • ½kx2 stored in deformed elastic bodies.
    • Springs, bows and catapults bank stretch energy.
    Remember
    • Extension squared - double stretch quadruples storage.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Elastic potential energy in stretched spring equals

    Solution: Average force (kx/2) times extension gives storage.
    Key Formulas · Elastic Potential Energy
    \(U=\frac12kx^{2}\) stretch squared storage
    \(F=-kx\) Hooke restoring pull

    Chapter 4 · Topic 13

    Conservation of mechanical energy

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsEnergyStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy and remains constant when only conservative forces do work on an isolated system. A conservative force depends on position but its work between two fixed points is independent of the path, allowing a potential-energy function with \(F=-dU/dr\). JEE energy problems are often fastest when velocity is eliminated by equating \(K+U\) at chosen events, but every non-conservative work term must be retained.
    Key formula(s). \[E_{\mathrm{mech}}=K+U=\frac12mv^2+U(r)\]; \[F=-\nabla U\]; \[K_i+U_i+W_{\mathrm{nc}}=K_f+U_f\]; \[K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f\quad\text{when }W_{\mathrm{nc}}=0\]
    Key points.
    • Gravitational potential near Earth's surface is \(U=mgy\) only when \(g\) is treated as constant.
    • A spring stores \(U_s=\frac12kx^2\), measured from the spring's natural length.
    • Kinetic energy is nonnegative and is zero at every turning point where the given coordinate's velocity vanishes.
    • Use a different reference potential in each subproblem if it simplifies arithmetic; only energy differences matter.
    • For a particle, \(\Delta K=-W_{\mathrm{net}}\), while for a rigid body kinetic energy may also contain a rotational part.
    Example 1.

    A \(0.20\,\mathrm{kg}\) ball is released from rest through a vertical height of \(20\,\mathrm{m}\). Neglect air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. Mechanical energy is conserved because gravity is conservative and the drag force is absent.
    2. Thus \(mgh=\frac12mv^2\), where \(v\) is the speed just before impact.
    3. Cancelling the common mass gives \(v^2=2gh=2\times10\times20=400\).
    4. Taking the positive speed as required at release, \(v=20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The impact speed is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) block moves on a smooth horizontal surface attached to a spring of stiffness \(16\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\). At \(x=1\,\mathrm{m}\), its speed is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its greatest displacement from the mean position.

    1. The conserved energy at the stated instant is \(E=\frac12mv^2+\frac12kx^2\).
    2. Substitution gives \(E=\frac12(1)(25)+\frac12(16)(1)=12.5+8=20.5\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. At the extreme position the speed is zero, so all of this energy is spring potential energy: \(\frac12kx_{\max}^2=20.5\).
    4. Hence \(8x_{\max}^2=20.5\), so \(x_{\max}^2=41/16\).
    5. The amplitude is symmetric about the mean position, so the greatest distance on either side is the positive value of \(x_{\max}\).

    Answer: The greatest displacement is \(\frac{\sqrt{41}}{4}\,\mathrm{m}\approx1.60\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Applying \(mgh=K\) after a non-conservative force has already done work.
    • Setting total energy equal to \(\frac12mv^2\) at a turning point.
    • Forgetting that the reference level for potential energy may be changed.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 14

    Conservative force

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsEnergyStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A force is conservative if the work it does depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path between them. Such a force has zero net work around every closed path and can be represented as the negative gradient of a scalar potential. If only conservative forces act on a body or isolated system, total mechanical energy \(K+U\) is conserved.
    Key formula(s). \[\oint\vec F_{\mathrm{cons}}\cdot d\vec r=0\] ; \[\vec F_{\mathrm{cons}}=-\nabla U\] ; \[W_{\mathrm{cons},A\to B}=-\left(U_B-U_A\right)\] ; \[K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f\] ; \[F(x)=-dU/dx\]
    Key points.
    • Zero closed-path work is a stronger test than observing that a force is sometimes zero.
    • Gravity and an ideal spring are conservative; kinetic friction generally is not.
    • Conservative forces can exchange energy between kinetic and potential forms without dissipating it.
    • Mechanical-energy conservation does not apply if nonconservative work or an external transfer is present.
    • Reversing a conservative trajectory reverses the change in potential energy, even if the path differs.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body descends \(10\,\mathrm{m}\) under gravity and no other force acts. Find the work done by gravity and the change in its gravitational potential energy. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. Gravity is a conservative force, so \(W_g=-\Delta U_g\).
    2. The work done is \(W_g=mg\Delta h=2(10)(10)\).
    3. Therefore \(W_g=200\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. The potential-energy change is \(\Delta U_g=-200\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(W_g=200\,\mathrm{J}\) and \(\Delta U_g=-200\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) block is attached to a vertical spring of constant \(100\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\), initially at its natural length. It is released from rest and reaches maximum extension \(x\). Find \(x\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), and neglect damping.

    1. Gravity and the spring are both conservative, so \(K+U\) is conserved.
    2. Initially the speed and deformation are zero, so the total energy may be taken as zero.
    3. At maximum extension, \(K=0\), gravitational loss is \(mgx\), and spring energy is \(\frac12kx^2\).
    4. Thus \(mgx=\frac12kx^2\), giving the nonzero solution \(x=2mg/k\).
    5. Substitution gives \(x=2(1)(10)/100=0.20\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: \(x=0.20\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Calling a force conservative solely because it is path independent in one chosen example.
    • Using \(K+U=\text{constant}\) when friction or another nonconservative force does work.
    • Forgetting to test both initial and final conditions, especially the zero kinetic energy at maximum spring extension.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 15

    Non-conservative force

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsEnergyStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A non-conservative force does work that cannot be recovered from a change in potential energy associated with position alone. Friction, air drag, and internal deformation convert ordered mechanical energy into internal energy, so the work of such a force generally depends on the physical path. For JEE problems, isolate these forces and use \(\Delta K=W_{\mathrm{other}}\), rather than assuming conservation of speed between two positions.
    Key formula(s). \[W_f=\int \mathbf f\cdot d\mathbf r=-\int f_k\,ds\]; \[\Delta K=W_{\mathrm{cons}}+W_{\mathrm{nc}}\]; \[E_{\mathrm{mech},i}-E_{\mathrm{mech},f}=-W_{\mathrm{nc}}\]
    Key points.
    • Static friction may do no work, but kinetic friction normally does negative work on the sliding object.
    • On a rough plane of inclination \(\theta\), \(f_k=\mu_k mg\cos\theta\) when the surface normal is \(mg\cos\theta\).
    • The energy dissipated by kinetic friction over a distance \(s\) is \(Q=\mu_k N s\), not generally \(\mu_k mg s\).
    • Motorized or driven objects can gain mechanical energy from a non-conservative external agent.
    • Compare any two points by writing \(W_{\mathrm{nc}}=-\int\mathbf f_{\mathrm{nc}}\cdot d\mathbf r\) with one consistent sign convention.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block starts from rest and slides \(5\,\mathrm{m}\) down a rough incline with \(\sin\theta=3/5\), \(\cos\theta=4/5\), and \(\mu_k=0.25\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The normal reaction is \(N=mg\cos\theta=2\times10\times4/5=16\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. Hence the kinetic friction is \(f_k=\mu_kN=0.25\times16=4\,\mathrm{N}\), opposite the displacement.
    3. Its work is \(W_f=-f_ks=-4\times5=-20\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. Gravity does \(W_g=mgs\sin\theta=2\times10\times5\times3/5=60\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. Therefore \(K_f-K_i=W_g+W_f=40\,\mathrm{J}\); since \(K_i=0\), \(K_f=40\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The work done by friction is \(-20\,\mathrm{J}\), and the block gains \(40\,\mathrm{J}\) of kinetic energy.

    Example 2.

    A \(0.50\,\mathrm{kg}\) block is launched up a rough incline with \(u=6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), where \(\mu_k=0.50\), \(\sin\theta=3/5\), and \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the distance travelled before it stops and the total mechanical energy dissipated.

    1. During ascent, gravity and friction both oppose the motion, so their combined retarding force is \(mg\sin\theta+\mu_kmg\cos\theta\).
    2. Numerically, \(F_{\mathrm{ret}}=0.5\times10(3/5)+0.50\times0.5\times10(4/5)=5\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. Work-energy gives \(0-\frac12mu^2=-F_{\mathrm{ret}}s\), hence \(s=\frac{0.5\times0.5\times36}{5}=1.8\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. The gravitational potential-energy gain is \(mgs\sin\theta=0.5\times10\times1.8\times3/5=5.4\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. Friction dissipates \(\mu_kmg\cos\theta\,s=2\times1.8=3.6\,\mathrm{J}\).
    6. These add to the initial \(9\,\mathrm{J}\), so the mechanical-energy loss from release to rest is \(9.0\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The stopping distance is \(1.8\,\mathrm{m}\), and the total mechanical energy dissipated is \(9.0\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating \(\mu_kN\) as \(\mu_kmg\) on an incline.
    • Using conservation of mechanical energy in a path on which friction acts.
    • Assigning friction zero work merely because the force is constant.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 16

    Power

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsPower and CollisionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Power measures the rate at which energy is transferred or work is done, rather than the total work itself. For a force acting on a particle, instantaneous power is the scalar product of force and velocity, so a force perpendicular to motion does no instantaneous work. In JEE problems, identify whether the useful power is being delivered, absorbed, or wasted before applying \(P=dW/dt\).
    Key formula(s). \[P_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{W}{t}\]; \[P=\frac{dW}{dt}=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=Fv\cos\theta\]; \[P_{\mathrm{net}}=\frac{dK}{dt}=\sum_i\mathbf F_i\cdot\mathbf v_i\]
    Key points.
    • SI unit of power is watt, with \(1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}\).
    • \(P\) is positive when the force has a velocity component in its direction and negative when opposed to it.
    • A perpendicular force may constrain motion without doing work, as with ideal string tension on a mass moving transversely.
    • The power required to lift a body at constant speed against gravity is \(mgv_{\mathrm{vertical}}\).
    • \(1\,\mathrm{kW}=10^3\,\mathrm{W}\) and \(1\,\mathrm{hp}=746\,\mathrm{W}\).
    Example 1.

    A person of mass \(60\,\mathrm{kg}\) climbs a height of \(4\,\mathrm{m}\) in \(8\,\mathrm{s}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), assume uniform motion, and neglect losses.

    1. The work done against gravity is \(W=mgh=60\times10\times4=2400\,\mathrm{J}\).
    2. Average power delivered to the person is \(P=W/t=2400/8=300\,\mathrm{W}\).
    3. Equivalently, the average vertical speed is \(h/t=4/8=0.50\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so \(P=mgv_{\mathrm{vertical}}=300\,\mathrm{W}\).
    4. No other mechanical work is needed if the idealized body is treated as a particle and energy losses are ignored.

    Answer: The power delivered is \(300\,\mathrm{W}\).

    Example 2.

    An engine drives a vehicle at a constant speed of \(72\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\) against a total resistive force of \(400\,\mathrm{N}\). Find the engine power if the drivetrain is ideal.

    1. Convert the speed: \(72\,\mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}=72/3.6=20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. At constant speed, the driving force balances the total resistance and has magnitude \(400\,\mathrm{N}\).
    3. Therefore the useful engine power is \(P=Fv=400\times20=8000\,\mathrm{W}\).
    4. This is also the rate at which kinetic and potential energies remain constant and the engine supplies lost work.

    Answer: The engine power is \(8.0\,\mathrm{kW}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Dividing force by time instead of work by time.
    • Using the full force when only its velocity component does work.
    • Confusing total energy dissipated with the power delivered to overcome it.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 17

    Average power

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsPower and CollisionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Average power is the total energy transferred divided by the elapsed time, and it describes only the net rate over an interval. When the net external work equals a change in kinetic energy, average power becomes \(\Delta K/\Delta t\), even if the force and velocity vary strongly during the interval. For a long journey, level portions may have zero average rate of change of kinetic or potential energy but still require power against resistance.
    Key formula(s). \[P_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{W_{\mathrm{net}}}{\Delta t}=\frac{\Delta K}{\Delta t}\]; \[P_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{\Delta U}{\Delta t}\quad\text{when }K\text{ is constant}\]; \[P_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{\mathbf F\cdot\Delta\mathbf r}{\Delta t}\quad\text{only for a constant force vector}\]
    Key points.
    • Average power is a time average and is not generally \(\mathbf F_{\mathrm{av}}\cdot\mathbf v_{\mathrm{av}}\).
    • With a constant net force and constant mass, \(P_{\mathrm{av}}=\mathbf F\cdot\frac{\Delta\mathbf r}{\Delta t}\).
    • For a vehicle moving at constant speed, useful engine power equals resistive force times speed.
    • A pump lifting volume flow rate \(Q\) through height \(h\) has minimum ideal power \(\rho gQh\).
    • A graph of power versus time has area equal to the work done during that interval.
    Example 1.

    A \(1000\,\mathrm{kg}\) car accelerates uniformly from \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to \(22\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) in \(5\,\mathrm{s}\). Neglect resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    1. The net work is the change in kinetic energy, \(W_{\mathrm{net}}=\Delta K\).
    2. The speed squared changes by \(22^2-2^2=484-4=480\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}\).
    3. Thus \(W_{\mathrm{net}}=\frac12(1000)(480)=240000\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. Average power is \(P_{\mathrm{av}}=240000/5=48000\,\mathrm{W}\).

    Answer: The average net power is \(4.8\times10^4\,\mathrm{W}\).

    Example 2.

    A pump lifts water at \(0.010\,\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}\) through a vertical height of \(15\,\mathrm{m}\). Take the density of water as \(1000\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) and \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), and neglect all losses.

    1. The mass flow rate is \(\dot m=\rho Q=1000\times0.010=10\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. Each kilogram gains gravitational potential energy \(gh=10\times15=150\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}\).
    3. The ideal average power is \(\dot mgh=10\times150=1500\,\mathrm{W}\).
    4. Any inefficiency increases the required input power above this ideal value.

    Answer: The ideal average power is \(1.5\,\mathrm{kW}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the average of endpoint powers without knowing the time dependence.
    • Replacing average speed with final speed in a variable-speed journey.
    • Using \(\Delta K/\Delta t\) when external forces also change potential energy.
