    Chapter 4 · Topic 18

    Instantaneous power

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsPower and CollisionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Instantaneous power is the limiting value of average power as the time interval shrinks around a given instant. For a particle, it is \(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\); consequently, only the component of force along velocity contributes. It also equals the rate of change of kinetic energy when \(\mathbf F\) is the resultant force, making power a useful bridge between force, velocity, and energy in JEE problems.
    Key formula(s). \[P=\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=Fv\cos\theta\]; \[P_{\mathrm{net}}=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac12mv^2\right)=\mathbf F_{\mathrm{net}}\cdot\mathbf v\]; \[P=\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\boldsymbol\omega\quad\text{for a rigid body about a fixed axis}\]
    Key points.
    • Unit dimensions are \(\mathrm{M L^2 T^{-3}}\).
    • At the top of a vertical projectile, the instantaneous power of gravity is zero because \(\mathbf g\) and \(\mathbf v\) are perpendicular.
    • Centripetal force is perpendicular to velocity for uniform circular motion and therefore has zero instantaneous power.
    • A constant force can have changing power when the angle between force and velocity changes.
    • For a motor, shaft power is \(P=\tau\omega\), with torque and angular velocity expressed in SI units.
    Example 1.

    At a certain instant, a \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle has velocity \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and experiences a net force of \(20\,\mathrm{N}\) along its direction of motion. Find its instantaneous net power.

    1. Instantaneous power from the resultant force is \(P_{\mathrm{net}}=\mathbf F_{\mathrm{net}}\cdot\mathbf v\).
    2. Force and velocity are parallel, so the included angle is \(0^\circ\).
    3. Therefore \(P_{\mathrm{net}}=20\times4\times\cos0^\circ=80\,\mathrm{W}\).
    4. This is also \(dK/dt\), even though the mass is not needed because the resultant force is already given.

    Answer: The instantaneous net power is \(80\,\mathrm{W}\).

    Example 2.

    A particle of mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves with \(\mathbf r(t)=t^2\mathbf i+2t^3\mathbf j\,\mathrm{m}\) and experiences \(\mathbf F(t)=2t\mathbf i\,\mathrm{N}\). Find its instantaneous power at \(t=2\,\mathrm{s}\).

    1. Differentiate the position to obtain velocity: \(\mathbf v(t)=2t\mathbf i+6t^2\mathbf j\).
    2. At \(t=2\,\mathrm{s}\), \(\mathbf v=4\mathbf i+24\mathbf j\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. The applied force is \(\mathbf F=4\mathbf i\,\mathrm{N}\).
    4. Taking their scalar product gives \(P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=4(4)+0(24)=16\,\mathrm{W}\).
    5. The large vertical velocity does no work because the applied force has no vertical component.

    Answer: The instantaneous power at \(t=2\,\mathrm{s}\) is \(16\,\mathrm{W}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Multiplying scalar magnitudes by \(\cos\theta\) when \(\theta>90^\circ\) and forgetting the negative sign.
    • Using speed when the force is not parallel to the path.
    • Treating centripetal power as the power needed to maintain speed.

    Chapter 4 · Topic 19

    Collisions

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsPower and CollisionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A collision is a short interaction in which bodies exert impulses on one another over a small interval, causing velocities to change. Total momentum is conserved during the collision only when the external impulse is negligible, but kinetic energy may be conserved, lost, or gained according to the physical interaction. The work done by the collision forces equals the change in kinetic energy, which is the cleanest way to quantify the energy loss.
    Key formula(s). \[\mathbf J=\int\mathbf F\,dt=m(\mathbf v_2-\mathbf v_1)\]; \[\mathbf P_i=\mathbf P_f\quad\text{if }J_{\mathrm{ext}}\simeq0\]; \[W_{\mathrm{coll}}=\Delta K=K_f-K_i\]; \[E_{\mathrm{loss}}=K_i-K_f\geq0\quad\text{for a passive collision}\]
    Key points.
    • Collisions are commonly approximated as instantaneous, so gravity contributes negligible impulse during impact.
    • The coefficient of restitution, not conservation of energy by itself, determines whether impact is elastic.
    • A passive collision has \(K_f\leq K_i\); an isolated system cannot acquire collision energy.
    • Impulse is an area on a force-time graph and momentum change has the same units as impulse.
    • For a wall treated as having infinite mass, the wall's speed change is negligible but its impulse is not.
    Example 1.

    A \(0.20\,\mathrm{kg}\) ball moving at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) strikes a stationary \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) ball. After impact the first ball rebounds at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the impulse on the first ball and the net work done by their collision forces.

    1. Take the incident direction as positive; the first ball's final velocity is \(v_{1f}=-6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. Its momentum change is \(\Delta p_1=m_1(v_{1f}-v_{1i})=0.20(-6-10)=-3.2\,\mathrm{N\,s}\), which is the impulse on it.
    3. Momentum conservation gives \(0.20(10)+2(0)=0.20(-6)+2v_2\), so the second ball leaves at \(v_2=1.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The net collision work equals the change in total kinetic energy: \(W=\frac12(0.20)(36-100)+\frac12(2)(1.6^2)\).
    5. This gives \(W=-6.4+2.56=-3.84\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The impulse on the first ball is \(-3.2\,\mathrm{N\,s}\), and the collision forces do \(-3.84\,\mathrm{J}\) of work on the two-ball system.

    Example 2.

    Two \(0.50\,\mathrm{kg}\) balls move along one line. Ball A has velocity \(+4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), ball B is at rest, and after impact A and B have equal velocities \(+2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the kinetic-energy loss.

    1. Before impact, the total momentum is \(p_i=(0.50)(4)+(0.50)(0)=2.0\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    2. After impact, \(p_f=(0.50)(2)+(0.50)(2)=2.0\,\mathrm{N\,s}\), verifying momentum conservation.
    3. The initial kinetic energy is \(K_i=\frac12(0.50)(4^2)=4.0\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. The final kinetic energy is \(K_f=2\left[\frac12(0.50)(2^2)\right]=2.0\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. For this passive collision, the mechanical energy dissipated is \(E_{\mathrm{loss}}=K_i-K_f=2.0\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The kinetic-energy loss is \(2.0\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Conserving kinetic energy without any collision condition.
    • Treating the external gravitational impulse as zero over a long fall instead of a short impact.
    • Using the sign of rebound velocity incorrectly in \(\Delta p=m(v_f-v_i)\).

    Chapter 4 · Topic 20

    Elastic collision

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsPower and CollisionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. An elastic collision is an ideal collision in which total kinetic energy and total momentum are both conserved. During a short impact, the interacting forces do a net-zero total work on the free system, even though each body may temporarily deform and exchange energy. The standard one-dimensional solutions follow directly from momentum conservation and \(v_{2f}-v_{1f}=u_1-u_2\).
    Key formula(s). \[m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2\]; \[v_2-v_1=u_1-u_2\]; \[v_1=\frac{(m_1-m_2)u_1+2m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}\]; \[v_2=\frac{2m_1u_1+(m_2-m_1)u_2}{m_1+m_2}\]
    Key points.
    • Elasticity is an idealization; real collisions dissipate some macroscopic kinetic energy.
    • A moving object striking a stationary wall reverses velocity only for a perfectly elastic normal collision.
    • Equal masses in one dimension exchange velocities after a head-on elastic collision.
    • In the centre-of-mass frame, elastic collision simply reverses every velocity.
    • Momentum conservation alone does not distinguish elastic from inelastic outcomes.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block moving at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) collides head-on with a stationary \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) block. Assume a perfectly elastic one-dimensional collision.

    1. Momentum conservation gives \(2(4)+1(0)=2v_1+1v_2\), so \(2v_1+v_2=8\).
    2. Elasticity gives \(v_2-v_1=u_1-u_2=4-0=4\).
    3. Substitution of \(v_2=v_1+4\) into momentum gives \(2v_1+v_1+4=8\).
    4. Hence \(v_1=4/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(v_2=16/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. The common centre-of-mass speed is \(8/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and reversing the relative velocities about it gives the same result.

    Answer: The final velocities are \(v_1=4/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(v_2=16/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) in the initial direction.

    Example 2.

    Two identical blocks, each of mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), collide head-on elastically. Before impact their velocities are \(+3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find both final velocities.

    1. For equal masses in one dimension, an elastic head-on collision exchanges the initial velocities.
    2. Thus the block initially at \(+3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) leaves with \(-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. The block initially at \(-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) leaves with \(+3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. Check momentum: the initial and final totals are both \(2(3-1)=4\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    5. Check energy: both states have total kinetic energy \(10\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The final velocities are exchanged: \(-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(+3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding rather than subtracting relative velocities for an elastic collision.
    • Assuming the heavier body stops in every elastic collision.
    • Solving from momentum conservation alone and omitting the elasticity condition.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 21

    Inelastic collision

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsPower and CollisionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. An inelastic collision conserves total momentum but not total kinetic energy; some energy becomes deformation, heat, sound, or other internal forms. The bodies need not stick together, provided the coefficient of restitution is less than one. In the centre-of-mass frame, an inelastic impact reduces the magnitude of relative velocity while keeping the centre-of-mass motion unchanged.
    Key formula(s). \[m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2\]; \[0\leq e=\frac{v_2-v_1}{u_1-u_2}<1\]; \[v_1=\frac{(m_1-em_2)u_1+m_2(1+e)u_2}{m_1+m_2}\]; \[E_{\mathrm{loss}}=\frac12\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}(u_1-u_2)^2(1-e^2)\]
    Key points.
    • Inelastic describes energy non-conservation, not necessarily zero relative velocity after impact.
    • The maximum energy loss for fixed masses and approach speed occurs at \(e=0\).
    • The energy-loss expression depends only on relative motion, not on the uniform centre-of-mass translation.
    • Splitting can be a physically active inelastic process if stored internal energy creates the fragments.
    • Momentum must be solved vectorially for oblique collisions and algebraically only with a consistent one-dimensional sign.
    Example 1.

    A \(0.20\,\mathrm{kg}\) ball moving at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) strikes a stationary \(0.30\,\mathrm{kg}\) block. After impact the ball continues at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the block's speed and the kinetic-energy loss.

    1. Take the initial direction as positive and use momentum conservation: \(0.20(10)=0.20(2)+0.30v\).
    2. Therefore \(v=[2.0-0.40]/0.30=16/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Initially, \(K_i=\frac12(0.20)(10^2)=10\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. Finally, \(K_f=\frac12(0.20)(2^2)+\frac12(0.30)(16/3)^2=\frac25+\frac{64}{15}=\frac{14}{3}\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. Therefore the passive impact loses \(K_i-K_f=10-14/3=16/3\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The block moves at \(16/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the kinetic-energy loss is \(16/3\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) body moving at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) suddenly fragments into \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) pieces. The \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) piece moves at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) in the original direction. Find the velocity of the \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) piece and the kinetic-energy change.

    1. The initial momentum is \(4(10)=40\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    2. Momentum conservation gives \(40=1(4)+3v_2\), hence \(v_2=12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. The initial kinetic energy is \(K_i=\frac12(4)(10^2)=200\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. The final kinetic energy is \(K_f=\frac12(1)(4^2)+\frac12(3)(12^2)=8+216=224\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. The difference is positive, so the supplied internal energy is \(24\,\mathrm{J}\), and the collision is not passive.

    Answer: The \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) piece moves at \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the kinetic-energy gain is \(24\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Calling every inelastic collision perfectly inelastic.
    • Obtaining \(K_f>K_i\) for a passive impact and failing to check physical admissibility.
    • Applying the reduced-mass energy-loss formula without reducing the masses correctly.

    Explanation

    Concept. In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies stick together immediately after contact and move with a common final velocity. Momentum conservation determines that velocity because the internal interaction impulse can be large while the external impulse remains negligible. The lost kinetic energy is maximum for the given approach velocity and equals the initial relative kinetic energy in the centre-of-mass frame.
    Key formula(s). \[v_f=\frac{m_1u_1+m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}\]; \[E_{\mathrm{loss}}=\frac12\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}(u_1-u_2)^2=\frac12\mu(u_1-u_2)^2\]; \[\mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}\]
    Key points.
    • The coefficient of restitution is \(e=0\) for a perfectly inelastic collision.
    • The common final velocity is always the initial centre-of-mass velocity.
    • Static friction after sticking is not automatically frictional loss; loss occurs during the deforming impact interval.
    • Momentum conservation is still valid, but kinetic-energy conservation is not used.
    • The greatest possible fractional loss occurs when the colliding masses are equal.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) cart moving at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) collides with and absorbs a stationary \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) block on a smooth horizontal surface. Find their common speed and energy dissipated.

    1. Since the bodies stick, apply \((m_1+m_2)v_f=m_1u_1+m_2u_2\).
    2. This gives \(6v_f=2(10)+4(0)=20\), hence \(v_f=10/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. The initial kinetic energy is \(K_i=\frac12(2)(10^2)=100\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. The final kinetic energy is \(K_f=\frac12(6)(10/3)^2=100/3\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. Thus \(E_{\mathrm{loss}}=100-100/3=200/3\,\mathrm{J}\), equal to \(\frac12\mu u_{\mathrm{rel}}^2\).

    Answer: Their common speed is \(10/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and \(200/3\,\mathrm{J}\) is dissipated.

    Example 2.

    A \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) cart moving at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) catches a \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) block moving in the same direction at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). They stick on a smooth surface. Find the common velocity and the kinetic-energy loss.

    1. Total initial momentum is \(3(6)+1(2)=20\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    2. Momentum conservation for the combined \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass gives \(4v_f=20\).
    3. Hence \(v_f=5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the relative approach speed was \(6-2=4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The reduced mass is \(\mu=(3)(1)/(3+1)=3/4\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    5. Therefore \(E_{\mathrm{loss}}=\frac12(3/4)(4^2)=6\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The common velocity is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the kinetic-energy loss is \(6\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Setting the final kinetic energy equal to the initial kinetic energy.
    • Using a weighted average that omits the relative direction of the initial velocities.
    • Assuming sticking dissipates zero energy because the bodies move together afterward.

    Explanation

    Concept. The coefficient of restitution measures the ratio of relative speed of separation to relative speed of approach along the line of impact. It ranges from zero for a perfectly inelastic collision to one for a perfectly elastic collision. For oblique collisions, restitution applies only to velocity components normal to the line of impact, while tangential components require additional collision-surface information.
    Key formula(s). \[e=-\frac{(\mathbf v_1-\mathbf v_2)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}}{(\mathbf u_1-\mathbf u_2)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}}\]; \[e=\frac{v_2-v_1}{u_1-u_2}\quad\text{in 1D with the right sign convention}\]; \[0\leq e\leq1\quad\text{for a passive impact}\]
    Key points.
    • Both masses do not appear directly in the definition; relative velocities determine the loss of relative kinetic energy.
    • A compliant body is more elastic, and thus has larger \(e\), when it compresses more during impact.
    • \(e\) is constant only for collisions between the same pair of materials over the relevant impact speed range.
    • In two dimensions, the impulse acts along the line of impact if the surfaces are smooth.
    • Solving momentum conservation together with \(e\) determines final velocities in one dimension.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body moving at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) strikes a stationary \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) body in one dimension. If \(e=0.50\), find both final velocities and the kinetic-energy loss.

    1. Momentum conservation gives \(2(4)=2v_1+v_2\).
    2. Restitution gives \(v_2-v_1=0.50(4-0)=2\).
    3. Using \(v_2=v_1+2\) in momentum yields \(2v_1+v_1+2=8\), so \(v_1=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. Consequently \(v_2=4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which indeed gives relative separation speed \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. The kinetic energies are \(K_i=16\,\mathrm{J}\) and \(K_f=\frac12(2)(2^2)+\frac12(1)(4^2)=12\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The final velocities are \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the energy loss is \(4\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(0.20\,\mathrm{kg}\) ball moving at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) catches a \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) cart moving in the same direction at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). After impact the ball continues forward at \(0.50\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the cart velocity, coefficient of restitution, and energy loss.

    1. Momentum conservation gives \(0.20(10)=0.20(0.50)+1v_c\), so \(v_c=1.90\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. The approach relative speed is \(u_1-u_2=10-4=6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. The separation relative speed is \(v_2-v_1=1.90-0.50=1.40\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so \(e=1.40/6=7/30\).
    4. The initial kinetic energy is \(K_i=\frac12(0.20)(10^2)+\frac12(1)(4^2)=18\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. Finally, \(K_f=\frac12(0.20)(0.50^2)+\frac12(1)(1.90^2)=1.83\,\mathrm{J}\), giving a passive loss of \(16.17\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The cart moves at \(1.90\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(e=7/30\), and the energy loss is \(16.17\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Dividing either velocity by the corresponding velocity of the other body.
    • Applying restitution to the tangential component in an oblique collision.
    • Ignoring the result \(e>1\), which signals incompatible or active-impact data.

    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 22

    One-dimensional collision

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsPower and CollisionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A one-dimensional collision requires one sign convention for all velocities, with magnitudes used only after the collision nature is identified. Momentum conservation supplies one equation and the coefficient of restitution supplies the second, or energy conservation may replace restitution for an elastic impact. A useful check is that the relative velocity reverses for \(e=1\), vanishes for \(e=0\), and is reduced by the factor \(e\) otherwise.
    Key formula(s). \[m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2\]; \[v_2-v_1=-e(u_2-u_1)\]; \[v_1=\frac{(m_1-em_2)u_1+m_2(1+e)u_2}{m_1+m_2}\]; \[v_2=\frac{m_1(1+e)u_1+(m_2-em_1)u_2}{m_1+m_2}\]
    Key points.
    • Choose rightward positive once and retain negative signs for leftward velocities.
    • For a rear-end impact, \(u_1-u_2>0\); for opposing motion, signed relative velocities automatically handle the reversal.
    • A final separation speed is expected for passive impact, not a continued approach after the bodies separate.
    • Verify the final velocities against both momentum and the definition of \(e\).
    • For same-direction impacts, blindly exchanging velocities or assuming one body stops is usually wrong.
    Example 1.

    A \(0.20\,\mathrm{kg}\) ball moving at \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) hits a stationary \(0.30\,\mathrm{kg}\) block in a direct one-dimensional impact with \(e=0.20\). Find the final velocities.

    1. The approach speed is \(u_1-u_2=20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. Restitution requires \(v_2-v_1=0.20(20)=4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Momentum conservation gives \(0.20(20)=0.20v_1+0.30v_2\), or \(0.20v_1+0.30v_2=4\).
    4. Substitution of \(v_2=v_1+4\) yields \(0.50v_1+1.20=4\), so \(v_1=5.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. Hence \(v_2=9.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); both move forward, but the block now has the greater speed.

    Answer: The final velocities are \(5.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(9.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) car moving at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) rear-ends a \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) car moving at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The coefficient of restitution is \(0.50\). Find the final velocities and kinetic-energy loss.

    1. Take the common direction as positive, so the approach relative speed is \(u_1-u_2=6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. Restitution gives \(v_2-v_1=0.50(6)=3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Momentum conservation gives \(4(10)+2(4)=4v_1+2v_2=48\).
    4. Substituting \(v_2=v_1+3\) gives \(6v_1+6=48\), hence \(v_1=7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(v_2=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. The initial kinetic energy is \(216\,\mathrm{J}\), while the final value is \(\frac12(4)(7^2)+\frac12(2)(10^2)=198\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The final velocities are \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), with an \(18\,\mathrm{J}\) energy loss.

    Common mistakes.
    • Replacing signed velocities by magnitudes before applying momentum conservation.
    • Assuming equal masses exchange velocities in a non-elastic same-direction collision.
    • Omitting the relative-velocity equation and assuming the impact is elastic.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 4 · Topic 23

    Two-dimensional collision

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsPower and CollisionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. In a two-dimensional collision, total momentum is conserved independently along two chosen axes. For smooth bodies the contact impulse acts along the line joining the impact points, so tangential velocity components of each smooth body are unchanged. The restitution condition constrains only the relative velocity component along that line, and physical admissibility requires that it correspond to separation rather than continued approach.
    Key formula(s). \[m_1\mathbf u_1+m_2\mathbf u_2=m_1\mathbf v_1+m_2\mathbf v_2\]; \[(\mathbf v_2-\mathbf v_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=-e(\mathbf u_2-\mathbf u_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\]; \[\mathbf u_{i\parallel}=\mathbf v_{i\parallel}\quad\text{for smooth surfaces}\]
    Key points.
    • Conservation along one Cartesian axis remains valid even when the other component changes.
    • Smoothness does not conserve each body's speed, only its tangential component and the system's normal momentum through restitution.
    • The line of impact is perpendicular to the common contact tangent at the instant of collision.
    • Equal smooth masses with one initially at rest have outgoing paths perpendicular after impact.
    • A final answer is invalid if the bodies approach each other along the line after a passive collision.
    Example 1.

    Two identical smooth balls collide on a smooth horizontal surface. Ball A approaches at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), ball B is at rest, and afterward A moves at \(30^\circ\) below the initial line while B moves at \(60^\circ\) above it. Find their speeds.

    1. Let the final speeds be \(v_A\) and \(v_B\); conserve vertical momentum: \(-v_A\sin30^\circ+v_B\sin60^\circ=0\).
    2. Thus \(v_B=v_A\sin30^\circ/\sin60^\circ=v_A/\sqrt3\).
    3. Horizontal momentum conservation gives \(5=v_A\cos30^\circ+v_B\cos60^\circ\).
    4. Substitution gives \(5=(\sqrt3/2)v_A+(1/2)(v_A/\sqrt3)=(2/\sqrt3)v_A\).
    5. Hence \(v_A=5\sqrt3/2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(v_B=5/2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    6. The two paths are perpendicular, as expected for a smooth oblique collision of equal masses when one is initially stationary.

    Answer: Ball A leaves at \(\frac{5\sqrt3}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and ball B at \(\frac52\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body moves at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along the \(x\)-axis and strikes a stationary \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) body. Afterward their paths make angles \(30^\circ\) and \(-30^\circ\) with the initial line. Find the two speeds and verify the energy change.

    1. Let the \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body leave with speed \(v\) at \(30^\circ\), and the \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) body with speed \(u\) at \(-30^\circ\).
    2. Vertical momentum gives \(2v\sin30^\circ-u\sin30^\circ=0\), hence \(u=2v\).
    3. Horizontal momentum gives \(2(10)=2v\cos30^\circ+u\cos30^\circ\), or \(20=\sqrt3(v+u/2)\).
    4. Using \(u=2v\), \(20=2\sqrt3v\), so \(v=10/\sqrt3\) and \(u=20/\sqrt3\).
    5. The final kinetic energy is \(\frac12(2)(100/3)+\frac12(1)(400/3)=100\,\mathrm{J}\).
    6. This equals the initial energy, so the specified outcome is an elastic collision with zero energy loss.

    Answer: The speeds are \(10/\sqrt3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(20/\sqrt3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), with zero kinetic-energy change.

    Common mistakes.
    • Applying scalar relative-velocity formula to components not along the line of impact.
    • Conserving kinetic energy for an unspecified oblique collision.
    • Ignoring transverse impulse when the colliding surfaces are rough.

    Vertical circular motion

    Work, Energy and PowerMechanicsPower and CollisionsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Vertical circular motion (string whirls, roller coasters, bucket swings) varies speed (gravity speeds descents, slows climbs) while tension adjusts (maximum bottom: mg plus mv2/r; minimum top: mv2/r minus mg). Loop-the-loop needs top speed √(gr) keeping strings taut (normal non-negative); energy conservation links heights to speeds throughout. Critical velocity √(rg) separates completing loops from falling short.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Speed varies with height; tension adjusts to provide centripetal needs.
    • Top needs v²/r ≥ g keeping strings taut.
    Vertical circle

    BottomMax tension: mg + mv²/r
    TopMin tension: mv²/r - mg ≥ 0
    Critical speed√(gr) completes loops

    Deep Dive · Spin doctors: mass points to rigid bodies

    Rotation builds on mass points: centre of mass (two-particle to continuous bodies, motion with momentum conservation plus rocket-collision extras) locates average mass; rotational kinematics (angular displacement-velocity-acceleration mirroring linear) describes spin; dynamics (torque as moment of force, angular momentum with conservation, moment of inertia with parallel-perpendicular theorems plus standard bodies, rotational kinetic energy with rolling extras) causes it; equilibrium (net force plus torque zero) plus rigid-body rotation equations (mirroring linear with θ-ω-α mapping) complete the toolkit. Translate linear results rotationally via mapping.
    NEET facts:

    • Angular momentum conserves without external torque (ice-skater spins faster).

    Chapter 5 · Topic 1

    Centre of mass

    Rotational MotionMechanicsCentre of MassStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The centre of mass of a system is the mass-weighted point whose position represents the system in equations for total momentum. Equal and opposite internal forces cancel pairwise, so they do not change total momentum or the acceleration of the centre of mass. Only the resultant external force changes that acceleration, which is the bridge between Newton's laws and many-particle problems.
    Key formula(s). \[\mathbf R_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{\sum_i m_i\mathbf r_i}{M},\qquad M=\sum_i m_i\]; \[\mathbf a_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}}{M}\]; \[\mathbf P=M\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}\]
    Key points.
    • The centre of mass need not coincide with any material point of the system.
    • Internal forces cancel only when they obey Newton's third law and act on the same pair.
    • Gravity and normal force can be treated as external when deciding the whole-system motion.
    • For a non-rigid system, the centre of mass can move even if every internal shape is unchanged.
    • On Earth, the locally measured \(g\) may be replaced by \(GM_{\mathrm E}/R^2\) when gravity varies significantly.
    Example 1.

    Three particles of masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), and \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) are at \(x=0\), \(2\,\mathrm{m}\), and \(5\,\mathrm{m}\) on a smooth line. A net external force of \(12\,\mathrm{N}\) acts in the positive \(x\)-direction for \(4\,\mathrm{s}\) from rest. Find the final velocity of the centre of mass.

    1. The total mass is \(M=2+3+1=6\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    2. The initial centre-of-mass coordinate is \(X_i=[2(0)+3(2)+1(5)]/6=11/6\,\mathrm{m}\).
    3. The external acceleration of the centre of mass is \(A_{\mathrm{cm}}=F_{\mathrm{ext}}/M=12/6=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    4. Starting from rest, \(V_{\mathrm{cm}}=A_{\mathrm{cm}}t=2(4)=8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. The coordinates of the individual particles need not be tracked because internal forces do not affect this result.

    Answer: The centre of mass moves at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle at \(x=1\,\mathrm{m}\) and a \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle at \(x=4\,\mathrm{m}\) are acted on only by their mutual interaction. Initially at rest, they become \(5\,\mathrm{m}\) closer after \(2\,\mathrm{s}\). Find the acceleration of the centre of mass.

    1. Internal mutual forces occur in equal-and-opposite pairs, so their resultant is zero.
    2. Therefore \(\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}=0\) and \(A_{\mathrm{cm}}=F_{\mathrm{ext}}/M=0\).
    3. The centre of mass initially has zero velocity, so it remains at rest even though both particles move.
    4. Their separation can decrease while their centre remains fixed, as in a head-on gravitational collapse.

    Answer: The centre-of-mass acceleration is zero.

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating internal forces as causing centre-of-mass acceleration.
    • Equating centre of mass with the geometric centre of the geometric extent regardless of mass distribution.
    • Using component-wise momentum of only one particle as total momentum.

    Explanation

    Concept. The position of the centre of mass is obtained by taking moments of all mass elements about a chosen origin and dividing by total mass. A convenient origin can reduce arithmetic; shifting the origin changes every reported coordinate but not the physical location of the centre of mass. For a two-body system, the heavier mass lies closer to the centre of mass than the lighter mass.
    Key formula(s). \[x_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{\sum_i m_ix_i}{\sum_i m_i}\]; \[\mathbf R_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{\sum_i m_i\mathbf r_i}{M}\]; \[\Delta x_{\mathrm{cm}}=x'_{\mathrm{cm}}-x_{\mathrm{cm}}=\Delta x_O\]
    Key points.
    • A shift of origin by \(-\mathbf a\) shifts every reported coordinate by \(-\mathbf a\).
    • The balance condition is \(\sum_i m_i x_i=Mx_{\mathrm{cm}}\).
    • Symmetry may locate the centre instantly only when the mass distribution shares that symmetry.
    • Coordinates of point particles may be averaged only if their masses are equal.
    • Taking moments about a proposed centre and setting their sum to zero is often the fastest JEE setup.
    Example 1.

    Particles of masses \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\), and \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) lie on the \(x\)-axis at \(x=-1\,\mathrm{m}\), \(4\,\mathrm{m}\), and an unknown \(x_3\). Find \(x_3\) if the centre of mass is at the origin.

    1. For a centre of mass at \(x=0\), the weighted coordinate sum must vanish.
    2. Thus \(3(-1)+5(4)+2x_3=0\).
    3. The known moment is \(-3+20=17\,\mathrm{kg\,m}\).
    4. Therefore \(2x_3=-17\), giving \(x_3=-8.5\,\mathrm{m}\).
    5. The negative sign places the third particle to the left of the origin, as required to cancel the positive moment.

    Answer: The unknown particle is at \(x_3=-8.5\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Example 2.

    Four particles of masses \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), and \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) are located at \(x=-3\), \(-1\), \(2\), and \(4\,\mathrm{m}\). Find the centre of mass.

    1. Sum the masses to obtain \(M=1+2+3+2=8\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    2. The first moment is \(\sum m_ix_i=1(-3)+2(-1)+3(2)+2(4)=-3-2+6+8=9\,\mathrm{kg\,m}\).
    3. Divide this moment by total mass: \(x_{\mathrm{cm}}=9/8\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. The result lies to the right of the origin but left of the mass-heavy cluster, as expected.

    Answer: The centre of mass is at \(x_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac98\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Averaging coordinates without mass weights.
    • Treating visual symmetry as sufficient when masses are unequal.
    • Using moments with distance but forgetting the required side.

    Chapter 5 · Topic 2

    Two-particle system

    Rotational MotionMechanicsCentre of MassStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. For two isolated point masses, the centre of mass divides the line joining them internally in the inverse ratio of their masses. The nearer mass has the larger share of total mass and therefore lies closer to the balancing point. The same result applies to two extended bodies by replacing each mass and position with its own centre of mass and total mass.
    Key formula(s). \[m_1\mathbf r_1+m_2\mathbf r_2=(m_1+m_2)\mathbf R_{\mathrm{cm}}\]; \[\frac{r_1}{r_2}=\frac{m_2}{m_1}\quad\text{where }r_i=|\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R_{\mathrm{cm}}|\]; \[d=|\mathbf r_2-\mathbf r_1|,\qquad r_1=\frac{m_2d}{m_1+m_2},\quad r_2=\frac{m_1d}{m_1+m_2}\]
    Key points.
    • A balance beam gives \(m_1r_1=m_2r_2\), not \(m_1r_2=m_2r_1\).
    • For equal masses, the centre of mass is the midpoint.
    • As \(m_2\to0\), the centre of mass approaches the location of \(m_1\).
    • For unequal masses, the centre of mass is closer to the heavier object.
    • The formula is valid in three dimensions and does not require \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) to be calculated separately.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass is at \(x=0\) and a \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass is at \(x=12\,\mathrm{m}\). Find the centre of mass and the two distances from it.

    1. Apply the weighted-coordinate formula: \(x_{\mathrm{cm}}=[2(0)+3(12)]/5=36/5\,\mathrm{m}\).
    2. The first mass is therefore \(r_1=36/5-0=36/5\,\mathrm{m}\) from the centre.
    3. The second mass is \(r_2=12-36/5=24/5\,\mathrm{m}\) from the centre.
    4. The inverse-mass check gives \(r_1/r_2=36/24=3/2=m_2/m_1\).

    Answer: The centre of mass is at \(36/5\,\mathrm{m}\), with distances \(36/5\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(24/5\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\) body has its centre \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\) from a balance point. Where must a \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body be placed on the opposite side for balance?

    1. Moment balance requires \(m_1r_1=m_2r_2\).
    2. Substituting gives \(6(8)=2r_2\), so \(r_2=48/2=24\,\mathrm{cm}\).
    3. The two bodies must lie on opposite sides of the pivot for opposing moments.
    4. Their separation from each other is \(8+24=32\,\mathrm{cm}\).

    Answer: The \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body must be placed \(24\,\mathrm{cm}\) from the balance point on the opposite side.

    Common mistakes.
    • Writing \(m_1/r_1=m_2/r_2\) instead of \(m_1r_1=m_2r_2\).
    • Measuring both distances in the same direction from the pivot.
    • Forgetting that the ratio is inverse when the two distances are compared.

    Explanation

    Concept. For many particles, the centre of mass is the mass-weighted sum of all position vectors divided by the total mass. Masses may be grouped when particles share a location or when a symmetric set contributes zero net moment. The method remains valid in any dimension, and checking symmetry after grouping usually detects arithmetic errors.
    Key formula(s). \[\mathbf R_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{m_1\mathbf r_1+m_2\mathbf r_2+\cdots+m_N\mathbf r_N}{m_1+m_2+\cdots+m_N}\]; \[\sum m_i(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R_{\mathrm{cm}})=\mathbf0\]
    Key points.
    • Every particle must appear with its own mass and position in the moment sum.
    • Equal and opposite pairs cancel only when they have equal mass and equal moment arm.
    • A uniform row of equal particles has its centre at the midpoint of the first and last positions.
    • The coordinate sum and the mass sum must use matching units.
    • A mass moved by a distance \(\Delta r\) changes the centre of mass by only \(m\Delta r/M\).
    Example 1.

    Four particles of masses \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), and \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) are at \(x=1\), \(3\), \(5\), and \(7\,\mathrm{m}\). Find the centre of mass.

    1. Total mass is \(M=1+2+3+4=10\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    2. The first moment is \(1(1)+2(3)+3(5)+4(7)=1+6+15+28=50\,\mathrm{kg\,m}\).
    3. Therefore \(x_{\mathrm{cm}}=50/10=5\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. The weighted moments about \(x=5\) are \(1(-4)+2(-2)+3(0)+4(2)=0\,\mathrm{kg\,m}\).

    Answer: The centre of mass is at \(x=5\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle at \(x=1\,\mathrm{m}\) is moved by \(3\,\mathrm{m}\) to the right, while a \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle at \(x=8\,\mathrm{m}\) is moved by \(2\,\mathrm{m}\) to the left. Find the initial and final centre-of-mass positions.

    1. Initially, \(M=3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(x_i=[2(1)+1(8)]/3=10/3\,\mathrm{m}\).
    2. The final particle positions are \(x_1'=4\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(x_2'=6\,\mathrm{m}\).
    3. Thus \(x_f=[2(4)+1(6)]/3=14/3\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. The centre shifts by \(\Delta x=(2)(3)+(1)(-2)\) divided by \(3\), which is \(4/3\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The centre moves from \(10/3\,\mathrm{m}\) to \(14/3\,\mathrm{m}\), a rightward shift of \(4/3\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Forgetting a particle when it is hidden inside a grouped term.
    • Cancelling unequal masses located at equal distances.
    • Using a coordinate change without its corresponding mass weighting.

    Chapter 5 · Topic 3

    Centre of mass of rigid body

    Rotational MotionMechanicsCentre of MassStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A continuous body's mass is spread over a volume, area, or line, so its centre of mass is obtained by integrating mass-weighted position over all elements. A uniform body reduces this to finding the geometric centroid because its mass density is constant. Symmetry and the subtraction or addition method are often much faster than evaluating an integral directly in JEE problems.
    Key formula(s). \[\mathbf R_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{1}{M}\int\mathbf r\,dm\]; \[dm=\rho\,dV\quad\text{for a volume},\qquad dm=\sigma\,dA\quad\text{for a lamina}\]; \[x_{\mathrm{rod}}=\frac{L}{2}\quad\text{for a uniform rod measured from one end}\]
    Key points.
    • The origin must be specified, but choosing a symmetry point can make the integral vanish automatically.
    • A uniform semicircular arc has its centre of mass at \(2R/\pi\) from the circle centre, whereas a semicircular lamina has it at \(4R/(3\pi)\).
    • A rectangular lamina has centre of mass at its geometric centre.
    • To find a hole, subtract the removed uniform portion with its own centroid and negative mass.
    • For a thin wire bent into a shape, use the length element \(dm=\lambda\,ds\).
    Example 1.

    A uniform rod of length \(2\,\mathrm{m}\) and mass \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\) has a point mass of \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) attached at its right end. Find the combined centre of mass.

    1. The uniform rod's own centre is at its midpoint, \(x_R=1\,\mathrm{m}\) from the left end.
    2. The attached point mass is at \(x_P=2\,\mathrm{m}\).
    3. Total mass is \(M=6+2=8\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    4. Taking moments, \(Mx_{\mathrm{cm}}=6(1)+2(2)=10\,\mathrm{kg\,m}\).
    5. Hence \(x_{\mathrm{cm}}=10/8=1.25\,\mathrm{m}\), closer to the larger rod mass.

    Answer: The combined centre of mass is \(1.25\,\mathrm{m}\) from the left end.

    Example 2.

    Three thin uniform rods, each of length \(1\,\mathrm{m}\) and linear density \(2\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}}\), form a triangular frame: one lies from \((0,0)\) to \((1,0)\), one from \((0,0)\) to \((0,1)\), and the third joins \((1,0)\) to \((0,1)\). Find the centre of mass.

    1. Each rod has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and its own centre at the geometric midpoint.
    2. The three mass centres are \((1/2,0)\), \((0,1/2)\), and \((1/2,1/2)\).
    3. The total mass is \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\), and the sum of mass moments is \((1,1)\mathrm{kg\,m}\).
    4. Dividing the vector moment by total mass gives \(\mathbf R_{\mathrm{cm}}=(1/3,1/3)\,\mathrm{m}\).
    5. The equal \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates follow from reflection symmetry about \(y=x\).

    Answer: The centre of mass is at \(\left(\frac13,\frac13\right)\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the geometric centre of a non-uniform body.
    • Applying the subtraction method to a hole with the positive sign.
    • Confusing the centre of a semicircular arc with that of a semicircular lamina.

    Chapter 5 · Topic 4

    Motion of centre of mass

    Rotational MotionMechanicsCentre of MassStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The motion of the centre of mass is determined by the total external force and total mass of the system. Internal motions, including separation after an explosion, can change individual speeds but cannot move the centre of mass when the net external impulse is zero. Consequently, the centre of mass either remains at rest, moves uniformly, or follows accelerated motion with acceleration \(\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}/M\).
    Key formula(s). \[\mathbf R_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{1}{M}\int\mathbf r\,dm\]; \[\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{d\mathbf R_{\mathrm{cm}}}{dt}=\frac{\mathbf P}{M}=\frac{1}{M}\int\mathbf v\,dm\]; \[\mathbf a_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}}{M}\]
    Key points.
    • The centre of mass can move when every internal part is initially at rest but a nonzero external force acts.
    • It is not necessary for the system to be rigid; particles, deformable bodies, and extended systems all obey the same result.
    • External force determines centre-of-mass acceleration, while internal energy changes determine kinetic-energy changes.
    • In a gravitational field, the centre of mass follows the projectile formula if it is the only external force.
    • For a system in free fall, gravitational acceleration acts on the centre of mass just as on each body.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block and a \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) block rest on a smooth horizontal surface. A force of \(6\,\mathrm{N}\) acts on the \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block for \(3\,\mathrm{s}\), while the blocks push each other. Find the velocity of their centre of mass.

    1. The total mass is \(M=3\,\mathrm{kg}\), and the only external horizontal force is \(F_{\mathrm{ext}}=6\,\mathrm{N}\).
    2. Hence the centre-of-mass acceleration is \(A_{\mathrm{cm}}=6/3=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
    3. The contact force between the blocks is internal and does not appear in this equation.
    4. Since the centre of mass starts from rest, \(V_{\mathrm{cm}}=A_{\mathrm{cm}}t=2(3)=6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The centre of mass moves at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(60\,\mathrm{kg}\) person walks \(3\,\mathrm{m}\) forward relative to a \(50\,\mathrm{kg}\) boat on frictionless water. Both are initially at rest. Find the displacement of the person and boat relative to the ground.

    1. There is no external horizontal force, so the horizontal centre of mass remains fixed.
    2. Let the ground displacement of the boat be \(x\), positive forward. The person displacement is then \(x+3\,\mathrm{m}\).
    3. Conservation of the centre-of-mass position gives \(50x+60(x+3)=0\).
    4. This becomes \(110x+180=0\), so the boat displacement is \(x=-18/11\,\mathrm{m}\).
    5. The person displacement is \(x+3=15/11\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The boat moves \(18/11\,\mathrm{m}\) backward and the person moves \(15/11\,\mathrm{m}\) forward relative to the ground.

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating the force between two chosen components as external for the complete system.
    • Setting \(m_p\Delta x_p+m_b\Delta x_b=0\) when relative distances are used incorrectly.
    • Assuming the centre of mass of an isolated system must remain at rest regardless of its initial velocity.

    Explanation

    Concept. The momentum of a system is the vector sum of the momenta of all its particles, including continuous mass elements through an integral. It equals the total mass times the velocity of the centre of mass. The impulse-momentum theorem for the whole system states that its momentum change is caused only by the resultant external impulse.
    Key formula(s). \[\mathbf P=\sum_i m_i\mathbf v_i=\int\mathbf v\,dm=M\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}\]; \[\mathbf P_f-\mathbf P_i=\mathbf J_{\mathrm{ext}}=\int\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}\,dt\]; \[\frac{d\mathbf P}{dt}=\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}\]
    Key points.
    • Momentum is a vector, so each component is evaluated independently.
    • The SI unit of momentum is \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), equivalent to \(\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    • Equal and opposite internal momenta can cancel without making external impulse zero.
    • Total momentum is conserved only for a closed system with negligible external impulse.
    • Momentum conservation is valid for external fields if the relevant field interaction is included in the system definition.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle at \((1,2)\,\mathrm{m}\) has velocity \((3,-1)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and a \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle at \((-2,1)\,\mathrm{m}\) has velocity \((4,5)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find total momentum and centre-of-mass velocity.

    1. The first momentum is \(2(3,-1)=(6,-2)\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    2. The second momentum is \(1(4,5)=(4,5)\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    3. Therefore \(\mathbf P=(10,3)\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    4. The total mass is \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), so \(\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}=\mathbf P/M=(10/3,1)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. The positions are unnecessary for this calculation; they would be needed only to find the instantaneous position of the centre of mass.

    Answer: \(\mathbf P=(10,3)\,\mathrm{N\,s}\) and \(\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}=(10/3,1)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(0.50\,\mathrm{kg}\) ball moving at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) is brought to rest in \(0.050\,\mathrm{s}\). Find the magnitude and direction of the average force on the ball.

    1. Its momentum change is \(\Delta p=m(v_f-v_i)=0.50(0-10)=-5.0\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    2. By the impulse-momentum theorem, the average force is \(\mathbf F_{\mathrm{av}}=\Delta\mathbf p/\Delta t\).
    3. Thus \(\mathbf F_{\mathrm{av}}=(-5.0)/(0.050)=-100\,\mathrm{N}\) if the initial direction is positive.
    4. The negative sign shows that the force is opposite the ball's initial motion.

    Answer: The average force has magnitude \(100\,\mathrm{N}\) and acts opposite the initial velocity.

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding momentum magnitudes without resolving directions.
    • Using an internal contact force to change total-system momentum.
    • Confusing momentum with kinetic energy, especially for a particle that simply stops.

    Explanation

    Concept. Total momentum is conserved when the net external impulse on a system is zero or negligible during the interaction. Internal forces, including explosive forces and collision impulses, occur in Newton's-third-law pairs and cannot change total momentum. The statement does not imply that kinetic energy or the velocity of each body is conserved.
    Key formula(s). \[\frac{d\mathbf P}{dt}=\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathbf P_f=\mathbf P_i\]; \[\mathbf P_f-\mathbf P_i=\mathbf J_{\mathrm{ext}}\simeq0\]; \[\sum_i\mathbf p_{i,f}=\sum_i\mathbf p_{i,i}\]
    Key points.
    • An isolated explosion is the standard example: kinetic energy may increase while total momentum remains fixed.
    • External impulse must be evaluated over the actual interaction interval, not merely called small.
    • A spring or string between components is internal if it is included in the chosen system.
    • Momentum conservation determines only one vector equation, so multiple unknowns may require geometry or another condition.
    • On a smooth horizontal surface, gravity and the normal force balance vertically and neither contributes a horizontal impulse.
    Example 1.

    A \(20\,\mathrm{kg}\) gun fires a \(0.020\,\mathrm{kg}\) shell horizontally at \(600\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) relative to the gun. The gun is initially at rest on a smooth horizontal support. Find the gun's recoil velocity.

    1. Initially, the gun-shell system's horizontal momentum is zero.
    2. After firing, take the shell direction as positive and let the gun velocity be \(V\).
    3. Momentum conservation gives \(0.020(600)+20V=0\).
    4. The shell's laboratory velocity is \(600\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) because the gun was initially at rest.
    5. Therefore \(V=-12/20=-0.60\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The gun recoils at \(0.60\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) opposite the shell direction.

    Example 2.

    A \(0.020\,\mathrm{kg}\) bullet moving at \(500\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) embeds itself in a stationary \(0.480\,\mathrm{kg}\) block on a frictionless surface. Find their common velocity and the kinetic-energy loss.

    1. Momentum conservation gives \(0.020(500)=(0.500)V\), so \(V=20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. The initial kinetic energy is \(K_i=\frac12(0.020)(500^2)=2500\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. The final kinetic energy is \(K_f=\frac12(0.500)(20^2)=100\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. The reduction \(2400\,\mathrm{J}\) becomes deformation, heat, and sound.
    5. No kinetic-energy equation is used during the inelastic impact; it would incorrectly predict a different common speed.

    Answer: The common velocity is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and \(2400\,\mathrm{J}\) is dissipated.

    Common mistakes.
    • Conserving mechanical energy in an inelastic collision.
    • Omitting recoil mass from a projectile-and-launcher system.
    • Claiming momentum is conserved when a sustained external force acts for a finite time.

    Explanation

    Concept. A variable-mass system exchanges matter with its surroundings, so the rate of change of its momentum is not simply the resultant force on the currently contained mass. The momentum carried by incoming or outgoing matter must be included. Choosing a rocket, an ejecting cart, or a receiving vehicle as the system makes the relevant momentum flux explicit.
    Key formula(s). \[m\frac{d\mathbf v}{dt}=\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}+(\mathbf u-\mathbf v)\frac{dm}{dt}\quad\text{for accretion with incoming velocity }\mathbf u\]; \[\mathbf F_{\mathrm{thrust}}=\mathbf u_{\mathrm{rel}}\frac{dm}{dt}\quad\text{where }\mathbf u_{\mathrm{rel}}\text{ points backward}\]; \[\frac{d(m\mathbf v)}{dt}=\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}+\mathbf u_{\mathrm{in}}\dot m_{\mathrm{in}}-\mathbf u_{\mathrm{out}}\dot m_{\mathrm{out}}\]
    Key points.
    • A fixed-mass equation \(m\mathbf a=\mathbf F\) cannot be used without accounting for momentum carried by exchanged mass.
    • For a rocket, \(\dot m<0\) and the thrust is opposite the exhaust velocity relative to the rocket.
    • If incoming material is at rest in the inertial frame, horizontal momentum conservation may still be used for a receiving body.
    • Mass transfer can cause acceleration even when the external force on the original body is zero.
    • The chosen system must not double-count incoming or outgoing momentum.
    Example 1.

    A \(2.0\,\mathrm{t}\) truck starts from rest on a smooth horizontal track while water strikes it horizontally at \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at a mass rate of \(0.10\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}\). Find its speed after \(5\,\mathrm{s}\).

    1. During \(5\,\mathrm{s}\), the received water mass is \(0.10(5)=0.50\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    2. The final truck-plus-water mass is \(2000+0.50=2000.50\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    3. There is no external horizontal force, so the final momentum equals the total momentum carried in by the water.
    4. The incoming horizontal momentum is \(0.50(20)=10\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    5. Hence \(V_{\mathrm{final}}=10/2000.50\approx0.005\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: After \(5\,\mathrm{s}\), the truck's horizontal speed is approximately \(5.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(1000\,\mathrm{kg}\) rail cart moves at \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) on a smooth track and ejects mass at \(2\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}\) vertically downward with negligible horizontal velocity relative to the cart. Find the cart's speed after \(1\,\mathrm{s}\).

    1. The expelled sand has the same horizontal velocity as the cart at release because its relative horizontal velocity is zero.
    2. Therefore the sand carries away no horizontal momentum in the ground frame.
    3. The cart has no external horizontal force, so its horizontal momentum remains \(P=1000(20)=20000\,\mathrm{N\,s}\).
    4. After \(1\,\mathrm{s}\), the remaining cart mass is \(998\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    5. Thus \(998V_f=20000\), giving \(V_f=20.040\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The cart's speed after \(1\,\mathrm{s}\) is approximately \(20.04\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Applying \(m\,dv/dt=F\) while silently discarding the momentum of exchanged mass.
    • Treating relative exhaust velocity as its ground-frame velocity.
    • Using \(\dot m>0\) for a rocket while also reversing the thrust direction.

    Explanation

    Concept. A rocket accelerates by ejecting mass backward, and the thrust is the momentum transferred per second to the remaining vehicle. Because rocket mass decreases continuously, acceleration usually increases even when thrust is constant, while gravity reduces the net acceleration. Integrating the rocket equation gives the ideal velocity change, after which gravity and other external effects must be added separately.
    Key formula(s). \[T=u_{\mathrm{rel}}\left(-\frac{dm}{dt}\right)\]; \[m\frac{dv}{dt}=-u_{\mathrm{rel}}\frac{dm}{dt}+F_{\mathrm{ext}}\]; \[\Delta v=u_{\mathrm{rel}}\ln\left(\frac{m_i}{m_f}\right)\quad\text{with no gravity}\]; \[\Delta v=u_{\mathrm{rel}}\ln\left(\frac{m_i}{m_f}\right)-g\,\Delta t\quad\text{for constant gravity}\]
    Key points.
    • The exhaust speed \(u_{\mathrm{rel}}\) is measured relative to the rocket, not the ground.
    • A larger mass ratio \(m_i/m_f\) gives a larger ideal delta-v for fixed exhaust speed.
    • Thrust \(T\) is a force, whereas \(T\,dt\) is the impulse supplied to the rocket.
    • For constant mass flow, thrust can be constant even while the rocket's mass and acceleration change.
    • Momentum conservation for rocket plus all exhaust includes changing vector directions in space; the rocket equation is simpler in one dimension.
    Example 1.

    A rocket has a dry mass of \(1000\,\mathrm{kg}\) and carries \(3000\,\mathrm{kg}\) of propellant. Its exhaust speed relative to the rocket is \(3.0\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). Neglect gravity and losses. Find the ideal velocity change after all propellant is used.

    1. The initial total mass is \(m_i=1000+3000=4000\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    2. After combustion, the final mass is the dry mass \(m_f=1000\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    3. The initial-to-final mass ratio is \(m_i/m_f=4\).
    4. Applying the ideal rocket equation, \(\Delta v=3000\ln4\).
    5. Since \(\ln4\approx1.3863\), \(\Delta v\approx4159\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The ideal velocity gain is about \(4.16\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(10000\,\mathrm{kg}\) rocket ejects fuel at \(100\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}\) with exhaust speed \(400\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) backward for \(20\,\mathrm{s}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and neglect other losses. Find the change in velocity.

    1. The final mass is \(m_f=10000-100(20)=8000\,\mathrm{kg}\).
    2. The ideal thrust-independent rocket term is \(400\ln(10000/8000)=400\ln(1.25)\).
    3. Numerically, this term is \(400(0.22314)=89.26\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. Gravity reduces velocity by \(g\Delta t=10(20)=200\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. Therefore \(\Delta v=89.26-200=-110.74\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The velocity changes by approximately \(-111\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), a decrease.

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the dry mass as the initial mass in the rocket equation.
    • Adding the gravity term with the wrong sign.
    • Treating thrust as constant acceleration without accounting for decreasing mass.

    Explanation

    Concept. The centre-of-mass frame is an inertial frame in which total momentum is zero and remains zero throughout an isolated collision. In this frame, only relative kinetic energy is available to be lost or transferred. For an elastic collision, relative velocities reverse completely; for a perfectly inelastic collision, all relative kinetic energy is lost while the centre-of-mass velocity is unchanged.
    Key formula(s). \[\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{m_1\mathbf u_1+m_2\mathbf u_2}{m_1+m_2}\]; \[\mathbf u_i'=\mathbf u_i-\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}},\qquad \mathbf v_i'=\mathbf v_i-\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}\]; \[K=K_{\mathrm{cm}}+K_{\mathrm{rel}},\qquad K_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac12M V_{\mathrm{cm}}^2\]
    Key points.
    • A frame moving at constant \(\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}\) remains an inertial frame for an isolated collision.
    • In the centre-of-mass frame, \(m_1\mathbf u_1'+m_2\mathbf u_2'=0\) at every instant of the impact.
    • Elastic collision sends \(\mathbf u_1'\) to \(-\mathbf u_1'\) and \(\mathbf u_2'\) to \(-\mathbf u_2'\).
    • Perfectly inelastic collision sets both final centre-of-mass-frame velocities to zero.
    • Kinetic-energy loss is the same in all Galilean frames when the centre-of-mass velocity is constant.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) block moving at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) collides elastically head-on with a stationary \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) block. Use the centre-of-mass frame to find the laboratory final velocities.

    1. The centre-of-mass speed is \(V_{\mathrm{cm}}=[2(4)+1(0)]/3=8/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. Initial centre-of-mass-frame velocities are \(u_1'=4-8/3=4/3\) and \(u_2'=0-8/3=-8/3\).
    3. Elastic impact reverses them: \(v_1'=-4/3\) and \(v_2'=+8/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. Transforming back, \(v_1=-4/3+8/3=4/3\) and \(v_2=8/3+8/3=16/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The laboratory final velocities are \(4/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(16/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) body moving at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) collides perfectly inelastically with a stationary \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) body. Find the common speed and the energy dissipated using centre-of-mass energy.

    1. The common speed is \(V_{\mathrm{cm}}=[2(5)+1(0)]/3=10/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. The initial centre-of-mass-frame velocities are \(5/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(-10/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. Hence \(K_{\mathrm{rel}}=\frac12(2)(5/3)^2+\frac12(1)(10/3)^2=25/3\,\mathrm{J}\).
    4. The centre-of-mass energy is \(\frac12(3)(10/3)^2=50/3\,\mathrm{J}\), and total initial energy is \(25\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. Sticking removes all \(K_{\mathrm{rel}}\), leaving only the \(50/3\,\mathrm{J}\) centre-of-mass energy.

    Answer: The common speed is \(10/3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the energy dissipated is \(25/3\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Reversing velocities in the laboratory frame instead of the centre-of-mass frame.
    • Calling \(K_{\mathrm{cm}}\) the lost energy in a perfectly inelastic collision.
    • Forgetting to add \(\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}\) after solving in the centre-of-mass frame.

    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 5 · Topic 6

    Angular displacement

    Rotational MotionMechanicsRotationStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Angular displacement describes the rotation of a rigid body about a chosen axis and is the angular version of linear displacement. For motion about a fixed axis, the magnitude of the net angular displacement is arc length divided by radius and is measured in radians. The direction is assigned by the right-hand rule, and angular displacements may be added algebraically when the axis remains fixed.
    Key formula(s). \[\Delta\theta=\frac{s}{r}\quad\text{for a fixed radius}\]; \[s=r|\Delta\theta|\]; \[\boldsymbol{\Delta\theta}=(\Delta\theta)\hat{\mathbf n}\]; \[1\ \mathrm{revolution}=2\pi\ \mathrm{rad}=360^\circ\]
    Key points.
    • One radian is the angle subtended when arc length equals radius.
    • A full revolution is \(2\pi\) radians and a half revolution is \(\pi\) radians.
    • Radians are dimensionless, while degrees are a non-SI angular unit.
    • Angular displacement is an oriented quantity; clockwise and anticlockwise rotations have opposite signs.
    • For a fixed axis, displacements add directly, so two opposite rotations of equal magnitude give zero net angular displacement.
    Example 1.

    A wheel of radius \(0.40\,\mathrm{m}\) rotates about a fixed axle through \(5/6\) of a revolution. Find its angular displacement in radians and the distance travelled by a point on the rim.

    1. One revolution is \(2\pi\) radians, so \(\Delta\theta=(5/6)(2\pi)=5\pi/3\,\mathrm{rad}\).
    2. The rim point follows a circular arc whose length is \(s=r|\Delta\theta|\).
    3. Thus \(s=0.40(5\pi/3)=2\pi/3\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. The axle is fixed, so this is angular displacement about a stationary axis rather than a rolling displacement.

    Answer: The angular displacement is \(5\pi/3\,\mathrm{rad}\), and the rim travel is \(2\pi/3\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Example 2.

    A body first rotates through \(3\pi/2\) radians anticlockwise about the \(z\)-axis and then through \(4\pi/3\) radians clockwise. Find the net angular displacement vector.

    1. Choose anticlockwise rotation about \(+\hat{\mathbf z}\) as positive; clockwise rotation is negative.
    2. The total signed angle is \(\Delta\theta_z=3\pi/2-4\pi/3=(9\pi-8\pi)/6=\pi/6\).
    3. Since the axis is unchanged, the angular displacements add algebraically.
    4. The net vector is \((\pi/6)\hat{\mathbf z}\,\mathrm{rad}\).

    Answer: The net angular displacement is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\hat{\mathbf z}\,\mathrm{rad}\), equivalent to \(30^\circ\) anticlockwise.

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding clockwise and anticlockwise angular displacements with the same sign.
    • Using \(s=r\theta\) while mixing degrees with radians.
    • Assigning an angular-displacement direction without defining a positive axis.

    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 5 · Topic 7

    Angular velocity

    Rotational MotionMechanicsRotationStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Angular velocity measures the rate of change of the angular position of a rigid body about a fixed axis. It is a vector whose instantaneous direction is found by the right-hand rule, while its magnitude gives the rate of rotation. In JEE problems, the correct axis and reference point must be identified before using angular-velocity relations.
    Key formula(s). \[\boldsymbol{\omega}_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\Delta t},\qquad \boldsymbol{\omega}=\frac{d\boldsymbol{\theta}}{dt}\]; \[\boldsymbol{\omega}=\frac{d\boldsymbol{\phi}}{dt}\hat{\boldsymbol e}_z,\qquad \boldsymbol v=\boldsymbol{\omega}\times\boldsymbol r\]
    Key points.
    • The SI unit of angular velocity is \(\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\); in dimensional analysis, radians are dimensionless.
    • The direction of \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) is along the axis of rotation according to the right-hand rule, not along the tangential motion.
    • For uniform rotation, \(\omega\) is constant even though the velocity vector of every moving point changes continuously.
    • One complete revolution corresponds to an angular displacement of \(2\pi\) radians.
    • The relation \(\boldsymbol v=\boldsymbol{\omega}\times\boldsymbol r\) applies when \(\boldsymbol r\) is measured from a point on the rotation axis.
    • Angular velocity is frame-dependent; for a moving axis, the simple formula applies to rotation relative to that axis.
    Example 1.

    A wheel completes 3 revolutions uniformly in 6 s. Find its angular velocity in \(\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).

    1. One revolution represents an angular displacement of \(2\pi\) radians.
    2. Hence the total angular displacement is \(\theta=3(2\pi)=6\pi\) radians.
    3. For uniform rotation, \(\omega=\theta/t\).
    4. \(\omega=\frac{6\pi}{6}=\pi\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The angular velocity is \(\pi\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A belt moves without slipping on two pulleys of radii \(0.15\ \mathrm m\) and \(0.25\ \mathrm m\). If the belt speed is \(3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), find the angular speeds of the pulleys.

    1. The no-slip condition gives the tangential speed at each pulley as \(v=R\omega\).
    2. For the first pulley, \(\omega_1=v/R_1=\frac{3}{0.15}=20\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. For the second pulley, \(\omega_2=v/R_2=\frac{3}{0.25}=12\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The smaller pulley therefore rotates faster, as expected from \(v=\omega R\).

    Answer: The angular speeds are \(20\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\) and \(12\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\), respectively.

    Common mistakes.
    • Counting revolutions without converting them to radians.
    • Choosing the direction of angular velocity along the tangential velocity.
    • Applying \(v=\omega R\) when \(R\) is not the perpendicular distance from the rotation axis.
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 5 · Topic 8

    Angular acceleration

    Rotational MotionMechanicsRotationStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Angular acceleration measures the rate of change of angular velocity and determines how quickly the tangential speed or direction of rotation changes. For fixed-axis rotation, it is a vector along the rotation axis, but its sign distinguishes speeding up from slowing down. It must not be confused with tangential acceleration, which also has a radial contribution when \(\omega\neq 0\).
    Key formula(s). \[\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}}{\Delta t},\qquad \boldsymbol{\alpha}=\frac{d\boldsymbol{\omega}}{dt}=\frac{d^2\boldsymbol{\theta}}{dt^2}\]; \[a_t=R|\alpha|,\qquad \omega_f=\omega_i+\alpha t,\qquad \theta=\omega_i t+\frac12\alpha t^2\quad(\alpha=\text{constant})\]
    Key points.
    • The SI unit of angular acceleration is \(\mathrm{rad\,s^{-2}}\).
    • Positive \(\alpha\) means angular velocity increases algebraically; it need not mean that the body's rotation becomes faster if \(\omega_i\) and \(\alpha\) have opposite signs.
    • For fixed \(R\), tangential acceleration is proportional to angular acceleration.
    • A body moving at constant angular velocity has \(\alpha=0\), but points with \(\omega\neq 0\) still possess centripetal acceleration.
    • For nonuniform angular velocity, the tangential acceleration is still \(R\alpha\); it does not include the centripetal term.
    • Over an interval, average angular acceleration can be used even when the angular acceleration itself varies with time.
    Example 1.

    A wheel slows uniformly from \(20\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\) to \(10\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\) in 2 s. Find its angular acceleration.

    1. The change in angular velocity is \(\Delta\omega=10-20=-10\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. The elapsed time is \(t=2\ \mathrm s\).
    3. By the definition of average angular acceleration, \(\alpha=\Delta\omega/t\).
    4. \(\alpha=\frac{-10}{2}=-5\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-2}}\).

    Answer: The angular acceleration is \(-5\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-2}}\), directed opposite to the initial angular velocity.

    Example 2.

    A wheel of radius \(0.4\ \mathrm m\) starts rotating at \(5\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\) and undergoes uniform angular acceleration \(3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-2}}\) for 4 s. Find its final angular speed and angular displacement.

    1. For uniform angular acceleration, \(\omega_f=\omega_i+\alpha t\).
    2. \(\omega_f=5+3(4)=17\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. The angular displacement is \(\theta=\omega_i t+\frac12\alpha t^2\).
    4. \(\theta=5(4)+\frac12(3)(4^2)=20+24=44\ \mathrm{rad}\).
    5. The corresponding tangential acceleration is \(a_t=R\alpha=1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

    Answer: The final angular speed is \(17\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\), and the angular displacement is \(44\ \mathrm{rad}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Reporting a positive magnitude when the body is actually slowing down.
    • Omitting the sign of \(\omega_i\) when deciding whether rotation is speeding up.
    • Treating total acceleration as \(R\alpha\) when the point also has centripetal acceleration.

    Chapter 5 · Topic 9

    Torque

    Rotational MotionMechanicsRotationStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Torque is the rotational effect of a force and equals the cross product of the position vector from the chosen axis to the point of application with the force. Only the component perpendicular to the lever arm produces rotation about the axis. For fixed-axis rigid bodies, the net external torque determines the angular acceleration, while power is supplied by \(P=\boldsymbol{\tau}\cdot\boldsymbol{\omega}\).
    Key formula(s). \[\boldsymbol{\tau}=\boldsymbol r\times\boldsymbol F,\qquad |\tau|=rF\sin\theta\]; \[P=\boldsymbol{\tau}\cdot\boldsymbol{\omega},\qquad \sum\tau_{\mathrm{ext},z}=I_z\alpha,\qquad \int\tau\,dt=\Delta L\]
    Key points.
    • The SI unit of torque is \(\mathrm{N\,m}\), dimensionally identical to energy.
    • The lever arm \(r\sin\theta\) is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of the force.
    • A force whose line of action passes through the axis has zero torque about that axis.
    • Torque is an axial vector, so its sign must be assigned with a chosen positive sense of rotation.
    • A radial force through the center produces no torque about the center even if it changes the translational motion.
    • On a frictionless axle, the support force can produce no torque about the axle because its lever arm is zero.
    Example 1.

    A force of \(20\ \mathrm N\) acts at the end of a \(0.4\ \mathrm m\) lever arm, making an angle of \(60^\circ\) with the lever. Find the torque.

    1. The torque magnitude is \(\tau=rF\sin\theta\).
    2. Here the perpendicular lever arm is \(r\sin60^\circ=0.4(\sqrt3/2)\ \mathrm m\).
    3. Thus \(\tau=(0.4)(20)(\sqrt3/2)\ \mathrm{N\,m}\).
    4. \(\tau=4\sqrt3\ \mathrm{N\,m}\).

    Answer: The torque is \(4\sqrt3\ \mathrm{N\,m}\).

    Example 2.

    A force of magnitude \(50\ \mathrm N\) has tangential and radial components \(30\ \mathrm N\) and \(40\ \mathrm N\) at a point \(0.5\ \mathrm m\) from a wheel's axis. The wheel rotates at \(4\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Find the net torque and power due to this force.

    1. The radial component has zero moment arm and therefore gives zero torque.
    2. The tangential component gives \(\tau=(0.5)(30)=15\ \mathrm{N\,m}\).
    3. Since the force is not opposed, the torque is in the direction of rotation and \(P=\tau\omega\).
    4. \(P=15(4)=60\ \mathrm W\).

    Answer: The torque is \(15\ \mathrm{N\,m}\), and the power delivered is \(60\ \mathrm W\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(rF\) without the perpendicular component of the force.
    • Confusing torque with force even though both can have units of \(\mathrm{N\,m}\).
    • Including a radial force in the torque calculation.
    • Forgetting the minus sign when opposing torque slows the rotation.

    Chapter 5 · Topic 10

    Moment of force

    Rotational MotionMechanicsRotationStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Moment of force (torque magnitude: force times perpendicular distance, τ=rFsinθ) twists bodies - door handles far from hinges, spanners lengthening leverage, seesaws balancing moments. Clockwise versus anticlockwise signs; couple (equal-opposite force pairs) gives pure rotation (steering wheels). Torque zero along force lines (sin0°) - pushing hinges turns nothing. Lever arms multiply forces into turning power.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Force times perpendicular distance twists bodies.
    • Longer arms, bigger twists - leverage physics.
    Remember
    • Push hinges (zero arm) turns nothing ever.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    SI unit of torque (moment of force) is

    Solution: Force-distances share energy units dimensionally.
    Key Formulas · Moment of Force
    \(\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F,\;\tau=rF\sin\theta\) twist magnitude plus axis
    \(\tau_{net}=I\alpha\) rotation second law
    Back to Index
    Index / Mechanics
    Chapter 5 · Topic 11

    Angular momentum

    Rotational MotionMechanicsRotationStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Angular momentum measures the rotational momentum of a system about a chosen origin or axis. For a particle it is the cross product of its linear momentum with position, and for a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis it is \(L=I\omega\). The rate of change of angular momentum equals the net external torque, making conservation of angular momentum a central tool for collisions and suddenly constrained systems.
    Key formula(s). \[\boldsymbol L=\sum_i\boldsymbol r_i\times m_i\boldsymbol v_i,\qquad L_z=I_z\omega\]; \[\frac{d\boldsymbol L}{dt}=\boldsymbol\tau_{\mathrm{ext}},\qquad L_i=L_f\quad\text{if}\ \int\tau_{\mathrm{ext}}dt=0\]
    Key points.
    • The SI unit of angular momentum is \(\mathrm{J\,s}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}\).
    • For a point particle, the lever arm in angular momentum is again the perpendicular distance from the axis to the momentum line.
    • For a rigid body, \(L=I\omega\) is direct for rotation about a principal axis or a fixed symmetry axis; otherwise the general tensor form is required.
    • The torque and angular momentum must be referred to the same origin and axis.
    • Internal torques cancel for a system, but only the net external torque determines \(dL/dt\).
    • Kinetic energy is generally not conserved in a perfectly inelastic impact even when angular momentum is conserved.
    Example 1.

    A uniform rod of mass \(3\ \mathrm{kg}\) and length \(1.2\ \mathrm m\) rotates about one end with angular speed \(6\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Find its angular momentum about the fixed end.

    1. For a uniform rod rotating about one end, \(I=\frac13 ML^2\).
    2. \(I=\frac13(3)(1.2)^2=1.44\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}\).
    3. The angular momentum about that end is \(L=I\omega\).
    4. \(L=1.44(6)=8.64\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The angular momentum is \(8.64\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A particle of mass \(0.1\ \mathrm{kg}\) moving at \(6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) strikes and sticks to a uniform rod of mass \(4\ \mathrm{kg}\) and length \(0.6\ \mathrm m\) at a point \(0.3\ \mathrm m\) from its center. The rod is free to rotate about its frictionless center pivot and lies in the plane of motion. Find the final angular speed.

    1. The initial angular momentum about the pivot is \(L_i=mvr\), since the impact is tangential.
    2. \(L_i=(0.1)(6)(0.3)=0.18\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. The rod's moment of inertia is \(I=\frac1{12}ML^2=\frac1{12}(4)(0.6)^2=0.12\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}\).
    4. With negligible external torque, \(mvr=I\omega_f\).
    5. \(\omega_f=\frac{0.18}{0.12}=1.5\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The combined rod-particle system rotates at \(1.5\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\) about its center.

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(mv\) instead of \(mvr\) for particle angular momentum.
    • Calculating angular momentum about an axis other than the pivot used in the equation.
    • Assuming momentum is conserved about any point in an impulsive collision.
    • Applying \(L=I\omega\) with the moment of inertia about the wrong axis.
