    Chapter 8 · Topic 9

    Adiabatic process

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsLaws and ProcessesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. An adiabatic process transfers no heat across its boundary, so any change in a closed system's internal energy results from work alone. For a reversible adiabatic change of a fixed amount of ideal gas, \(PV^\gamma=\text{constant}\) and temperature changes as volume changes. Adiabatic does not mean isothermal, and the power-law relation is not valid for every irreversible adiabatic path.
    Key formula(s). \[\delta Q=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Delta U=-W_{\mathrm{by}}\]; \[PV^\gamma=\text{constant},\qquad TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant}\]; \[W_{\mathrm{by}}=\frac{P_1V_1-P_2V_2}{\gamma-1}=n\frac{R}{\gamma-1}(T_1-T_2)\]
    Key points.
    • The defining condition is \(Q=0\), not constant temperature.
    • Reversible adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas cools the gas, while reversible adiabatic compression heats it.
    • \(\gamma=C_P/C_V\); it is \(5/3\) for a monatomic ideal gas and \(7/5\) for a diatomic ideal gas at ordinary temperatures.
    • The relations \(PV^\gamma=\text{constant}\) and \(TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant}\) require a reversible ideal-gas path.
    • In an adiabatic free expansion into a vacuum, external pressure is zero, so work is zero even though volume increases.
    • A closed adiabatic system can have its internal energy and temperature changed by any nonzero boundary work.
    Example 1.

    A \(1.00\,\mathrm{mol}\) monatomic ideal gas at \(300\,\mathrm{K}\) expands reversibly and adiabatically from volume \(V_1\) to \(2V_1\). Find its final temperature and the work done by the gas. Use \(R=8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\).

    1. For a monatomic ideal gas, \(\gamma=5/3\), so \(\gamma-1=2/3\).
    2. The reversible adiabatic relation gives \(T_1V_1^{\gamma-1}=T_2V_2^{\gamma-1}\).
    3. Thus \(T_2=300(V_1/(2V_1))^{2/3}=300/2^{2/3}=189.0\,\mathrm{K}\).
    4. Since \(Q=0\), the work done by the gas is \(W_{\mathrm{by}}=-\Delta U=nC_V(T_1-T_2)\).
    5. With \(C_V=3R/2=12.471\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\), \(W_{\mathrm{by}}=1(12.471)(300-189.0)=1.38\times10^3\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The final temperature is approximately \(189\,\mathrm{K}\), and the gas does \(1.38\,\mathrm{kJ}\) of work.

    Example 2.

    An ideal gas is separated from an evacuated region by a partition in a thermally insulated, rigid vessel. The partition is removed and the gas expands to twice its original volume. Find \(Q\), \(W_{\mathrm{by}}\), \(\Delta U\), and the change in temperature.

    1. The vessel is adiabatic, so \(Q=0\) across the system boundary.
    2. Expansion is into a vacuum with \(P_{\mathrm{ext}}=0\), hence \(W_{\mathrm{by}}=\int P_{\mathrm{ext}}\,dV=0\).
    3. The first law gives \(\Delta U=Q-W_{\mathrm{by}}=0\).
    4. For a fixed amount of ideal gas, zero internal-energy change means \(T_2=T_1\), despite the doubling of volume and fall in pressure.

    Answer: \(Q=0,\ W_{\mathrm{by}}=0,\ \Delta U=0\), and \(\Delta T=0\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Assuming every adiabatic process is isothermal.
    • Applying \(PV^\gamma=\text{constant}\) to free expansion or another irreversible adiabatic process.
    • Using the reversible adiabatic work formula when the external pressure is zero.

    Chapter 8 · Topic 10

    Isobaric process

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsLaws and ProcessesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. An isobaric process occurs at constant pressure while heat transfer, expansion, or both take place. For an ideal gas, \(P,V,T\) obey \(V/T=\text{constant}\), and the work done by the gas is \(P\Delta V=nR\Delta T\). The heat supplied is \(Q=nC_P\Delta T\), so process-work calculations must be separated carefully from the change in internal energy.
    Key formula(s). \[P=P_0=\text{constant}, \qquad \frac{V}{T}=\text{constant}\] ; \[W_{\rm by}=P(V_2-V_1)=nR(T_2-T_1)\] ; \[\Delta U=nC_V(T_2-T_1), \qquad Q=\Delta U+W_{\rm by}=nC_P(T_2-T_1)\]
    Key points.
    • Constant pressure does not imply constant temperature; \(PV=nRT\) gives \(V\propto T\) for a fixed amount of ideal gas.
    • With the convention \(\Delta U=Q-W_{\rm by}\), expansion at positive pressure gives positive work by the gas.
    • For an isobaric process, \(C_P-C_V=R\), hence \(C_P>C_V\).
    • The work \(nR\Delta T\) vanishes only for an isochoric process or when \(\Delta T=0\).
    • Pressure must be expressed consistently with volume in \(P\Delta V\); SI gives work in joules.
    • In a \(P\)-\(V\) graph, an isobaric path is horizontal and its enclosed area equals the work by the gas.
    Example 1.

    Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas expand isobarically from \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) to \(450\ \mathrm{K}\). Find the work done by the gas, the change in internal energy, and the heat supplied, using \(R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\).

    1. For a monatomic gas, \(C_V=\frac{3}{2}R\), so \(\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T=2\left(\frac{3}{2}R\right)(150)=750R\).
    2. The isobaric work done by the gas is \(W_{\rm by}=nR\Delta T=2R(150)=300R\).
    3. Numerically, \(\Delta U=750(8.314)=6235.5\ \mathrm{J}\) and \(W_{\rm by}=300(8.314)=2494.2\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. From the first law, \(Q=\Delta U+W_{\rm by}=750R+300R=1050R\).

    Answer: \(W_{\rm by}=2.49\ \mathrm{kJ}\), \(\Delta U=6.24\ \mathrm{kJ}\), and \(Q=8.73\ \mathrm{kJ}\).

    Example 2.

    One mole of a diatomic ideal gas with \(C_P=\frac{7}{2}R\) expands at constant pressure from \(2.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^3}\) to \(6.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^3}\) at \(2.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\). Calculate its initial and final temperatures and the heat supplied.

    1. The boundary work is \(W_{\rm by}=P\Delta V=(2.0\times10^5)(6.0-2.0)\times10^{-2}=8.0\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}\).
    2. Since \(W_{\rm by}=nR\Delta T\), \(\Delta T=8000/8.314=962.1\ \mathrm{K}\).
    3. From \(T_1=PV_1/(nR)\), \(T_1=(2.0\times10^5)(2.0\times10^{-2})/8.314=481.1\ \mathrm{K}\).
    4. Hence \(T_2=481.1+962.1=1443.2\ \mathrm{K}\).
    5. The heat supplied is \(Q=nC_P\Delta T=\frac{7}{2}(8000)=2.80\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(T_1=481.1\ \mathrm{K}\), \(T_2=1.443\times10^3\ \mathrm{K}\), and \(Q=28.0\ \mathrm{kJ}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating constant pressure as constant temperature.
    • Using \(Q=nC_V\Delta T\) for an isobaric process; that is valid only when the volume is constant.
    • Reporting work as positive when the gas is compressed instead of following the sign of \(P\,dV\).

    Chapter 8 · Topic 11

    Isochoric process

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsLaws and ProcessesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. An isochoric, or constant-volume, process takes place in a rigid container, so the boundary work is zero. For an ideal gas at fixed \(n,V\), pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature, and all heat supplied changes the internal energy. This makes isochoric heating and cooling especially useful for measuring molar heat capacities.
    Key formula(s). \[V=V_0=\text{constant}, \qquad W_{\rm by}=\int P\,dV=0\] ; \[\frac{P}{T}=\text{constant}, \qquad \Delta U=nC_V\Delta T\] ; \[Q=\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T\]
    Key points.
    • A rigid piston is required to realize the ideal isochoric condition; a freely moving piston generally permits volume change.
    • At constant volume, \(P/T\) is constant, not \(V/T\).
    • The molar heat capacity in an isochoric process is \(C_V\), while \(C_P\) applies at constant pressure.
    • On a \(P\)-\(V\) diagram, an isochoric path is vertical and contributes no area.
    • An ideal gas can be compressed or heated at constant volume, but it is heated if its pressure rises at fixed \(n\) and \(V\).
    • The work done on the gas is also zero because the container boundary does not move.
    Example 1.

    Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas are heated at constant volume from \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) to \(450\ \mathrm{K}\). Find the work done, the change in internal energy, and the heat supplied, with \(R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\).

    1. The volume cannot change, so \(W_{\rm by}=\int P\,dV=0\) and \(W_{\rm on}=0\).
    2. For a monatomic gas, \(C_V=\frac{3}{2}R\), hence \(\Delta U=2\left(\frac{3}{2}R\right)(150)=750R\).
    3. Thus \(\Delta U=750(8.314)=6235.5\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. The first law gives \(Q=\Delta U+W_{\rm by}=\Delta U\).

    Answer: \(W_{\rm by}=0\), \(\Delta U=+6.24\ \mathrm{kJ}\), and \(Q=+6.24\ \mathrm{kJ}\).

    Example 2.

    Four moles of an ideal gas occupy \(0.10\ \mathrm{m^3}\) at \(300\ \mathrm{K}\). The gas is heated at constant volume to \(450\ \mathrm{K}\). Find the initial and final pressures and the heat supplied, assuming \(C_V=\frac{3}{2}R\).

    1. Initially, \(P_1=nRT_1/V=4(8.314)(300)/0.10=9.9768\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\).
    2. At fixed \(V,n\), \(P_2/P_1=T_2/T_1=450/300=3/2\).
    3. Therefore \(P_2=1.4965\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\).
    4. The heat supplied is \(Q=nC_V\Delta T=4\left(\frac{3}{2}R\right)(150)=900R\).
    5. Numerically, \(Q=900(8.314)=7482.6\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(P_1=99.8\ \mathrm{kPa}\), \(P_2=150\ \mathrm{kPa}\), and \(Q=7.48\ \mathrm{kJ}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding \(P\Delta V\) work even though \(V\) is constant.
    • Using the Celsius temperature ratio in \(P/T\); only absolute temperature is valid.
    • Confusing \(C_P\) with \(C_V\) in the heat calculation.

    Chapter 8 · Topic 12

    Reversible process

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsLaws and ProcessesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A reversible process is ideal and quasi-static, proceeding through equilibrium states without friction, finite temperature differences, or other dissipative effects, so reversing the path restores the system and surroundings exactly. An irreversible process involves such finite gradients or dissipative effects and generates entropy. Although entropy generation is zero for a reversible process, the total entropy of an isolated system increases for every real irreversible process.
    Key formula(s). \[\oint \frac{\delta Q_{\rm rev}}{T}=0, \qquad \Delta S_{\rm univ}=\Delta S_{\rm sys}+\Delta S_{\rm surroundings}\ge 0\] ; \[\Delta S_{\rm gen}\ge 0, \qquad \Delta S_{\rm univ}=\Delta S_{\rm gen}\] ; \[W_{\rm reversible}\ge W_{\rm actual} \text{ for the same end states and reservoir conditions}\]
    Key points.
    • Quasi-static does not by itself guarantee reversibility; friction and finite temperature differences must also be absent.
    • Heat flowing directly between bodies at unequal temperatures is irreversible, even when it is transferred very slowly.
    • Friction converts organized mechanical work into internal energy and creates entropy.
    • For a cyclic device, \(\Delta S_{\rm sys}=0\), but \(\Delta S_{\rm univ}=\Delta S_{\rm gen}>0\) for an irreversible cycle.
    • The equality \(\Delta S_{\rm univ}=0\) identifies an ideal reversible process, not merely one for which entropy happens to be calculated as zero along an irreversible path.
    • A reversible process gives maximum work output or minimum work input between specified states.
    Example 1.

    An engine operating between cyclic states receives \(1000\ \mathrm{J}\) of heat from a reservoir at \(600\ \mathrm{K}\) and rejects heat to a reservoir at \(300\ \mathrm{K}\). Find the entropy changes of the system, surroundings, and universe, and comment on reversibility.

    1. Since the engine returns to its initial state after each cycle, \(\Delta S_{\rm sys}=0\).
    2. The reservoir of finite temperature loses heat, so \(\Delta S_{\rm hot}=-1000/600=-1.667\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).
    3. The cold reservoir gains heat \(1000\ \mathrm{J}\), giving \(\Delta S_{\rm cold}=1000/300=3.333\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).
    4. Hence \(\Delta S_{\rm univ}=-1.667+3.333=+1.667\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).
    5. Positive entropy generation proves that heat transfer across the finite temperature difference makes the cycle irreversible.

    Answer: \(\Delta S_{\rm sys}=0\), \(\Delta S_{\rm surroundings}=+1.667\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\), and \(\Delta S_{\rm univ}=+1.667\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\); the cycle is irreversible.

    Example 2.

    A cyclic engine absorbs \(1200\ \mathrm{J}\) from a \(600\ \mathrm{K}\) source and rejects heat to a \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) sink. If the total entropy generation per cycle is \(0.400\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\), find the rejected heat, net work, and efficiency.

    1. The cyclic working fluid has \(\Delta S_{\rm sys}=0\), so \(0.400=-1200/600+Q_C/300=-2+Q_C/300\).
    2. Solving gives \(Q_C/300=2.400\), hence \(Q_C=720\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. The first law over a cycle gives \(W=Q_H-Q_C=1200-720=480\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. The efficiency is \(\eta=W/Q_H=480/1200=0.400\).
    5. A reversible engine would have \(\eta_{\rm C}=1-300/600=0.500\), confirming that entropy generation lowers efficiency.

    Answer: \(Q_C=720\ \mathrm{J}\), \(W=480\ \mathrm{J}\), and \(\eta=40.0\%\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Assuming every quasi-static process is reversible.
    • Writing \(\Delta S_{\rm univ}=0\) for every cyclic process; this holds only for an ideal reversible cycle.
    • Ignoring reservoir entropy changes and calculating only the working system's entropy.

    Explanation

    Concept. In a cyclic process, a system returns to its initial thermodynamic state after undergoing a sequence of transformations. Since internal energy is a state function, \(\Delta U_{\rm cycle}=0\), so the net heat supplied equals the net work done by the system. The sign of the enclosed area on a \(P\)-\(V\) diagram determines whether the cycle is an engine or a refrigerator.
    Key formula(s). \[\Delta U_{\rm cycle}=0, \qquad Q_{\rm net}=W_{\rm net}\] ; \[W_{\rm net}=\oint P\,dV\] ; \[W_{\rm net}>0 \text{ for clockwise operation}, \qquad \eta=\frac{W_{\rm net}}{Q_{\rm in}}\]
    Key points.
    • A cyclic process is not necessarily a thermodynamic cycle of a heat engine; positive efficiency requires both \(W_{\rm net}>0\) and \(Q_{\rm in}>0\).
    • The net area is positive for clockwise traversal and negative for counterclockwise traversal in a \(P\)-\(V\) diagram.
    • Heat may enter during one or more legs and leave during the others; \(Q_{\rm net}\) is not the same as \(Q_{\rm in}\).
    • The enclosed area has dimensions of energy even when pressure is plotted against volume.
    • Internal-energy changes of individual legs need not vanish, but their algebraic sum is zero.
    • A reversible cycle has no net entropy generation, but ordinary cyclic heat engines are usually irreversible.
    Example 1.

    A gas follows the cycle \(A(0.10\ \mathrm{m^3},2.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})\to B(0.30\ \mathrm{m^3},2.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})\to C(0.10\ \mathrm{m^3},1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})\to A\). Find the net work and net heat, and state the direction of heat flow.

    1. On \(A\to B\), the work is \(W_{AB}=2.0\times10^5(0.30-0.10)=4.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}\).
    2. The leg \(B\to C\) is linear, so \(W_{BC}=\frac{P_B+P_C}{2}(V_C-V_B)=1.5\times10^5(-0.20)=-3.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. The leg \(C\to A\) is isochoric, so \(W_{CA}=0\).
    4. Therefore \(W_{\rm net}=(4.0-3.0)\times10^4=1.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}\).
    5. Since \(\Delta U_{\rm cycle}=0\), \(Q_{\rm net}=W_{\rm net}=10.0\ \mathrm{kJ}\).

    Answer: The cycle does \(10.0\ \mathrm{kJ}\) of net work and absorbs the same net amount of heat; it is clockwise.

    Example 2.

    The triangular cycle in the preceding example is traversed in the same order and the gas is monatomic. Find the total heat absorbed during the two heat-input legs and the thermal efficiency of the cycle.

    1. For \(A\to B\), \(\Delta(PV)=P\Delta V=2.0\times10^5(0.20)=4.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}\).
    2. Thus \(\Delta U_{AB}=\frac{3}{2}\Delta(PV)=6.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}\) and \(Q_{AB}=\Delta U_{AB}+W_{AB}=1.00\times10^5\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. For \(C\to A\), the volume is fixed, so \(W_{CA}=0\) and \(\Delta(PV)=V\Delta P=0.10(1.0\times10^5)=1.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. Hence \(Q_{CA}=\Delta U_{CA}=\frac{3}{2}(1.0\times10^4)=1.50\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}\); heat enters on this leg.
    5. Therefore \(Q_{\rm in}=115.0\ \mathrm{kJ}\), while the net work is \(10.0\ \mathrm{kJ}\).
    6. The efficiency is \(\eta=10/115=0.08696\).

    Answer: \(Q_{\rm in}=115\ \mathrm{kJ}\) and \(\eta=8.70\%\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Claiming that internal energy is constant during each leg; it is only unchanged over the complete cycle.
    • Treating all heat entering the gas as net heat when some heat may leave on another leg.
    • Reversing the sign of work from the clockwise enclosed area.

    Explanation

    Concept. A \(P\)-\(V\) diagram displays pressure against volume and encodes the work and direction of thermodynamic processes geometrically. The work done by a gas during a quasistatic path is the signed area under its curve, while a closed path encloses an area equal to the net work. Slopes identify process types: horizontal isobars, vertical isochores, and curves connecting the two are adiabats or isotherms.
    Key formula(s). \[W_{\rm by}=\int_{V_1}^{V_2}P(V)\,dV\] ; \[\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_T=-\frac{P}{V} \text{ for an isotherm}, \qquad \left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_S=-\gamma\frac{P}{V}\] ; \[W_{\rm cycle}=\oint P\,dV=\text{signed enclosed area}\]
    Key points.
    • Expansion gives positive work; on a \(P\)-\(V\) plot it is traversed from smaller to larger volume.
    • A straight-line process is not isothermal or adiabatic unless its slope satisfies the corresponding relation.
    • Isothermal curves for an ideal gas are flatter than adiabats because \(\gamma>1\).
    • The area under a process curve gives only that process's work, not the heat transferred.
    • Clockwise cycles produce positive work, while counterclockwise cycles require net work input.
    • Axes and scales are essential when finding the numerical area under a curve.
    Example 1.

    A gas expands quasistatically along a straight line from \((V_1,P_1)=(1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3},2.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})\) to \((V_2,P_2)=(3.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3},1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})\). Calculate the work done by the gas.

    1. The area under a straight line on a \(P\)-\(V\) graph is the trapezoidal area \(\frac{P_1+P_2}{2}(V_2-V_1)\).
    2. Here \(\Delta V=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}\) and \(P_{\rm avg}=(2.0+1.0)\times10^5/2=1.5\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\).
    3. Therefore \(W_{\rm by}=P_{\rm avg}\Delta V=(1.5\times10^5)(2.0\times10^{-3})\).
    4. The product is \(3.0\times10^2\ \mathrm{J}\), with a positive sign because the expansion is left to right.

    Answer: \(W_{\rm by}=300\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    One mole of monatomic ideal gas executes the cycle \(A(V=1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3},P=1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})\to B(4.0\times10^{-3},1.0\times10^5)\to C(4.0\times10^{-3},2.0\times10^5)\to D(1.0\times10^{-3},2.0\times10^5)\to A\). Find the net work, heat absorbed, and efficiency.

    1. The clockwise rectangular area gives \(W_{\rm net}=(2.0-1.0)\times10^5(4.0-1.0)\times10^{-3}=300\ \mathrm{J}\).
    2. On \(A\to B\), \(Q_{AB}=(1+\frac{3}{2})P\Delta V=\frac{5}{2}(300)=750\ \mathrm{J}\), so heat enters.
    3. On \(B\to C\), \(Q_{BC}=(\frac{3}{2})V\Delta P=\frac{3}{2}(400)=600\ \mathrm{J}\), so heat also enters.
    4. On \(C\to D\), \(Q_{CD}=\frac{5}{2}P\Delta V=\frac{5}{2}(-600)=-1500\ \mathrm{J}\).
    5. On \(D\to A\), \(Q_{DA}=\frac{3}{2}V\Delta P=\frac{3}{2}(-100)=-150\ \mathrm{J}\).
    6. Thus \(Q_{\rm in}=750+600=1350\ \mathrm{J}\) and \(\eta=300/1350\).

    Answer: \(W_{\rm net}=300\ \mathrm{J}\), \(Q_{\rm in}=1.35\ \mathrm{kJ}\), and \(\eta=22.2\%\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(P\Delta V\) for a non-isobaric process without taking the pressure average.
    • Taking unsigned area when a compression or counterclockwise cycle requires a negative sign.
    • Equating the area under a path with heat supplied; that area is work, not heat.

    Chapter 8 · Topic 13

    Irreversible process

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsLaws and ProcessesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Irreversible processes (free expansion, friction heating, uncontrolled heat flow, diffusion mixing) cannot retrace exactly - entropy rises, universe gains disorder. All real processes are irreversible; reversible (quasi-static, infinitesimal gradients) is an ideal limit approached by slow engines. Second law forbids perfect reversal (Kelvin-Planck, Clausius statements). Irreversibility arrows time itself - broken eggs never unbreak.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Real processes irreversible; reversible is ideal slow limit.
    • Entropy rise marks irreversibility direction.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    All natural processes are

    Solution: Finite-gradient real processes cannot retrace exactly.
    Key Formulas · Irreversible Process
    \(\Delta S_{universe}>0\) entropy rises in real processes
    \(\eta_{real}<1-\frac{T_{c}}{T_{h}}\) real engines trail Carnot cap

    Chapter 8 · Topic 14

    Second law

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsLaws and ProcessesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The second law of thermodynamics determines the direction of spontaneous processes and the efficiency limits of heat devices. Its Kelvin-Planck form states that no cyclic device can extract heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work without another effect. Its entropy formulation states that total entropy generation is nonnegative, so no engine can operate between two reservoirs with efficiency exceeding the Carnot limit.
    Key formula(s). \[\eta=1-\frac{Q_C}{Q_H}\le 1-\frac{T_C}{T_H}\] ; \[\Delta S_{\rm univ}=\Delta S_{\rm sys}+\Delta S_{\rm surroundings}\ge 0\] ; \[\oint \delta Q_{\rm rev}/T\le 0\]
    Key points.
    • The first law conserves energy, but the second law imposes an additional restriction on how that energy may be transformed.
    • Heat naturally flows from a hotter body to a colder body; reversing this flow requires work or another compensating change.
    • Complete conversion of heat from a single reservoir into work in a cyclic device is impossible.
    • The Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements are equivalent and lead to the Carnot efficiency bound.
    • A calculated positive work output that makes \(\Delta S_{\rm univ}<0\) is thermodynamically impossible.
    • The second law does not forbid energy loss; it forbids an energy transformation that produces negative total entropy.
    Example 1.

    A reversible engine operates between reservoirs at \(1000\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) and absorbs \(5000\ \mathrm{J}\) from the hot reservoir. Find the maximum work, the minimum heat rejected, and the efficiency.

    1. For reversible operation, \(\eta_{\max}=1-T_C/T_H=1-300/1000=0.700\).
    2. The maximum work is \(W_{\max}=\eta_{\max}Q_H=0.700(5000)=3500\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. Energy conservation over a cycle gives \(Q_C=Q_H-W=5000-3500=1500\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. The entropy balance is consistent: \(-Q_H/T_H+Q_C/T_C=-5+5=0\).

    Answer: \(W_{\max}=3500\ \mathrm{J}\), \(Q_{C,\min}=1500\ \mathrm{J}\), and \(\eta_{\max}=70.0\%\).

    Example 2.

    A proposed cyclic engine absorbs \(1000\ \mathrm{J}\) from a \(1000\ \mathrm{K}\) reservoir, does \(700\ \mathrm{J}\) of work, and rejects \(300\ \mathrm{J}\) to a \(400\ \mathrm{K}\) reservoir. Test the proposal using the second law and find the maximum permissible efficiency.

    1. Energy balance is satisfied because \(W+Q_C=700+300=1000\ \mathrm{J}\).
    2. The engine is cyclic, so its entropy change over one cycle is zero.
    3. The reservoirs' entropy change is \(\Delta S_{\rm univ}=-1000/1000+300/400=-0.250\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).
    4. A negative value violates the second law, so the proposed engine is impossible.
    5. The Carnot limit between \(1000\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(400\ \mathrm{K}\) is \(\eta_{\max}=1-400/1000=0.600\).

    Answer: The proposal violates the second law; the maximum permissible efficiency is \(60.0\%\), corresponding to \(W_{\max}=600\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using energy conservation alone to declare a proposed heat engine possible.
    • Comparing reservoir temperatures in degrees Celsius in an efficiency formula.
    • Claiming that spontaneous heat flow may occur from a cold reservoir to a hot one without work or another change.

    Explanation

    Concept. Entropy is a thermodynamic state function that measures the number of accessible microscopic configurations and the tendency of energy dispersal. For a reversible transfer, its change in a system is \(dS=\delta Q_{\rm rev}/T\), where the temperature is the absolute boundary temperature. Because entropy is a state function, it can be calculated using any convenient reversible path connecting the initial and final equilibrium states.
    Key formula(s). \[\Delta S=\int_i^f\frac{\delta Q_{\rm rev}}{T}, \qquad \oint \frac{\delta Q_{\rm rev}}{T}=0\] ; \[\Delta S_{\rm univ}\ge 0, \qquad [S]=\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\] ; \[\Delta S_{\rm rev}=-Q/T, \qquad \Delta S_{\rm surr}=Q/T\]
    Key points.
    • Entropy is not generally \(Q/T\) for an irreversible process; that expression requires a reversible heat-transfer path.
    • The entropy of an isolated system never decreases in a spontaneous physical process.
    • Entropy is a state function, so path reversibility does not prevent using an alternative reversible path for calculation.
    • A change in temperature, volume, phase, or composition can all change entropy.
    • Entropy has units of joules per kelvin and is not heat capacity.
    • Reversible isothermal work and reversible isothermal heat have the same magnitude for an ideal gas because \(\Delta U=0\).
    Example 1.

    Two moles of an ideal gas expand reversibly and isothermally at \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) from volume \(V\) to \(10V\). Calculate the entropy change of the gas and the heat absorbed reversibly.

    1. At constant temperature for an ideal gas, \(\Delta U=0\), so \(Q_{\rm rev}=W_{\rm rev}=nRT\ln(V_f/V_i)\).
    2. Thus \(Q_{\rm rev}=2(8.314)(300)\ln10=1.152\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. The entropy change is \(\Delta S=Q_{\rm rev}/T=(1.152\times10^4)/300\).
    4. Equivalently, \(\Delta S=2R\ln10=2(8.314)(2.302585)\).
    5. Both routes give \(\Delta S=38.39\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\), positive for the expansion.

    Answer: \(\Delta S=38.39\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\) and \(Q_{\rm rev}=11.52\ \mathrm{kJ}\).

    Example 2.

    One mole of monatomic ideal gas changes from \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}\) to \(600\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}\). Find its entropy change.

    1. The entropy differential of an ideal gas is \(dS=(C_V/T)dT+R(dV/V)\).
    2. For a monatomic gas, \(C_V=\frac{3}{2}R\).
    3. Therefore \(\Delta S=C_V\ln(T_2/T_1)+R\ln(V_2/V_1)\).
    4. Both ratios equal \(2\), so \(\Delta S=(\frac{3}{2}R+R)\ln2=\frac{5}{2}R\ln2\).
    5. Numerically, \(\Delta S=2.5(8.314)(0.693147)=14.41\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(\Delta S=+14.41\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(Q/T\) with the final temperature when the heat transfer is not reversible.
    • Treating entropy as a path-dependent quantity.
    • Confusing entropy with heat capacity or with temperature in kelvin.

    Explanation

    Concept. An entropy change can be positive or negative for a system, but the total entropy change of the system and surroundings cannot be negative. For an ideal gas, temperature and volume changes contribute separate logarithmic terms to \(\Delta S\). Free expansion illustrates that \(\Delta S\) can be positive even when an isolated gas exchanges no heat and does no work.
    Key formula(s). \[\Delta S_{\rm univ}=\Delta S_{\rm sys}+\Delta S_{\rm surroundings}\] ; \[\Delta S_{\rm ideal}=nC_V\ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)+nR\ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)\] ; \[\Delta S_{\rm mix}=-nR\sum_i x_i\ln x_i\] ; \[\Delta S_{\rm univ}=\Delta S_{\rm gen}\ge 0\]
    Key points.
    • A positive \(\Delta S_{\rm sys}\) does not require heat to enter the system; internal irreversible processes can generate entropy.
    • An ideal gas has \(\Delta U=0\) in Joule free expansion because no work is done and its internal energy depends only on temperature.
    • For reservoir entropy changes, use the reservoir temperature and the signed heat received by the reservoir.
    • State-function entropy differences can be evaluated even if the actual path is not reversible.
    • Mixing distinguishable gases is irreversible and produces an entropy increase even when no energy is supplied externally.
    • The second law constrains the combined change, not the sign of the system's entropy change alone.
    Example 1.

    Two moles of an ideal gas undergo Joule free expansion in an insulated container from volume \(V\) to \(2V\). Find \(Q\), \(W_{\rm by}\), \(\Delta U\), the system's entropy change, and the universe's entropy change.

    1. The expansion is into a vacuum, so the external pressure is zero and \(W_{\rm by}=0\).
    2. The container is insulated, so \(Q=0\), and the first law gives \(\Delta U=Q-W_{\rm by}=0\).
    3. For an ideal gas, constant internal energy means constant temperature, so the isothermal state-function formula applies.
    4. Hence \(\Delta S_{\rm sys}=nR\ln(V_2/V_1)=2R\ln2=11.53\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).
    5. There is no heat transfer and the surroundings is unchanged, so \(\Delta S_{\rm univ}=11.53\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}>0\).

    Answer: \(Q=0\), \(W_{\rm by}=0\), \(\Delta U=0\), and \(\Delta S_{\rm sys}=\Delta S_{\rm univ}=11.53\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(2.0\ \mathrm{kg}\) sample of ice at \(273.15\ \mathrm{K}\) melts completely and the resulting water is heated to \(300\ \mathrm{K}\). Take \(L_f=3.34\times10^5\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}\) and \(c_w=4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}\). Find the total entropy change of the sample.

    1. The entropy increase during reversible melting at \(273.15\ \mathrm{K}\) is \(\Delta S_1=mL_f/T_f\).
    2. Thus \(\Delta S_1=2.0(3.34\times10^5)/273.15=2.446\times10^3\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).
    3. For heating liquid water, \(\Delta S_2=mc_w\ln(T_2/T_f)=2.0(4200)\ln(300/273.15)\).
    4. The logarithmic factor is approximately \(0.09376\), giving \(\Delta S_2=787.6\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).
    5. Entropy is additive over the two state changes, so \(\Delta S=\Delta S_1+\Delta S_2=3.233\times10^3\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).

    Answer: The total entropy change of the sample is \(+3.23\times10^3\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Writing \(Q/T\) for a system that undergoes free expansion, for which \(Q=0\) but \(\Delta S\ne0\).
    • Using one reservoir temperature for all heat transfer when a process spans changing temperatures.
    • Omitting the latent-entropy term during a phase change.

    Chapter 8 · Topic 15

    Heat engines

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsEnginesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A heat engine is a cyclic device that absorbs heat from a high-temperature source, converts part of it into net work, and rejects the remainder to a low-temperature sink. Its efficiency is the ratio of net work output to total heat input, not the ratio of work to the heat rejected. A useful JEE strategy is to mark every heat-input and heat-output leg on the \(P\)-\(V\) diagram before applying the first law.
    Key formula(s). \[Q_{\rm net}=Q_{\rm in}-Q_{\rm out}, \qquad W_{\rm net}=Q_{\rm in}-Q_{\rm out}\] ; \[\eta=\frac{W_{\rm net}}{Q_{\rm in}}=1-\frac{Q_{\rm out}}{Q_{\rm in}}\] ; \[\eta<1-\frac{T_C}{T_H}\quad\text{for an irreversible engine}\]
    Key points.
    • An engine operates cyclically, so its working fluid has \(\Delta U=0\) over a complete cycle.
    • \(Q_{\rm in}\) is heat absorbed on all positive heat-input legs, while \(Q_{\rm out}\) is the positive magnitude of all rejected heat.
    • Net work is positive only for clockwise operation on a \(P\)-\(V\) diagram.
    • A source or sink reservoir is external to the cyclic working fluid and does not return to its initial state.
    • The thermal efficiency can never equal unity and is always below the Carnot limit for the highest and lowest reservoir temperatures.
    • Mechanical efficiency and thermal efficiency are different quantities and should not be interchanged.
    Example 1.

    A heat engine absorbs \(2500\ \mathrm{J}\) of heat per cycle and rejects \(1800\ \mathrm{J}\) to the sink. Calculate its net work output and thermal efficiency.

    1. The first law for a complete cycle gives \(W_{\rm net}=Q_{\rm in}-Q_{\rm out}\).
    2. Therefore \(W_{\rm net}=2500-1800=700\ \mathrm{J}\) per cycle.
    3. The efficiency is defined using the heat input, so \(\eta=700/2500=0.280\).
    4. The rejected heat is the remaining \(1800\ \mathrm{J}\), confirming that only \(28\%\) of the input becomes work.

    Answer: \(W_{\rm net}=700\ \mathrm{J}\) per cycle and \(\eta=28.0\%\).

    Example 2.

    One mole of monatomic ideal gas executes the cycle \(A(V=1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3},P=1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})\to B(4.0\times10^{-3},1.0\times10^5)\to C(4.0\times10^{-3},2.0\times10^5)\to D(1.0\times10^{-3},2.0\times10^5)\to A\). Find the net work, heat absorbed, and efficiency.

    1. The clockwise rectangular area gives \(W_{\rm net}=(2.0-1.0)\times10^5(4.0-1.0)\times10^{-3}=300\ \mathrm{J}\).
    2. On the isobaric expansion \(A\to B\), \(Q=\frac{5}{2}P\Delta V=\frac{5}{2}(300)=750\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. On the isochoric heating \(B\to C\), \(Q=\frac{3}{2}V\Delta P=\frac{3}{2}(400)=600\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. The other two legs reject heat, so the total heat input is \(Q_{\rm in}=750+600=1350\ \mathrm{J}\).
    5. Thus \(\eta=W_{\rm net}/Q_{\rm in}=300/1350=0.2222\).

    Answer: \(W_{\rm net}=300\ \mathrm{J}\), \(Q_{\rm in}=1350\ \mathrm{J}\), and \(\eta=22.2\%\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Defining efficiency as \(W/(Q_{\rm in}+Q_{\rm out})\).
    • Taking \(Q_{\rm net}\) to be the same as total heat absorbed.
    • Omitting heat-input legs that have zero boundary work, as during isochoric heating.

    Chapter 8 · Topic 16

    Refrigerator

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsEnginesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A refrigerator is a cyclic device run in reverse that removes heat from a low-temperature region and delivers it, together with work, to a high-temperature region. Its performance is measured by the coefficient of performance rather than thermal efficiency. Since it moves heat uphill, its coefficient of performance can legitimately exceed one.
    Key formula(s). \[Q_H=Q_C+W,\qquad \eta=\frac{W}{Q_H}\] ; \[\mathrm{COP}_R=\frac{Q_C}{W},\qquad \mathrm{COP}_{HP}=\frac{Q_H}{W}\] ; \[\mathrm{COP}_{HP}=\mathrm{COP}_R+1\]
    Key points.
    • A refrigerator requires work input; a reversed heat engine operating in this mode is called a refrigerator or heat pump.
    • \(Q_C\) is the heat removed from the refrigerated space and \(Q_H\) is the heat delivered at the hot end.
    • The first law requires \(Q_H=Q_C+W\) for the complete cycle.
    • \(\mathrm{COP}_R\) is a performance ratio, not a thermodynamic efficiency and not bounded by one.
    • A heat pump and the same device used as a refrigerator have identical \(W\) and \(Q_C\), but heat-pump COP is one greater.
    • The best theoretical refrigerator operating between two reservoirs is the Carnot refrigerator.
    Example 1.

    A refrigerator removes \(200\ \mathrm{J}\) of heat from its contents in each cycle and consumes \(80\ \mathrm{J}\) of work. Find the heat delivered to the surroundings, the refrigerator COP, and the heat-pump COP.

    1. Energy conservation gives \(Q_H=Q_C+W=200+80=280\ \mathrm{J}\).
    2. The refrigerator coefficient of performance is \(\mathrm{COP}_R=Q_C/W=200/80=2.50\).
    3. The heat-pump coefficient of performance is \(\mathrm{COP}_{HP}=Q_H/W=280/80=3.50\).
    4. As required, \(\mathrm{COP}_{HP}=\mathrm{COP}_R+1=3.50\).

    Answer: \(Q_H=280\ \mathrm{J}\), \(\mathrm{COP}_R=2.50\), and \(\mathrm{COP}_{HP}=3.50\).

    Example 2.

    An ideal refrigerator operates between a \(250\ \mathrm{K}\) refrigerated space and a \(350\ \mathrm{K}\) room. It removes \(1200\ \mathrm{J}\) of heat from the cold space in each cycle. Calculate the work required, the heat delivered, and the COP.

    1. For a Carnot refrigerator, \(\mathrm{COP}_R=T_C/(T_H-T_C)=250/(350-250)=2.50\).
    2. Since \(Q_C=\mathrm{COP}_R W\), the work is \(W=1200/2.50=480\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. The heat delivered to the room is \(Q_H=Q_C+W=1200+480=1680\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. Equivalently, \(Q_H/Q_C=T_H/T_C=350/250=1.40\).
    5. A real refrigerator needs at least this much work for the same extraction.

    Answer: \(W=480\ \mathrm{J}\), \(Q_H=1680\ \mathrm{J}\), and \(\mathrm{COP}_R=2.50\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Calling the heat removed from the cold body the work input.
    • Using \(Q_H/W\) when the requested coefficient is the refrigerator COP.
    • Expecting every COP to be less than one; refrigerator and heat-pump COPs may exceed one.
    Back to Index
    Index / Heat and Thermodynamics
    Chapter 8 · Topic 17

    Coefficient of performance

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsEnginesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The coefficient of performance measures the useful thermal output of a refrigerator or heat pump per unit work input. The appropriate numerator depends on the desired effect: removed cooling for a refrigerator and delivered heat for a heat pump. For reversible devices operating between fixed reservoirs, the Carnot formulas provide upper bounds that are useful for judging the performance of real machines.
    Key formula(s). \[\mathrm{COP}_R=\frac{Q_C}{W}=\frac{Q_C}{Q_H-Q_C}\] ; \[\mathrm{COP}_{HP}=\frac{Q_H}{W}=1+\mathrm{COP}_R\] ; \[\mathrm{COP}_{R,C}=\frac{T_C}{T_H-T_C}, \qquad \mathrm{COP}_{HP,C}=\frac{T_H}{T_H-T_C}\]
    Key points.
    • A COP can be greater than one because the device may move several units of heat for each unit of work supplied.
    • The refrigerator COP and heat-pump COP cannot be interchanged; their numerators describe different useful effects.
    • A real refrigerator has a lower COP than the Carnot refrigerator for the same two reservoir temperatures.
    • At fixed \(T_C\), increasing \(T_H\) lowers the ideal refrigerator COP.
    • COP is not a heat-engine efficiency and has no universal upper bound of one.
    • For a given cooling load, a larger COP means less work and less electrical consumption per cycle.
    Example 1.

    A refrigerator removes \(600\ \mathrm{J}\) from a \(270\ \mathrm{K}\) compartment while consuming \(180\ \mathrm{J}\) of work. Find the heat delivered to a \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) room, the refrigerator COP, and the heat-pump COP.

    1. The first law for the cycle gives \(Q_H=Q_C+W=600+180=780\ \mathrm{J}\).
    2. The refrigerator COP is \(\mathrm{COP}_R=600/180=3.333\).
    3. The heat-pump COP is \(\mathrm{COP}_{HP}=780/180=4.333\).
    4. The Carnot refrigerator COP is \(270/(300-270)=9.00\), so the stated machine is far from ideal.
    5. The relation \(\mathrm{COP}_{HP}=\mathrm{COP}_R+1\) is satisfied.

    Answer: \(Q_H=780\ \mathrm{J}\), \(\mathrm{COP}_R=3.33\), and \(\mathrm{COP}_{HP}=4.33\).

    Example 2.

    A refrigerator must remove \(1000\ \mathrm{J}\) from a space at \(250\ \mathrm{K}\) and reject it to a room at \(300\ \mathrm{K}\). Find the minimum theoretical work and the required heat delivery; an actual refrigerator has COP \(2.50\). Find its actual work and heat delivery.

    1. The ideal COP is \(\mathrm{COP}_{R,C}=250/(300-250)=5.00\).
    2. The minimum work is \(W_{\min}=Q_C/\mathrm{COP}_{R,C}=1000/5=200\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. For the ideal device, \(Q_{H,\min}=Q_C+W_{\min}=1200\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. For the actual device, \(W_{\rm actual}=Q_C/\mathrm{COP}_R=1000/2.50=400\ \mathrm{J}\).
    5. Its heat delivery is \(Q_{H,\rm actual}=1000+400=1400\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: Ideally \(W_{\min}=200\ \mathrm{J}\) and \(Q_{H,\min}=1200\ \mathrm{J}\); actually \(W=400\ \mathrm{J}\) and \(Q_H=1400\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(Q_C/Q_H\) instead of \(Q_C/W\) for refrigerator COP.
    • Writing \(\mathrm{COP}_R=\mathrm{COP}_{HP}\) although their difference is exactly one.
    • Comparing a real COP directly with unity rather than with the appropriate Carnot COP.

    Index / Heat and Thermodynamics
    Chapter 8 · Topic 18

    Carnot engine

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsEnginesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A Carnot engine is the ideal reversible engine operating between two fixed-temperature reservoirs and consists of two isothermal and two adiabatic reversible processes. The isotherms provide heat exchange, while the quick reversible adiabats connect the temperatures without heat transfer. The adiabatic legs also imply equal volume ratios on the two isothermal legs for the same working gas.
    Key formula(s). \[\eta_C=1-\frac{T_C}{T_H}, \qquad \frac{Q_C}{Q_H}=\frac{T_C}{T_H}\] ; \[Q_H=nRT_H\ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right), \qquad Q_C=nRT_C\ln\left(\frac{V_3}{V_4}\right)\] ; \[\frac{V_3}{V_2}=\frac{V_4}{V_1}=\left(\frac{T_H}{T_C}\right)^{1/(\gamma-1)}, \qquad \frac{V_2}{V_1}=\frac{V_3}{V_4}\ \text{for a closed Carnot cycle}\]
    Key points.
    • The two isothermal processes are not isochoric; finite heat transfer in a reversible engine requires finite temperature difference between the working gas and reservoir.
    • The two adiabatic processes have no heat exchange, so their entropy changes are zero.
    • \(T_H\) and \(T_C\) must be absolute temperatures in kelvin.
    • For a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, \(\Delta U=0\), so the heat absorbed equals the work done.
    • A larger hot-to-cold temperature ratio gives a larger Carnot efficiency, but all real efficiencies remain below it.
    • The Carnot engine is an efficiency benchmark, not a practical maximum-power engine.
    Example 1.

    Two moles of monatomic ideal gas operate a Carnot engine between \(500\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(300\ \mathrm{K}\). During hot isothermal expansion the volume doubles. Find the heat absorbed, heat rejected, and net work per cycle.

    1. The hot isotherm has \(Q_H=nRT_H\ln(V_2/V_1)=2R(500)\ln2\).
    2. Thus \(Q_H=1000(8.314)(0.693147)=5.762\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. For a Carnot cycle, \(Q_C/Q_H=T_C/T_H=300/500=0.600\), so \(Q_C=3457\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. The net work is \(W=Q_H-Q_C=(1-0.600)Q_H=2305\ \mathrm{J}\).
    5. The cold isothermal volume ratio is also \(2\), and the adiabatic ratio is \((500/300)^{3/2}=1.814\).

    Answer: \(Q_H=5.76\ \mathrm{kJ}\), \(Q_C=3.46\ \mathrm{kJ}\), and \(W=2.30\ \mathrm{kJ}\) per cycle.

    Example 2.

    Three moles of a diatomic ideal gas \((\gamma=1.40)\) form a Carnot engine between \(400\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(250\ \mathrm{K}\). The hot reservoir supplies \(6000\ \mathrm{J}\). Find \(Q_C\), \(W\), the hot-isothermal volume ratio, and the adiabatic volume ratio.

    1. The Carnot relation gives \(Q_C=Q_H(T_C/T_H)=6000(250/400)=3750\ \mathrm{J}\).
    2. Therefore \(W=Q_H-Q_C=6000-3750=2250\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. From \(Q_H=nRT_H\ln(V_2/V_1)\), \(\ln(V_2/V_1)=6000/[3(8.314)(400)]=0.6014\).
    4. Hence \(V_2/V_1=e^{0.6014}=1.825\).
    5. For a diatomic gas, the common adiabatic ratio is \((T_H/T_C)^{1/(\gamma-1)}=(1.6)^{2.5}=3.238\).

    Answer: \(Q_C=3750\ \mathrm{J}\), \(W=2250\ \mathrm{J}\), \(V_2/V_1=1.825\), and \(V_3/V_2=V_4/V_1=3.238\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Placing the reservoirs at equal temperatures and concluding that an engine can have nonzero work.
    • Using Celsius temperatures in the heat ratio.
    • Applying the adiabatic volume formula to the isothermal expansion leg.

    Chapter 8 · Topic 19

    Efficiency

    ThermodynamicsHeat and ThermodynamicsEnginesStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Carnot efficiency is the maximum efficiency of any heat engine operating between two specified reservoir temperatures. It depends only on the absolute temperatures and not on the working substance, amount of gas, or path details. Reversible Carnot operation attains this limit, while all irreversible engines necessarily have lower efficiency.
    Key formula(s). \[\eta_C=1-\frac{T_C}{T_H}=\frac{T_H-T_C}{T_H}\] ; \[W_{\rm rev}=Q_H\left(1-\frac{T_C}{T_H}\right), \qquad Q_{C,\rm rev}=Q_H\frac{T_C}{T_H}\] ; \[\eta_{\rm engine}\le\eta_C\]
    Key points.
    • Both reservoir temperatures must be in kelvin.
    • The efficiency is a ratio, so multiplying numerator and denominator by a temperature scale factor does not change it.
    • Carnot efficiency is independent of the quantity and molar heat capacity of the working substance.
    • Increasing \(T_H\) or decreasing \(T_C\) increases the maximum possible efficiency.
    • Equality with Carnot efficiency requires every process of the cycle to be reversible.
    • A reversible engine need not deliver maximum power; irreversibilities such as friction may increase power at the cost of efficiency.
    Example 1.

    A Carnot engine operates between \(800\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) and absorbs \(3000\ \mathrm{J}\) from the source in each cycle. Calculate the heat rejected and the work produced.

    1. The maximum efficiency is \(\eta_C=1-300/800=500/800=0.625\).
    2. The work produced is \(W=\eta_CQ_H=0.625(3000)=1875\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. The rejected heat is \(Q_C=Q_H-W=3000-1875=1125\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. The ratio \(Q_C/Q_H=1125/3000=0.375=T_C/T_H\), as required.

    Answer: \(Q_C=1125\ \mathrm{J}\) and \(W=1875\ \mathrm{J}\) per cycle.

    Example 2.

    An actual engine absorbs \(2500\ \mathrm{J}\) from a \(1000\ \mathrm{K}\) source in each cycle and has efficiency \(40.0\%\). Find its work and rejected heat. If a reversible engine is to produce the same work from the same source, what must be the sink temperature?

    1. The actual work output is \(W=\eta Q_H=0.400(2500)=1000\ \mathrm{J}\).
    2. Its rejected heat is \(Q_C=Q_H-W=2500-1000=1500\ \mathrm{J}\).
    3. For a reversible engine with the same source temperature and work, \(1-T_C/1000=W/Q_H=1000/2500=0.400\).
    4. Solving gives \(T_C/1000=0.600\), hence \(T_C=600\ \mathrm{K}\).
    5. This is a bound: the actual engine with the same sink cannot exceed \(40\%\) without irreversibility elsewhere.

    Answer: \(W=1000\ \mathrm{J}\), \(Q_C=1500\ \mathrm{J}\), and the required reversible sink temperature is \(600\ \mathrm{K}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Substituting \(300\ \mathrm{K}/800\ \mathrm{K}\) directly as the efficiency.
    • Treating Carnot efficiency as the actual efficiency of every engine.
    • Increasing Carnot efficiency by changing the working substance while keeping both reservoirs fixed.

    Chapter 9 · Topic 1

    Ideal gas

    Kinetic Theory of GasesHeat and ThermodynamicsGas LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. An ideal gas is a hypothetical gas whose particles have negligible volume, exert no intermolecular forces except during perfectly elastic collisions, and obey the ideal-gas equation exactly. It is the simplest working substance for thermodynamics and models most real gases accurately at low pressure and sufficiently high temperature. The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, not on pressure or volume.
    Key formula(s). \[PV=nRT,\qquad pV=Nk_BT\] ; \[n=\frac{m}{M},\qquad PV=\frac{m}{M}RT\] ; \[\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T,\qquad U=U(T)\text{ for an ideal gas}\]
    Key points.
    • The universal gas constant is \(R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\), while \(k_B=1.381\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).
    • \(n\) is the amount in moles, \(N\) is the molecule count, \(m\) is gas mass, and \(M\) is molar mass.
    • Temperature in the equation must be in kelvin.
    • The ideal-gas equation applies to each gas in a nonreacting ideal-gas mixture, with its own partial pressure and mole fraction.
    • Real gases deviate most strongly at high pressure and low temperature, when molecular size and attractions become important.
    • \(PV/T\) is constant for a fixed sample over a sequence of equilibrium states.
    Example 1.

    Find the volume occupied by \(0.50\) mol of ideal gas at \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(1.5\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\).

    1. Rearrange the ideal-gas equation as \(V=nRT/P\).
    2. Substitute the data: \(V=(0.50)(8.314)(300)/(1.5\times10^5)\).
    3. The numerator is \(1247.1\ \mathrm{J}\), and volume has units \(\mathrm{J\,Pa^{-1}}=\mathrm{m^3}\).
    4. Hence \(V=8.314\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}=8.314\ \mathrm{L}\).

    Answer: \(V=8.31\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}\), or \(8.31\ \mathrm{L}\).

    Example 2.

    Two moles of ideal gas with molar mass \(28\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\) occupy \(0.10\ \mathrm{m^3}\) at \(27^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Find the pressure and the mass of gas.

    1. Convert the temperature to \(T=27+273=300\ \mathrm{K}\).
    2. The pressure is \(P=nRT/V=2(8.314)(300)/0.10=4.9884\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\).
    3. Converting molar mass gives \(M=0.028\ \mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\).
    4. The sample mass is \(m=nM=2(0.028)=0.056\ \mathrm{kg}\).
    5. The two results follow from \(PV=nRT\) and \(n=m/M\), respectively.

    Answer: \(P=4.99\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\) and \(m=0.056\ \mathrm{kg}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Substituting Celsius temperature into the ideal-gas equation.
    • Mixing the meanings of molar mass and total mass.
    • Using SI pressure with volume in litres without converting units.

    Index / Heat and Thermodynamics
    Chapter 9 · Topic 2

    Gas laws

    Kinetic Theory of GasesHeat and ThermodynamicsGas LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The gas laws are special cases of the ideal-gas equation for a fixed amount of gas. Boyle's law applies at constant temperature, Charles's law at constant pressure, and Gay-Lussac's law at constant volume, always with absolute temperature. For a process spanning several such stages, the combined relation \(P_1V_1/T_1=P_2V_2/T_2\) applies only if the endpoints have the same fixed amount of gas.
    Key formula(s). \[P=\text{constant}: \qquad \frac{V}{T}=\text{constant}\] ; \[V=\text{constant}: \qquad \frac{P}{T}=\text{constant}\] ; \[T=\text{constant}: \qquad PV=\text{constant}, \qquad \frac{P_1V_1}{T_1}=\frac{P_2V_2}{T_2}\]
    Key points.
    • The temperature in every gas law is the absolute temperature in kelvin.
    • At constant pressure, doubling absolute temperature doubles volume for a fixed sample.
    • At constant volume, a pressure ratio equals the corresponding absolute-temperature ratio.
    • At constant temperature, pressure and volume vary inversely.
    • The combined gas law is the equation of state, not a statement that \(PV/T\) remains constant during every arbitrary process.
    • A change in the number of gas molecules invalidates comparisons that assume a closed sample.
    Example 1.

    A fixed sample of ideal gas is heated at constant pressure from \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) to \(600\ \mathrm{K}\). If its initial volume is \(4.0\ \mathrm{L}\), find its final volume and explain the applicable law.

    1. At constant pressure for a fixed amount of gas, Charles's law gives \(V/T=\text{constant}\).
    2. Therefore \(V_2=V_1(T_2/T_1)\).
    3. Substituting the values, \(V_2=4.0(600/300)=8.0\ \mathrm{L}\).
    4. Absolute, not Celsius, temperature must be used in the ratio.

    Answer: \(V_2=8.0\ \mathrm{L}\), using Charles's law.

    Example 2.

    A gas starts at \(P_1=1.2\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\), \(V_1=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}\), and \(T_1=300\ \mathrm{K}\). It expands isothermally to \(6.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}\), then is heated at constant volume to \(450\ \mathrm{K}\). Find the intermediate and final pressures.

    1. During the isothermal expansion, \(P_1V_1=P_2V_2\).
    2. Thus \(P_2=1.2\times10^5(2.0/6.0)=4.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\).
    3. During the constant-volume heating, Gay-Lussac's law gives \(P_3/P_2=T_3/T_2\).
    4. The intermediate temperature is still the initial temperature, \(T_2=300\ \mathrm{K}\).
    5. Therefore \(P_3=4.0\times10^4(450/300)=6.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\).

    Answer: \(P_2=4.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\) and \(P_3=6.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using a Celsius temperature ratio in a gas law.
    • Applying Boyle's law during the constant-volume heating stage.
    • Applying the combined gas law across a process that leaks gas or changes the number of moles.

    Chapter 9 · Topic 3

    Equation of state

    Kinetic Theory of GasesHeat and ThermodynamicsGas LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The equation of ideal gas relates pressure, volume, amount, and absolute temperature for a gas in thermodynamic equilibrium. It applies to the total gas and independently to each component of an ideal-gas mixture. Partial pressure is the pressure a component would exert if it alone occupied the container volume at the same temperature, and mole fraction times total pressure gives the partial pressure.
    Key formula(s). \[PV=nRT=\frac{m}{M}RT\] ; \[pV=Nk_BT,\qquad \frac{PV}{T}=\text{constant for a fixed sample}\] ; \[p_i=x_iP,\qquad x_i=\frac{n_i}{\sum n_i},\qquad P=\sum_i p_i\]
    Key points.
    • A thermodynamic pressure is a macroscopic equilibrium quantity obtained after averaging enormous numbers of molecular collisions.
    • The equation determines only changes consistent with the constraints; heat supplied and work done must be found separately.
    • For a mixture of nonreacting ideal gases, each gas expands to fill the whole volume.
    • A heavier gas at the same temperature has the same average translational kinetic energy as a lighter gas.
    • The equation does not directly give heat or work during a non-isothermal or non-isobaric process.
    • Compressibility factor \(Z=PV/(nRT)\) equals one for an ideal gas and is a common measure of real-gas deviation.
    Example 1.

    Three moles of ideal gas are confined at \(400\ \mathrm{K}\) by a pressure of \(3.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\). Find the volume in cubic metres and litres.

    1. From \(PV=nRT\), \(V=nRT/P\).
    2. Substituting gives \(V=3(8.314)(400)/(3.0\times10^5)\).
    3. The numerator is \(9976.8\ \mathrm{J}\), which is equal to \(P V\).
    4. Therefore \(V=3.3256\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^3}\).
    5. Since \(1\ \mathrm{m^3}=1000\ \mathrm{L}\), this is \(33.256\ \mathrm{L}\).

    Answer: \(V=3.33\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^3}=33.3\ \mathrm{L}\).

    Example 2.

    A mixture contains \(2.0\) mol of gas A and \(3.0\) mol of gas B at \(500\ \mathrm{K}\) and total pressure \(1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\). Find the mole fractions, partial pressures, and mixture volume.

    1. The total amount is \(n=2.0+3.0=5.0\ \mathrm{mol}\).
    2. Thus \(x_A=2/5=0.40\) and \(x_B=3/5=0.60\).
    3. Dalton's law gives \(p_A=x_AP=0.40(1.0\times10^5)=4.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\).
    4. Similarly, \(p_B=6.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\), and \(p_A+p_B=P\).
    5. The mixture volume is \(V=nRT/P=5.0(8.314)(500)/(1.0\times10^5)=0.20785\ \mathrm{m^3}\).

    Answer: \(x_A=0.40\), \(x_B=0.60\), \(p_A=40\ \mathrm{kPa}\), \(p_B=60\ \mathrm{kPa}\), and \(V=0.208\ \mathrm{m^3}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Equating partial pressure with mole fraction instead of multiplying it by total pressure.
    • Using the component mole count in \(p_iV=nRT\); the whole mixture volume must be used.
    • Reporting the ideal-gas equation as if it supplied \(Q\) or \(W\) automatically.

    Molecular interpretation

    Kinetic Theory of GasesHeat and ThermodynamicsGas LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Molecular interpretation reads gas laws as molecular statistics: pressure is molecular bombardment momentum rate, temperature is average kinetic energy (3/2 kT per molecule), Boyle law (fewer hits per volume), Charles law (faster hits per heat). Maxwell-Boltzmann speeds distribute statistically (most probable below average below RMS). Bulk laws emerge from molecular chaos - thermodynamics meets mechanics statistically.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Pressure hits, temperature motion, laws statistics.
    • 3/2 kT per molecule links heat to motion.
    Remember
    • Temperature IS average molecular kinetic energy.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Temperature of a gas measures average

    Solution: 3/2 kT per molecule defines absolute temperature kinetically.
    Key Formulas · Molecular Interpretation
    \(pV=NkT,\;k=\frac{R}{N_{A}}\) gas law per molecule
    \(\bar{KE}=\frac32kT\) temperature is mean kinetic energy

    Index / Heat and Thermodynamics
    Chapter 9 · Topic 5

    Kinetic theory

    Kinetic Theory of GasesHeat and ThermodynamicsGas LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Kinetic theory explains macroscopic gas behavior through the random motion and elastic collisions of a very large number of molecules. Pressure arises from the normal momentum transferred when molecules strike a container wall, while temperature measures average molecular translational kinetic energy. Isotropy of molecular motion allows the three Cartesian mean-square components to contribute equally to pressure.
    Key formula(s). \[\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2}=\frac{3}{2}k_BT,\qquad \frac{1}{2}M\overline{c^2}=\frac{3}{2}RT\] ; \[P=\frac{1}{3}\frac{Nm}{V}\overline{v^2}=\frac{1}{3}\rho\overline{c^2}\] ; \[PV=\frac{1}{3}Nm\overline{v^2}=nRT\]
    Key points.
    • The brackets denote a long-time average over enormous numbers of collisions.
    • Temperature is proportional to mean-square speed, not to the mean or most probable speed.
    • Pressure has two equivalent microscopic origins: momentum transfer at the wall and random molecular motion in the bulk.
    • The relation \(P=\frac{1}{3}\rho\overline{c^2}\) is exact for the translational degrees under the kinetic-theory assumptions.
    • Mass density \(\rho\) and molar mass enter the speed through \(\rho=Nm/V\).
    • Removing the last molecule or making the particle count too small invalidates the statistical averaging underlying the law.
    Example 1.

    Two moles of monatomic ideal gas are at \(300\ \mathrm{K}\). Find the total translational kinetic energy of its molecules.

    1. Each molecule has average translational kinetic energy \(\frac{3}{2}k_BT\).
    2. For \(n\) moles, \(E_{\rm tr}=n(\frac{3}{2}RT)\).
    3. Here \(E_{\rm tr}=2(\frac{3}{2})(8.314)(300)=3RT\).
    4. Numerically, \(E_{\rm tr}=3(8.314)(300)=7482.6\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(E_{\rm tr}=7.48\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    A gas of total mass \(2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}\) occupies \(2.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^3}\). Microscopic measurement gives a mean-square molecular speed of \(9.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{m^2s^{-2}}\). Find the gas pressure.

    1. Kinetic theory gives \(P=\frac{1}{3}\rho\overline{v^2}\), where \(\rho=m_{\rm tot}/V\).
    2. The mass density is \((2.0\times10^{-3})/(2.0\times10^{-2})=0.100\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\).
    3. Substitution gives \(P=\frac{1}{3}(0.100)(9.0\times10^4)\).
    4. Equivalently, \(P=Nm\overline{v^2}/(3V)\), obtained from wall-collision momentum transfer.
    5. The unit is \((\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}})(\mathrm{m^2s^{-2}})=\mathrm{Pa}\).

    Answer: \(P=3.0\times10^3\ \mathrm{Pa}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Replacing mean-square speed with the square of mean speed in the pressure formula.
    • Omitting the factor \(1/3\) arising from isotropy.
    • Using total molar mass instead of the mass of one molecule in a single-particle kinetic relation.

    Explanation

    Concept. The kinetic theory of an ideal gas relies on a set of simplifying assumptions about an enormous collection of particles. Molecules are treated as point particles, collisions are perfectly elastic, and intermolecular forces are negligible except during instantaneous collisions. Random isotropic motion and equilibrium exchange of energy with walls establish uniform pressure and temperature throughout a real gas sample.
    Key formula(s). \[N\gg1, \qquad \frac{Nd^3}{V}\ll1, \qquad \tau_{\rm coll}\gg d,\qquad \tau_{\rm coll}\ll\tau_{\rm macro}\] ; \[\text{Elastic collision: }K_i=K_f\] ; \[dU_{\rm wall}+dU_{\rm molecules}=0\]
    Key points.
    • The number of molecules must be large enough for statistical averages and pressure to remain stable.
    • The time between molecular collisions is much shorter than the macroscopic observation time, establishing local equilibrium.
    • Molecular dimensions are negligible compared with the average separation in the ideal-gas model.
    • Molecules have no forces on one another when separated, so internal energy is stored in molecular degrees of freedom.
    • Wall collisions are elastic, so temperature remains unchanged through thermal equilibrium.
    • Real molecules possess finite size and attraction or repulsion, causing equation-of-state deviations at high density or low temperature.
    Example 1.

    One mole of monatomic ideal gas is maintained at \(400\ \mathrm{K}\). Find the total translational kinetic energy of all molecules and use it to identify which microscopic mean is fixed by temperature.

    1. The mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is \(\frac{3}{2}k_BT\).
    2. Multiplication by Avogadro's number gives \(\frac{3}{2}RT\) per mole.
    3. Thus \(E_{\rm tr}=\frac{3}{2}(8.314)(400)=4988.4\ \mathrm{J}\).
    4. It follows that the mean-square speed is fixed, not the arithmetic mean speed or most probable speed.
    5. Specifically, \(M\overline{c^2}/2=3RT/2\) for a molar mass \(M\).

    Answer: \(E_{\rm tr}=4.99\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}\), and temperature fixes the mean-square translational speed.

    Example 2.

    At STP, one mole occupies \(2.24\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^3}\). Estimate the fraction of volume occupied by molecules if their effective diameter is \(3.0\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\).

    1. The number of molecules is \(N=PV/(k_BT)\approx2.69\times10^{25}\) at STP.
    2. Modeling one molecule as a sphere of diameter \(d\), its effective volume is \(v_m=\frac{\pi}{6}d^3\).
    3. Thus \(v_m=\frac{\pi}{6}(3.0\times10^{-10})^3=1.414\times10^{-29}\ \mathrm{m^3}\).
    4. The total effective molecular volume is \(Nv_m\approx3.80\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3}\).
    5. Therefore the occupied fraction is \(3.80\times10^{-4}/2.24\times10^{-2}=1.70\times10^{-2}=1.70\%\).

    Answer: The molecules occupy approximately \(1.70\%\) of the container volume, supporting the negligible-volume approximation.

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating molecular collisions as perfectly inelastic.
    • Allowing long-range intermolecular attractions in the ideal-gas model.
    • Inferring a zero mean vector molecular velocity from a nonzero average molecular speed.

    Index / Heat and Thermodynamics
    Chapter 9 · Topic 6

    Pressure of gas

    Kinetic Theory of GasesHeat and ThermodynamicsGas LawsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The pressure exerted by an ideal gas is the macroscopic result of continuous molecular impacts on the container walls. A perfectly elastic normal collision reverses a molecule's normal velocity and transfers momentum twice that amount, producing force on the wall. Isotropy divides the mean-square speed equally among three coordinates, leading to \(P=\frac{1}{3}\rho\overline{v^2}\), which is equivalent to the ideal-gas law.
    Key formula(s). \[\Delta p_{\rm molecule}=2m v_x,\qquad F=\frac{N}{2}\frac{\overline{|v_x|}}V\Delta p\] ; \[P=\frac{Nm\overline{v_x^2}}V=\frac{Nm\overline{v^2}}{3V}\] ; \[P=\frac{1}{3}\rho\overline{v^2}=\frac{nRT}{V}=\sum_i p_i\]
    Key points.
    • The factor \(1/3\) comes from \(\overline{v_x^2}=\overline{v_y^2}=\overline{v_z^2}=\frac{1}{3}\overline{v^2}\).
    • Absolute pressure is nonnegative and has SI unit \(\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{Pa}\).
    • At fixed \(V,T,n\), pressure is independent of molecular mass even though different gases have different rms speeds.
    • Partial pressures add in an ideal-gas mixture according to Dalton's law.
    • Molecular mass does not affect pressure directly at fixed temperature because lighter molecules move faster.
    • Gauge pressure excludes atmospheric pressure, whereas thermodynamic calculations use absolute pressure.
    Example 1.

    A \(1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}\) rigid vessel contains \(0.010\) mol of ideal gas at \(300\ \mathrm{K}\). Calculate the absolute pressure.

    1. The number of moles, volume, and temperature are fixed, so use \(P=nRT/V\).
    2. Substitution gives \(P=(0.010)(8.314)(300)/(1.0\times10^{-3})\).
    3. The numerator is \(24.942\ \mathrm{J}\), equal to \(PV\).
    4. Since one pascal is one joule per cubic metre, \(P=2.4942\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\).

    Answer: \(P=2.49\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}=24.9\ \mathrm{kPa}\).

    Example 2.

    A rigid vessel at uniform temperature contains \(2.0\) mol of helium and \(3.0\) mol of nitrogen, with total absolute pressure \(1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\). Find each partial pressure and the mole fraction of nitrogen.

    1. The total amount is \(n=2.0+3.0=5.0\ \mathrm{mol}\).
    2. Dalton's law gives \(p_i=(n_i/n)P\), independent of the different molecular masses.
    3. The helium partial pressure is \(p_{\rm He}=(2/5)(1.0\times10^5)=4.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\).
    4. The nitrogen partial pressure is \(p_{\rm N_2}=(3/5)(1.0\times10^5)=6.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}\).
    5. Their sum is the total pressure, \(4.0\times10^4+6.0\times10^4=1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\).

    Answer: \(p_{\rm He}=40\ \mathrm{kPa}\), \(p_{\rm N_2}=60\ \mathrm{kPa}\), and \(x_{\rm N_2}=0.60\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Omitting the factor \(1/3\) in the pressure derivation.
    • Assuming the heavier gas contributes more partial pressure solely because its molecules are heavier.
    • Adding the two component pressures without dividing by the total number of moles.
    Back to Index
    Index / Heat and Thermodynamics
    Chapter 9 · Topic 7

    RMS speed

    Kinetic Theory of GasesHeat and ThermodynamicsMolecular SpeedsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Root-mean-square speed is the square root of the average squared molecular speed of an ideal gas. It is the speed statistic directly connected to temperature and to the pressure expression in kinetic theory. For a given gas, \(v_{\rm rms}\propto\sqrt{T}\); for gases at the same temperature, it varies inversely with the square root of molar mass.
    Key formula(s). \[v_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{\overline{v^2}}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}=\sqrt{\frac{3k_BT}{m}}\] ; \[P=\frac{1}{3}\rho v_{\rm rms}^2\] ; \[\frac{v_{\rm rms,1}}{v_{\rm rms,2}}=\sqrt{\frac{T_1M_2}{T_2M_1}}\]
    Key points.
    • The root-mean-square speed is always greater than the average speed and greater than the most probable speed.
    • Temperature must be in kelvin and molar mass in compatible SI units, usually \(\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\).
    • At fixed temperature, all gases have the same mean-square speed per molecule, not the same rms speed.
    • A molecule selected at random is not most likely to have exactly the rms speed.
    • Doubling absolute temperature increases rms speed by \(\sqrt{2}\), while quadrupling it doubles rms speed.
    • For a gas mixture at one temperature, the total translational kinetic energy depends on total moles, not the mass-weighted arithmetic mean of individual rms speeds.
    Example 1.

    Calculate the rms speed of nitrogen molecules, for which \(M=28\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\), at \(300\ \mathrm{K}\).

    1. Use \(v_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{3RT/M}\).
    2. Substitute \(v_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{3(8.314)(300)/(28\times10^{-3})}\).
    3. The ratio inside the square root is \(3.7413\times10^6\ \mathrm{m^2s^{-2}}\).
    4. Taking the square root gives \(v_{\rm rms}=1.934\times10^3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(v_{\rm rms}=1.93\times10^3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    A mixture contains \(2.0\) mol of hydrogen \(M=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\) and \(1.0\) mol of helium \(M=4.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\) at \(600\ \mathrm{K}\). Find the rms speed over all molecules.

    1. The total translational energy is \(E_{\rm tr}=\frac{3}{2}n_{\rm total}RT=\frac{3}{2}(3.0)(8.314)(600)\).
    2. The total mass is \(m_{\rm tot}=2(2.0\times10^{-3})+1(4.0\times10^{-3})=8.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}\).
    3. Since \(E_{\rm tr}=\frac{1}{2}m_{\rm tot}\overline{v^2}\), \(\overline{v^2}=2E_{\rm tr}/m_{\rm tot}\).
    4. This gives \(\overline{v^2}=5.612\times10^6\ \mathrm{m^2s^{-2}}\).
    5. Taking the square root yields \(v_{\rm rms}=2.369\times10^3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(v_{\rm rms}=2.37\times10^3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Squaring the average of molecular speeds instead of averaging their squares.
    • Taking a mole-weighted arithmetic mean of component rms speeds.
    • Using Celsius temperature in the speed ratio.

    Chapter 9 · Topic 8

    Average speed

    Kinetic Theory of GasesHeat and ThermodynamicsMolecular SpeedsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The average speed of gas molecules is the arithmetic mean of their speeds, while their mean vector velocity is zero in equilibrium because molecular motion is isotropic. The Maxwell distribution predicts a nonzero average speed proportional to \(\sqrt{T/M}\). It is smaller than the rms speed and greater than the most probable speed, a standard comparison tested in JEE questions.
    Key formula(s). \[\overline{\mathbf v}=0 \text{ in an equilibrium gas with no bulk flow}\] ; \[\overline v=\sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}=\sqrt{\frac{8k_BT}{\pi m}}\] ; \[v_p<v_{\rm avg}<v_{\rm rms}\]
    Key points.
    • Average speed is always nonnegative; averaging signed velocity components over equilibrium gives zero.
    • The factor \(8/\pi\) arises from averaging speed over the Maxwell speed distribution.
    • At fixed molar mass, average speed increases as \(\sqrt{T}\).
    • At fixed temperature, average speed is inversely proportional to \(\sqrt{M}\).
    • Average speed is not the speed associated with average kinetic energy; that is the rms speed.
    • A simple arithmetic average is valid for a specified discrete set of speeds but not for all speeds in a continuous Maxwell distribution.
    Example 1.

    Find the average molecular speed of an ideal gas of molar mass \(32\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\) at \(300\ \mathrm{K}\).

    1. For the Maxwell distribution, \(\overline v=\sqrt{8RT/(\pi M)}\).
    2. Substitute the data: \(\overline v=\sqrt{8(8.314)(300)/[\pi(32\times10^{-3})]}\).
    3. The ratio inside the square root is \(6.2355\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^2s^{-2}}\).
    4. Taking the square root gives \(\overline v=7.90\times10^2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(\overline v=790\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    Three groups containing equal numbers of gas molecules have speeds \(100\), \(200\), and \(300\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the average speed, rms speed, and most probable speed of all molecules.

    1. Equal numbers make each group count one third, so \(\overline v=(100+200+300)/3=200\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. The mean-square speed is \((100^2+200^2+300^2)/3=46666.7\ \mathrm{m^2s^{-2}}\).
    3. Hence \(v_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{46666.7}=216.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. Each discrete speed occurs equally often, so there is a threefold tie rather than one unique most probable speed; conventionally all three speeds are equally most probable.

    Answer: \(\overline v=200\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(v_{\rm rms}=216\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the modes are \(100\), \(200\), and \(300\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) with equal weight.

    Common mistakes.
    • Averaging the positive and negative components of molecular velocities and calling the nonzero result average speed.
    • Using \(\sqrt{3RT/M}\), which gives rms speed instead.
    • Assuming average speed equals rms speed even though the Maxwell distribution is not sharply peaked.

    Chapter 9 · Topic 9

    Most probable speed

    Kinetic Theory of GasesHeat and ThermodynamicsMolecular SpeedsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The most probable speed is the speed at which the Maxwell speed distribution has its maximum, meaning the largest range of nearby speeds is occupied. It is zero at both \(v=0\) and \(v\to\infty\), with a unique maximum at finite speed. It scales as \(\sqrt{T/M}\), just like the other characteristic speeds, but has a different numerical coefficient.
    Key formula(s). \[f(v)=4\pi\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2}v^2e^{-mv^2/(2k_BT)}\] ; \[\frac{df}{dv}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_p=\sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}=\sqrt{\frac{2k_BT}{m}}\] ; \[v_p:v_{\rm avg}:v_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{2}:\sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}}:\sqrt{3}\]
    Key points.
    • Most probable does not mean the same as average or rms; it is the distribution's mode.
    • For a fixed gas, \(v_p\propto\sqrt{T}\), and for fixed temperature, \(v_p\propto M^{-1/2}\).
    • The distribution is zero at \(v=0\) because both the spherical shell area and the number of possible directions vanish there.
    • The ratio \(v_{\rm rms}/v_p=\sqrt{3/2}\) is independent of molar mass and temperature.
    • Differential probability is \(P(v\text{ to }v+dv)=f(v)\,dv\), while a finite interval requires integration.
    • A gas mixture has one molecular speed distribution determined by total mass and total number at a common temperature, rather than simply two separate modes.
    Example 1.

    Find the most probable speed of hydrogen molecules, \(M=2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\), at \(300\ \mathrm{K}\).

    1. Use \(v_p=\sqrt{2RT/M}\).
    2. Substitution gives \(v_p=\sqrt{2(8.314)(300)/(2.0\times10^{-3})}\).
    3. The quantity inside the square root is \(2.4942\times10^6\ \mathrm{m^2s^{-2}}\).
    4. Taking the square root yields \(v_p=1.579\times10^3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(v_p=1.58\times10^3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    For a gas at a fixed temperature, the rms speed is \(600\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the most probable speed and the ratio of average speed to most probable speed.

    1. From the universal ratios, \(v_{\rm rms}/v_p=\sqrt{3/2}\).
    2. Thus \(v_p=v_{\rm rms}\sqrt{2/3}=600(0.816497)\).
    3. The result is \(v_p=489.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. Also, \(\overline v/v_p=\sqrt{(8/\pi)/2}=\sqrt{4/\pi}=1.1284\).
    5. The ratios do not depend on temperature or molar mass.

    Answer: \(v_p=490\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(\overline v/v_p=\sqrt{4/\pi}=1.128\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Equating the most probable speed with the rms speed.
    • Using \(v=0\) as the mode because the function begins there.
    • Comparing most probable and average speeds without accounting for their different distribution coefficients.

    Chapter 9 · Topic 10

    Degrees of freedom

    Kinetic Theory of GasesHeat and ThermodynamicsMolecular SpeedsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A degree of freedom is an independent quadratic term needed to describe the molecular energy or motion of a gas molecule. Every such term in the equipartition theorem contributes \(\frac{1}{2}k_BT\) per molecule at thermal equilibrium. Translational motion always contributes three degrees; rotation and vibration contribute only when their characteristic modes are thermally active.
    Key formula(s). \[\langle E\rangle_{\rm molecule}=\frac{f}{2}k_BT,\qquad U=\frac{f}{2}nRT\] ; \[C_V=\frac{f}{2}R,\qquad C_P=\frac{f}{2}R+R,\qquad \gamma=\frac{C_P}{C_V}=1+\frac{2}{f}\] ; \[f_{\rm mono}=3,\qquad f_{\rm diatomic}=5\ \text{at ordinary temperatures}\]
    Key points.
    • A monatomic ideal gas has \(C_V=\frac{3}{2}R\), \(C_P=\frac{5}{2}R\), and \(\gamma=5/3\) when vibration is ignored.
    • A rigid diatomic ideal gas has two rotational degrees, so \(C_V=\frac{5}{2}R\) and \(\gamma=7/5\).
    • A nonlinear polyatomic molecule has three translational and three rotational degrees, giving \(f=6\) before vibration is included.
    • A linear polyatomic molecule has two rotational degrees in addition to three translational degrees.
    • Each vibrational mode contributes two degrees, one kinetic and one potential.
    • The active value of \(f\) can change with temperature when vibrational excitation becomes appreciable.
    Example 1.

    Two moles of monatomic ideal gas are heated from \(300\ \mathrm{K}\) to \(450\ \mathrm{K}\). Calculate the change in internal energy.

    1. A monatomic molecule has three translational degrees, so \(C_V=\frac{3}{2}R\).
    2. The temperature change is \(\Delta T=450-300=150\ \mathrm{K}\).
    3. For an ideal gas, \(\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T=2\left(\frac{3}{2}R\right)(150)=750R\).
    4. Numerically, \(\Delta U=750(8.314)=6235.5\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(\Delta U=+6.24\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Example 2.

    One mole of a diatomic ideal gas with \(\gamma=1.40\) expands reversibly and adiabatically from \(V_1=2.0\ \mathrm{L}\), \(T_1=300\ \mathrm{K}\) to \(V_2=8.0\ \mathrm{L}\). Find the final temperature and the work done by the gas.

    1. For a reversible adiabatic process, \(TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant}\).
    2. Hence \(T_2=T_1(V_1/V_2)^{\gamma-1}=300(2.0/8.0)^{0.40}\).
    3. Since \(4^{0.40}=1.741\), \(T_2=300/1.741=172.3\ \mathrm{K}\).
    4. The gas is diatomic, so \(C_V=\frac{R}{\gamma-1}=2.5R\).
    5. With \(Q=0\), the work done by the gas is \(W_{\rm by}=nC_V(T_1-T_2)=2.5(8.314)(300-172.3)\).

    Answer: \(T_2=172.3\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(W_{\rm by}=2.65\times10^3\ \mathrm{J}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Assigning rotational degrees to a monatomic molecule.
    • Counting a vibrational mode as one degree rather than two.
    • Applying the constant-adiabatic-temperature law to an ordinary isochoric heating process.
