    Chapter 13 · Topic 1

    Electric potential

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentPotentialStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity to that point. It is a scalar quantity and is defined to be zero at infinity, while the potential difference between two points is independent of the path in electrostatics. The field and potential are related by \(\vec E=-\nabla V\), so a rapid decrease of potential indicates a strong field component.
    Key formula(s). \[V(P)=\frac{W_{\mathrm{ext}}(\infty\to P)}{q_0}=-\int_{\infty}^{P}\vec E\cdot d\vec l,\qquad V_B-V_A=-\int_A^B\vec E\cdot d\vec l,\qquad \vec E=-\nabla V,\qquad [V]=\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}\]
    Key points.
    • Potential is a scalar, so charge signs are added algebraically and no vector direction is assigned to \(V\).
    • Setting \(V=0\) at infinity is the standard reference for isolated charge distributions.
    • The potential difference is \(V_B-V_A\), while the work done by the electric field is \(-q(V_B-V_A)\).
    • In a uniform field, the potential changes linearly along the field and remains constant along a perpendicular equipotential line.
    • The relation \(\vec E=-\nabla V\) means that the electric field points toward decreasing potential.
    • A zero-potential surface is not necessarily a zero-field surface; only \(\nabla V=0\) gives zero field.
    Example 1.

    A uniform electric field \(200\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\) points from point \(A\) to point \(B\), and \(B\) is \(0.30\,\mathrm m\) from \(A\) along the field. Find \(V_B-V_A\).

    1. Along the field direction, \(\vec E\cdot d\vec l=E\,dl\) because the path element and field have the same direction.
    2. The potential difference is \(V_B-V_A=-\int_A^B E\,dl=-Ed\).
    3. Substitution gives \(V_B-V_A=-(200)(0.30)=-60\,\mathrm V\).
    4. Thus the potential decreases by \(60\,\mathrm V\) when moving from \(A\) to \(B\) along the field.

    Answer: \(V_B-V_A=-60\,\mathrm V\).

    Example 2.

    Charges \(+3.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) and \(-1.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) are located at \(x=0\) and \(x=0.40\,\mathrm m\), respectively. Taking \(V=0\) at infinity, find the potential at the midpoint.

    1. The midpoint is \(0.20\,\mathrm m\) from each charge.
    2. By superposition, \(V=k(3.0\times10^{-6})/(0.20)+k(-1.0\times10^{-6})/(0.20)\).
    3. The equivalent charge factor is \((3.0-1.0)\times10^{-6}/0.20=1.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C\,m^{-1}}\).
    4. Therefore \(V=(8.99\times10^9)(1.0\times10^{-5})=8.99\times10^4\,\mathrm V\).
    5. The potential is positive because the positive charge's contribution is larger.

    Answer: The potential at the midpoint is \(8.99\times10^4\,\mathrm V\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(V_B-V_A=+Ed\) when moving in the direction of the electric field.
    • Treating potential as a vector and trying to add its directions.
    • Forgetting that the reference potential is zero at infinity.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 2

    Potential difference

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentPotentialStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Potential difference between two points is the change in electric potential and equals the work done per unit charge by an external agent in moving a test charge quasistatically between them. In electrostatics it is path-independent because the electric field is conservative, but the sign still depends on the order of the endpoints. JEE problems often ask for the work done by the field, which has the opposite sign to the external work for a slow move.
    Key formula(s). \[V_B-V_A=-\int_A^B\vec E\cdot d\vec l,\qquad \Delta V=\frac{W_{\mathrm{ext}}}{q_0},\qquad W_{\mathrm{field}}=-q_0\Delta V,\qquad \Delta V=\sum_i k\frac{q_i}{r_{iB}}-\sum_i k\frac{q_i}{r_{iA}}\]
    Key points.
    • The notation \(V_B-V_A\) fixes the sign; reversing the endpoints reverses the potential difference.
    • Work per unit charge is a potential difference, not the potential itself unless the reference is specified.
    • The electric field does work \(W_{\mathrm{field}}=-q\Delta V\), while a quasistatic external agent does \(W_{\mathrm{ext}}=q\Delta V\).
    • In electrostatics the same potential difference is obtained for any path connecting \(A\) and \(B\).
    • A larger distance from a positive source changes the potential even when no force is explicitly calculated.
    • A negative test charge reverses the direction of the force but does not reverse the definition of potential difference.
    Example 1.

    A point charge \(+4.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) is at the origin. Find the potential difference between a point \(A\) at \(r_A=0.20\,\mathrm m\) and a point \(B\) at \(r_B=0.50\,\mathrm m\), with \(V(\infty)=0\).

    1. For a point charge, \(V(r)=kq/r\), so \(V_A=(8.99\times10^9)(4.0\times10^{-6})/(0.20)=1.798\times10^5\,\mathrm V\).
    2. Similarly, \(V_B=(8.99\times10^9)(4.0\times10^{-6})/(0.50)=7.192\times10^4\,\mathrm V\).
    3. Taking the difference in the stated order gives \(\Delta V=V_B-V_A=7.192\times10^4-1.798\times10^5\).
    4. Hence \(\Delta V=-1.079\times10^5\,\mathrm V\), because \(B\) is farther from the positive charge.

    Answer: \(V_B-V_A=-1.079\times10^5\,\mathrm V\).

    Example 2.

    A fixed point charge \(+0.40\,\mu\mathrm C\) is at the origin. A \(+0.40\,\mu\mathrm C\) test charge is moved quasistatically from \(A\) at \(r_A=0.40\,\mathrm m\) to \(B\) at \(r_B=0.10\,\mathrm m\). Find the work done by the field and by the external agent.

    1. The source potentials are \(V_A=k(0.40\times10^{-6})/(0.40)=8.99\times10^3\,\mathrm V\) and \(V_B=k(0.40\times10^{-6})/(0.10)=3.596\times10^4\,\mathrm V\).
    2. Thus \(\Delta V=V_B-V_A=2.697\times10^4\,\mathrm V\).
    3. The work done by the field is \(W_{\mathrm{field}}=-q\Delta V=-(0.40\times10^{-6})(2.697\times10^4)=-1.079\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J\).
    4. For a quasistatic move, the external agent does the opposite amount, \(W_{\mathrm{ext}}=+1.079\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J\).

    Answer: \(W_{\mathrm{field}}=-1.08\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J\) and \(W_{\mathrm{ext}}=+1.08\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Reporting the potential difference with the endpoints reversed without changing its sign.
    • Using \(W_{\mathrm{field}}=q\Delta V\) instead of the negative sign.
    • Assuming the potential difference is positive merely because the endpoint is closer to a positive charge.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 3

    Potential due to point charge

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentPotentialStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The potential due to a point charge is proportional to the charge and inversely proportional to its distance from the observation point, with the zero of potential at infinity. The total potential at a point is the algebraic sum of the potentials due to all charges. Unlike electric field, potential has no direction, so a negative charge contributes a negative potential at every finite point.
    Key formula(s). \[V=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r}=\frac{kq}{r},\qquad V_{\mathrm{net}}=\sum_i\frac{kq_i}{r_i},\qquad V(\infty)=0,\qquad \Delta V=V_B-V_A\]
    Key points.
    • A positive charge gives positive potential and a negative charge gives negative potential relative to infinity.
    • At a fixed point, doubling every source charge doubles the total potential.
    • The potential due to a point charge is a scalar, so contributions are added with their charge signs.
    • The \(1/r\) dependence is one power weaker than the \(1/r^2\) dependence of the point-charge field.
    • The reference potential can be shifted by a constant without changing any electric field, but \(V=0\) at infinity is the usual convention.
    • To compare two points, subtract their total potentials rather than subtracting the distances themselves.
    Example 1.

    A point charge \(+5.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) is at the origin. Find its potential at a point \(0.25\,\mathrm m\) away, taking \(V=0\) at infinity.

    1. The point-charge potential is \(V=kq/r\).
    2. Substitute \(q=5.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm C\) and \(r=0.25\,\mathrm m\).
    3. \(V=(8.99\times10^9)(5.0\times10^{-6})/(0.25)\).
    4. The numerator is \(4.495\times10^4\,\mathrm{V\,m}\), so division by \(0.25\,\mathrm m\) gives \(1.798\times10^5\,\mathrm V\).

    Answer: The potential is \(1.80\times10^5\,\mathrm V\).

    Example 2.

    A \(+2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) charge is at \(x=0.20\,\mathrm m\) and a \(-1.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) charge is at \(x=0.30\,\mathrm m\). Find the total potential at the origin.

    1. The origin is \(0.20\,\mathrm m\) from the positive charge and \(0.30\,\mathrm m\) from the negative charge.
    2. The positive contribution is \(V_+=k(2.0\times10^{-6})/(0.20)=8.99\times10^4\,\mathrm V\).
    3. The negative contribution is \(V_-=k(-1.0\times10^{-6})/(0.30)=-2.997\times10^4\,\mathrm V\).
    4. Superposition gives \(V=V_++V_-=5.993\times10^4\,\mathrm V\).

    Answer: The total potential at the origin is \(5.99\times10^4\,\mathrm V\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Forgetting the minus sign in the potential of a negative point charge.
    • Adding source-charge distances instead of dividing each charge by its own distance.
    • Confusing the \(1/r\) potential dependence with the \(1/r^2\) field dependence.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 4

    Potential due to dipole

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentPotentialStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The potential of an ideal electric dipole falls as the inverse square of distance and also depends on the angle between the dipole moment and the line to the observation point. It is positive on the axial side in the direction of the moment and negative on the equatorial line. The potential is a scalar, so reversing the dipole reverses the sign at every fixed observation direction.
    Key formula(s). \[V=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p\cos\theta}{r^2}=\frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2},\qquad V_{\mathrm{axial}}=\frac{kp}{r^2},\qquad V_{\mathrm{equatorial}}=-\frac{kp}{r^2},\qquad r\gg d\]
    Key points.
    • The ideal-dipole potential applies when the observation distance is much larger than the charge separation.
    • At the positive-charge end of the dipole axis, \(V\) is positive; at the negative end it is negative.
    • The equatorial potential is exactly opposite in sign to the axial potential for the same \(p\) and \(r\).
    • The potential vanishes on the plane perpendicular to the dipole moment through its centre.
    • The sign of \(\cos\theta\) determines whether the point is on a positive-potential or negative-potential angular region.
    • The dipole potential is not obtained by adding two point-charge magnitudes; the signed charge contributions must be retained.
    Example 1.

    An ideal dipole has \(p=5.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C\,m}\). Find the potential at points on the positive axis and on the equatorial line, each at \(r=0.25\,\mathrm m\), and find their difference.

    1. On the positive axial side, \(\cos\theta=1\), so \(V_{\mathrm{ax}}=kp/r^2\).
    2. \(V_{\mathrm{ax}}=(8.99\times10^9)(5.0\times10^{-6})/(0.25)^2=7.19\times10^5\,\mathrm V\).
    3. On the equatorial line, \(\cos\theta=0\), giving \(V_{\mathrm{eq}}=-kp/r^2=-7.19\times10^5\,\mathrm V\).
    4. Therefore \(V_{\mathrm{ax}}-V_{\mathrm{eq}}=1.438\times10^6\,\mathrm V\).

    Answer: \(V_{\mathrm{ax}}=+7.19\times10^5\,\mathrm V\), \(V_{\mathrm{eq}}=-7.19\times10^5\,\mathrm V\), and the difference is \(1.44\times10^6\,\mathrm V\).

    Example 2.

    An ideal dipole has \(p=4.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C\,m}\). Find the potential at a point \(r=0.30\,\mathrm m\) from its centre in a direction making \(60^\circ\) with the dipole moment.

    1. The angular factor is \(\cos60^\circ=0.50\).
    2. Hence \(V=kp(0.50)/(0.30)^2\).
    3. The numerator is \((8.99\times10^9)(4.0\times10^{-6})(0.50)=1.798\times10^4\,\mathrm{V\,m^2}\).
    4. Dividing by \((0.30)^2=0.0900\,\mathrm{m^2}\) gives \(V=1.998\times10^5\,\mathrm V\).
    5. The potential is positive because the point lies in the hemisphere where \(\vec p\cdot\hat r>0\).

    Answer: The potential is \(2.00\times10^5\,\mathrm V\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the axial value for every point on a sphere around a dipole.
    • Omitting the \(\cos\theta\) factor and treating potential as independent of angle.
    • Using the dipole field formula \(1/r^3\) where the dipole potential \(1/r^2\) is required.
    Back to Index
    Index / Electrostatics and Current
    Chapter 13 · Topic 5

    Equipotential surfaces

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentPotentialStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. An equipotential surface is a surface on which the electric potential has the same value at every point. No work is done by the electric field when a charge moves along such a surface, and the electric field is perpendicular to it wherever the field is nonzero. Equipotential surfaces never intersect, and closer surfaces indicate a stronger normal electric field.
    Key formula(s). \[V(x,y,z)=\text{constant},\qquad dV=-\vec E\cdot d\vec l,\qquad \vec E\perp\text{equipotential surface},\qquad E_n=\left|\frac{dV}{dn}\right|,\qquad E_1A_1=E_2A_2\ \text{for a flux tube}\]
    Key points.
    • Moving a charge along one equipotential surface requires no work by the electric field.
    • The electric field is normal to an equipotential surface because the tangential field would change the potential.
    • Two distinct equipotential surfaces cannot intersect, since an intersection would have two different potential values.
    • A uniform electric field has plane equipotential surfaces perpendicular to the field.
    • The field of a point charge has spherical equipotential surfaces centred on the charge.
    • Equipotential surfaces become closer together where the field is stronger for a fixed potential interval.
    Example 1.

    A uniform electric field of \(200\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\) is directed along \(+\hat i\). Two equipotential planes are separated by \(0.050\,\mathrm m\) in the \(x\)-direction. Find the magnitude of the potential difference between the planes and the direction of decreasing potential.

    1. Equipotential planes are perpendicular to the field, so the separation is measured along \(\hat i\).
    2. The magnitude of the potential difference is \(|\Delta V|=E\,d\).
    3. Substitution gives \(|\Delta V|=200(0.050)=10\,\mathrm V\).
    4. Since \(\vec E=-\nabla V\), the potential decreases in the \(+\hat i\) direction, which is the direction of the field.

    Answer: The planes differ by \(10\,\mathrm V\), with decreasing potential in the \(+\hat i\) direction.

    Example 2.

    A point charge \(+2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) produces equipotential spherical surfaces at \(100\,\mathrm V\) and \(50\,\mathrm V\). Find their radii and the ratio of their areas.

    1. For a point charge, \(V=kq/r\), so \(r=kq/V\).
    2. For the \(100\,\mathrm V\) surface, \(r_{100}=(8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-6})/100=179.8\,\mathrm m\).
    3. For the \(50\,\mathrm V\) surface, \(r_{50}=(8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-6})/50=359.6\,\mathrm m\).
    4. Since area is proportional to \(r^2\), \(A_{50}/A_{100}=(359.6/179.8)^2=4\).
    5. The lower-potential surface is farther from the positive charge, where the field is weaker.

    Answer: \(r_{100}=180\,\mathrm m\), \(r_{50}=360\,\mathrm m\), and \(A_{50}/A_{100}=4\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Drawing equipotential lines parallel to the electric field instead of perpendicular to it.
    • Claiming that a charge moves freely along a surface where the potential changes.
    • Comparing radii instead of areas when asked for the ratio of spherical surface areas.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 6

    Potential energy

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentPotentialStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Electrostatic potential energy is the energy required to assemble a charge configuration from infinitely separated charges, with zero energy defined at infinite separation. For two charges it is \(kq_1q_2/r\), and for several charges the pairwise contributions are added once each. Only changes in potential energy are physically relevant, and the work done by the field is the negative of the change in electrostatic potential energy for a quasistatic process.
    Key formula(s). \[U=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1q_2}{r}=\frac{kq_1q_2}{r},\qquad U=\sum_{i<j}\frac{kq_iq_j}{r_{ij}},\qquad U=qV_{\mathrm{other}},\qquad \Delta U=W_{\mathrm{ext,qs}}=-W_{\mathrm{field}}\]
    Key points.
    • Like charges have positive interaction energy, while unlike charges have negative interaction energy.
    • The zero of energy is conventionally chosen at infinite separation, so only energy differences are meaningful.
    • In a many-charge system, include each distinct pair exactly once; do not add both \(i,j\) and \(j,i\).
    • \(U=qV_{\mathrm{other}}\) uses the potential produced by all other charges, not the test charge's self-potential.
    • For a quasistatic change, external work equals \(\Delta U\), while field work equals \(-\Delta U\).
    • A bound or neutral object can have zero net charge but still possess internal electrostatic potential energy.
    Example 1.

    Two charges \(+2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) and \(+3.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) are separated by \(0.40\,\mathrm m\). Find their electrostatic potential energy and the work done by an external agent in separating them quasistatically to infinity.

    1. The two-charge energy is \(U=kq_1q_2/r\).
    2. The charge product is \(6.0\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C^2}\), so \(U=(8.99\times10^9)(6.0\times10^{-12})/(0.40)\).
    3. Evaluating gives \(U=0.1349\,\mathrm J\).
    4. At infinite separation the final energy is zero, so the quasistatic external work for the stated outward motion is \(W_{\mathrm{ext}}=\Delta U=0-0.1349=-0.1349\,\mathrm J\).
    5. The negative sign means the electric field releases energy while doing \(+0.1349\,\mathrm J\) of work; an external agent extracts energy during the quasistatic separation.

    Answer: \(U=+0.135\,\mathrm J\) initially, \(W_{\mathrm{ext}}=-0.135\,\mathrm J\), and the electric field does \(+0.135\,\mathrm J\) of work.

    Example 2.

    Three charges \(+2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\), \(-3.0\,\mu\mathrm C\), and \(+4.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side \(0.50\,\mathrm m\). Find the total electrostatic potential energy relative to infinite separation.

    1. Label the charges \(q_1=+2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\), \(q_2=-3.0\,\mu\mathrm C\), and \(q_3=+4.0\,\mu\mathrm C\); all pair distances are \(r=0.50\,\mathrm m\).
    2. The three pair products are \(q_1q_2=-6.0\,\mu\mathrm{C^2}\), \(q_1q_3=+8.0\,\mu\mathrm{C^2}\), and \(q_2q_3=-12.0\,\mu\mathrm{C^2}\).
    3. Their sum is \(-10.0\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{C^2}\), so \(U=k(-10.0\times10^{-12})/(0.50)\).
    4. Therefore \(U=(8.99\times10^9)(-10.0\times10^{-12})/0.50=-0.1798\,\mathrm J\).
    5. The negative sign means the final arrangement has lower electrostatic energy than three charges at infinite separation.

    Answer: The total potential energy is \(-0.180\,\mathrm J\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding only the attractive pairs and omitting the repulsive contribution.
    • Using a total-charge expression for a neutral or non-neutral configuration instead of summing pair interactions.
    • Taking \(qV\) with the potential due to the same charge included.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 7

    Conductors

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentCapacitorsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium has zero electric field everywhere in its material because free charges would otherwise continue to move. All excess charge resides on the surface, and the entire conductor is at one potential, although a cavity may contain a separate field if charge is placed inside it. The field immediately outside a conductor is normal to its surface and equals \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\), which is a common route to surface charge, force, and pressure questions.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec E_{\mathrm{inside}}=0,\qquad V_{\mathrm{conductor}}=\text{constant},\qquad E_{\mathrm{just\ outside}}=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \oint_S\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\frac{Q_{\mathrm{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \vec F=q\vec E\]
    Key points.
    • The field inside the conducting material is zero, not necessarily the field inside every empty cavity.
    • A conductor in equilibrium is an equipotential body, so no charge flows within it.
    • Excess charge is distributed on the outer surface unless charge is deliberately placed within a cavity, which induces charge on the inner surface.
    • The surface field is perpendicular to the surface and has magnitude \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\) immediately outside in vacuum.
    • A Gaussian surface drawn inside the metal encloses zero net charge even if external charges alter the surrounding field.
    • Surface charge density is generally not uniform; it is larger near sharp regions of high curvature.
    Example 1.

    An isolated conducting sphere of radius \(0.10\,\mathrm m\) carries a total charge \(+2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\). Find the electric field at \(r=0.05\,\mathrm m\) and at the surface \(r=0.10\,\mathrm m\).

    1. At \(r=0.05\,\mathrm m\), the point is inside the conducting material, where \(E=0\) in electrostatic equilibrium.
    2. At the surface, the field just outside is \(E=kQ/R^2\) for a conducting sphere.
    3. Substitution gives \(E=(8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-6})/(0.10)^2\).
    4. Hence \(E=1.798\times10^6\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\), directed radially outward.
    5. The potential is constant throughout the metal even though the field changes at the surface.

    Answer: \(E(0.05\,\mathrm m)=0\) and \(E(0.10\,\mathrm m)=1.80\times10^6\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\) outward.

    Example 2.

    A point charge \(+2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) is placed at the centre of the cavity of a thick conducting spherical shell whose inner radius is \(0.10\,\mathrm m\), outer radius is \(0.20\,\mathrm m\), and whose net charge is initially zero. Find the induced charges on the inner and outer surfaces and the fields at \(r=0.05\,\mathrm m\), in the metal, and at \(r=0.30\,\mathrm m\).

    1. A Gaussian surface in the metal has \(E=0\), so its enclosed charge must be zero; the inner surface therefore carries \(-2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    2. Since the shell is initially neutral, the outer surface must carry \(+2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    3. In the cavity at \(r=0.05\,\mathrm m\), the centered point charge gives \(E=kq/r^2=(8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-6})/(0.05)^2=7.19\times10^6\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\), outward.
    4. Throughout the conducting material, \(E=0\) because the induced charges make the net enclosed charge zero for a Gaussian surface there.
    5. Outside the shell, the total enclosed charge is \(+2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\), so at \(r=0.30\,\mathrm m\), \(E=kq/r^2=2.00\times10^5\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\), outward.

    Answer: The induced charges are \(-2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) on the inner surface and \(+2.0\,\mu\mathrm C\) on the outer surface; the fields are \(7.19\times10^6\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\) in the cavity, zero in the metal, and \(2.00\times10^5\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\) outside.

    Common mistakes.
    • Claiming that the field is zero throughout every cavity merely because the conductor is an equipotential.
    • Forgetting that a Gaussian surface in the metal must enclose zero net charge.
    • Assuming surface charge density is uniform on every conductor shape.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 8

    Dielectrics

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentCapacitorsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A dielectric is an insulating polarizable medium in which positive and negative bound charges separate under an applied electric field. Its polarization is \(\mathbf P=\varepsilon_0\chi_e\mathbf E\), and its relative permittivity is \(\kappa=1+\chi_e\), which reduces the internal field produced by free charges. For JEE slab problems, the dielectric-filled and unfilled lengths act as capacitors in series.
    Key formula(s). \[\mathbf p=q\boldsymbol{\ell},\qquad \mathbf P=n\mathbf p,\qquad \mathbf D=\varepsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P=\varepsilon\mathbf E,\qquad \kappa=1+\chi_e,\qquad C=\frac{\kappa\varepsilon_0A}{d}\];
    Key points.
    • Dielectric molecules need not contain free charges; their induced dipoles create bound charges.
    • For a linear isotropic dielectric, \(\mathbf P\parallel\mathbf E\) and \(\varepsilon=\kappa\varepsilon_0\).
    • The bound surface-charge density on a face normal to polarization has magnitude \(|\sigma_b|=|\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}|\).
    • A dielectric slab placed between the plates always has its two faces treated as bound-charge surfaces, even though it carries no free charge.
    • For a full-area slab of thickness \(t\), \(C=\varepsilon_0A/[d-t+t/\kappa]\), showing that even an infinitesimal void layer has a large effective thickness.
    Example 1.

    A dielectric slab of relative permittivity \(4\) and thickness \(1\,\mathrm{mm}\) covers the full area of one \(4\,\mathrm{mm}\)-long parallel-plate capacitor whose plates have area \(100\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Find its capacitance.

    1. The slab and air gap are series dielectric layers because the same free charge appears on both.
    2. Their total effective thickness is \((d-t)+t/\kappa=3\,\mathrm{mm}+(1\,\mathrm{mm})/4=3.25\,\mathrm{mm}\).
    3. Convert the area: \(100\,\mathrm{cm^2}=10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}\).
    4. Hence \(C=\varepsilon_0A/[3.25\times10^{-3}]=(8.854\times10^{-12})(10^{-2})/(3.25\times10^{-3})\).
    5. The result is \(C=2.72\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm F\).

    Answer: The capacitance is \(27.2\,\mathrm{pF}\).

    Example 2.

    A linear dielectric of relative permittivity \(3\) is placed in a uniform field \(2.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\). Find its polarization and the magnitude of bound surface charge density at an interface normal to the field.

    1. For a linear dielectric, \(\chi_e=\kappa-1=2\), so \(\mathbf P=\varepsilon_0(\kappa-1)\mathbf E\).
    2. Its magnitude is \(P=(8.854\times10^{-12})(2)(2.0\times10^5)\).
    3. Therefore \(P=3.54\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}\).
    4. On a surface perpendicular to \(\mathbf P\), the bound surface charge has magnitude \(|\sigma_b|=P\).
    5. The signs are opposite on the two dielectric faces.

    Answer: \(P=3.54\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}\) and \(|\sigma_b|=3.54\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Assuming every material is a linear dielectric; ferroelectric materials are not generally linear.
    • Adding dielectric thicknesses directly instead of replacing air thickness by \(t/\kappa\).
    • Confusing free surface charge \(\sigma_f=\mathbf D\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\) with bound charge \(\sigma_b\).

    Explanation

    Concept. Inserting a dielectric increases capacitance because polarization reduces the electric field produced by free charges. The resulting changes in charge, voltage, and energy depend critically on whether the capacitor remains connected to a battery. A connected battery holds voltage fixed, whereas an isolated capacitor conserves free charge; recognizing the invariant first prevents most energy-bookkeeping errors.
    Key formula(s). \[C_f=\kappa C_i,\qquad (V\text{ fixed})\,:\ Q_f=\kappa Q_i,\ U_f=\kappa U_i,\qquad (Q\text{ fixed})\,:\ V_f=V_i/\kappa,\ U_f=U_i/\kappa,\qquad C_{\mathrm{slab}}=\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d-t+t/\kappa}\];
    Key points.
    • Complete insertion multiplies capacitance by \(\kappa=1+\chi_e\); partial insertion changes it according to the two series regions.
    • With a battery connected, voltage is the invariant and the source supplies additional charge.
    • With the battery disconnected, free charge is the invariant and voltage and energy both decrease by a factor \(\kappa\).
    • The mechanical force tends to pull a dielectric into a region of stronger electric field.
    • On removing a dielectric at fixed \(Q\), the rising field energy comes from positive external mechanical work.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor is connected to a \(50\,\mathrm V\) battery. After the connection is made, a dielectric of relative permittivity \(3\) is fully inserted. Find the final charge and the work done by the battery.

    1. Since the battery remains connected, the voltage stays \(50\,\mathrm V\) and the capacitance becomes \(C_f=3C_i=6\,\mu\mathrm F\).
    2. The initial charge is \(Q_i=C_iV=(2\,\mu\mathrm F)(50\,\mathrm V)=100\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    3. The final charge is \(Q_f=C_fV=(6\,\mu\mathrm F)(50\,\mathrm V)=300\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    4. The battery work is \(W_{\mathrm{bat}}=V(Q_f-Q_i)=50(300-100)\,\mu\mathrm C=1.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J\).
    5. The field-energy increase is only \(U_f-U_i=(7.50-2.50)\,\mathrm{mJ}=5.00\,\mathrm{mJ}\).

    Answer: \(Q_f=300\,\mu\mathrm C\) and \(W_{\mathrm{bat}}=1.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J\).

    Example 2.

    A \(3\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor charged to \(40\,\mathrm V\) is isolated from its battery. A dielectric of relative permittivity \(4\) is then fully inserted. Find the final voltage, final energy, and energy converted into mechanical work.

    1. Isolation fixes the charge at \(Q=C_iV_i=(3\,\mu\mathrm F)(40\,\mathrm V)=120\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    2. Full insertion raises capacitance to \(C_f=4C_i=12\,\mu\mathrm F\).
    3. Therefore \(V_f=Q/C_f=120/12=10\,\mathrm V\).
    4. The initial energy is \(U_i=\tfrac12C_iV_i^2=2.40\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J\), and the final energy is \(U_f=\tfrac12C_fV_f^2=0.600\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J\).
    5. The decrease \(U_i-U_f=1.80\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J\) is the work associated with insertion of the dielectric.

    Answer: \(V_f=10\,\mathrm V\), \(U_f=6.00\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J\), and mechanical work is \(1.80\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Saying charge stays fixed even though a battery remains connected.
    • Applying the constant-voltage energy rule to an isolated capacitor.
    • Counting all lost field energy as heat when a movable dielectric is inserted.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 9

    Capacitance

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentCapacitorsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Capacitance measures a conductor system's ability to store charge and is defined by \(C=Q/\Delta V\) in a linear electrostatic system. For a definite geometry and dielectric environment, \(C\) is fixed, so the stored charge is proportional to the potential difference. JEE problems are most efficiently solved by identifying whether the object is an isolated sphere, a parallel-plate arrangement, or a two-conductor system before applying the corresponding formula.
    Key formula(s). \[C=\frac{Q}{V_A-V_B},\qquad C_{\mathrm{sphere}}=4\pi\varepsilon_0R,\qquad C_{\mathrm{concentric}}=4\pi\varepsilon_0\frac{ab}{b-a},\qquad [C]=[\varepsilon_0]\];
    Key points.
    • A single isolated conductor is compared with infinity, so \(Q=CV\) gives its potential relative to infinity.
    • For nested spheres, \(a<b\), and the result tends to \(4\pi\varepsilon_0a\) as the outer radius becomes very large.
    • Increasing conductor area increases capacitance, while increasing separation of two charged plates decreases it.
    • The SI unit of capacitance is the farad, with \(1\,\mathrm F=1\,\mathrm{C\,V^{-1}}\) and \(1\,\mathrm{pF}=10^{-12}\,\mathrm F\).
    • When conductors touch and are then separated with no external path, total charge is conserved but each final potential is obtained from the new geometry.
    Example 1.

    A conducting sphere of radius \(4\,\mathrm{cm}\) is given a charge of \(2\,\mu\mathrm C\). Find its capacitance and potential relative to infinity.

    1. For an isolated sphere, \(C=4\pi\varepsilon_0R\), with \(R=0.04\,\mathrm m\) and \(\varepsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}\).
    2. Substitution gives \(C=4\pi(8.854\times10^{-12})(0.04)=4.45\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm F\).
    3. The potential is \(V=Q/C=(2\times10^{-6})/(4.45\times10^{-12})\).
    4. Hence \(V=4.49\times10^5\,\mathrm V\).

    Answer: \(C=4.45\,\mathrm{pF}\) and \(V=4.49\times10^5\,\mathrm V\).

    Example 2.

    Two widely separated conducting spheres of radii \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(3\,\mathrm{cm}\) carry charges \(4\,\mu\mathrm C\) and \(6\,\mu\mathrm C\), respectively. They are touched together and then separated far apart. Find their final common potential.

    1. Touching makes the two spheres equipotential, while no charge escapes, so \(Q_{\mathrm{total}}=10\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    2. The final potential satisfies \(V=Q_{\mathrm{total}}/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(R_1+R_2)]\), since capacitances add at common voltage.
    3. With \(R_1+R_2=0.05\,\mathrm m\), the denominator is \(4\pi(8.854\times10^{-12})(0.05)=5.56\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm F\).
    4. Thus \(V=(10\times10^{-6})/(5.56\times10^{-12})\).
    5. Each sphere retains the same potential because they are far apart after separation.

    Answer: The final potential of each sphere is \(1.80\times10^6\,\mathrm V\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating capacitance as proportional to charge; for fixed geometry, \(Q=CV\) is the correct relation.
    • Using \(a+b\) instead of \(b-a\) for a concentric-sphere capacitor.
    • Losing the sign or total charge when identical spheres are separated after contact.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 10

    Parallel plate capacitor

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentCapacitorsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A parallel-plate capacitor stores equal and opposite free charges on plates having area \(A\) and separation \(d\), while fringing is neglected. In a uniform dielectric of permittivity \(\varepsilon\), the uniform field is \(E=V/d\), and the capacitance follows directly from the free-surface charge density. The electrostatic force between the plates can be derived either from Maxwell pressure or from the energy change at constant charge.
    Key formula(s). \[E=\frac{V}{d},\qquad C=\frac{\varepsilon A}{d},\qquad Q=\frac{\varepsilon AV}{d},\qquad F=\frac{\varepsilon AV^2}{2d^2}=\frac{Q^2}{2\varepsilon A},\qquad p=\frac{F}{A}=\frac{\varepsilon E^2}{2}\];
    Key points.
    • Capacitance is directly proportional to plate area and inversely proportional to plate separation.
    • In vacuum, \(C=\varepsilon_0A/d\); in a linear dielectric, replace \(\varepsilon_0\) by \(\kappa\varepsilon_0\).
    • Equal and opposite charges appear on the two conducting plates, although the algebraic charges are opposite.
    • The force is attractive and remains finite even as \(d\to0\) under the ideal fixed-voltage model.
    • The factor \(1/2\) prevents counting a plate's own field on its charge; only the other plate's field produces the net force.
    Example 1.

    A parallel-plate capacitor has area \(2\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), plate separation \(1\,\mathrm{mm}\), and a dielectric of relative permittivity \(4\). Find its capacitance and the charge on each plate when connected to a \(300\,\mathrm V\) battery.

    1. Convert the data to SI units: \(A=0.02\,\mathrm{m^2}\), \(d=10^{-3}\,\mathrm m\), and \(\varepsilon=4\varepsilon_0\).
    2. The capacitance is \(C=\varepsilon A/d=4(8.854\times10^{-12})(0.02)/(10^{-3})\).
    3. Hence \(C=7.08\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm F=708\,\mathrm{pF}\).
    4. While connected to the battery, the capacitor remains at \(V=300\,\mathrm V\), so \(Q=CV\).
    5. Therefore \(Q=(7.08\times10^{-10})(300)=2.12\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm C\).

    Answer: \(C=708\,\mathrm{pF}\) and \(Q=2.12\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm C=212\,\mathrm{nC}\) on each plate.

    Example 2.

    A parallel-plate capacitor with area \(1\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), separation \(2\,\mathrm{mm}\), and relative permittivity \(2\) is held at \(100\,\mathrm V\). Find the attractive force between its plates.

    1. Its permittivity is \(\varepsilon=2\varepsilon_0=1.7708\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}\).
    2. The field is \(E=V/d=100/(2\times10^{-3})=5.0\times10^4\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\).
    3. The Maxwell pressure is \(p=\varepsilon E^2/2\).
    4. Thus \(p=(1.7708\times10^{-11})(2.5\times10^9)/2=2.21\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{Pa}\).
    5. Multiplying by area gives \(F=pA=2.21\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm N\).

    Answer: Each plate experiences an attractive force of \(2.21\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm N\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Omitting the dielectric constant from \(C=\kappa\varepsilon_0A/d\).
    • Using \(E=V\) instead of \(E=V/d\) for parallel plates.
    • Omitting the factor \(1/2\) in the plate-force or pressure formula.

    Dielectric capacitor

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentCapacitorsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Dielectric-slab capacitors (K-filled: C=Kε0A/d, field reduced E0/K, voltage drops V0/K with isolated charge; battery-connected voltage fixed, charge rises K-fold) store more energy safely. Partial slabs (series/series-parallel combos), conducting slabs (K-infinite limit), and dielectric breakdown limits (kV/mm ratings) extend cases. Slab insertion with battery on/off splits behaviours - charge versus voltage constancy decides.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • K multiplies capacitance; isolated charge keeps Q (V falls), battery keeps V (Q rises).
    • Breakdown fields limit safe voltages.
    Slab cases
    PointDetail
    Isolated (Q fixed)V falls K-fold, energy falls
    Battery (V fixed)Q rises K-fold, energy rises
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Dielectric slab inserted in isolated charged capacitor

    Solution: Fixed charge with K-fold capacitance drops voltage proportionally.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 12

    Combination of capacitors

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentCapacitorsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Capacitors connected in parallel share the same potential difference, so their capacitances add. Capacitors connected in series carry equal-magnitude charges, so their equivalent capacitance is the reciprocal of the sum of their reciprocals. In network problems, repeatedly identify nodes at equal potential and replace the simplest parallel or series group until one equivalent capacitor remains.
    Key formula(s). \[C_{\mathrm{parallel}}=\sum_i C_i,\qquad \frac{1}{C_{\mathrm{series}}}=\sum_i\frac{1}{C_i},\qquad C_{\mathrm{series}}=(C_1C_2)/(C_1+C_2),\qquad Q_{\mathrm{series}}=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V,\qquad V_{\mathrm{parallel,i}}=V_{\mathrm{eq}}\];
    Key points.
    • A series equivalent is smaller than the smallest capacitor, while a parallel equivalent is larger than the largest.
    • In series, charge is equal but potential differences add; in parallel, voltage is equal but charges add.
    • The series formula for capacitance uses reciprocals, unlike the direct addition rule for series resistance.
    • Floating intermediate nodes must initially be neutral, so redistributions of capacitor charge are not generally possible.
    • A capacitor joined by a zero-resistance wire is in parallel even if the diagram makes its geometric position unusual.
    Example 1.

    Capacitors of \(2\,\mu\mathrm F\), \(3\,\mu\mathrm F\), and \(6\,\mu\mathrm F\) are connected in series across a \(60\,\mathrm V\) source. Find the equivalent capacitance, charge on each capacitor, and stored energy.

    1. The series equivalent obeys \(1/C_{\mathrm{eq}}=1/2+1/3+1/6=1\), all in units of \((\mu\mathrm F)^{-1}\).
    2. Hence \(C_{\mathrm{eq}}=1\,\mu\mathrm F\).
    3. Every series capacitor carries \(Q=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V=(1\,\mu\mathrm F)(60\,\mathrm V)=60\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    4. The total electrostatic energy is \(U=Q^2/(2C_{\mathrm{eq}})=(60\times10^{-6})^2/(2\times10^{-6})\).
    5. Thus \(U=1.80\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J\).

    Answer: \(C_{\mathrm{eq}}=1\,\mu\mathrm F\), each capacitor has charge \(60\,\mu\mathrm C\), and \(U=1.80\,\mathrm{mJ}\).

    Example 2.

    Three \(3\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitors are first connected in parallel. That group is in series with a \(6\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor, and the combination is in parallel with a \(4.4\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor. A \(90\,\mathrm V\) battery is connected across the network. Find the equivalent capacitance and voltage across the \(6\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor.

    1. The three parallel capacitors combine to \(C_a=3+3+3=9\,\mu\mathrm F\).
    2. The series pair has \(C_s=(9\times6)/(9+6)\,\mu\mathrm F=3.6\,\mu\mathrm F\).
    3. Its final parallel combination with \(4.4\,\mu\mathrm F\) gives \(C_{\mathrm{eq}}=3.6+4.4=8.0\,\mu\mathrm F\).
    4. The charge on the series branch is \(Q=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V=(8\,\mu\mathrm F)(90\,\mathrm V)=720\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    5. Therefore the voltage across the \(6\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor is \(720/6=120\,\mathrm V\); the \(9\,\mu\mathrm F\) group has \(80\,\mathrm V\).

    Answer: \(C_{\mathrm{eq}}=8.0\,\mu\mathrm F\) and the voltage across the \(6\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor is \(120\,\mathrm V\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding capacitance reciprocals in a parallel group.
    • Assigning the full battery voltage to every capacitor in a series chain.
    • Applying series or parallel rules before simplifying all nearby branches.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 13

    Series

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentCapacitorsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Series capacitors share charge (same Q flows through chain), voltages divide inversely (V=Q/C each), reciprocal adds (1/C=1/C1+1/C2+...) - smallest dominates equivalent (below smallest individual). Breakdown-safe (high voltage splits), charge-matched applications (tuning circuits). Two equal C give C/2 - series always reduces below minimum member.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Same charge; voltages split inversely; reciprocal sums.
    • Equivalent below smallest member always.
    Remember
    • Series shares charge; parallel shares voltage - dual rules.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Three 6μF capacitors in series give equivalent

    Solution: Reciprocal sum thirds: 1/6+1/6+1/6 halves twice to 2.
    Key Formulas · Series Capacitors
    \(\frac1C=\sum\frac1{C_{i}}\) reciprocals add
    \(Q\;\mathrm{same},\;V=\sum V_{i}\) charge shared, voltages split
    \(C_{eq}<\min(C_{i})\) below smallest member always

    Chapter 13 · Topic 14

    Parallel

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentCapacitorsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Parallel capacitors share voltage (same V across plates), charges add proportionally (Q=CV each), capacitances sum directly (C=C1+C2+...) - biggest dominates equivalent. Charge-storage banks (power supplies, flash circuits) parallel for capacity; voltage ratings stay single-unit. Two equal C give 2C - parallel always exceeds maximum member.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • Same voltage; charges add; capacitances sum.
    • Equivalent above largest member always.
    Remember
    • Parallel adds capacity; series divides voltage.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    Three 6μF capacitors in parallel give equivalent

    Solution: Direct sum triples capacity at shared voltage.
    Key Formulas · Parallel Capacitors
    \(C=\sum C_{i}\) capacitances add directly
    \(V\;\mathrm{same},\;Q=\sum Q_{i}\) voltage shared, charges add
    \(C_{eq}>\max(C_{i})\) above largest member always

    Chapter 13 · Topic 15

    Energy stored

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentCapacitorsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The electrostatic energy of a capacitor is the work required to separate its charges and equals \(U=Q^2/(2C)=\tfrac12CV^2\). These equivalent forms correspond respectively to fixed charge and fixed voltage, allowing a quick choice of the energy change after a connection. When a charged capacitor is connected to another without a source, charge is conserved, but the missing energy appears as heat, radiation, and transient circuit energy.
    Key formula(s). \[U=\frac{Q^2}{2C}=\frac12CV^2=\frac12QV,\qquad W_{\mathrm{source}}=V\Delta Q,\qquad U_{\mathrm{loss}}=\frac{Q^2C_2}{2C_1(C_1+C_2)}\quad(C_2\text{ initially uncharged})\];
    Key points.
    • The SI unit of capacitor energy is the joule, and \(1\,\mu\mathrm F\) at \(1\,\mathrm V\) stores \(\tfrac12\,\mu\mathrm J\).
    • At fixed \(C\), energy increases as \(V^2\) and decreases as \(1/Q^2\).
    • Holding a capacitor at fixed voltage requires a battery, so the battery does more work than the increase in field energy.
    • Connecting an isolated charged capacitor to an uncharged one conserves total charge but not electrostatic energy.
    • The final voltage of a parallel connection is the charge-weighted average, \(V_f=(C_1V_1+C_2V_2)/(C_1+C_2)\), using signed voltages.
    Example 1.

    A \(4\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor is charged by a \(100\,\mathrm V\) source. Find the charge on it and its stored electrostatic energy.

    1. The capacitance and voltage give \(Q=CV=(4\times10^{-6})(100)=4.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm C\).
    2. As a consistency check, the final voltage is \(Q/C=(4.0\times10^{-4})/(4\times10^{-6})=100\,\mathrm V\).
    3. The stored energy is \(U=\tfrac12CV^2=\tfrac12(4\times10^{-6})(100)^2\).
    4. This gives \(U=2.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J\).
    5. The same result follows from \(U=Q^2/(2C)\).

    Answer: \(Q=4.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm C=400\,\mu\mathrm C\) and \(U=2.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J\).

    Example 2.

    A \(6\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor charged to \(100\,\mathrm V\) is disconnected from its battery and connected in parallel with an initially uncharged \(3\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor. Find the final voltage and the energy dissipated during connection.

    1. Initially \(Q_i=C_iV_i=(6\,\mu\mathrm F)(100\,\mathrm V)=600\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    2. Because the battery is absent, this total charge is conserved: \(Q_f=600\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    3. The final capacitance is \(C_f=6+3=9\,\mu\mathrm F\), so \(V_f=600/9=66.7\,\mathrm V\).
    4. The initial energy is \(U_i=\tfrac12(6\times10^{-6})(100)^2=0.030\,\mathrm J\), and \(U_f=\tfrac12(9\times10^{-6})(66.7)^2=0.020\,\mathrm J\).
    5. Therefore the dissipated energy is \(U_i-U_f=0.010\,\mathrm J\).

    Answer: The final voltage is \(66.7\,\mathrm V\), and \(1.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm J\) is dissipated.

    Common mistakes.
    • Dropping the factor \(1/2\) from the capacitor-energy formula.
    • Conserving charge as well as energy when an isolated capacitor is reconnected.
    • Using \(Q=CV\) for both original capacitors in a series chain at arbitrary voltages.

    Explanation

    Concept. A series \(RC\) circuit obeys a first-order charging or discharging law whenever the source, resistance, and capacitance are constant. The characteristic time \(\tau=RC\) is the time for the difference between the instantaneous value and its final value to fall to \(1/e\). During charging, \(dq/dt=(V-q/C)/R\); during discharge, \(dq/dt=-q/(RC)\).
    Key formula(s). \[\tau=RC,\qquad q_{\mathrm{ch}}=CV\left(1-e^{-t/RC}\right),\qquad i_{\mathrm{ch}}=\frac VR e^{-t/RC},\qquad q_{\mathrm{dis}}=q_0e^{-t/RC},\qquad i_{\mathrm{dis}}=-\frac{q_0}{RC}e^{-t/RC}\];
    Key points.
    • At \(t=0^+\) an uncharged capacitor behaves like a short circuit, while a fully charged ideal capacitor in a discharge circuit initially behaves like a source of voltage \(q_0/C\).
    • At \(t=\tau\), charging reaches \(63.2\%\) of the final charge, while discharging leaves \(36.8\%\).
    • The voltage decays exactly as a fraction of charge because \(V=q/C\) for a fixed capacitor.
    • The half-life is \(t_{1/2}=(RC)\ln2\), which is not \(RC/2\).
    • A battery charging an ideal capacitor supplies \(CV^2\), of which only \(CV^2/2\) remains stored and the other half is dissipated in the resistance.
    Example 1.

    A \(2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\) resistor charges a \(5\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor from a \(12\,\mathrm V\) ideal battery. Find the charge and charging current \(20\,\mathrm{ms}\) after connection.

    1. The time constant is \(\tau=RC=(2\times10^3)(5\times10^{-6})=0.010\,\mathrm s\).
    2. The elapsed time is \(t/\tau=20\,\mathrm{ms}/10\,\mathrm{ms}=2\).
    3. The charge is \(q=CV(1-e^{-2})=(12)(5\times10^{-6})(1-0.1353)\).
    4. Thus \(q=5.19\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm C=51.9\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    5. The current is \(i=(V/R)e^{-2}=6.0\times10^{-3}\times0.1353=8.12\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm A\).

    Answer: At \(20\,\mathrm{ms}\), \(q=51.9\,\mu\mathrm C\) and \(i=81.2\,\mu\mathrm A\).

    Example 2.

    A \(10\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor initially charged to \(100\,\mathrm V\) is discharged through a \(1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\) resistor. Find the time for its voltage to halve and the resistor current at that instant.

    1. The time constant is \(\tau=RC=(10^3)(10\times10^{-6})=0.010\,\mathrm s\).
    2. For discharge, \(V=V_0e^{-t/\tau}\).
    3. Setting \(V=V_0/2\) gives \(e^{-t/\tau}=1/2\), so \(t=\tau\ln2\).
    4. Hence \(t_{1/2}=(0.010)(0.6931)=6.93\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm s\).
    5. At this time \(V=50\,\mathrm V\), hence the current magnitude is \(i=V/R=50/1000=0.050\,\mathrm A\).

    Answer: The half-voltage time is \(6.93\,\mathrm{ms}\), and the discharge current has magnitude \(50\,\mathrm{mA}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(1-e^{-t/(2RC)}\) or another incorrect exponential time scale.
    • Treating the capacitor voltage as constant throughout a charging process.
    • Assigning a negative current as charge when a problem requests the conventional current direction.

    Explanation

    Concept. In any capacitor process, first identify whether the battery is connected, because that fixes voltage and permits charge flow, or disconnected, because that fixes free charge. Dielectric insertion, removal, and subsequent reconnection must then be treated as separate state changes. For connected and disconnected cases, the ratios \(C:Q:V:U\) provide fast JEE-level answers without unnecessary integration.
    Key formula(s). \[V\text{ fixed}:\ (C,Q,V,U)\to(\kappa C,\kappa Q,V,\kappa U),\qquad Q\text{ fixed}:\ (C,Q,V,U)\to(\kappa C,Q,V/\kappa,U/\kappa)\];
    Key points.
    • The circuit topology determines \(C\), while the battery condition determines which of \(Q\) and \(V\) remains constant.
    • A connected battery contributes work \(V\Delta Q\), which need not equal \(\Delta U\) during insertion or removal.
    • If the battery is disconnected after charging, subsequent operations conserve the newly established free charge.
    • Removing a dielectric at constant charge raises voltage and field energy, requiring positive external work.
    • Energy is conserved when the work of the battery and the mechanical agent are included alongside \(\Delta U\).
    Example 1.

    A \(4\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor is charged to \(60\,\mathrm V\), disconnected from its battery, and then filled with a dielectric of relative permittivity \(5\). Find the final capacitance, voltage, and energy.

    1. Before disconnection, \(Q=C_iV_i=(4\,\mu\mathrm F)(60\,\mathrm V)=240\,\mu\mathrm C\).
    2. With the battery absent, this charge remains constant during insertion.
    3. The capacitance increases to \(C_f=\kappa C_i=20\,\mu\mathrm F\).
    4. Thus \(V_f=Q/C_f=240/20=12\,\mathrm V\).
    5. The final energy is \(U_f=Q^2/(2C_f)=(240\times10^{-6})^2/[2(20\times10^{-6})]=1.44\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J\).

    Answer: \(C_f=20\,\mu\mathrm F\), \(V_f=12\,\mathrm V\), and \(U_f=1.44\,\mathrm{mJ}\).

    Example 2.

    A \(2\,\mu\mathrm F\) capacitor is connected to a \(30\,\mathrm V\) battery and filled with a dielectric of relative permittivity \(3\). The battery is then removed, and finally the dielectric is removed while charge remains conserved. Find the final voltage, energy, and external work required in the last step.

    1. With the battery connected, \(C_1=3C_0=6\,\mu\mathrm F\), \(Q=180\,\mu\mathrm C\), and \(V=30\,\mathrm V\).
    2. The energy at the end of insertion is \(U_1=\tfrac12(6\times10^{-6})(30)^2=2.70\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J\).
    3. Removing the battery fixes \(Q=180\,\mu\mathrm C\) throughout dielectric removal.
    4. When the capacitance returns to \(2\,\mu\mathrm F\), \(V_2=Q/C_0=90\,\mathrm V\) and \(U_2=\tfrac12C_0V_2^2=8.10\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J\).
    5. There is no battery during the last step, so external mechanical work is \(W_{\mathrm{ext}}=U_2-U_1=5.40\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm J\).

    Answer: The final voltage is \(90\,\mathrm V\), the final energy is \(8.10\,\mathrm{mJ}\), and the required external work is \(5.40\,\mathrm{mJ}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Continuing to hold voltage fixed after the battery has been removed.
    • Applying a connected-battery ratio after an intermediate disconnection.
    • Equating battery work alone with the final increase in field energy.

    Chapter 13 · Topic 16

    Energy density

    Electrostatic Potential and CapacitanceElectrostatics and CurrentCapacitorsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Energy density is the electric-field energy per unit volume and equals \(u=\tfrac12\varepsilon E^2\) in a linear dielectric. It is a local quantity, whereas total capacitor energy is its volume integral. JEE comparisons must state whether the same electric field or the same free surface charge is maintained, because reversing that condition reverses the dependence on permittivity.
    Key formula(s). \[u=\frac12\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D=\frac12\varepsilon E^2=\frac12\frac{\sigma_f^2}{\varepsilon}=\frac{\sigma_fE}{2},\qquad U=uV_{\mathrm{vol}},\qquad p=\frac{F}{A}=u\quad\text{for parallel plates in a linear dielectric}\];
    Key points.
    • In vacuum, \(u=\varepsilon_0E^2/2\), and in a linear dielectric \(u=\kappa\varepsilon_0E^2/2\).
    • At fixed free charge density, the field scales as \(1/\kappa\), so the energy density scales as \(1/\kappa\).
    • At fixed electric field, increasing permittivity increases the energy density because more dielectric is polarized.
    • Energy density has units \(\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\) and is also equal to \(\mathrm{Pa}\).
    • For a uniformly filled capacitor, \(U=\tfrac12CV^2=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0A(V/d)^2\kappa\).
    Example 1.

    A region of vacuum has a uniform field \(2.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\) and volume \(5.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Find its energy density and total field energy.

    1. In vacuum, \(u=\varepsilon_0E^2/2\).
    2. The squared field is \(E^2=(2.0\times10^5)^2=4.0\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{V^2\,m^{-2}}\).
    3. Hence \(u=(8.854\times10^{-12})(4.0\times10^{10})/2=0.177\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\).
    4. Because the field is uniform, \(U=uV_{\mathrm{vol}}\).
    5. Therefore \(U=(0.177)(5.0\times10^{-4})=8.85\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J\).

    Answer: The energy density is \(0.177\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\) and the total energy is \(8.85\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J\).

    Example 2.

    The space between parallel plates is completely filled by a dielectric of relative permittivity \(4\). The field is \(1.0\times10^6\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\) and the field-filled volume is \(1.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^3}\). Find the stored energy and compare it with the same field in vacuum.

    1. The dielectric permittivity is \(\varepsilon=4\varepsilon_0\).
    2. Its energy density is \(u=\tfrac12\varepsilon E^2=\tfrac12(4\varepsilon_0)(1.0\times10^6)^2\).
    3. Thus \(u=17.7\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\).
    4. The total energy is \(U=uV_{\mathrm{vol}}=(17.7)(1.0\times10^{-5})=1.77\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J\).
    5. In vacuum the energy density would be \(4.43\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\), and the total energy would be \(4.43\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm J\).

    Answer: The dielectric stores \(1.77\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm J\), which is four times the vacuum value at the same field.

    Common mistakes.
    • Comparing dielectric and vacuum at constant field but assuming the energy decreases.
    • Confusing energy density in \(\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\) with total energy.
    • Using \(\sigma^2\varepsilon/2\) instead of \(\sigma^2/(2\varepsilon)\) at fixed free charge density.

    Index / Electrostatics and Current
    Chapter 14 · Topic 1

    Electric current

    Current ElectricityElectrostatics and CurrentBasicsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Electric current is the rate at which net charge crosses a chosen oriented surface. By convention, positive charge motion defines positive current, while conventional current is opposite to electron drift. In a conductor, multiplying carrier number density, charge magnitude, cross-sectional area, and drift speed gives the microscopic current.
    Key formula(s). \[I=\frac{dQ}{dt},\qquad I=\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}\text{ for constant average rate},\qquad I=n|q|Av_d,\qquad \mathbf J=nq\mathbf v_d,\qquad 1\,\mathrm A=1\,\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}\];
    Key points.
    • Conventional current through a wire points from higher to lower potential for an ordinary resistive conductor.
    • The current-density vector points in the direction of positive-charge transport, so electron motion contributes current opposite to its velocity.
    • Current may be steady while individual carriers move with a small drift velocity superimposed on random thermal motion.
    • Equal positive and negative charges crossing an area in opposite directions can yield zero net current.
    • A neutral conductor contains many mobile electrons but normally carries no net current when there is no applied field.
    Example 1.

    A conductor carries \(6\,\mathrm C\) of net charge through a cross-section in \(3\,\mathrm{ms}\). Find the average current and state its direction if the positive charge moves rightward.

    1. Convert the time to seconds: \(3\,\mathrm{ms}=3\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm s\).
    2. The average current is \(I=\Delta Q/\Delta t\).
    3. Substitution gives \(I=6/(3\times10^{-3})=2.0\times10^3\,\mathrm A\).
    4. Since positive charge moves rightward, conventional current is also rightward.

    Answer: The average current is \(2.0\,\mathrm{kA}\), directed rightward.

    Example 2.

    A semiconductor contains \(5\times10^{21}\) electrons per cubic metre and \(1\times10^{21}\) holes per cubic metre. Their drift speeds are \(4\times10^4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(1\times10^4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), respectively, with electrons and holes moving in opposite directions. Find the current density.

    1. Electrons move opposite the conventional current, while holes move with it, so their speed contributions add.
    2. The electron contribution is \(n_eev_e=(5\times10^{21})(1.602\times10^{-19})(4\times10^4)\).
    3. The hole contribution is \(n_pev_h=(1\times10^{21})(1.602\times10^{-19})(1\times10^4)\).
    4. Therefore \(J=n_eev_e+n_pev_h=3.204\times10^7+1.602\times10^6\).
    5. Thus \(J=3.364\times10^7\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\), directed along hole motion.

    Answer: The current density is \(3.364\times10^7\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Substituting electron drift velocity with its charge sign as though it were positive.
    • Adding electron and hole current magnitudes with a minus sign between them.
    • Confusing the number of carriers passing per second with total current in amperes.
    Back to Index
    Index / Electrostatics and Current
    Chapter 14 · Topic 2

    Drift velocity

    Current ElectricityElectrostatics and CurrentBasicsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Drift velocity is the small average velocity component of charge carriers that contributes to current, after averaging their random thermal motion. A microscopic current is \(I=n|q|Av_d\), so a smaller carrier density, charge, or area requires a larger drift velocity for the same current. The direction of electron drift is opposite to conventional current and opposite to the applied electric field in a metal.
    Key formula(s). \[\mathbf J=nq\mathbf v_d,\qquad I=n|q|Av_d,\qquad v_d=\frac{I}{n|q|A},\qquad v_d\ll v_{\mathrm{thermal}},\qquad e=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C,\qquad v_d=\mu E\ \text{at constant mobility}\];
    Key points.
    • Drift speed is an average over large numbers of carriers, not the instantaneous random speed of an electron.
    • Both electrons and positive ions can contribute current in an electrolyte, and their conventional current contributions point in the direction of their respective charge motion.
    • Increasing cross-sectional area lowers drift speed for fixed current and carrier density.
    • The time for a carrier to traverse a wire is length divided by drift speed, not by random thermal speed.
    • Current density is independent of wire length, whereas drift velocity is also independent of length for a uniform wire.
    Example 1.

    A copper wire of cross-sectional area \(2\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2}\) carries \(6\,\mathrm A\). If the free-electron density is \(8.5\times10^{28}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), find the drift speed of the electrons.

    1. Rearrange the microscopic current relation: \(v_d=I/(neA)\).
    2. Using \(e=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\), the denominator is \(neA=(8.5\times10^{28})(1.602\times10^{-19})(2\times10^{-5})\).
    3. This denominator equals \(2.723\times10^5\,\mathrm{C\,m^{-1}}\).
    4. Therefore \(v_d=6/(2.723\times10^5)=2.20\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    5. The electron velocity is opposite the conventional current direction.

    Answer: The electron drift speed is \(2.20\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    Example 2.

    An electrolyte contains positive and negative ions, each species having number density \(2\times10^{25}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\) and charge magnitude \(e\). Both species drift at \(5\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), with positive ions along the field and negative ions against it. Find the current density.

    1. Positive-ion current density is \(J_+=n_+ev_+\).
    2. Negative ions have charge \(-e\), and their conventional current also points along the field, so \(J_-=n_-ev_-\).
    3. Thus \(J=n_+ev_++n_-ev_-=(2\times10^{25})(1.602\times10^{-19})(10^{-3})\).
    4. Numerically, \(J=3.204\times10^3\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\).
    5. The total current density is along the electric field.

    Answer: The current density is \(3.20\times10^3\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Reporting the electron drift direction as the conventional-current direction.
    • Using \(n\) as total atoms per cubic metre when the problem gives mobile charge carriers.
    • Forgetting the factor \(e\) in \(I=neAv_d\).
    Back to Index
    Index / Electrostatics and Current
    Chapter 14 · Topic 3

    Mobility

    Current ElectricityElectrostatics and CurrentBasicsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Mobility measures how quickly a carrier's drift speed changes with applied field, with \(\mu=v_d/E\) using drift-speed magnitude. In an isotropic homogeneous conductor, scalar drift speed is proportional to field magnitude even for electrons, although their vector drift is opposite the field. Adding all charge species gives the general conductivity \( \sigma=\sum n|q|\mu\).
    Key formula(s). \[\mu=\frac{|v_d|}{E},\qquad |\mathbf v_d|=\mu E,\qquad \sigma=\sum_i n_i|q_i|\mu_i,\qquad J=\sigma E,\qquad [\mu]=\mathrm{m^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}\,V^{-1}}\];
    Key points.
    • Mobility is speed per unit electric field, not a speed and not a dimensionless ratio.
    • A smaller mobility at fixed field means a smaller drift-speed magnitude.
    • Electrons and holes both produce conductivity along the field, although their drift vectors are opposite.
    • Conductivity is the sum of carrier contributions for their number densities and charge magnitudes.
    • Mobility generally varies with temperature, impurity concentration, and material structure.
    Example 1.

    The electron mobility in a material is \(1.3\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\). If \(E=500\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\), find the magnitude and direction of electron drift velocity.

    1. The drift-speed magnitude is \(v_d=\mu E\).
    2. Substitute the data: \(v_d=(1.3\times10^{-4})(500)=6.5\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    3. This is the magnitude, not the vector direction.
    4. Electrons have negative charge, so their force and acceleration oppose the electric field.
    5. Their drift vector is therefore opposite to \(\mathbf E\).

    Answer: The electron drift speed is \(0.065\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), directed opposite to the field.

    Example 2.

    An intrinsic semiconductor has \(n_e=n_h=10^{20}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), electron mobility \(0.13\,\mathrm{m^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\), hole mobility \(0.05\,\mathrm{m^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\), and \(E=200\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}\). Find the hole drift speed and total current density.

    1. The hole drift speed is \(v_h=\mu_hE=(0.05)(200)=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), along the field.
    2. The electron speed is \(v_e=\mu_eE=(0.13)(200)=26\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), opposite the field.
    3. Since their conventional currents both point along the field, \(J=n_eev_e+n_pev_h\).
    4. Therefore \(J=(1.602\times10^{-19})(10^{20})(26+10)\).
    5. This gives \(J=0.576\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\).

    Answer: \(v_h=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along the field and \(J=0.576\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Calling mobility itself the drift velocity.
    • Subtracting electron and hole current densities because their motions are opposite.
    • Ignoring that a carrier's drift vector may oppose \(\mathbf E\) while its speed is \(\mu E\).
    Back to Index
    Index / Electrostatics and Current
    Chapter 14 · Topic 4

    Current density

    Current ElectricityElectrostatics and CurrentBasicsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Current density describes the current per unit area and retains the local direction of charge flow. For uniform current perpendicular to a wire, \(J=I/A\); in the general case, a current element is \(dI=\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf A\). Integrating over a cross-section is essential when \(\mathbf J\) is spatially nonuniform or has components parallel to the surface.
    Key formula(s). \[\mathbf J=\frac{dI}{d\mathbf A},\qquad I=\int_A\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf A,\qquad J_n=\frac{I}{A}\ \text{when uniform and normal},\qquad \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0,\qquad [J]=\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\];
    Key points.
    • Current density is a vector, while current through one oriented surface is a signed scalar.
    • For a circular wire of radius \(R\), the uniform cross-sectional area is \(\pi R^2\), not \(2\pi R\).
    • Current is \(\int\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf A\), not \(\int J\,dA\), unless the field is everywhere normal to the surface.
    • In steady one-dimensional flow, charge conservation requires the same current through every cross-section, even if wire area changes.
    • Joule heating depends on current density through the local electric power density \(p=\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E\).
    Example 1.

    A current of \(5\,\mathrm A\) flows uniformly through a circular wire of radius \(2\,\mathrm{mm}\). Find the current density.

    1. The radius is \(R=2\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm m\), so the area is \(A=\pi R^2\).
    2. Numerically, \(A=\pi(2\times10^{-3})^2=1.257\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2}\).
    3. Since the current is uniform, \(J=I/A\).
    4. Thus \(J=5/(1.257\times10^{-5})=3.98\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\).

    Answer: The current density is \(3.98\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\).

    Example 2.

    In a cylindrical wire of radius \(R\), current density varies radially as \(J(r)=J_0(1-r/R)\) and is directed along the axis. If the total current is \(6\,\mathrm A\) and \(R=3\,\mathrm{mm}\), find \(J_0\).

    1. Take a concentric annulus of area \(dA=2\pi r\,dr\), for which \(dI=J(r)dA\).
    2. Integrate from the axis to the surface: \(I=2\pi J_0\int_0^R(1-r/R)r\,dr\).
    3. The integral is \(R^2/2-R^2/3=R^2/6\), so \(I=\pi J_0R^2/3\).
    4. Hence \(J_0=3I/(\pi R^2)=18/[\pi(3\times10^{-3})^2]\).
    5. Numerically, \(J_0=6.37\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\).

    Answer: The axial current-density coefficient is \(J_0=6.37\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using diameter instead of radius in \(A=\pi R^2\).
    • Taking \(\int J\,dA\) without checking whether \(\mathbf J\) is normal to the surface.
    • Assuming constant area is required for constant current density in a varying-area wire.

    Chapter 14 · Topic 5

    Ohm's law

    Current ElectricityElectrostatics and CurrentBasicsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Ohm's law states that, for a conductor at fixed physical conditions, current is directly proportional to potential difference. Equivalently, voltage drop is proportional to current and a constant resistance characterizes the system. For nonlinear devices, the ratio \(V/I\) gives only a static resistance, while the slope \(dV/dI\) at an operating point gives the differential resistance used in advanced problems.
    Key formula(s). \[I=\frac{V}{R},\qquad V=IR,\qquad G=\frac1R,\qquad J=\sigma E,\qquad R_{\mathrm{static}}=\frac VI,\qquad r_d=\left(\frac{dI}{dV}\right)^{-1}\ \text{at the operating point}\];
    Key points.
    • Ohm's law applies to an ohmic material over a stated range and at fixed temperature and geometry.
    • Resistance is positive for a passive resistor, and conductance \(G\) is its reciprocal.
    • Joule power can be written as \(P=VI=I^2R=V^2/R\).
    • The linear \(I\)-\(V\) graph passes through the origin for an ideal ohmic conductor.
    • For a nonlinear \(I\)-\(V\) relation, use the tangent slope rather than an endpoint chord for dynamic resistance.
    Example 1.

    A \(22\,\Omega\) resistor carries a current of \(0.50\,\mathrm A\). Find the potential difference across it and the electrical power dissipated.

    1. Apply \(V=IR\).
    2. The potential difference is \(V=(22)(0.50)=11\,\mathrm V\).
    3. Joule power can be calculated as \(P=VI\).
    4. Thus \(P=(11)(0.50)=5.5\,\mathrm W\).
    5. The equivalent calculation \(I^2R=(0.50)^2(22)\) gives the same result.

    Answer: The voltage drop is \(11\,\mathrm V\) and the dissipated power is \(5.5\,\mathrm W\).

    Example 2.

    A nonlinear element obeys \(I=\alpha V^2\). At \(V=10\,\mathrm V\), its current is \(0.020\,\mathrm A\). Find its static and differential resistances at this operating point.

    1. From \(0.020=\alpha(10)^2\), obtain \(\alpha=2.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{A\,V^{-2}}\).
    2. The static resistance is \(R_s=V/I=10/0.020=500\,\Omega\).
    3. Differentiate the characteristic: \(dI/dV=2\alpha V\).
    4. At \(10\,\mathrm V\), \(dI/dV=(2)(2.0\times10^{-4})(10)=4.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A\,V^{-1}}\).
    5. Hence \(r_d=(dI/dV)^{-1}=250\,\Omega\), showing that the element is nonlinear.

    Answer: \(R_s=500\,\Omega\) and \(r_d=250\,\Omega\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using static resistance where a tangent or differential resistance is required.
    • Writing Ohm's law as \(I/V\) is constant for all materials and all voltages.
    • Computing power as \(V^2/R\) using a voltage not actually across the chosen resistance.

    Chapter 14 · Topic 6

    Resistance

    Current ElectricityElectrostatics and CurrentBasicsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Resistance is the opposition offered by a complete conducting body to steady current and is defined as \(R=V/I\). For a uniform conductor of length \(L\), cross-sectional area \(A\), material resistivity \(\rho\), and fixed temperature, it becomes \(R=\rho L/A\). Geometric changes must therefore be applied to length and area separately.
    Key formula(s). \[R=\frac VI,\qquad R=\frac{\rho L}{A}=\frac{4\rho L}{\pi d^2},\qquad \frac{R_2}{R_1}=\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}\frac{L_2}{L_1}\frac{A_1}{A_2},\qquad P=I^2R=V^2/R=VI,\qquad [R]=\mathrm V\,\mathrm A^{-1}=\Omega\];
    Key points.
    • Resistance depends on geometry as well as material and temperature.
    • Doubling length doubles \(R\), whereas halving area also doubles \(R\).
    • Because area is proportional to diameter squared, doubling diameter makes resistance one-fourth for an otherwise identical wire.
    • In series, resistances add directly; in parallel, their reciprocals add.
    • The value \(V/I\) defines resistance only for a chosen two-terminal state and can depend on temperature in a non-ohmic device.
    Example 1.

    A uniform wire of length \(4\,\mathrm m\), cross-sectional area \(2\,\mathrm{mm^2}\), and resistivity \(1.7\times10^{-7}\,\Omega\,\mathrm m\) is connected across a potential difference. Find its resistance.

    1. Convert the area: \(2\,\mathrm{mm^2}=2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2}\).
    2. For a uniform wire, \(R=\rho L/A\).
    3. Substitute to obtain \(R=(1.7\times10^{-7})(4)/(2\times10^{-6})\).
    4. The numerator is \(6.8\times10^{-7}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m^2}\).
    5. Therefore \(R=0.34\,\Omega\).

    Answer: The wire resistance is \(0.34\,\Omega\).

    Example 2.

    A wire initially has resistance \(12\,\Omega\). Its length is increased by \(25\%\), its radius is increased by \(20\%\), and its material and temperature are unchanged. Find the final resistance.

    1. At fixed \(\rho\), \(R\) is proportional to \(L/A\).
    2. The new length factor is \(L_2/L_1=1.25\).
    3. Since \(A=\pi r^2\), the new area factor is \(A_2/A_1=(1.20)^2=1.44\).
    4. Hence \(R_2/R_1=1.25/1.44=0.8681\).
    5. Therefore \(R_2=12(0.8681)=10.42\,\Omega\).

    Answer: The final resistance is \(10.42\,\Omega\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Applying a diameter change linearly instead of using \(A\propto d^2\).
    • Ignoring resistivity changes when temperature or material is altered.
    • Forgetting that \(R=V/I\) is not the same quantity as resistivity \(\rho\).

    Chapter 14 · Topic 7

    Resistivity

    Current ElectricityElectrostatics and CurrentBasicsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Resistivity is the material property that opposes current per unit length and per unit area, with \( \rho=RA/L=E/J\). It is independent of a wire's dimensions but generally depends on temperature, impurity content, and microscopic relaxation time. For JEE calculations, macroscopic and microscopic expressions provide complementary checks on the same current.
    Key formula(s). \[\rho=\frac{RA}{L}=\frac EJ=\frac1\sigma,\qquad \sigma=\frac1\rho,\qquad \rho(T)=\rho_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)],\qquad \rho_{\mathrm{micro}}=\frac{m}{ne^2\tau},\qquad [\rho]=\Omega\,\mathrm m=\mathrm{A^{-1}m^3\,s^{-3}}\];
    Key points.
    • Resistivity is independent of wire length and area at fixed material state, while resistance depends on both.
    • Increasing electron number density reduces resistivity if the relaxation time is held fixed.
    • The relaxation time is the average time between momentum-relaxing collisions, not the mean free path itself.
    • The SI unit of resistivity is \(\Omega\,\mathrm m\), while conductivity has units \(\mathrm{S\,m^{-1}}\).
    • Over a limited temperature range, both resistance and resistivity of the same material have the same fractional change.
    Example 1.

    A wire of length \(5\,\mathrm m\) and area \(2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2}\) has resistance \(0.070\,\Omega\). Find the resistivity of its material.

    1. Rearrange \(R=\rho L/A\) to obtain \(\rho=RA/L\).
    2. The area is already in square metres, so no conversion is required.
    3. Substitute: \(\rho=(0.070)(2\times10^{-6})/5\).
    4. The numerator is \(1.4\times10^{-7}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m^2}\).
    5. Hence \(\rho=2.8\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\mathrm m\).

    Answer: The material has resistivity \(2.8\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\,\mathrm m\).

    Example 2.

    A semiconductor has carrier number density \(5.0\times10^{16}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), carrier mass \(9.1\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}\), charge magnitude \(1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\), and mean relaxation time \(2.2\times10^{-14}\,\mathrm s\). Find its resistivity.

    1. Use the microscopic relation \(\rho=m/(ne^2\tau)\).
    2. The charge squared is \(e^2=(1.602\times10^{-19})^2=2.566\times10^{-38}\,\mathrm{C^2}\).
    3. The denominator is \(ne^2\tau=(5.0\times10^{16})(2.566\times10^{-38})(2.2\times10^{-14})=2.82\times10^{-35}\).
    4. Therefore \(\rho=(9.1\times10^{-31})/(2.82\times10^{-35})\).
    5. The resistivity is \(3.23\times10^4\,\Omega\,\mathrm m\).

    Answer: The semiconductor resistivity is \(3.23\times10^4\,\Omega\,\mathrm m\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Writing \(\rho=\sigma\) instead of \(\rho=1/\sigma\).
    • Using \(e\) rather than \(e^2\) in \(\rho=m/(ne^2\tau)\).
    • Concluding that doubling conductivity halves resistivity without stating that other state variables remain fixed.
