    Chapter 15 · Topic 8

    Circular loop

    Moving Charges and MagnetismMagnetism, EMI and ACLaws and WiresStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A circular current loop produces a magnetic field that is especially simple on its axis, where all elemental contributions have equal magnitude and a common direction. The field decreases away from the center along the axis, while the axial field is exactly zero in the plane of the loop at a general point. These results are foundational for magnetic dipoles, solenoids, and moving-coil instruments.
    Key formula(s). \[B_{\mathrm{axis}}=\frac{\mu_0 I a^2}{2(a^2+x^2)^{3/2}}\quad\text{(single loop at distance }x\text{)};\] \[B_{\mathrm{center}}=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2a};\qquad B_N=\frac{\mu_0NI}{2a}\quad\text{(\(N\) turns)}\]
    Key points.
    • The axial field of a circular loop points along its magnetic moment on the axis but opposite to it in the plane outside the loop.
    • At the center, the result follows from adding contributions of all current elements.
    • For \(x\ll a\), the axial variation near the center is approximately \(B=\frac{\mu_0I}{2a}(1-\frac{3x^2}{2a^2})\).
    • The magnetic moment of one loop is \(\mu=IA\), and for \(N\) turns it is \(NIA\).
    • For a slowly varying axial field over a small loop, a net torque generally exists, but the net force is approximately zero.
    Example 1.

    A single circular turn of radius \(0.20\,\mathrm{m}\) carries \(3.0\,\mathrm{A}\). Find the magnetic field at the center of the loop.

    1. The center field of one circular turn is \(B=\mu_0I/(2a)\).
    2. Substitute \(a=0.20\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(I=3.0\,\mathrm{A}\).
    3. \(B=4\pi\times10^{-7}\frac{3.0}{0.40}=4\pi\times10^{-7}(7.5)\).
    4. Hence \(B=3.0\pi\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    5. The direction is normal to the loop according to the right-hand rule.

    Answer: \(\boxed{B=3\pi\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T}\approx9.42\,\mu\mathrm{T}}\)

    Example 2.

    A charge \(q=2.0\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}\) moves in a circular path of radius \(0.10\,\mathrm{m}\) with frequency \(1.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{Hz}\), equivalent to a current loop. Find the magnetic field at the center.

    1. The period is \(T=1/f=1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}\).
    2. The equivalent current is \(I=q/T=qf=2.0\times10^{-16}\,\mathrm{A}\).
    3. For one loop of radius \(a\), \(B=\mu_0I/(2a)\).
    4. Substitution gives \(B=4\pi\times10^{-7}\frac{2.0\times10^{-16}}{0.20}\).
    5. Therefore \(B=4\pi\times10^{-22}\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B=4\pi\times10^{-22}\,\mathrm{T}}\)

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the center-loop formula at an arbitrary point on the axis.
    • Treating \(x\) in the axial formula as distance measured along the wire.
    • Omitting the number of turns when replacing one loop by an \(N\)-turn coil.

    Explanation

    Concept. The magnetic field at the center of a circular current arc is proportional to the angle subtended by the arc and inversely proportional to its radius. Each elemental field at the center has the same direction, so their contributions add directly. Radial leads and symmetry axes are especially useful in problems asking for the field due to a composite current path.
    Key formula(s). \[B_{\mathrm{arc}}=\frac{\mu_0I\theta}{4\pi R}\quad(\theta\text{ in radians})\]; \[\theta_{\mathrm{rad}}=\theta_{\mathrm{deg}}\frac{\pi}{180}\]; \[B_{\mathrm{full\ loop}}=\frac{\mu_0I}{2R}\]
    Key points.
    • The arc angle must be in radians when using the standard Biot-Savart expression.
    • At the center, the field is perpendicular to the plane of the arc and is given by the right-hand rule.
    • A semicircle contributes one-half the field of the complete loop, while a quarter circle contributes one-fourth.
    • Straight segments lying along a radius through the observation point produce zero field there because \(d\boldsymbol{\ell}\) is parallel to \(\hat{\mathbf r}\).
    • In a composite path, add arc contributions as vectors after assigning each direction.
    Example 1.

    A semicircular arc of radius \(0.20\,\mathrm{m}\) carries \(3.0\,\mathrm{A}\). Find the magnetic field at its center.

    1. The semicircle subtends \(\theta=\pi\) radians.
    2. Use \(B=\mu_0I\theta/(4\pi R)\).
    3. Substitution gives \(B=\frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.0)(\pi)}{4\pi(0.20)}\).
    4. The factors \(\pi\) and \(4\pi\) simplify, leaving \(B=1.5\pi\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    5. This is half the field of a complete loop of the same radius and current.

    Answer: \(\boxed{B=1.5\pi\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T}\approx4.71\,\mu\mathrm{T}}\)

    Example 2.

    A current of \(2.0\,\mathrm{A}\) flows along a \(270^\circ\) circular arc of radius \(0.10\,\mathrm{m}\). The arc is completed by two radial straight segments. Find the field at the arc center.

    1. Convert the arc angle: \(\theta=270^\circ\frac{\pi}{180^\circ}=\frac{3\pi}{2}\).
    2. The two radial segments give zero field at the center because their vectors to the center are parallel to \(d\boldsymbol{\ell}\).
    3. Thus only the arc contributes, with \(B=\mu_0I\theta/(4\pi R)\).
    4. Substitution gives \(B=10^{-7}\frac{(2.0)(3\pi/2)}{0.10}\).
    5. Hence \(B=3\pi\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B=3\pi\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T}\approx9.42\,\mu\mathrm{T}}\)

    Common mistakes.
    • Inserting an angle in degrees without converting it to radians.
    • Treating radial segments as nonzero contributors at the center.
    • Using the complete-loop field for an arc whose angle is not \(2\pi\).

    Chapter 15 · Topic 9

    Solenoid

    Moving Charges and MagnetismMagnetism, EMI and ACLaws and WiresStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A solenoid is a tightly wound helical coil for which an idealization treats all turns as circular loops at nearly the same axial position. In its central region, the magnetic field is uniform and parallel to the axis, while the field outside is negligible. The relevant winding density is turns per unit length, not the total number of turns.
    Key formula(s). \[n=\frac{N}{l};\] \[B_{\mathrm{inside}}=\mu_0nI=\frac{\mu_0NI}{l};\] \[L_s=\frac{\mu_0N^2A}{l};\qquad U=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}Al=\frac12L_sI^2\]
    Key points.
    • The ideal-solenoid approximation is best when the solenoid is long compared with its radius and closely wound.
    • Near an open end, the axial field is approximately \(\mu_0nI/2\), half the interior value.
    • Inserting a high-permeability core increases \(B\) by approximately \(\mu_r\) while the coil remains unsaturated.
    • Magnetic-field energy density in vacuum is \(u=B^2/(2\mu_0)\), not \(B^2/(2\mu_0^2)\).
    • The field direction is fixed by current winding direction and remains the same inside and outside near the ends.
    Example 1.

    A long solenoid has \(600\) turns over a length of \(0.30\,\mathrm{m}\) and carries \(0.50\,\mathrm{A}\). Find its magnetic field near the center.

    1. The turns per unit length are \(n=600/0.30=2000\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\).
    2. The interior field is \(B=\mu_0nI\).
    3. Substitution gives \(B=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2000)(0.50)\).
    4. Hence \(B=4\pi\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    5. Near the center, edge effects are negligible.

    Answer: \(\boxed{B=4\pi\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}\approx1.26\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}}\)

    Example 2.

    An air-core solenoid has \(500\) turns, length \(0.50\,\mathrm{m}\), cross-sectional area \(\pi(0.010\,\mathrm{m})^2\), and current \(2.0\,\mathrm{A}\). Find its stored magnetic energy.

    1. The field is \(B=\mu_0\frac{N}{l}I=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1000)(2.0)=8\pi\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    2. The volume is \(Al=\pi(0.010)^2(0.50)=1.5708\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3}\).
    3. The magnetic energy density is \(u=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}=\frac{(8\pi\times10^{-4})^2}{2(4\pi\times10^{-7})}=2.513\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\).
    4. Therefore \(U=uAl=(2.513)(1.5708\times10^{-4})\).
    5. This gives \(U=3.95\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{U=3.95\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}}\)

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(N\) directly in \(B=\mu_0NI/l\) without dividing by length.
    • Applying the ideal interior field exactly at an open end.
    • Replacing \(\mu_0\) by \(\mu_0^2\) in the magnetic energy-density formula.

    Explanation

    Concept. A toroid is a solenoid bent into a closed ring, so current windings lie along the circumference and the field is confined mainly to the toroidal core. At a fixed radius in the core, the field is tangential and inversely proportional to that radius. This geometry makes the toroid a standard application of Ampere's law.
    Key formula(s). \[B(r)=\frac{\mu_0NI}{2\pi r}\quad\text{(within the core)};\] \[\mathbf B\ \text{is azimuthal};\qquad B_{\mathrm{ideal}}\approx0\ \text{outside the core}\]
    Key points.
    • \(N\) is the total number of turns linked with the magnetic path.
    • \(r\) is the mean distance from the center of the toroid to the observation point within the core.
    • The field is not exactly uniform over a thick toroidal cross-section because it varies as \(1/r\).
    • An iron core raises the field by its permeability ratio only below saturation.
    • The field direction is tangential and follows the right-hand rule around the toroid.
    Example 1.

    A toroid has \(1000\) turns, mean radius \(0.10\,\mathrm{m}\), and carries \(2.0\,\mathrm{A}\). Find the magnetic field in its core.

    1. For the toroidal core, \(B=\mu_0NI/(2\pi r)\).
    2. Substitute \(N=1000\), \(I=2.0\,\mathrm{A}\), and \(r=0.10\,\mathrm{m}\).
    3. \(B=\frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1000)(2.0)}{2\pi(0.10)}\).
    4. The numerator is \(8\pi\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T\,m}\) and the denominator is \(0.20\pi\,\mathrm{m}\).
    5. Thus \(B=4.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B=4.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}}\)

    Example 2.

    A toroidal core has mean radius \(0.20\,\mathrm{m}\), relative permeability \(100\), and \(500\) turns. It carries \(0.50\,\mathrm{A}\). Assuming a linear core with no saturation, find the magnetic field in the core.

    1. In the core, \(\mu=\mu_0\mu_r=100\mu_0\).
    2. Use \(B=\frac{\mu NI}{2\pi r}=\frac{\mu_0\mu_rNI}{2\pi r}\).
    3. Substitution gives \(B=\frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(100)(500)(0.50)}{2\pi(0.20)}\).
    4. The numerator is \(0.010\pi\) and the denominator is \(0.40\pi\).
    5. Hence \(B=2.5\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B=2.5\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}=25\,\mathrm{mT}}\)

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the inner surface radius as a constant for a thick toroid.
    • Omitting the core's relative permeability.
    • Applying the toroid formula to a straight solenoid without changing the geometry.

    Chapter 15 · Topic 10

    Torque on current loop

    Moving Charges and MagnetismMagnetism, EMI and ACLoops and MetersStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A current loop in a uniform magnetic field experiences a torque equal to the cross product of its magnetic moment and the field. The torque tends to align the loop's magnetic moment with the field and vanishes when the moment is parallel or antiparallel. Parallel and antiparallel orientations have different potential energies, so one is stable and the other unstable.
    Key formula(s). \[\boldsymbol{\mu}=NIA\hat{\mathbf n};\qquad \boldsymbol{\tau}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\times\mathbf B\]; \[\tau=\mu B\sin\theta\]; \[U=-\boldsymbol{\mu}\cdot\mathbf B=-\mu B\cos\theta;\qquad W_{\mathrm{field}}=\mu B(\cos\theta_f-\cos\theta_i)\]
    Key points.
    • The loop area vector is normal to the plane according to the right-hand rule.
    • A rectangular loop of sides \(a\) and \(b\) has area \(A=ab\).
    • The torque is maximum when the magnetic moment is perpendicular to the field.
    • The moment parallel to the field is a minimum-energy stable equilibrium; antiparallel is a maximum-energy unstable equilibrium.
    • In a uniform field, the net force on a complete loop is zero even when its torque is nonzero.
    Example 1.

    A \(100\)-turn coil of area \(0.010\,\mathrm{m^2}\) carries \(2.0\,\mathrm{A}\). It is placed in a \(0.30\,\mathrm{T}\) field with its normal at \(30^\circ\) to the field. Find the torque.

    1. The magnetic moment is \(\mu=NIA=(100)(2.0)(0.010)=2.0\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\).
    2. The torque magnitude is \(\tau=\mu B\sin\theta\).
    3. Substitution gives \(\tau=(2.0)(0.30)\sin30^\circ\).
    4. Since \(\sin30^\circ=0.5\), \(\tau=0.30\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
    5. The direction is along \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\times\mathbf B\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{\tau=0.30\,\mathrm{N\,m}}\)

    Example 2.

    A loop has magnetic moment \(0.50\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\) in a uniform \(0.20\,\mathrm{T}\) field. It is rotated quasistatically from \(30^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\) relative to the field. Find the work done by the magnetic field and by the external agent.

    1. The potential energy at angle \(\theta\) is \(U=-\mu B\cos\theta\).
    2. Initially \(U_i=-(0.50)(0.20)\cos30^\circ=-0.0866\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. Finally \(U_f=-(0.50)(0.20)\cos90^\circ=0\).
    4. The magnetic field's work is \(W_{\mathrm{field}}=U_i-U_f=-0.0866\,\mathrm{J}\).
    5. A quasistatic external agent does the opposite work, \(W_{\mathrm{ext}}=U_f-U_i=0.0866\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{W_{\mathrm{field}}=-0.0866\,\mathrm{J},\quad W_{\mathrm{ext}}=0.0866\,\mathrm{J}}\)

    Common mistakes.
    • Writing \(U=+\mu B\cos\theta\) instead of \(-\mu B\cos\theta\).
    • Treating the parallel and antiparallel orientations as equally stable.
    • Calculating a net force in a uniform field instead of a torque.

    Chapter 15 · Topic 11

    Magnetic dipole

    Moving Charges and MagnetismMagnetism, EMI and ACLoops and MetersStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A magnetic dipole is a small current loop or magnet characterized in external space by its magnetic moment vector. On the axial line its field is twice the equatorial value, and its energy in an external field is \(-\boldsymbol{\mu}\cdot\mathbf B\). These facts determine the forces, torques, and stable orientation of magnetic dipoles in JEE problems.
    Key formula(s). \[\boldsymbol{\mu}=NIA\hat{\mathbf n}\]; \[B_{\mathrm{axis}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2\mu}{r^3};\qquad B_{\mathrm{equator}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{\mu}{r^3}\]; \[U=-\mu B\cos\theta;\qquad \tau=\mu B\sin\theta\]
    Key points.
    • A small loop is a good point-dipole approximation when the observation distance is much larger than its radius.
    • The magnetic moment is a current times area, with SI unit \(\mathrm{A\,m^2}\).
    • On the axis, \(\mathbf B\) is parallel to \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\); on the equatorial line, it is antiparallel.
    • The dipole aligns with the field to minimize \(U=-\mu B\cos\theta\).
    • Two aligned coaxial dipoles attract, while two side-by-side antiparallel magnetic moments repel.
    Example 1.

    An electron of charge magnitude \(1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}\) moves in a circular orbit of radius \(1.0\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}\) with speed \(2.2\times10^6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its orbital magnetic moment.

    1. The equivalent current is \(I=ev/(2\pi r)\), where \(e\) is the magnitude of electron charge.
    2. The loop area is \(A=\pi r^2\), so \(\mu=IA=\frac{ev}{2\pi r}\pi r^2\).
    3. Therefore \(\mu=\frac{evr}{2}=\frac{(1.6\times10^{-19})(2.2\times10^6)(1.0\times10^{-10})}{2}\).
    4. The magnitude is \(1.76\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\).
    5. The vector is normal to the orbit and opposite to the conventional-current direction defined by positive charge.

    Answer: \(\boxed{\mu=1.76\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}}\)

    Example 2.

    A magnetic dipole of moment \(0.80\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\) is placed in a uniform \(0.30\,\mathrm{T}\) field. Find its torque and potential energy when the moment makes \(60^\circ\) with the field.

    1. The torque magnitude is \(\tau=\mu B\sin\theta\).
    2. Substitution gives \(\tau=(0.80)(0.30)\sin60^\circ\).
    3. Since \(\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\tau=0.208\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
    4. The potential energy is \(U=-\mu B\cos\theta=-(0.80)(0.30)(0.5)\).
    5. Hence \(U=-0.120\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{\tau=0.208\,\mathrm{N\,m},\quad U=-0.120\,\mathrm{J}}\)

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(B=\mu_0\mu/(4\pi r^3)\) on the axis without the factor of two.
    • Omitting the negative sign in \(U=-\mu B\cos\theta\).
    • Treating electron magnetic moment as parallel to the conventional-current normal.

    Chapter 15 · Topic 12

    Moving coil galvanometer

    Moving Charges and MagnetismMagnetism, EMI and ACLoops and MetersStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A moving-coil galvanometer uses the torque on a current-carrying coil in a radial magnetic field to produce angular deflection, while a mechanical spring provides a restoring torque. In equilibrium these torques balance, so deflection is directly proportional to current. The radial field keeps the torque nearly independent of the coil's angular position.
    Key formula(s). \[\tau_B=N I A B;\qquad \tau_s=\kappa\theta\]; \[\theta=\frac{NAB}{\kappa}I;\qquad S_I=\frac{\theta}{I}=\frac{NAB}{\kappa}\]
    Key points.
    • \(N\), \(A\), and \(B\) are the turn number, loop area, and radial field strength.
    • The angular restoring constant \(\kappa\) has SI unit \(\mathrm{N\,m\,rad^{-1}}\).
    • A moving-coil instrument is a PMMC type and normally measures direct current.
    • At steady deflection, the electromagnetic and spring torques are equal and opposite.
    • With magnetic damping and negligible drag, the undamped natural period is \(T_0=2\pi\sqrt{J/\kappa}\), where \(J\) is the coil's moment of inertia.
    Example 1.

    A moving coil has \(100\) turns, area \(1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), and operates in a radial field of \(0.40\,\mathrm{T}\). Its restoring constant is \(1.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{N\,m\,rad^{-1}}\). Find the deflection for a current of \(0.50\,\mathrm{mA}\).

    1. The electromagnetic torque constant is \(NAB=(100)(1.0\times10^{-3})(0.40)=0.040\,\mathrm{N\,m\,A^{-1}}\).
    2. For \(I=0.50\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}\), \(\tau_B=NABI=2.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
    3. At equilibrium, \(\kappa\theta=\tau_B\).
    4. Therefore \(\theta=\frac{2.0\times10^{-5}}{1.0\times10^{-4}}=0.20\,\mathrm{rad}\).
    5. The deflection is therefore linear with current in the elastic range.

    Answer: \(\boxed{\theta=0.20\,\mathrm{rad}}\)

    Example 2.

    A moving-coil galvanometer has moment of inertia \(J=2.0\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}\) and torsional constant \(\kappa=1.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{N\,m\,rad^{-1}}\). Neglecting damping and magnetic effects on frequency, find its natural oscillation period.

    1. The restoring equation is \(J\ddot{\theta}+\kappa\theta=0\).
    2. Its angular frequency is \(\omega_0=\sqrt{\kappa/J}\).
    3. Substituting gives \(\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{1.0\times10^{-4}}{2.0\times10^{-9}}}=\sqrt{5.0\times10^4}=223.6\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).
    4. The natural period is \(T_0=2\pi/\omega_0\).
    5. Hence \(T_0=2\pi/223.6=0.0281\,\mathrm{s}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{T_0=2.81\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}}\)

    Common mistakes.
    • Forgetting that the area is that of one turn before multiplication by \(N\).
    • Omitting the radial-field constant when computing torque.
    • Using \(2\pi\sqrt{J/\kappa}\) for a permanently damped instrument without qualification.

    Explanation

    Concept. A galvanometer is converted into an ammeter by connecting a low-resistance shunt in parallel so that most measured current bypasses the coil. It is converted into a voltmeter by connecting a high resistance in series so that nearly all applied voltage appears across that resistance. The original galvanometer resistance and full-scale current are essential for both conversions.
    Key formula(s). \[I=I_g+I_s;\qquad I_sG=I_gR_s\]; \[R_s=\frac{I_gG}{I-I_g}\quad\text{(ammeter shunt)}\]; \[R_m=\frac{V}{I_g}-G\quad\text{(voltmeter multiplier)}\]
    Key points.
    • A shunt lowers the equivalent resistance, while a multiplier raises it.
    • The voltage drop across a shunt equals the voltage drop across the galvanometer because they are parallel.
    • The current through an ammeter shunt is generally much larger than the galvanometer current.
    • The series multiplier in a voltmeter carries the small full-scale galvanometer current.
    • An ideal ammeter has zero resistance and an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance; real conversions approach these limits.
    Example 1.

    A galvanometer has resistance \(50\,\Omega\) and full-scale current \(0.20\,\mathrm{mA}\). Find the shunt resistance required to convert it into a \(5.0\,\mathrm{A}\) ammeter.

    1. The galvanometer voltage at full scale is \(V_g=I_gG=(0.20\times10^{-3})(50)=0.010\,\mathrm{V}\).
    2. At full scale, the shunt current is \(I_s=I-I_g=5.0-0.00020=4.9998\,\mathrm{A}\).
    3. Since the shunt is parallel to the galvanometer, \(R_s=V_g/I_s\).
    4. Thus \(R_s=0.010/4.9998=2.00008\times10^{-3}\,\Omega\).
    5. To the justified precision, the required resistance is \(2.0\,\mathrm{m}\Omega\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{R_s=2.0\times10^{-3}\,\Omega}\)

    Example 2.

    A galvanometer of resistance \(100\,\Omega\) has a full-scale current of \(0.50\,\mathrm{mA}\). Find the series resistance required to convert it into a \(0\) to \(20\,\mathrm{V}\) voltmeter.

    1. A full-scale total voltage must produce only \(I_g=0.50\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}\) through the galvanometer.
    2. The required total resistance is \(R_{\mathrm{total}}=V/I_g=\frac{20}{0.50\times10^{-3}}\).
    3. This gives \(R_{\mathrm{total}}=4.0\times10^4\,\Omega\).
    4. The multiplier resistance is \(R_m=R_{\mathrm{total}}-G=40000-100\).
    5. Therefore \(R_m=3.99\times10^4\,\Omega=39.9\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{R_m=3.99\times10^4\,\Omega=39.9\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}\)

    Common mistakes.
    • Connecting a shunt in series or a multiplier in parallel.
    • Using total current as shunt current in an ammeter conversion.
    • Adding the multiplier resistance instead of subtracting the galvanometer resistance.

    Chapter 15 · Topic 13

    Ammeter

    Moving Charges and MagnetismMagnetism, EMI and ACLoops and MetersStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. An ammeter is an instrument that measures current by allowing only a known small current through a sensitive galvanometer and diverting the remainder through a low-resistance shunt. For JEE problems, the current-sharing relation, not the total circuit resistance, is the key to converting a galvanometer into an ammeter.
    Key formula(s). \(I_g=G I\); \[I_g=I\frac{R_s}{R_g+R_s},\qquad I_g(1+G)=I,\qquad G=\frac{I_g}{R_g}\]; \[R_s=\frac{I_g}{I-I_g}=\frac{G R_g}{I-I_g},\qquad R_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{R_gR_s}{R_g+R_s}.\]
    Key points.
    • An ammeter is connected in series with the branch whose current is to be measured.
    • The shunt is connected in parallel with the galvanometer and has very small resistance.
    • For a nearly ideal ammeter, \(I_g\ll I\), so \(R_s\ll R_g\) and \(G=I/R_g\).
    • The ranges of the galvanometer and the ammeter are different currents, not the same quantity.
    • The common potential difference is \(V=I_gR_g=I_sR_s\); this is the fastest current-divider method.
    • Increasing the ammeter range requires decreasing shunt resistance.
    Example 1.

    A galvanometer has resistance \(100\,\Omega\) and full-scale current \(1\,\mathrm{mA}\). Find the shunt resistance needed to convert it into an ammeter of range \(11\,\mathrm{mA}\).

    1. The conversion factor is \(G=I_g/R_g=(1\times10^{-3})/100=10^{-5}\,\mathrm{S}\).
    2. The current through the shunt must be \(I_s=I-I_g=11-1=10\,\mathrm{mA}\).
    3. Since the galvanometer and shunt have the same voltage, \(R_s=I_gR_g/I_s=(10^{-3})(100)/(10^{-2})=10\,\Omega\).
    4. The resulting ammeter resistance is \(R_gR_s/(R_g+R_s)=1000/110\approx9.09\,\Omega\).

    Answer: The required shunt resistance is \(\boxed{10\,\Omega}\), giving an effective ammeter resistance of approximately \(9.09\,\Omega\).

    Example 2.

    A \(50\,\Omega\) galvanometer has a full-scale current of \(2\,\mathrm{mA}\). Find the shunt required to convert it into an ammeter of range \(20\,\mathrm{A}\).

    1. Its conversion factor is \(G=I_g/R_g=(2\times10^{-3})/50=4.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{S}\).
    2. Apply \(I=I_g(1+G/R_s)\), so \(R_s=G R_g/(I-I_g)\).
    3. Substituting gives \(R_s=(4.0\times10^{-5})(50)/(20-2\times10^{-3})\).
    4. Hence \(R_s\approx1.001\times10^{-4}\,\Omega=0.1001\,\mathrm{m}\Omega\).
    5. This is far below the galvanometer resistance, as required for a high-range ammeter.

    Answer: \(\boxed{R_s\approx1.00\times10^{-4}\,\Omega=0.1001\,\mathrm{m}\Omega}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Connecting an ammeter in parallel instead of series.
    • Using total current \(I\) where the shunt current \(I-I_g\) is required.
    • Omitting the parallel combination when asked for the effective ammeter resistance.

    Chapter 15 · Topic 14

    Voltmeter

    Moving Charges and MagnetismMagnetism, EMI and ACLoops and MetersStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A voltmeter measures potential difference by passing a small known current through a sensitive galvanometer connected to a very large series resistance. A JEE problem is usually solved by requiring the full-scale current through the entire voltmeter to equal the galvanometer current.
    Key formula(s). \(V=V_gG\); \[G=\frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{total}}},\qquad V_g=I_gR_g,\qquad V=I_g(R_g+R_m)\]; \[R_{\mathrm{total}}=\frac{V}{I_g}=\frac{V}{G},\qquad R_m=\frac{V}{G}-R_g=\frac{V}{I_g}-R_g.\]
    Key points.
    • A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the element across which the voltage is required.
    • The series multiplier resistance is very large so that the voltmeter draws negligible current.
    • A larger voltage range requires more series resistance.
    • The resistance of the ideal voltmeter tends to infinity and its current tends to zero.
    • The effective voltmeter resistance is \(V/I_g\), not just the multiplier resistance \(R_m\).
    • When the measured voltage is a fraction \(f\) of full scale, the galvanometer current is \(fI_g\).
    Example 1.

    A galvanometer of resistance \(100\,\Omega\) and full-scale current \(1\,\mathrm{mA}\) is to be converted into a voltmeter of range \(10\,\mathrm{V}\). Find the required series resistance.

    1. At full scale, the required total resistance is \(R_{\mathrm{total}}=V/I_g=10/(1\times10^{-3})=10^4\,\Omega\).
    2. The multiplier carries the galvanometer current but has a larger drop, so \(V_g=I_gR_g=0.1\,\mathrm{V}\).
    3. The remaining voltage across the series resistor is \(V_m=10-0.1=9.9\,\mathrm{V}\).
    4. Thus \(R_m=V_m/I_g=9.9/(1\times10^{-3})=9.9\times10^3\,\Omega\).
    5. Equivalently, \(R_m=V/I_g-R_g=10^4-100=9.9\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\).

    Answer: A series resistance of \(\boxed{9.9\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}\) is required.

    Example 2.

    A galvanometer has resistance \(50\,\Omega\) and full-scale current \(0.1\,\mathrm{mA}\). It is converted into a voltmeter whose percentage error must not exceed \(1\%\) for a measured voltage of \(0.1\,\mathrm{V}\). Find the series resistance needed.

    1. The largest permissible voltage error is \(0.01(0.1\,\mathrm{V})=0.001\,\mathrm{V}\).
    2. Full-scale current is \(I_g=0.1\,\mathrm{mA}=10^{-4}\,\mathrm{A}\), so the required total resistance is \(0.001/10^{-4}=10^3\,\Omega\).
    3. The voltmeter drop in the galvanometer is \(I_gR_g=(10^{-4})(50)=0.005\,\mathrm{V}\).
    4. Therefore the added resistance is \(R_m=1000-50=950\,\Omega\).
    5. This choice makes the voltmeter resistance \(1.0\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{R_m=950\,\Omega}\), giving a total voltmeter resistance of \(1.0\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Connecting a voltmeter in series rather than across the component.
    • Forgetting that the series resistor also carries the full-scale current.
    • Treating \(R_m=V/G\) as the added resistance instead of the total resistance.

Susceptibility (negative dia, small positive para, huge positive ferro) plus Curie temperature (ferro-to-para transition) classify everything.

    • Hysteresis loop area equals energy loss per cycle.

    Chapter 16 · Topic 1

    Bar magnet

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMagnetsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A bar magnet is a permanently magnetized body with north and south poles, and in the pole model its magnetic moment is the pole strength multiplied by its magnetic length. The magnetic length is the distance between the two poles and is slightly smaller than the geometric length of a finite bar.
    Key formula(s). \[m=q_m(2l),\qquad \tau=mB\sin\theta,\qquad \vec\tau=\vec m\times\vec B,\qquad U=-\vec m\cdot\vec B.\]
    Key points.
    • Magnetic moment points from the south pole to the north pole inside the magnet.
    • Pole strength is represented by \(q_m\) and has SI unit \(\mathrm{A\,m}\); magnetic moment has unit \(\mathrm{A\,m^2}\).
    • A bar of geometric length \(L_g\) has magnetic length \(L_m<L_g\), often estimated roughly as \(L_m\approx0.9L_g\).
    • The resultant force on a magnetic dipole in a uniform field is zero because the pole forces are equal and opposite.
    • The torque magnitude is maximum when the magnetic moment is perpendicular to the field.
    • Stable equilibrium corresponds to \(m\) parallel to \(B\), while unstable equilibrium corresponds to \(m\) antiparallel to \(B\).
    Example 1.

    A bar magnet of magnetic length \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\) has pole strength \(12\,\mathrm{A\,m}\). Find its magnetic moment and torque in a uniform field of \(0.04\,\mathrm{T}\) when the magnet makes an angle of \(30^\circ\) with the field.

    1. Convert the magnetic length: \(2l=0.10\,\mathrm{m}\).
    2. The magnetic moment is \(m=q_m(2l)=12(0.10)=1.2\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\).
    3. The torque is \(\tau=mB\sin\theta=1.2(0.04)\sin30^\circ\).
    4. Since \(\sin30^\circ=1/2\), \(\tau=1.2(0.04)/2=0.024\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{m=1.2\,\mathrm{A\,m^2},\quad \tau=2.4\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N\,m}}\).

    Example 2.

    A magnetic dipole has magnetic moment \(4.32\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\) and is placed in a uniform field of \(0.15\,\mathrm{T}\). Find the torque when the dipole makes angles \(0^\circ\), \(30^\circ\), and \(90^\circ\) with the field.

    1. At \(0^\circ\), \(\tau=mB\sin0^\circ=0\).
    2. At \(30^\circ\), \(\tau=4.32(0.15)(0.5)=0.324\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
    3. At \(90^\circ\), \(\sin90^\circ=1\), so \(\tau=4.32(0.15)=0.648\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).
    4. The maximum torque occurs at \(90^\circ\), while \(0^\circ\) is the stable orientation.

    Answer: \(\boxed{\tau_{0^\circ}=0,\quad \tau_{30^\circ}=0.324\,\mathrm{N\,m},\quad \tau_{90^\circ}=0.648\,\mathrm{N\,m}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using geometric length directly instead of magnetic length.
    • Forgetting that the magnetic moment direction is south to north.
    • Adding unequal-looking pole forces in a uniform field instead of recognizing that the net force is zero.

    Explanation

    Concept. Magnetic field lines are directed curves whose tangent at any point gives the direction of the magnetic field and whose local density indicates its magnitude. They are continuous closed curves with no intersections, and a JEE graph should be interpreted through field direction, density, boundary shape, and flux represented by the number of lines.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec B\parallel \vec\tau_{\mathrm{line}},\qquad |\vec B|\propto\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta A},\qquad \Phi_B=BA\cos\theta,\qquad \vec B=-\nabla V_m.\]
    Key points.
    • Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from north to south; inside it, they run from south to north.
    • Two magnetic field lines never intersect, since a unique field direction exists at each point.
    • Closer spacing represents a stronger field; spacing alone is not a precise quantitative scale.
    • Field lines are normal to the surfaces of constant magnetic scalar potential.
    • The number of field lines crossing a surface is proportional to magnetic flux, not generally to line spacing alone.
    • A closed surface has zero net magnetic flux, although positive and negative fluxes through its parts can both be nonzero.
    Example 1.

    A uniform magnetic field of \(0.25\,\mathrm{T}\) is perpendicular to a surface of area \(8.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}\). Find the flux and the field-line density represented in a sketch with one line per weber.

    1. For a perpendicular field, \(\cos\theta=1\).
    2. The magnetic flux is \(\Phi_B=BA=(0.25)(8.0\times10^{-4})\).
    3. Multiplication gives \(\Phi_B=2.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Wb}\).
    4. With the stated convention, this corresponds to \(2.0\times10^{-4}\) field lines crossing the surface.

    Answer: \(\boxed{\Phi_B=2.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Wb}}\), represented by the same numerical number of lines under the given convention.

    Example 2.

    A field sketch represents the same number of field lines crossing two surfaces. For the first, \(B_1=0.20\,\mathrm{T}\), \(A_1=0.020\,\mathrm{m^2}\), and the field makes \(30^\circ\) with the normal. The field is perpendicular to the second surface of area \(A_2=0.010\,\mathrm{m^2}\). Find \(B_2\).

    1. The first flux is \(\Phi_1=B_1A_1\cos30^\circ=(0.20)(0.020)(\sqrt3/2)\).
    2. Evaluating this product gives \(\Phi_1=3.464\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Wb}\).
    3. The same number of lines means the same flux, so \(B_2A_2=\Phi_1\).
    4. Hence \(B_2=(3.464\times10^{-3})/(0.010)=0.3464\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B_2\approx0.346\,\mathrm{T}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Drawing magnetic field lines as intersecting curves.
    • Treating field lines as actual material strings that begin or end at magnetic poles.
    • Using \(BA\) when the field is specified relative to the surface tangent instead of its normal.

    Magnetic field

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMagnetsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Magnetic field (B, tesla - vector with magnitude plus direction shown by compass needles and field lines) fills space around magnets and currents - Earth field (~30-60 μT guiding compasses), lab electromagnets (teslas lifting cars), MRI scanners (superconducting teslas imaging bodies). Field versus induction (B versus H in materials) splits vacuum response from magnetisation. Lines exit north poles, enter south, never cross - mapping rules shared with electric fields.
    NEET Snapshot:
    • B in tesla; lines north-to-south outside, never crossing.
    • Earth microteslas guide; MRI teslas image bodies.
    Remember
    • Compass needles align with local B direction.
    NEET Practice MCQ
    1

    SI unit of magnetic field (magnetic flux density) is

    Solution: Tesla measures B; weber measures flux through areas.

    \(\vec F=q\vec v\times\vec B\) Lorentz force bends movers
    \(1\,\mathrm{T}=1\,\mathrm{N\,s/C\,m}\) tesla in base units
    \(B_{earth}\approx30\text{-}60\,\mu\mathrm{T}\) compass-scale planetary field

    Chapter 16 · Topic 3

    Magnetic dipole

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMagnetsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A magnetic dipole is a pair of equal and opposite magnetic poles separated by a small distance, represented by a vector magnetic moment directed from south to north. Its external field is obtained from the axial and equatorial expressions, while a nonuniform field can also exert a net force on it.
    Key formula(s). \[m=q_m d,\qquad \vec\tau=\vec m\times\vec B,\qquad U=-mB\cos\theta;\] \[B_{\mathrm{axial}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{r^3},\qquad B_{\mathrm{equatorial}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m}{r^3};\] \[\vec B(r,\theta)=\frac{\mu_0m}{4\pi r^3}(3\cos\theta\,\hat r+\sin\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}),\qquad \vec F=\nabla(\vec m\cdot\vec B).\]
    Key points.
    • At equal distance from the center, the axial field is twice the equatorial field.
    • The dipole approximation assumes \(r\gg d\), the separation between the poles.
    • A magnetic dipole in a uniform field experiences torque but no net translational force.
    • The torque tends to align \(\vec m\) with \(\vec B\), and \(U=-mB\cos\theta\) has its minimum at alignment.
    • An antiparallel orientation is unstable because a small displacement lowers the potential energy.
    • In a nonuniform field, \(\vec F=\nabla(\vec m\cdot\vec B)\) can be nonzero; replace \(\vec B\) by a vector, not just its magnitude, inside the gradient.
    Example 1.

    A magnetic dipole of moment \(0.80\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\) is placed on the axis at a distance \(0.10\,\mathrm{m}\) from the observation point. Calculate the field there using \(\mu_0/(4\pi)=10^{-7}\,\mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-2}}\).

    1. The observation point lies on the dipole axis, so use \(B=2\mu_0m/(4\pi r^3)\).
    2. Substitute \(m=0.80\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\) and \(r=0.10\,\mathrm{m}\): \(B=2(10^{-7})(0.80)/(0.10)^3\).
    3. The denominator is \(r^3=10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}\).
    4. Therefore \(B=1.6\times10^{-4}/10^{-3}=1.6\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B=1.6\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}}\) on the axis.

    Example 2.

    A magnetic dipole \(m=1.2\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\) is slowly rotated from \(30^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\) relative to a uniform field \(B=4.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}\). Find the external work required.

    1. The potential energy at angle \(\theta\) is \(U(\theta)=-mB\cos\theta\).
    2. Initially \(U_i=-mB\cos30^\circ\), while finally \(U_f=-mB\cos90^\circ=0\).
    3. The increase in potential energy is \(W=U_f-U_i=mB(1-\cos30^\circ)\).
    4. Substituting gives \(W=(1.2)(4.0\times10^{-4})(1-\sqrt3/2)\).
    5. Thus \(W=6.43\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: The required external work is \(\boxed{6.43\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{J}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using the equatorial formula on the axis or the axial formula in the equatorial plane.
    • Writing the dipole force as \(\vec m\times\vec B\), which is actually torque.
    • Taking the gradient of \(mB\) when the field direction itself varies with position.

    Chapter 16 · Topic 4

    Earth's magnetism

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMagnetsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Earth's magnetism is described by a geomagnetic field whose direction need not coincide with the geographic axis. Magnetic declination and inclination specify the horizontal direction and vertical tilt, respectively, and JEE problems usually require resolving the total field into horizontal and vertical components.
    Key formula(s). \[D=\angle(\text{geographic north},\text{magnetic north}),\qquad I=\angle(\text{horizontal},\text{total field});\] \[B_H=B\cos I,\qquad B_V=B\sin I,\qquad B=\sqrt{B_H^2+B_V^2},\qquad \tan I=\frac{B_V}{B_H}.\]
    Key points.
    • Positive declination means magnetic north lies east of geographic north; negative declination means west.
    • Positive inclination or dip in the northern geographic hemisphere means the field points downward.
    • The horizontal component is the projection of the total field on the horizontal plane.
    • \(B_H=B\cos I\), not \(B\sin I\), and \(B_V=B\sin I\).
    • The declination is a horizontal-plane angle and is independent of inclination.
    • A compass aligns with the local horizontal magnetic field, so magnetic declination is the difference between its north and geographic north.
    Example 1.

    At a location the magnetic field has magnitude \(5.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\), an inclination of \(60^\circ\), and a declination of \(2^\circ\) west. Find the horizontal field and the direction of magnetic north.

    1. The horizontal component is \(B_H=B\cos I=(5.0\times10^{-5})\cos60^\circ\).
    2. Since \(\cos60^\circ=1/2\), \(B_H=2.5\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    3. A \(2^\circ\) west declination means magnetic north is \(2^\circ\) west of geographic north.
    4. Inclination affects the vertical tilt but does not alter this horizontal direction statement.

    Answer: \(\boxed{B_H=2.5\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}}\), with magnetic north \(2^\circ\) west of geographic north.

    Example 2.

    At a place the total terrestrial magnetic field is \(5.4\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\) and its horizontal component is \(4.5\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\). Calculate the inclination.

    1. From \(\cos I=B_H/B\), obtain \(\cos I=4.5/5.4=5/6\).
    2. Therefore \(I=\cos^{-1}(5/6)\).
    3. The vertical component is \(B_V=B\sin I=(5.4\times10^{-5})\sqrt{1-25/36}\).
    4. Hence \(B_V=(5.4\times10^{-5})(\sqrt{11}/6)=3.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    5. Equivalently, \(I=\tan^{-1}(3.0/4.5)\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{I\approx33.7^\circ\text{ downward}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Calling inclination an angle from the vertical instead of the horizontal.
    • Losing the east or west sign when interpreting declination.
    • Applying \(\cos I\) to the vertical component.

    Explanation

    Concept. Earth's magnetic field is weak, varies with position and time, and is approximately horizontal near the magnetic equator and increasingly vertical toward the magnetic poles. For local calculations, it is represented by the vector total field whose horizontal and vertical components set its local direction.
    Key formula(s). \[B_E=\sqrt{B_H^2+B_V^2},\qquad B_H=B_E\cos I,\qquad B_V=B_E\sin I,\qquad \tan I=\frac{B_V}{B_H};\] \[1\,\mathrm{G}=10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T},\qquad B_E\sim(25\text{ to }65)\,\mu\mathrm{T}\text{ typically}.\]
    Key points.
    • The horizontal component \(B_H\) is important for a freely rotating compass needle.
    • The vertical component is zero approximately at the magnetic equator and greatest near the magnetic poles.
    • The usual magnitude of Earth's field is of order \(10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\), not \(10^{-4}\) or \(10^{-6}\,\mathrm{T}\) in SI.
    • A positive dip in the northern hemisphere means the field points into the ground.
    • The local field is obtained from magnetic survey data and may change slowly with time.
    • In a uniform approximation, superposition allows a known laboratory field to be added vectorially to \(B_E\).
    Example 1.

    At a place the total Earth's magnetic field is \(50\,\mu\mathrm{T}\) and the dip is \(45^\circ\). Find its horizontal and vertical components.

    1. Use \(B_H=B_E\cos I=(50\,\mu\mathrm{T})\cos45^\circ\).
    2. Use \(B_V=B_E\sin I=(50\,\mu\mathrm{T})\sin45^\circ\).
    3. Since both trigonometric factors equal \(1/\sqrt2\), each component is \(50/\sqrt2\,\mu\mathrm{T}\).
    4. The equal components are consistent with an inclination of \(45^\circ\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B_H=B_V\approx35.4\,\mu\mathrm{T}}\).

    Example 2.

    At a location the horizontal and vertical components of Earth's field are \(36\,\mu\mathrm{T}\) and \(48\,\mu\mathrm{T}\). Find the total field and inclination.

    1. The components are perpendicular, so \(B_E=\sqrt{36^2+48^2}\,\mu\mathrm{T}\).
    2. Since \(36^2+48^2=1296+2304=3600\), \(B_E=60\,\mu\mathrm{T}\).
    3. The inclination follows from \(\tan I=B_V/B_H=48/36=4/3\).
    4. Thus \(I=\tan^{-1}(4/3)\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B_E=60\,\mu\mathrm{T},\quad I\approx53.1^\circ\text{ downward}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating Earth's field as exactly uniform over large regions.
    • Confusing gauss and tesla: \(1\,\mathrm{G}=10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    • Using \(B_H=B_E\sin I\).

    Chapter 16 · Topic 5

    Magnetic elements

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMagnetsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The principal magnetic elements describing Earth's field at a place are the horizontal component \(B_H\), the declination \(D\), and the inclination or dip \(I\). Declination fixes the horizontal direction of the field, while inclination fixes its tilt above or below the horizontal plane.
    Key formula(s). \[D=\angle(\text{geographic north},\text{magnetic north}),\qquad I=\angle(\text{horizontal plane},\text{total field});\] \[B_H=B\cos I,\qquad B_V=B\sin I,\qquad B=\sqrt{B_H^2+B_V^2},\qquad \tan I=\frac{B_V}{B_H}.\]
    Key points.
    • A compass needle aligns with \(B_H\), and its horizontal angular displacement from geographic north gives the declination.
    • Positive declination means magnetic north is east of geographic north; negative declination means west.
    • Dip is measured from the horizontal, not from the vertical, and is positive downward in the northern geographic hemisphere.
    • The horizontal component is commonly measured by a magnetometer or compass-based survey instrument.
    • Given \(B_H\) and \(I\), both the total field and vertical component can be found without a separate measurement.
    • Declination, inclination, and the field magnitude vary spatially and also change slowly with time.
    Example 1.

    At a location the horizontal component of Earth's field is \(3.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\) and the inclination is \(30^\circ\). Find the total field and vertical component.

    1. From \(B_H=B\cos I\), the total field is \(B=B_H/\cos30^\circ\).
    2. Since \(\cos30^\circ=\sqrt3/2\), \(B=(3.0\times10^{-5})(2/\sqrt3)\).
    3. Therefore \(B=2\sqrt3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\approx3.46\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    4. The vertical component is \(B_V=B_H\tan30^\circ=(3.0\times10^{-5})/\sqrt3\).
    5. Thus \(B_V=\sqrt3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\approx1.73\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B\approx3.46\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T},\quad B_V\approx1.73\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}}\).

    Example 2.

    At another place the total terrestrial field is \(6.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\), its inclination is \(30^\circ\), and its declination is \(5^\circ\) east of geographic north. Find the horizontal and vertical components and state the magnetic-north direction.

    1. The horizontal component is \(B_H=B\cos30^\circ=(6.0\times10^{-5})(\sqrt3/2)\).
    2. Hence \(B_H=3\sqrt3\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\approx5.20\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    3. The vertical component is \(B_V=B\sin30^\circ=3.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    4. Eastward declination means magnetic north lies \(5^\circ\) east of geographic north.
    5. The result is consistent with \(B=\sqrt{B_H^2+B_V^2}=6.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B_H\approx5.20\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T},\quad B_V=3.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{T},\quad D=5^\circ\text{ east}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Measuring inclination from the vertical instead of the horizontal.
    • Confusing the horizontal component \(B_H\) with the total field \(B\).
    • Losing the east-west sign of declination.
    • Treating Earth's magnetic and geographic axes as identical.

    Chapter 16 · Topic 6

    Magnetic materials

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMaterialsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Magnetic materials are classified mainly by the sign and magnitude of their response to an applied field as diamagnetic, paramagnetic, or ferromagnetic. For a linear material, susceptibility links magnetization to field intensity, while ferromagnetic behavior is dominated by domains and must be described through nonlinear or hysteretic data in JEE problems.
    Key formula(s). \[\chi_m=\frac{M}{H},\qquad \mu_r=1+\chi_m\quad\text{(linear isotropic material)},\qquad B=\mu_0(H+M).\]
    Key points.
    • Diamagnetic materials have \(\chi_m<0\) and \(\mu_r<1\); paramagnetic materials have \(0<\chi_m\ll1\).
    • Ferromagnetic materials have a very large positive susceptibility and can remain magnetized after the field is removed.
    • A field \(H\) that magnetizes a material can produce a field \(B\) different from \(\mu_0H\) because of the material's magnetization.
    • Domains are aligned in ferromagnets; disordering by heating above the Curie temperature produces a transition to paramagnetism.
    • High permeability lowers magnetic reluctance but does not eliminate saturation.
    • The relation \(B=\mu_0(H+M)\) is the general macroscopic average relation; \(B=\mu_0\mu_rH\) requires a linear response.
    Example 1.

    A magnetic material has susceptibility \(600\) and is placed in \(H=800\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\). Find its magnetization and \(B\), assuming linear behavior.

    1. Magnetization is \(M=\chi_mH=600(800)=4.8\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    2. The effective magnetic field term is \(H+M=800+4.8\times10^5=4.808\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    3. Therefore \(B=\mu_0(H+M)=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(4.808\times10^5)\).
    4. Evaluating gives \(B\approx0.604\,\mathrm{T}\).
    5. The result exceeds \(\mu_0H\) because the material is strongly magnetized in the field direction.

    Answer: \(\boxed{M=4.8\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},\quad B\approx0.604\,\mathrm{T}}\).

    Example 2.

    Three samples have relative permeabilities \(0.999\), \(1.00001\), and \(500\). Classify each and find their susceptibilities.

    1. Since \(\chi_m=\mu_r-1\), the first sample has \(\chi_m=-0.001\).
    2. Its \(\mu_r<1\) and negative susceptibility identify it as diamagnetic.
    3. The second sample has \(\chi_m=1.00001-1=10^{-5}\), so it is weakly paramagnetic.
    4. The third sample has \(\chi_m=500-1=499\), indicating strong ferromagnetic behavior in the idealized classification.

    Answer: \(\boxed{\text{diamagnetic: }-10^{-3};\ \text{paramagnetic: }10^{-5};\ \text{ferromagnetic: }499}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Applying \(B=\mu_0\mu_rH\) to a ferromagnetic sample deep in its nonlinear or hysteretic region.
    • Confusing permeability with permeability relative to free space.
    • Treating the same susceptibility law as exact for all magnetic temperatures and fields.

    Chapter 16 · Topic 7

    Diamagnetic

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMaterialsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A diamagnetic material develops an induced magnetic moment opposite to the applied field because electronic orbital changes produce a net current direction that opposes the change in flux. The effect is weak, reversible, and persists only while the field is present, although superconductors provide an extreme diamagnetic case through the Meissner effect.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec M=\chi_m\vec H,\qquad \chi_m<0,\qquad \mu_r=1+\chi_m<1,\qquad B=\mu_0(H+M),\qquad \chi_m=-\frac{C}{T}\quad(C>0).\]
    Key points.
    • Diamagnetism occurs in substances such as bismuth, copper, water, and nitrogen because their atoms have no permanent net moment.
    • The induced moment is antiparallel to the applied field, so the material is weakly repelled.
    • The induced effect disappears when the applied field is removed, apart from transient induced-current effects.
    • In weak fields, \(|M|\ll H\), so \(\mu_r\) is close to one rather than zero.
    • A superconductor is a perfect diamagnet and expels magnetic flux when cooled below its critical temperature in the Meissner state.
    • For ordinary diamagnets over limited temperature ranges, a common model is \(\chi_m=-C/T\).
    Example 1.

    A diamagnetic material has susceptibility \(-4.0\times10^{-5}\) and is placed in \(H=1.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\). Find \(M\), \(\mu_r\), and \(B\).

    1. Magnetization is \(M=\chi_mH=(-4.0\times10^{-5})(1.0\times10^5)=-4.0\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    2. The relative permeability is \(\mu_r=1+\chi_m=0.99996\).
    3. The field is \(B=\mu_0(H+M)=4\pi\times10^{-7}(10^5-4.0)\).
    4. Since \(10^5-4=99996\), \(B\approx0.12566\,\mathrm{T}\).
    5. The negative magnetization makes \(B\) very slightly smaller than \(\mu_0H=0.12566\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{M=-4.0\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},\quad \mu_r=0.99996,\quad B\approx0.12566\,\mathrm{T}}\).

    Example 2.

    A diamagnetic sample has \(\chi_m=-3.0\times10^{-5}\) at \(300\,\mathrm{K}\). If \(\chi_m=-C/T\), find \(C\) and the susceptibility at \(450\,\mathrm{K}\).

    1. From \(\chi_m=-C/T\), the magnitude relation is \(C=-\chi_mT\).
    2. At \(300\,\mathrm{K}\), \(C=(3.0\times10^{-5})(300)=9.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{K}\).
    3. At \(450\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\chi_m=-(9.0\times10^{-3})/450\).
    4. Evaluating gives \(\chi_m=-2.0\times10^{-5}\).
    5. The negative sign is retained; the absolute susceptibility decreases as temperature rises in this model.

    Answer: \(\boxed{C=9.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{K},\quad \chi_m(450\,\mathrm{K})=-2.0\times10^{-5}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Taking the induced moment parallel to the applied field.
    • Omitting the negative sign when finding susceptibility or magnetization.
    • Assuming a diamagnetic material remains permanently magnetized after unloading.
    Back to Index
    Index / Magnetism, EMI and AC
    Chapter 16 · Topic 8

    Paramagnetic

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMaterialsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Paramagnetic materials contain atoms or ions with permanent magnetic moments that are predominantly random without a field but acquire a net moment when a field aligns some of them. Their response is weak, positive, and strongly temperature dependent, with magnetization disappearing when the field is removed.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec M=\chi_m\vec H,\qquad \chi_m>0,\qquad \chi_m=\frac{C}{T},\qquad M=\frac{CH}{T},\qquad \chi_m=\frac{C}{T-\theta}.\]
    Key points.
    • Paramagnetism arises from unpaired electron spins or orbital moments, as in aluminium, oxygen, and many transition-metal ions.
    • The net magnetization is parallel to the applied field, producing weak attraction.
    • Increasing temperature increases thermal agitation and reduces magnetization for a fixed field.
    • Below the Curie temperature of a ferromagnet, exchange interaction may produce spontaneous magnetization; ordinary paramagnets do not show that ordering.
    • For small \(\chi_m\), \(M\ll H\), so \(B\) is only slightly greater than \(\mu_0H\).
    • The Curie-Weiss constant \(\theta\) is zero in the ideal Curie law and may differ from zero when interactions are relevant.
    Example 1.

    A paramagnetic material has \(\chi_m=2.0\times10^{-5}\) at \(300\,\mathrm{K}\). If \(H=1.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\), find \(M\) and \(B\) at \(300\,\mathrm{K}\).

    1. From \(M=\chi_mH\), \(M=(2.0\times10^{-5})(1.0\times10^5)=2.0\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    2. The total field term is \(H+M=1.0\times10^5+2.0=100002\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    3. Therefore \(B=\mu_0(H+M)=4\pi\times10^{-7}(100002)\).
    4. This is approximately \(0.12566\,\mathrm{T}\), only slightly above \(\mu_0H=0.12566\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{M=2.0\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},\quad B\approx0.12566\,\mathrm{T}}\).

    Example 2.

    A paramagnetic material has susceptibilities \(0.015\) at \(300\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(0.010\) at \(450\,\mathrm{K}\). Assuming \(\chi=C/(T-\theta)\), determine \(C\) and \(\theta\).

    1. Invert the law: \(1/\chi=(T-\theta)/C\), which is linear in \(T\).
    2. At \(300\,\mathrm{K}\), \(1/\chi_1=66.667\,\mathrm{K}\); at \(450\,\mathrm{K}\), \(1/\chi_2=100\,\mathrm{K}\).
    3. The slope is \((100-66.667)/(450-300)=0.22222\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}=1/C\).
    4. Thus \(C=4.50\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\theta=300-C/0.015=300-300=0\).
    5. The data are consistent with the Curie law \(\chi=C/T\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{C=4.50\,\mathrm{K},\quad \theta=0}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating paramagnetic magnetization as permanent after the field is removed.
    • Reversing the temperature dependence in Curie's law.
    • Using \(B=\mu_0(H-M)\) for a paramagnet instead of \(B=\mu_0(H+M)\).
    Back to Index
    Index / Magnetism, EMI and AC
    Chapter 16 · Topic 9

    Ferromagnetic

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMaterialsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A ferromagnetic material contains many magnetic domains whose moments align strongly through exchange interaction, producing very large magnetization and remanence. Its response is nonlinear and history dependent below the Curie temperature, so a JEE calculation may require a given susceptibility, saturation field, or hysteresis-loop area rather than a single constant \(\mu_r\).
    Key formula(s). \[\vec M=\chi_m\vec H\ \text{(linear region only)},\qquad B=\mu_0(H+M),\qquad \mu_r=1+\chi_m,\qquad W_h=\oint H\,dB,\qquad P_h=fV W_h,\qquad \chi_m=\frac{C}{T-T_C}\ \text{(ideal, above }T_C\text{)}.\]
    Key points.
    • Ferromagnetic materials such as iron, cobalt, and nickel have unpaired moments and strong exchange coupling.
    • Domains can remain aligned after the external field is removed, producing remanent magnetization.
    • The \(B-H\) curve is nonlinear and hysteretic; one universal permeability does not describe the whole curve.
    • The Curie temperature is the transition point below which spontaneous ferromagnetic order is possible.
    • Soft magnetic materials have small coercivity and narrow loops; hard magnetic materials have large coercivity and large energy products.
    • Hysteresis-loop area gives energy dissipated per unit volume in one complete cycle.
    Example 1.

    A ferromagnetic sample is treated as linear with \(\chi_m=5000\) at \(H=400\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\). Find \(M\) and \(B\).

    1. The magnetization is \(M=\chi_mH=5000(400)=2.0\times10^6\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    2. The field term is \(H+M=400+2.0\times10^6=2.0004\times10^6\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    3. Use \(B=\mu_0(H+M)=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.0004\times10^6)\).
    4. The dominant contribution is \(8\pi\times10^{-1}=2.513\,\mathrm{T}\), with the small \(H\) term included above.
    5. Evaluating exactly gives \(B\approx2.514\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{M=2.0\times10^6\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},\quad B\approx2.514\,\mathrm{T}}\).

    Example 2.

    The area of a ferromagnetic hysteresis loop is \(0.80\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\) per cycle. A core of volume \(2.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}\) is operated at \(50\,\mathrm{Hz}\). Find the hysteresis power loss.

    1. Energy dissipated per cycle is the loop area times core volume: \(E_{\mathrm{cycle}}=W_hV\).
    2. Thus \(E_{\mathrm{cycle}}=(0.80)(2.0\times10^{-3})=1.6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{J}\).
    3. The number of cycles per second is \(f=50\), so \(P_h=fE_{\mathrm{cycle}}\).
    4. \(P_h=50(1.6\times10^{-3})=8.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{W}\).
    5. The calculation assumes the loop area remains unchanged at the operating conditions.

    Answer: \(\boxed{P_h=8.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{W}=80\,\mathrm{mW}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Applying a linear \(M=\chi H\) law after the material has saturated.
    • Reporting hysteresis-loop area as energy without multiplying by volume when finding total loss.
    • Confusing Curie temperature with a temperature at which all ferromagnets instantly lose their remanence.
    Back to Index
    Index / Magnetism, EMI and AC
    Chapter 16 · Topic 10

    Magnetization

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMaterialsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Magnetization is the magnetic moment per unit volume of a material and measures the net alignment of microscopic magnetic moments. In a finite sample, surface and demagnetizing effects mean that the applied field \(H\), the magnetization \(M\), and the measured \(B\) must be related with the correct macroscopic convention.
    Key formula(s). \[\vec M=\frac{\sum_i\vec m_i}{V},\qquad m=MV,\qquad \vec B=\mu_0(\vec H+\vec M);\] \[\vec H_d=-N\vec M,\qquad K_b=M\quad\text{for a uniformly magnetized long cylinder},\qquad \chi_m=\frac{M}{H}.\]
    Key points.
    • The SI unit of magnetization is \(\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\), while magnetic moment has unit \(\mathrm{A\,m^2}\).
    • For a uniformly magnetized specimen, total moment \(m\) equals \(M\) multiplied by volume.
    • In SI, \(B=\mu_0(H+M)\) for volume-averaged macroscopic quantities; this is not \(B=\mu_0H\) unless \(M\) is neglected.
    • Magnetization is a vector; its direction is the net direction of the microscopic magnetic moments.
    • A uniformly magnetized long cylinder is equivalent to a solenoid with surface current per unit length \(K_b=M\).
    • The demagnetizing field opposes magnetization and depends on shape through the dimensionless demagnetizing factor \(N\).
    Example 1.

    A uniformly magnetized specimen of volume \(2.0\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3}\) has total magnetic moment \(0.080\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\). It is in \(H=120\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\). Find \(M\) and \(B\), assuming \(M\) is parallel to \(H\) and neglecting demagnetizing effects.

    1. Magnetization is moment per unit volume: \(M=m/V\).
    2. \(M=0.080/(2.0\times10^{-4})=400\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    3. The field term is \(H+M=120+400=520\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    4. Therefore \(B=\mu_0(H+M)=4\pi\times10^{-7}(520)\).
    5. Evaluating gives \(B=6.5345\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{M=400\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},\quad B\approx6.53\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}}\).

    Example 2.

    A long cylinder of radius \(0.020\,\mathrm{m}\) is uniformly magnetized with \(M=3.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\). An external field \(H=1.0\times10^3\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\) is applied along the magnetization. Find \(B\) and the equivalent solenoid surface current per unit length.

    1. For a long cylinder, the demagnetizing field is negligible in the ideal approximation.
    2. The total field is \(B=\mu_0(H+M)=4\pi\times10^{-7}(1.0\times10^3+3.0\times10^5)\).
    3. The bracket is \(301000\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\), giving \(B\approx0.378\,\mathrm{T}\).
    4. A uniformly magnetized cylinder is equivalent to a solenoid with \(K_b=M\).
    5. Thus \(K_b=3.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\); its total circumferential current is \(K_b(2\pi r)\), if required.

    Answer: \(\boxed{B\approx0.378\,\mathrm{T},\quad K_b=3.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Dividing magnetic moment by area instead of volume.
    • Omitting magnetization when calculating \(B\) in a strongly magnetized sample.
    • Confusing the surface current density \(K_b\) of a magnetized cylinder with the current per turn.

    Explanation

    Concept. Permeability describes how readily a medium develops magnetic flux for a given magnetizing field, with absolute permeability and relative permeability distinguished. It is useful as a constant only in a linear regime; ferromagnetic materials show nonlinear, hysteretic, and saturating behavior.
    Key formula(s). \[\mu=\frac{B}{H},\qquad \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}},\qquad \mu_r=\frac{\mu}{\mu_0}=\frac{B}{\mu_0H};\] \[\mu_r=1+\chi_m,\qquad u=\frac12BH\quad\text{(linear medium)}.\]
    Key points.
    • Absolute permeability \(\mu=B/H\) has SI unit \(\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}\), while relative permeability \(\mu_r\) is dimensionless.
    • For air and free space, \(\mu\simeq\mu_0\); the approximation is not exact for all practical air samples.
    • In a linear isotropic medium, \(B=\mu_0\mu_rH\) and \(\mu_r=1+\chi_m\).
    • In a ferromagnetic core, \(\mu_r\) can vary with field, temperature, and magnetic history.
    • Large permeability lowers reluctance and concentrates magnetic flux, but saturation still limits the attainable \(B\).
    • Magnetic energy density in a linear medium is \(u=BH/2=B^2/(2\mu)=H^2\mu/2\).
    Example 1.

    A linear magnetic material has \(\mu_r=100\) and is placed in \(H=200\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\). Find \(B\), \(\mu\), and the magnetic energy density.

    1. Apply \(B=\mu_0\mu_rH=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(100)(200)\).
    2. The product \(\mu_rH=20000\), so \(B=8\pi\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}=0.02513\,\mathrm{T}\).
    3. Absolute permeability is \(\mu=\mu_r\mu_0=100(4\pi\times10^{-7})=4\pi\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}\).
    4. The energy density is \(u=\frac12BH=\frac12(0.02513)(200)\).
    5. Thus \(u=2.513\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B=2.513\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T},\quad \mu=1.257\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}},\quad u=2.513\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}}\).

    Example 2.

    A long solenoid has \(n=5000\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\) and carries \(I=0.10\,\mathrm{A}\). Compare its air-core field with the field after inserting a linear core of relative permeability \(200\).

    1. In air, \(B_{\mathrm{air}}=\mu_0nI\).
    2. With \(nI=500\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), \(B_{\mathrm{air}}=4\pi\times10^{-7}(500)\).
    3. Thus \(B_{\mathrm{air}}=6.283\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}=0.6283\,\mathrm{mT}\).
    4. For the linear core, \(B_{\mathrm{core}}=\mu_0\mu_rnI=200B_{\mathrm{air}}\).
    5. Therefore \(B_{\mathrm{core}}=0.12566\,\mathrm{T}\), provided the core is not saturated and end effects are neglected.

    Answer: \(\boxed{B_{\mathrm{air}}=0.6283\,\mathrm{mT},\quad B_{\mathrm{core}}=0.12566\,\mathrm{T},\quad B_{\mathrm{core}}/B_{\mathrm{air}}=200}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(\mu_r\) with units of \(\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}\).
    • Treating \(\mu=B/H\) as constant for a saturated ferromagnetic core.
    • Forgetting the factor \(1/2\) in the energy density of a linear field.

    Chapter 16 · Topic 11

    Magnetic susceptibility

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMaterialsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Magnetic susceptibility measures how strongly a material magnetizes under an applied field and is dimensionless in SI. It is the slope of the appropriate magnetization response, so for nonlinear ferromagnetic or hysteretic material a small-signal or differential susceptibility may be more meaningful than a single constant.
    Key formula(s). \[\chi_m=\frac{M}{H}\quad\text{(linear sample)},\qquad \chi_m=\frac{dM}{dH}\quad\text{(differential value)};\] \[\mu_r=1+\chi_m,\qquad B=\mu_0(1+\chi_m)H\quad\text{when linear}.\]
    Key points.
    • Susceptibility has no SI unit because both \(M\) and \(H\) are measured in \(\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    • \(\chi_m<0\) for diamagnetic, \(0<\chi_m\ll1\) for paramagnetic, and \(\chi_m\gg1\) can occur for ferromagnetic materials.
    • A small measured \(M/H\) is valid only if the field state lies in the linear regime.
    • In a hysteresis loop, the secant susceptibility from the origin and the differential slope can differ.
    • For a material in a fixed ambient state, the induced response is often described by \(\delta M=\chi\,\delta H\).
    • The relation \(B=\mu_0(H+M)\) always uses the actual magnetization, including a possible reversible component.
    Example 1.

    A magnetic rod has \(\chi_m=100\) and is placed in \(H=500\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\). Find \(M\) and \(B\) under the linear-material assumption.

    1. Apply \(M=\chi_mH=100(500)=5.0\times10^4\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    2. Then \(B=\mu_0(H+M)=4\pi\times10^{-7}(500+50000)\).
    3. The field term is \(50500\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    4. Therefore \(B=0.06346\,\mathrm{T}\), which is much larger than \(\mu_0H\) because of the large susceptibility.

    Answer: \(\boxed{M=5.0\times10^4\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},\quad B=6.346\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}}\).

    Example 2.

    On a linear branch of a magnetic sample, \(M=4.0\times10^4\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\) at \(H=400\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\), and \(M=6.0\times10^4\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\) at \(H=600\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\). Find \(\chi_m\) and \(M\) at \(H=500\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\), assuming the line passes through the origin.

    1. The susceptibility is the slope \(\chi_m=\Delta M/\Delta H\).
    2. \(\Delta M=(6.0-4.0)\times10^4=2.0\times10^4\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    3. \(\Delta H=600-400=200\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\), so \(\chi_m=2.0\times10^4/200=100\).
    4. Since the line passes through the origin, \(M=100H\).
    5. At \(H=500\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\), \(M=5.0\times10^4\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{\chi_m=100,\quad M(500\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}})=5.0\times10^4\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Assigning units of \(\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\) to susceptibility.
    • Using a single \(M/H\) across a hysteresis loop without specifying the operating state.
    • Writing \(B=\mu_0H\) and ignoring the \(M\) term in a high-susceptibility sample.

    Chapter 16 · Topic 12

    Hysteresis

    Magnetism and MatterMagnetism, EMI and ACMaterialsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Hysteresis is the lag of magnetic flux density or magnetization behind the magnetizing field during a cyclic change, and it appears as a closed \(B-H\) or \(M-H\) loop. Its area measures energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle and helps classify soft and hard magnetic materials.
    Key formula(s). \[W_h=\oint H\,dB\quad\text{in }\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}},\qquad P_h=fV\oint H\,dB;\] \[B_r=B\big|_{H=0},\qquad H_c=-H\big|_{B=0},\qquad B_s=\text{saturation flux density}.\]
    Key points.
    • Retentivity \(B_r\) is the flux density remaining after the magnetizing field is reduced to zero.
    • Coercivity \(H_c\) is the reverse field needed to reduce the flux density to zero.
    • Saturation flux density \(B_s\) is the maximum attainable flux density on the magnetization curve.
    • The loop area is energy lost per unit volume in one complete cycle, not a simple \(BH\) product unless the loop shape is specified.
    • A narrow loop with small \(H_c\) indicates a soft magnetic material suitable for transformer cores.
    • A wide loop with large \(H_c\) and \(B_r\) indicates a hard magnetic material suitable for permanent magnets.
    • Reversing the field produces a two-branch loop; the upper and lower branches must not be treated as the same line.
    Example 1.

    A magnetic material has retentivity \(0.35\,\mathrm{T}\) and coercivity \(500\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\). Its full hysteresis loop is approximated by a rectangle with \(B\)-axis intercepts \(\pm B_r\) and \(H\)-axis intercepts \(\pm H_c\). Find the energy lost per unit volume per cycle.

    1. The full vertical height of the loop is \(2B_r=0.70\,\mathrm{T}\).
    2. The full horizontal width is \(2H_c=1000\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\).
    3. The enclosed area is \(W_h=(2B_r)(2H_c)=4B_rH_c\).
    4. Substituting gives \(W_h=4(0.35)(500)=700\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\).
    5. This is energy per unit volume for one complete cycle, not total energy for an unspecified core volume.
    6. A power calculation would additionally require the operating frequency and volume.

    Answer: \(\boxed{W_h=700\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\text{ per cycle}}\).

    Example 2.

    A magnetic core has hysteresis-loop area \(40\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\), volume \(3.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}\), and operates at \(50\,\mathrm{Hz}\). Find the hysteresis loss per second.

    1. Energy lost in one cycle is \(E=W_hV=(40)(3.0\times10^{-3})\).
    2. Hence \(E=0.120\,\mathrm{J}\) per cycle.
    3. There are \(50\) cycles per second, so the power is \(P=fE\).
    4. \(P=50(0.120)=6.0\,\mathrm{W}\).
    5. This ignores eddy-current and other losses and assumes the loop area is constant.

    Answer: \(\boxed{P_h=6.0\,\mathrm{W}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Confusing retentivity with coercivity or reading them from the wrong axis.
    • Calling the loop area total energy without multiplying by volume.
    • Forgetting the factor of frequency when converting energy per cycle to power.

    Explanation

    Concept. A permanent magnet retains a substantial magnetization after the external field is removed because its material has a large coercivity and retentivity. Its useful performance is characterized by a high magnetic moment and a large maximum energy product, while temperature, shock, and opposing fields can demagnetize it.
    Key formula(s). \[m=q_mL_m,\qquad \tau=mB\sin\theta,\qquad U=-mB\cos\theta;\] \[(BH)_{\max}=\text{maximum area of the useful demagnetization curve},\qquad E_{\max}\approx V(BH)_{\max}.\]
    Key points.
    • A hard magnetic material has a wide hysteresis loop and remains magnetized after the magnetizing field is removed.
    • Retentivity is the residual flux density at \(H=0\), while coercivity is the reverse field needed to reduce the flux density to zero.
    • The maximum energy product measures magnetic energy per unit volume available from a magnet of suitable shape.
    • Permanent magnets are commonly characterized by \(B_r\) and \(H_c\); an ideal rectangular demagnetization curve gives \((BH)_{\max}=B_rH_c/4\).
    • A magnetic moment points from south to north, and a nonuniform field can exert a force as well as a torque.
    • Heating above a material-dependent limit, a strong reverse field, or mechanical shock can reduce or reverse its magnetization.
    Example 1.

    A permanent bar magnet has pole strength \(8.0\,\mathrm{A\,m}\) and magnetic length \(0.15\,\mathrm{m}\). Find its moment and torque in a \(0.25\,\mathrm{T}\) field at \(60^\circ\).

    1. The moment is \(m=q_mL_m=8.0(0.15)=1.20\,\mathrm{A\,m^2}\).
    2. The torque magnitude is \(\tau=mB\sin\theta\).
    3. Substitute \(m=1.20\), \(B=0.25\), and \(\sin60^\circ=\sqrt3/2\): \(\tau=1.20(0.25)(\sqrt3/2)\).
    4. The product \(1.20(0.25)=0.30\), so \(\tau\approx0.260\,\mathrm{N\,m}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{m=1.20\,\mathrm{A\,m^2},\quad \tau\approx0.260\,\mathrm{N\,m}}\).

    Example 2.

    A hard magnet has \(B_r=0.80\,\mathrm{T}\) and \(H_c=2.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}\). Approximate its rectangular demagnetization curve, find its maximum energy density, and find the ideal stored energy in a volume \(2.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^3}\).

    1. For the rectangular approximation, \((BH)_{\max}=B_rH_c/4\).
    2. The product is \(B_rH_c=0.80(2.0\times10^5)=1.6\times10^5\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}\).
    3. Dividing by four gives \((BH)_{\max}=4.0\times10^4\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}=40\,\mathrm{kJ\,m^{-3}}\).
    4. The ideal total energy is \(E_{\max}=V(BH)_{\max}=(2.0\times10^{-3})(4.0\times10^4)\).
    5. Therefore \(E_{\max}=80\,\mathrm{J}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{(BH)_{\max}=40\,\mathrm{kJ\,m^{-3}},\quad E_{\max}=80\,\mathrm{J}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(\mu_0B_rH_c/4\) instead of the material energy product \(B_rH_c/4\).
    • Neglecting the demagnetizing field when using the \(B_rH_c/4\) estimate.
    • Assuming a magnet remains unchanged at arbitrarily high temperature or reverse field.

    Explanation

    Concept. An electromagnet produces a controlled magnetic field by passing current through a coil, usually wound around a soft ferromagnetic core of high permeability. The core raises the magnetic flux and makes attraction or switching controllable, but saturation, coil resistance, and magnetic hysteresis limit its performance.
    Key formula(s). \[B_{\mathrm{air}}=\mu_0nI,\qquad B_{\mathrm{core}}\simeq\mu_0\mu_rnI;\] \[\Phi_B=\frac{NI}{\mathcal R_m},\qquad B=\frac{\Phi_B}{A},\qquad \mathcal R_m\ \text{has units }\mathrm{A\,Wb^{-1}}.\]
    Key points.
    • For a long solenoid, \(n=N/\ell\) is the number of turns per unit length and the field is nearly uniform inside.
    • A high-permeability core increases magnetic flux and lowers the magnetic reluctance of the magnetic circuit.
    • An electromagnet has a controllable field, unlike a permanent magnet, but its field disappears when the coil current is removed apart from remanence.
    • Soft iron or another low-coercivity material is preferred for repeated switching because a narrow hysteresis loop loses little energy.
    • The field relation \(B\simeq\mu_0\mu_rnI\) assumes a linear core, negligible end effects, and no severe saturation.
    • Real electromagnets must be checked for coil heating, core saturation, and the pull-in behavior of an armature.
    Example 1.

    A long solenoid has \(n=2000\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), carries \(I=0.80\,\mathrm{A}\), and contains a linear core with \(\mu_r=1000\). Find the core field and the air-core field for comparison.

    1. The air-core field is \(B_{\mathrm{air}}=\mu_0nI=4\pi\times10^{-7}(2000)(0.80)\).
    2. Since \(nI=1600\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\), \(B_{\mathrm{air}}=2.0106\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}\).
    3. With a linear core, \(B_{\mathrm{core}}=\mu_rB_{\mathrm{air}}=1000(2.0106\times10^{-3})\).
    4. Thus \(B_{\mathrm{core}}=2.0106\,\mathrm{T}\), provided the core is not saturated.
    5. The enhancement factor is \(B_{\mathrm{core}}/B_{\mathrm{air}}=\mu_r=1000\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{B_{\mathrm{core}}\approx2.01\,\mathrm{T},\quad B_{\mathrm{air}}\approx2.01\,\mathrm{mT}}\).

    Example 2.

    A coil of \(1200\) turns is in a magnetic circuit of reluctance \(2.0\times10^5\,\mathrm{A\,Wb^{-1}}\). If the current is \(0.20\,\mathrm{A}\) and the core cross-sectional area is \(1.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), find the flux and core flux density.

    1. The magnetomotive force is \(NI=(1200)(0.20)=240\,\mathrm{A\,turn}\).
    2. Magnetic flux is \(\Phi_B=NI/\mathcal R_m=240/(2.0\times10^5)\).
    3. Therefore \(\Phi_B=1.20\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Wb}\).
    4. Divide by the area: \(B=\Phi_B/A=(1.20\times10^{-3})/(1.0\times10^{-2})\).
    5. Thus \(B=0.120\,\mathrm{T}\).

    Answer: \(\boxed{\Phi_B=1.20\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Wb},\quad B=0.120\,\mathrm{T}}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Applying the core permeability formula after the core has saturated.
    • Omitting the factor \(\mu_r\) in the ideal field of a solenoid with a core.
    • Treating reluctance as \(B/H\) instead of using \(\Phi=NI/\mathcal R_m\).

Lenz minus sign enforces energy conservation (opposition costs work); inductance inertia parallels mechanical mass.
