    Human eye

    Ray Optics and Optical InstrumentsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsInstrumentsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. The human eye is a refracting system whose relaxed power is about \(+60\ \mathrm{D}\), focused so that a distant object images exactly on the retina about 1.7 cm behind the cornea. By changing the curvature of its lens the eye can increase its power and focus nearer objects, down to the least distance of distinct vision \(D = 25\ \mathrm{cm}\); the range of this change is the power of accommodation. The JEE insight is that every eye problem is one of two operations: place a corrective lens in front of an eye of known far or near point and demand that the final image land on the retina.
    Key formula(s). \[ P_{eye} \approx +60\ \mathrm{D},\quad f \approx 1.67\ \mathrm{cm} \]; \[ P_{max}-P_{min} \approx 17\ \mathrm{D} \text{ (power of accommodation)} \]; \[ D = 25\ \mathrm{cm},\ \text{far point of a normal eye} = \infty \]; \[ \frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \]
    Key points.
    • The near point of a normal young eye is 25 cm and the far point is at infinity, so a normal eye focuses objects from 25 cm to infinity.
    • The image formed on the retina is real, inverted and diminished, which is why the perceived world is the right way up.
    • Power of accommodation is roughly 17 D, falling steadily with age; its loss is presbyopia, not a refractive error.
    • The relaxed eye has minimum power and is focused at the far point; maximum power is used at the near point.
    • A hypermetropic eye has insufficient power for its axial length, a myopic eye too much, and the retina position relative to the far point image decides which.
    • Clinical powers are quoted in dioptres, so a myopic correction of \(-2\ \mathrm{D}\) means a concave lens of focal length \(-0.5\ \mathrm{m}\).
    Example 1.

    A person's far point is 50 cm. Find the power of the lens that enables him to see distant objects, and find his near point when he wears it, given that his near point without the lens is 25 cm.

    1. To correct the far point, the lens must form a virtual image of a distant object at the far point: \(u = -\infty\), \(v = -0.5\ \mathrm{m}\).
    2. \(1/f = 1/v-1/u = -2-0 = -2\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\), so \(P = -2\ \mathrm{D}\) (a concave lens of focal length \(-0.5\ \mathrm{m}\)).
    3. For the near point, an object at 25 cm must be imaged virtually at the eye's near point, which is also 25 cm away: \(u = -0.25\ \mathrm{m}\), \(v = -0.25\ \mathrm{m}\).
    4. \(1/f = 1/v-1/u = -4+4 = 0\), so \(f = \infty\); the corrective lens changes nothing at 25 cm.
    5. The corrected range of vision is therefore from 25 cm to infinity, exactly the normal range.

    Answer: Corrective power \(P = -2\ \mathrm{D}\); the near point with the lens is \(25\ \mathrm{cm}\), so the range is 25 cm to infinity.

    Example 2.

    The far point of a myopic eye is 2 m and its near point is 10 cm. (a) Find the power of the lens needed to see distant objects clearly. (b) Find the near point when this lens is worn.

    1. (a) \(u = -\infty\), \(v = -2\ \mathrm{m}\), so \(P = 1/v-1/u = -0.5\ \mathrm{D}\), a concave lens of focal length \(-2\ \mathrm{m}\).
    2. (b) With the lens worn, an object at distance \(d\) must be imaged virtually at the eye's near point, \(v = -0.10\ \mathrm{m}\).
    3. \(-10+1/d = -0.5\), so \(1/d = 9.5\) and \(d = 0.1053\ \mathrm{m}\).
    4. The near point has moved from 10 cm to about 10.5 cm, i.e. it recedes slightly, as it must for a myopic eye corrected at the far point.

    Answer: (a) \(P = -0.5\ \mathrm{D}\); (b) the corrected near point is about \(10.5\ \mathrm{cm}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Setting the image of the corrective lens at the near point when it is the far point that is being corrected
    • Forgetting that accommodation still adds about 17 D, so the near point moves outwards after far-point correction
    • Treating the eye as a lens in air and forgetting that its image must fall on the retina
    • Assigning the maximum eye power to the relaxed state instead of the near point

    Explanation

    Concept. The common defects of vision are all statements about where the far point and near point of the defective eye lie, so each is corrected by a single lens of calculable power. Myopia (far point finite) needs a concave lens, hypermetropia and presbyopia (near point beyond 25 cm or power of accommodation lost) need a convex lens, and astigmatism needs a cylindrical lens because different meridians have different focal lengths. The JEE insight is never to draw the eye as a generic lens: place the corrective lens, write the image it must produce at the far or near point, and read off the power.
    Key formula(s). \[ \text{Myopia: } f = -F,\quad P = -\frac{1}{F} \]; \[ \text{Hypermetropia: } \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{D}+\frac{1}{N} \text{ for near point } N>D \]; \[ \text{Presbyopia: convex for near and concave for far (bifocals)} \]; \[ \text{Astigmatism: cylindrical/torric lens} \]
    Key points.
    • Myopia: the far point is finite and the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina; a concave lens of focal length equal in magnitude to the far point shifts the far point to infinity.
    • Hypermetropia: the near point lies beyond 25 cm because the eye is too weak for its axial length; a convex lens forms a virtual image at the eye's near point.
    • Presbyopia is a loss of accommodation with age, not a refractive error, so it is corrected with a convex lens for near work and often a concave lens for distance.
    • Astigmatism arises from a non-spherical cornea; it is corrected with a cylindrical lens, and the near point differs in the two principal meridians.
    • Correcting the far point pushes the near point outwards, and correcting the near point pulls the far point inwards; a single lens rarely does both.
    • Normal vision means a range of 25 cm to infinity, and the correction should be reported together with the new range.
    Example 1.

    A myopic person's far point is 4 m and his near point without any lens is 50 cm. (a) Find the power of the lens needed for normal distance vision. (b) Find his near point while wearing this lens.

    1. (a) The lens must image a distant object virtually at the far point: \(v = -4\ \mathrm{m}\), \(u = -\infty\).
    2. \(P = 1/v-1/u = -0.25\ \mathrm{D}\), a concave lens of focal length \(-4\ \mathrm{m}\).
    3. (b) An object at distance \(d\) must then be imaged virtually at the eye's near point, \(v = -0.5\ \mathrm{m}\).
    4. \(-2+1/d = -0.25\), so \(1/d = 1.75\) and \(d = 0.5714\ \mathrm{m}\).
    5. The near point has receded from 50 cm to 57.1 cm, which is the correct qualitative change for a myope.

    Answer: (a) \(P = -0.25\ \mathrm{D}\); (b) the corrected near point is about \(57.1\ \mathrm{cm}\).

    Example 2.

    A person uses a lens of power \(-0.5\ \mathrm{D}\) to see distant objects. His near point without any lens is 40 cm. (i) Find the far point of the uncorrected eye. (ii) Find his near point while wearing the lens. (iii) State the range of clear vision then.

    1. (i) The lens has focal length \(-2\ \mathrm{m}\), and a distant object is imaged at the far point, so the far point is \(2\ \mathrm{m}\).
    2. (ii) With the lens worn, an object at \(d\) is imaged virtually at the eye's near point \(v = -0.40\ \mathrm{m}\).
    3. \(1/u = 1/v-1/f = -2.5+0.5 = -2\), so \(u = -0.5\ \mathrm{m}\).
    4. (iii) The far point is now infinity (by construction of the correction) and the near point is 50 cm.
    5. Hence the range of clear vision is 50 cm to infinity, i.e. normal vision with a slightly receded near point.

    Answer: (i) far point \(2\ \mathrm{m}\); (ii) near point with the lens \(50\ \mathrm{cm}\); (iii) range of clear vision from \(50\ \mathrm{cm}\) to infinity.

    Common mistakes.
    • Prescribing a convex lens for myopia
    • Setting the corrective image at the near point when the far point is being corrected
    • Forgetting that a single lens cannot restore both the near point and the far point to normal
    • Ignoring that a myopic eye's near point moves outwards after far-point correction

    Chapter 20 · Topic 17

    Microscope

    Ray Optics and Optical InstrumentsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsInstrumentsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A compound microscope uses an objective of small focal length to produce a real, inverted, enlarged intermediate image of a tiny object, and an eyepiece of larger focal length to magnify that image angularly for the eye. Because the two stages are independent, the total magnifying power is the product of a linear magnification and an angular magnification. The JEE insight is to fix the final image condition (at the near point or at infinity) before choosing the eyepiece factor, and to use the instrument's near point \(D = 25\ \mathrm{cm}\) for the objective in the standard approximation.
    Key formula(s). \[ M = m_o m_e \]; \[ m_o = \frac{v_o}{u_o} \approx \frac{D}{f_o} \]; \[ m_e = 1+\frac{D}{f_e} \text{ (final image at } D),\quad m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} \text{ (at infinity)} \]; \[ L = f_o + \frac{D}{m_o} + f_e \]
    Key points.
    • The two magnifications multiply, and since each stage inverts once, the final image of a compound microscope is erect relative to the object.
    • The objective has the shorter focal length and the larger aperture; the eyepiece has the longer focal length and the smaller aperture.
    • The approximation \(m_o \approx D/f_o\) assumes the intermediate image lies close to the first focal plane beyond the objective, and it is accurate when \(f_o \ll D\).
    • For the final image at the near point the eyepiece factor is \(1+D/f_e\), and at infinity it is exactly \(D/f_e\).
    • The magnifying power of a single-lens magnifier is \(1+D/f\), so a compound microscope is always the more powerful instrument.
    • The tube length is \(f_o+D/m_o+f_e\), so a longer tube raises the objective magnification but narrows the field of view.
    Example 1.

    A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 0.4 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 2.5 cm, and the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision 25 cm. Find the magnifying power of the microscope.

    1. Objective magnification \(m_o \approx D/f_o = 25/0.4 = 62.5\).
    2. Since the final image is at the near point, the eyepiece magnification is \(m_e = 1+D/f_e = 1+25/2.5 = 11\).
    3. The total magnifying power is \(M = m_o m_e = 62.5\times 11 = 687.5\).
    4. Check the thin-lens validity: \(f_o = 0.4\ \mathrm{cm} \ll 25\ \mathrm{cm}\), so the approximation for \(m_o\) is well justified.

    Answer: \(M \approx 688\), and the final image is erect relative to the object and inverted once at each stage.

    Example 2.

    The objective of a compound microscope has focal length 1 cm and forms a real, inverted image 20 cm from itself. The eyepiece has focal length 5 cm and the final image is formed at the near point 25 cm. Find the magnifying power and the tube length.

    1. Objective: \(1/v_o-1/u_o = 1/f_o\) gives \(1/20-1/u_o = 1\), so \(1/u_o = -0.95\) and \(u_o = -1.053\ \mathrm{cm}\).
    2. Linear magnification of the objective \(m_o = v_o/u_o = 20/(-1.053) = -19.0\).
    3. Eyepiece: final image at \(D = 25\ \mathrm{cm}\), so \(m_e = 1+25/5 = 6\).
    4. Total \(M = (-19.0)(6) = -114\); the two inversions make the final image erect relative to the object, magnitude 114.
    5. For the tube length, the intermediate image is \(6.25\ \mathrm{cm}\) in front of the eyepiece, since \(1/u_e = 1/25-1/5 = -4/25\).
    6. So the distance between the lenses is \(20 + 6.25 = 26.25\ \mathrm{cm}\); the overall instrument length, measured from the objective to the final image, is \(26.25+25 = 51.25\ \mathrm{cm}\).

    Answer: \(M = 114\) (erect, magnitude 114) and the tube length (objective to eyepiece) is \(26.25\ \mathrm{cm}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding the two magnifications instead of multiplying them
    • Using \(1+D/f_e\) when the final image is formed at infinity
    • Writing the tube length as \(f_o+f_e\), omitting the \(D/m_o\) term
    • Reporting the final image as inverted, forgetting that the objective and eyepiece each invert once

    Chapter 20 · Topic 18

    Telescope

    Ray Optics and Optical InstrumentsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsInstrumentsStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A telescope magnifies the angular size of a distant object by using an objective of long focal length to gather light and form a small real image at its focus, which an eyepiece of short focal length then magnifies for the eye. Since the object is effectively at infinity, the geometry is trivial and the whole instrument is described by \(f_o\), \(f_e\) and the final image condition. The JEE insight is that there are only two standard conditions, normal adjustment and final image at the near point, and identifying which one applies reduces the problem to a single line.
    Key formula(s). \[ M = -\frac{f_o}{f_e} \quad \text{(normal adjustment)} \]; \[ M = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1+\frac{f_e}{D}\right) \quad \text{(final image at } D) \]; \[ L = f_o+f_e \quad \text{(normal adjustment)},\quad L = f_o+\frac{D f_e}{D+f_e} \]
    Key points.
    • In normal adjustment the final image is at infinity, the tube length is \(f_o+f_e\), and the magnification is \(-f_o/f_e\), the minus sign denoting an inverted image.
    • An astronomical (refracting) telescope gives an inverted image; a terrestrial telescope contains an erecting lens or an extra convex-concave pair and gives an erect image.
    • The objective needs a large focal length and a large aperture to gather light and to resolve; the eyepiece needs a small focal length and a small aperture.
    • The angular resolution is \(\theta_{\min} = 1.22\lambda/D_{ap}\), entirely independent of the focal lengths.
    • Useful magnification is limited: beyond roughly the value that expands the resolution limit to about one arcminute, extra magnification shows no new detail.
    • The magnifying power quoted for normal adjustment applies only to distant objects, since the derivation assumes the object at infinity.
    Example 1.

    An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. Find the magnifying power and the tube length in normal adjustment.

    1. A distant object lies at the front focus of the objective, so the intermediate image is formed at the back focus, a distance \(f_o\) from the objective.
    2. In normal adjustment the eyepiece is placed so that this intermediate image lies at its own front focus.
    3. The separation of the lenses is therefore the sum of the two focal lengths: \(L = f_o+f_e = 100+5 = 105\ \mathrm{cm}\).
    4. The magnifying power is \(M = -f_o/f_e = -100/5 = -20\).
    5. The negative sign means the image is inverted, as expected for an astronomical telescope.

    Answer: \(M = -20\) (magnification 20, inverted) and the tube length is \(105\ \mathrm{cm}\).

    Example 2.

    The same telescope is adjusted so that the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision 25 cm. Find the magnifying power and the tube length.

    1. With the final image at \(D = 25\ \mathrm{cm}\) (virtual, on the object side), the eyepiece obeys \(1/v_e-1/u_e = 1/f_e\) with \(v_e = -25\ \mathrm{cm}\).
    2. \(-1/25-1/u_e = 1/5\), so \(1/u_e = -1/25-1/5 = -6/25\) and \(u_e = -25/6 = -4.167\ \mathrm{cm}\).
    3. The distance between the lenses is \(L = f_o+|u_e| = 100+4.167 = 104.17\ \mathrm{cm}\).
    4. The magnifying power becomes \(M = -(f_o/f_e)(1+f_e/D) = -20\times(1+5/25) = -20\times 1.2 = -24\).
    5. For a near-point adjustment the magnification increases slightly over the normal-adjustment value, and the tube shortens a little, since the intermediate image moves inside the focal point.

    Answer: \(M = -24\) and the tube length is about \(104.2\ \mathrm{cm}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Reporting \(M = +f_o/f_e\) for an astronomical telescope, which is always inverted
    • Using \(L = f_o+f_e\) when the final image is at the near point
    • Confusing the resolving power \(1.22\lambda/D\) with the magnifying power \(f_o/f_e\)
    • Swapping the objective and eyepiece focal lengths, which inverts the magnification

    Explanation

    Concept. Optical instruments share one idea: they enlarge the angular size of an object, and the enlargement that matters is limited either by the accommodation of the eye or by the diffraction limit of the objective. A simple magnifier helps the eye accommodate; a microscope increases the linear size of a tiny object before the eyepiece magnifies it; a telescope increases the angular size of a distant object. The JEE insight is that once the final image condition is declared, every instrument collapses to a product of two factors, and the resolution limit explains why further magnification is useless.
    Key formula(s). \[ M_{mag} = 1+\frac{D}{f} \]; \[ M_{micro} = m_o m_e,\quad m_o\approx\frac{D}{f_o},\ m_e = 1+\frac{D}{f_e} \text{ or } \frac{D}{f_e} \]; \[ M_{tele} = \frac{f_o}{f_e} \]; \[ \theta_{\min} \approx \frac{\lambda}{A} \]
    Key points.
    • The eye resolves about one minute of arc, so an instrument is useful only while its resolution stays finer than that.
    • Magnification beyond the diffraction limit of the objective merely enlarges the diffraction pattern and reveals no new detail.
    • Angular magnification equals (image size / object size) multiplied by (object distance / near point) for a relaxed eye, which unifies all three instruments.
    • A simple magnifier gives \(1+D/f\); the objective alone gives \(D/f_o\); the compound microscope gives their product.
    • Sharing the power between two eyes halves the magnification needed from each eye for the same total effect.
    • The final image condition decides the formula: at the near point use the \(+1\) term, at infinity use the bare ratio.
    Example 1.

    A compound microscope uses an objective of focal length 0.5 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 2 cm, and the final image is formed at the near point 25 cm. Find the total magnification.

    1. Objective magnification \(m_o = D/f_o = 25/0.5 = 50\).
    2. Eyepiece magnification, final image at the near point, \(m_e = 1+D/f_e = 1+25/2 = 13.5\).
    3. Total \(M = m_o m_e = 50\times 13.5 = 675\).
    4. The two inversions cancel, so the final image is erect relative to the object.

    Answer: The total magnification is \(675\), with the final image erect relative to the object.

    Example 2.

    A telescope has an objective aperture of 20 cm and is used with light of wavelength 500 nm. Find its resolving power in radians and in arcseconds, and the magnification needed for the eye to exploit the full resolution of the instrument.

    1. The Rayleigh criterion gives \(\theta_{\min} = 1.22\lambda/D = 1.22\times 500\times 10^{-9}/0.2 = 3.05\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad}\).
    2. Converting to arcseconds using \(1\ \mathrm{rad} = 206265\) arcseconds gives \(3.05\times 10^{-6}\times 206265 = 0.63\) arcseconds.
    3. The eye can just resolve about 1 arcminute, i.e. 60 arcseconds, so the angular image must be enlarged by a factor \(60/0.63 \approx 95\).
    4. Any magnification beyond about 95 adds no information, since the two stars are then already as large as the eye can separate.

    Answer: \(\theta_{\min} = 3.05\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad} \approx 0.63\) arcseconds, and the useful magnification is about 95.

    Common mistakes.
    • Confusing magnification with resolution, or quoting a magnification that exceeds the diffraction limit
    • Using the aperture in centimetres without converting to metres in \(1.22\lambda/D\)
    • Omitting the \(+1\) in the simple magnifier factor when the final image is at the near point
    • Adding magnifications instead of multiplying them for a compound instrument

Coherence (laser vs sunlight) plus path difference (constructive nλ, destructive (2n+1)λ/2) decide fringe patterns.

    • Brewster tan ip=μ polarises reflected rays fully.

    Chapter 21 · Topic 1

    Huygens principle

    Wave OpticsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsWavefront and InterferenceStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Huygens' principle states that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that travel with the speed of the wave, and the wavefront at a later instant is the envelope of all those wavelets. The principle is a geometric construction of wave propagation rather than a prediction in its own right, and it becomes a law of propagation only when combined with the requirement that the wavelets interfere constructively to define the new front. That combination is the origin of Fermat's principle, since the envelope picks out the path of least optical time.
    Key formula(s). \[ v = f\lambda = \frac{\lambda}{T} \]; \[ \Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta \]; \[ \text{envelope: the common tangent to all secondary wavelets} \]; \[ k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \]
    Key points.
    • The principle has three ingredients: secondary wavelets, forward propagation at speed \(v\), and constructive-interference selection of the envelope.
    • Huygens' construction alone is satisfied by backward wavelets as well; the restriction to the forward region is a later refinement.
    • With the constructive-interference clause, the principle gives Fermat's principle of least time, the unifying statement of ray optics.
    • A wavefront is always normal to the direction of travel of the wave, so a tilted front implies tilted rays.
    • The principle explains reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference with a single mechanism, which is why it is the foundation of wave optics.
    • The number of wavelets that can reach a point in time \(t\) determines the path difference there, so interference is a Huygens construction.
    Example 1.

    A wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.66 m. Find the speed of the wave, and the phase difference between two points whose path difference is 1.32 m.

    1. The speed is \(v = f\lambda = 500\times 0.66 = 330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
    2. The phase difference corresponding to a path difference \(\Delta\) is \(\Delta\phi = 2\pi\Delta/\lambda\).
    3. With \(\Delta = 1.32\ \mathrm{m}\) and \(\lambda = 0.66\ \mathrm{m}\), the ratio \(\Delta/\lambda = 2\).
    4. Hence \(\Delta\phi = 2\pi\times 2 = 4\pi\ \mathrm{rad}\), which is two full cycles, so the two points are in phase.

    Answer: \(v = 330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the phase difference is \(4\pi\ \mathrm{rad}\) (in phase).

    Example 2.

    Two coherent sound sources each producing a pressure amplitude of 2 mPa at a point differ in path by 2.75 m, and the wavelength is 0.55 m. State whether the interference is constructive or destructive and find the resultant amplitude.

    1. The path difference in wavelengths is \(\Delta/\lambda = 2.75/0.55 = 5\).
    2. Since \(\Delta = 5\lambda = n\lambda\) with \(n=5\) integer, the interference is constructive.
    3. The two waves are in phase at the point, so amplitudes add: \(A_{res} = 2+2 = 4\ \mathrm{mPa}\).
    4. The corresponding phase difference is \(2\pi\times 5 = 10\pi\ \mathrm{rad}\).

    Answer: The interference is constructive and the resultant amplitude is \(4\ \mathrm{mPa}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating Huygens' principle as a statement that waves always travel in straight lines, with no mention of interference
    • Applying the envelope construction without the constructive-interference condition
    • Confusing a phase difference measured in radians with a path difference measured in metres
    • Omitting the factor \(2\pi\) when converting a path difference into a phase difference

    Chapter 21 · Topic 2

    Wavefront

    Wave OpticsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsWavefront and InterferenceStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. A wavefront is a surface of constant phase, and by definition it is everywhere normal to the direction in which the wave travels. Its shape records the geometry of the source, since a point source in a uniform medium produces spherical fronts while a distant or collimated source produces nearly plane fronts. Evolving a wavefront is done purely by Huygens' construction, and the number and spacing of the secondary wavelets encode the phase at each point. The JEE insight is that the fastest route to a correct construction is to draw normals, mark wavelets of radius \(vt\), and take the common tangent.
    Key formula(s). \[ \phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta = 2\pi f t \]; \[ k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \]; \[ \text{successive fronts separated by } \lambda;\ \text{at time } t \text{ the wavelet radius is } vt \]
    Key points.
    • A point source in an isotropic medium gives spherical wavefronts; a distant source in the same medium gives effectively plane wavefronts.
    • In the Huygens construction each point of the old front becomes a source of a secondary wavelet of radius \(vt\); the new front is their common tangent.
    • A plane wavefront incident on a spherical or cylindrical surface becomes curved, and a curved front becomes plane after passage through a lens: this is wave-optics lens action.
    • Because all points of a wavefront are in phase, the path difference between any two of its points is an integer number of wavelengths.
    • The count of wavelets that can reach a point in time \(t\) fixes the interference order at that point, so fringes and wavefronts are two descriptions of one process.
    • A wavefront can be drawn in any section of the medium; the section containing the rays is the most informative.
    Example 1.

    A plane sound wave of wavelength 0.5 m travelling in air at 3.3 x 10^2 m/s enters glass, in which its speed is 1.65 x 10^3 m/s. Find the wavelength in glass and the ratio of the wavenumbers in the two media.

    1. The frequency is fixed by the source and does not change on entering a medium, so \(f = v_{air}/\lambda_{air} = 330/0.5 = 660\ \mathrm{Hz}\).
    2. In glass, \(\lambda_{glass} = v_{glass}/f = 1650/660 = 2.5\ \mathrm{m}\).
    3. The wavenumber is \(k = 2\pi/\lambda\), so \(k_{air} = 2\pi/0.5 = 4\pi\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\).
    4. Similarly \(k_{glass} = 2\pi/2.5 = 0.8\pi\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\).
    5. The ratio is \(k_{glass}/k_{air} = 0.8\pi/4\pi = 0.2 = v_{air}/v_{glass}\).

    Answer: \(\lambda_{glass} = 2.5\ \mathrm{m}\), and \(k_{glass}/k_{air} = 0.2\) (equivalently \(k_{air}/k_{glass} = 5\)).

    Example 2.

    A plane wavefront of wavelength 0.5 m in air falls on a plane glass surface at an incidence of 30 degrees. The refractive index of the glass is 1.5. Find the wavelength in glass, the angle of refraction, and the phase difference between rays that entered the glass at the two ends of a wavefront 1 cm wide.

    1. The frequency is unchanged, so \(\lambda_{glass} = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333\ \mathrm{m} = 33.3\ \mathrm{cm}\).
    2. Refraction: \(\sin r = \sin 30^\circ/1.5 = 0.3333\), so \(r = 19.5^\circ\).
    3. Inside the glass the geometric path difference between the two edge rays is \(d\sin r = 1\times 0.3333 = 0.3333\ \mathrm{cm}\).
    4. The optical (phase-counting) path difference is \(\mu\,d\sin r = 1.5\times 0.3333 = 0.5\ \mathrm{cm}\), which equals exactly one wavelength in air, \(0.5\ \mathrm{cm}\).
    5. In wavelengths of the incident beam this is \(\Delta/\lambda = 1\), so the phase difference is \(2\pi\); the two edge rays remain in phase, as every wavefront must.

    Answer: \(\lambda_{glass} = 33.3\ \mathrm{cm}\), \(r = 19.5^\circ\), and the phase difference is \(2\pi\) (zero net lag).

    Common mistakes.
    • Drawing a wavefront oblique to the ray direction, which is impossible by definition
    • Claiming the frequency changes when light enters a medium
    • Taking the envelope to be an arbitrary common tangent rather than the forward one
    • Using the geometric path difference instead of the optical path difference when comparing phases in a medium

    Explanation

    Concept. Under the wave picture, reflection is explained by the Huygens construction: every point of the incident wavefront becomes a source of secondary wavelets, and the only direction in which these wavelets build up a new front is the backward one, at the mirror angle. The new wavefront is the mirror image of the incident wavefront in the surface, so the law of reflection follows for any wave, of any wavelength, without any extra assumption. Total internal reflection is the same construction with the refracted front failing to exist.
    Key formula(s). \[ i = r \]; \[ \text{constructive: } \Delta = n\lambda \text{ (two reflected waves from the same type of boundary)} \]; \[ \text{destructive: } \Delta = \left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda \text{ if one reflection inverts the phase} \]; \[ \sin c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \]
    Key points.
    • The \(\pi\) phase change at reflection from a denser medium is what allows a backward wavefront to form at all in the Huygens picture.
    • Sound reflecting from a hard wall has a phase change of \(\pi\); reflection from a soft, rarefied boundary has none.
    • Light reflected from a rarer medium has no phase change, while reflection from a denser medium shifts the phase by \(\pi\).
    • When reflection at one of two paths inverts the phase, the constructive condition becomes \(\Delta = (2n+1)\lambda/2\).
    • Total internal reflection is the case in which the refracted wavefront cannot be constructed at all, so only the reflected front survives.
    • The law of reflection \(i=r\) holds for sound, light, water waves and matter waves alike, which is the wave picture's main success.
    Example 1.

    A sound wave of pressure amplitude 2 x 10^-4 Pa is incident normally on a rigid wall, and the incident and reflected waves overlap. Find the pressure amplitude of the resulting standing wave at a point where the two waves are (i) in phase and (ii) exactly out of phase, and state the phase change at the rigid wall.

    1. A rigid wall is a rarer-to-denser boundary for the wave, so the reflected wave suffers a phase change of \(\pi\).
    2. At a point where the two waves are in phase (an antinode of pressure), the amplitudes add: \(p_{max} = 2\times 10^{-4}+2\times 10^{-4} = 4\times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Pa}\).
    3. At a point where they are exactly out of phase (a pressure node), the amplitudes cancel: \(p_{min} = 2\times 10^{-4}-2\times 10^{-4} = 0\).
    4. The complete reflection means the incident and reflected amplitude magnitudes are equal, which is why the node is a true node.
    5. Because of the \(\pi\) reversal at the wall, the wall itself is a pressure antinode and nodes occur at odd multiples of \(\lambda/4\) from the wall.

    Answer: (i) \(4\times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Pa}\) at an antinode; (ii) zero at a node; the rigid wall introduces a phase change of \(\pi\).

    Example 2.

    A loudspeaker is placed 0.4 m in front of a rigid wall and emits sound of wavelength 0.1 m. Find the positions of the antinodes and nodes between the speaker and the wall, and the separation between consecutive nodes.

    1. Let \(x\) be the distance from the speaker. The direct path is \(x\), while the reflected path is \(2\times 0.4 - x = 0.8-x\).
    2. The path difference is therefore \(\Delta = (0.8-x)-x = 0.8-2x\).
    3. A rigid wall reverses the phase, so an antinode (constructive) requires \(\Delta = n\lambda = 0.1n\): \(0.8-2x = 0.1n\).
    4. This gives \(x = 0.4-0.05n\), i.e. antinodes at \(x = 0, 0.05, 0.10, \ldots, 0.40\ \mathrm{m}\), nine in all, the first and last coinciding with the speaker and the wall.
    5. A node requires \(\Delta = (2n+1)\lambda/2 = 0.05(2n+1)\), so \(x = 0.4-0.025(2n+1)\), i.e. nodes at 0.025, 0.075, 0.125, \ldots 0.375 \mathrm{m}.
    6. Consecutive nodes are separated by \(0.05\ \mathrm{m} = \lambda/2\), as required for a standing wave.

    Answer: Antinodes at 5 cm intervals from 0 to 40 cm (nine of them) and nodes at 2.5, 7.5, 12.5, \ldots 37.5 cm (eight of them), with a node spacing of \(5\ \mathrm{cm}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Omitting the \(\pi\) phase change at reflection from a denser medium when computing interference
    • Applying \(\Delta = n\lambda\) for a node in a case where one reflection inverts the phase
    • Expecting a different law of reflection for sound and light; it is identical
    • Forgetting that a node is a true zero only when the incident and reflected amplitudes are equal

    Explanation

    Concept. In the wave picture refraction is nothing but a change of speed: when a tilted wavefront crosses into a medium in which it travels more slowly, the leading part of the front advances less than the trailing part, so the front tilts while staying continuous with itself. The direction of the ray is the normal to the wavefront, so the tilting of the front is the bending of the ray, and Snell's law follows from the geometry of that construction with no dynamical input. The JEE insight is that the correct picture to draw is the wavefront bending, not the ray, and that the frequency never changes.
    Key formula(s). \[ \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{v_1}{v_2} = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \]; \[ n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r \]; \[ v = \frac{c}{n},\quad \lambda = \frac{v}{f},\quad f = \text{constant} \]
    Key points.
    • Refraction is a kinematic consequence of the change of speed; the wavefront must remain continuous at the boundary.
    • The frequency is fixed by the source and is unchanged, while the speed and the wavelength both change in the new medium.
    • Entering a slower (optically denser) medium tilts the front towards the normal, and the ray bends towards the normal.
    • Snell's law emerges with \(n\) simply as a speed ratio, so the same construction explains the bending of sound, light and water waves.
    • If the tangential component of the wavevector exceeds the available speed, no real refraction angle exists and total internal reflection occurs.
    • A wavefront hitting a boundary normally is not tilted, so there is no bending for normal incidence whatever the two indices.
    Example 1.

    A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz passes from air, where its speed is 330 m/s, into water, where its speed is 1500 m/s. (a) Find the wavelength in each medium. (b) A ray is incident at 10 degrees on the water surface; find the angle of refraction and the deviation.

    1. (a) In air \(\lambda = v/f = 330/500 = 0.66\ \mathrm{m}\); in water \(\lambda = 1500/500 = 3.0\ \mathrm{m}\). The frequency stays 500 Hz in both.
    2. (b) From the wavefront construction, \(\sin i/\sin r = v_1/v_2 = 330/1500 = 0.22\).
    3. Hence \(\sin r = \sin 10^\circ/0.22 = 0.1736/0.22 = 0.789\), so \(r = 52.1^\circ\).
    4. Since water is the faster medium, the ray bends away from the normal, as the large value of \(r\) shows.
    5. The deviation is \(\delta = r-i = 52.1-10 = 42.1^\circ\).

    Answer: (a) \(0.66\ \mathrm{m}\) in air and \(3.0\ \mathrm{m}\) in water at 500 Hz; (b) \(r = 52.1^\circ\) with a deviation of \(42.1^\circ\).

    Example 2.

    A light ray travelling in water of refractive index 4/3 is incident on a plane glass surface of refractive index 1.5 at 40 degrees. The wavelength in water is 560 nm. Find the angle of refraction and the wavelength in the glass.

    1. Snell's law in wave form: \(\sin i/\sin r = (v_w/v_g) = (n_g/n_w) = 1.5/(4/3) = 1.125\).
    2. Therefore \(\sin r = \sin 40^\circ/1.125 = 0.6428/1.125 = 0.5714\), giving \(r = 34.8^\circ\).
    3. Glass is optically denser, so the ray bends towards the normal: \(r < i\), as required.
    4. The frequency is unchanged, so the wavelength scales as the speed: \(\lambda_g/\lambda_w = v_g/v_w = n_w/n_g = 0.8889\).
    5. Hence \(\lambda_g = 0.8889\times 560 = 497.8\ \mathrm{nm}\).

    Answer: \(r = 34.8^\circ\) and \(\lambda_{glass} \approx 498\ \mathrm{nm}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Claiming that the frequency changes on refraction
    • Bending the ray in the diagram instead of redrawing the wavefront that has tilted
    • Letting the wavefront break at the interface, or assuming the same speed in both media, either of which destroys the construction
    • Missing total internal reflection when \(\sin r > 1\): for sound entering water from air this happens above about 12.7 degrees

    Chapter 21 · Topic 3

    Interference

    Wave OpticsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsWavefront and InterferenceStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Interference is the redistribution of intensity produced by the superposition of two or more waves of fixed phase relationship, and its measurable signature is the variation of intensity with position or time. Because intensity is proportional to the square of the resultant amplitude, the interference term is \(2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi\), so complete darkness requires equal intensities. The JEE insight is that the ratio \(I_{max}/I_{min}\), which is what an experiment actually measures, depends only on the two intensities and not on the phase.
    Key formula(s). \[ I = I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi \]; \[ I_{max} = (\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2})^2,\quad I_{min} = (\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2})^2 \]; \[ \phi = \frac{2\pi\Delta}{\lambda} \]; \[ V = \frac{I_{max}-I_{min}}{I_{max}+I_{min}} \]
    Key points.
    • Sustained interference requires the same frequency, a constant phase difference (coherence) and comparable intensities.
    • Intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude, so amplitudes are what must be added, never intensities.
    • Interference redistributes rather than destroys energy: what is missing at a node appears at the antinodes, since \(I_1+I_2 = (I_{max}+I_{min})/2\).
    • Complete destructive interference (\(I_{min}=0\)) requires \(I_1 = I_2\), so equal intensities are essential for a dark fringe.
    • The visibility \(V = 2\sqrt{I_1I_2}/(I_1+I_2)\) is a direct measure of how nearly coherent and how nearly equal the two beams are.
    • The pattern in space and the pattern in time are the same physics, with the path difference replaced by an arrival-time difference.
    Example 1.

    Two waves of intensities 9 I_0 and 16 I_0 interfere with a phase difference of 60 degrees. Find the resultant intensity, the maximum and minimum intensities, and the ratio \(I_{max}/I_{min}\).

    1. The interference term is \(2\sqrt{9\times 16}\,I_0\cos 60^\circ = 2\times 12\,I_0\times 0.5 = 12\ I_0\).
    2. The resultant intensity is \(I = 9I_0+16I_0+12I_0 = 37\ I_0\).
    3. At maximum, \(I_{max} = (3+4)^2 I_0 = 49\ I_0\).
    4. At minimum, \(I_{min} = (3-4)^2 I_0 = 1\ I_0\); the minimum is not zero because the amplitudes, \(3\) and \(4\), differ.
    5. The check is exact: \((I_{max}+I_{min})/2 = (49+1)/2 = 25\ I_0 = I_1+I_2\), so energy is conserved.

    Answer: \(I = 37\ I_0\), \(I_{max} = 49\ I_0\), \(I_{min} = 1\ I_0\), and \(I_{max}/I_{min} = 49\).

    Example 2.

    Two coherent sources produce waves whose individual intensities are in the ratio 4:1. Find the visibility of the interference pattern and the intensity at a point where the phase difference is 90 degrees.

    1. Let \(I_1 = 4I_0\) and \(I_2 = I_0\), so \(\sqrt{I_1} = 2\sqrt{I_0}\) and \(\sqrt{I_2} = \sqrt{I_0}\).
    2. \(I_{max} = (2+1)^2 I_0 = 9I_0\) and \(I_{min} = (2-1)^2 I_0 = 1I_0\).
    3. Visibility \(V = (9-1)/(9+1) = 0.8\), equivalently \(V = 2\sqrt{I_1I_2}/(I_1+I_2) = 2\times 2/5 = 0.8\).
    4. At a phase difference of 90 degrees, \(\cos\phi = 0\), so \(I = I_1+I_2 = 5I_0\), the mean value.

    Answer: Visibility \(V = 0.8\) (80 per cent) and the intensity at 90 degrees is \(5I_0\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Adding intensities directly instead of adding amplitudes and then squaring
    • Forgetting the factor \(2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\) in the interference term
    • Assuming \(I_{min}=0\) whenever interference is observed
    • Treating two independent sources as coherent and hence expecting a stationary pattern

    Young's double-slit experiment

    Wave OpticsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsWavefront and InterferenceStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Young's double-slit experiment divides a single wavefront into two coherent secondary sources, whose overlapping beams produce equally spaced interference fringes on a distant screen. The positions of the fringes are fixed entirely by the path difference created by the geometry of the two slits, and the uniformity of the spacing follows from the small-angle approximation. The JEE insight is that the ratio \(D/d\) is the same for every fringe, which is precisely why the fringe width does not depend on the order of the fringe.
    Key formula(s). \[ \Delta = S_2P-S_1P = d\sin\theta \approx \frac{dx}{D} \]; \[ \text{bright: } d\sin\theta = n\lambda \]; \[ \text{dark: } d\sin\theta = \left(2n+1\right)\frac{\lambda}{2} \]; \[ \beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d} \]
    Key points.
    • The path difference at a point at distance \(x\) from the central maximum is exactly \(d\sin\theta\) and approximately \(dx/D\).
    • Bright fringes are at \(d\sin\theta = n\lambda\) and dark ones at \(d\sin\theta=(2n+1)\lambda/2\), with \(n = 0,1,2,\ldots\).
    • The angular fringe width is \(\lambda/d\) and the linear fringe width is \(\lambda D/d\); the two are independent quantities.
    • The fringe width is independent of the order \(n\) because the approximation \(x/D = \tan\theta\) is the same for every fringe.
    • Coherence is guaranteed by illuminating both slits from one source, which is why two lamps will not produce fringes.
    • The angular width of the central bright maximum is \(2\lambda/d\), i.e. twice the fringe width.
    Example 1.

    In a Young's double-slit experiment the slits are 0.4 mm apart and the screen is 1.2 m away. Light of wavelength 600 nm is used. Find the fringe width, the width of the central maximum, and the angular width of the central maximum.

    1. Fringe width \(\beta = \lambda D/d = 600\times 10^{-9}\times 1.2/(0.4\times 10^{-3})\).
    2. \(D/d = 1.2/(0.4\times 10^{-3}) = 3000\), so \(\beta = 600\times 10^{-9}\times 3000 = 1.8\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 1.8\ \mathrm{mm}\).
    3. The central maximum spans from the first minimum on one side to the first minimum on the other, so its width is \(2\beta = 3.6\ \mathrm{mm}\).
    4. The angular width is \(2\lambda/d = 2\times 600\times 10^{-9}/(0.4\times 10^{-3}) = 3.0\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}\).
    5. Check: angular width times \(D\) gives \(3.0\times 10^{-3}\times 1.2 = 3.6\ \mathrm{mm}\), matching the linear width.

    Answer: Fringe width \(\beta = 1.8\ \mathrm{mm}\), central maximum width \(3.6\ \mathrm{mm}\), angular width \(3.0\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad}\).

    Example 2.

    In a Young's double-slit experiment with slit separation 0.5 mm and screen distance 1 m, light of wavelength 500 nm is used. A thin glass plate of thickness 4 micrometres and refractive index 1.5 is placed in front of one slit. Find the shift of the pattern and the number of fringes that cross the central point.

    1. The plate adds an optical path \((\mu-1)t = 0.5\times 4\times 10^{-6} = 2\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m} = 2000\ \mathrm{nm}\) to that path.
    2. The number of fringes that pass the centre is the extra path in wavelengths: \(N = (\mu-1)t/\lambda = 2000/500 = 4\).
    3. The original fringe width is \(\beta = \lambda D/d = 500\times 10^{-9}\times 1/(0.5\times 10^{-3}) = 1.0\ \mathrm{mm}\).
    4. The whole pattern shifts by \(N\beta = 4\times 1.0 = 4.0\ \mathrm{mm}\), and the shift is towards the slit in front of which the plate is placed.

    Answer: The pattern shifts by \(4.0\ \mathrm{mm}\) towards the plate, and \(4\) fringes cross the central point.

    Common mistakes.
    • Using \(d\cos\theta\) instead of \(d\sin\theta\) for the path difference
    • Adding \(2\mu t\) instead of \((\mu-1)t\) for the extra optical path introduced by a plate
    • Forgetting that the shift is towards the slit before which the plate is placed
    • Assuming the fringe width grows with the order of the fringe

    Chapter 21 · Topic 5

    Fringe width

    Wave OpticsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsWavefront and InterferenceStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Fringe width is the distance between two consecutive bright fringes (or two consecutive dark fringes) and equals \(\lambda D/d\) in a double-slit arrangement, so it grows with wavelength and screen distance and shrinks as the slits are brought closer. The uniform spacing is a direct consequence of the paraxial approximation, since every fringe subtends the same small angle to the order of \(\lambda/d\). The JEE insight is that any change in the apparatus, including immersing it in a medium or inserting a plate, acts on this single expression.
    Key formula(s). \[ \beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d} \]; \[ \text{independent of the order } n \]; \[ \text{shift} = \frac{(\mu-1)tD}{d} \]; \[ \text{width of central maximum} = \frac{2\lambda D}{d} \]
    Key points.
    • \(\beta\) is proportional to \(\lambda\) and to \(D\), and inversely proportional to \(d\).
    • The fringe width does not depend on the order, so all bright fringes are equally spaced.
    • Immersing the whole apparatus in a medium of index \(n_m\) multiplies \(\beta\) by \(1/n_m\), since the wavelength shrinks.
    • The number of fringes within the central maximum is \(2d/a\) if each slit is also a source of diffraction of width \(a\).
    • Inserting a plate of thickness \(t\) and index \(\mu\) in one path shifts the pattern by \((\mu-1)tD/d\), which is the classic JEE combined question.
    • Moving the screen changes only the scale of the pattern, not the angular fringe width, and the fringes always scale about the central point.
    Example 1.

    In a Young's double-slit experiment the slit separation is 0.3 mm, the screen is 2 m from the slits, and the wavelength used is 600 nm. Find the fringe width, the width of the central maximum, and the number of bright fringes inside the central maximum.

    1. \(\beta = \lambda D/d = 600\times 10^{-9}\times 2/(0.3\times 10^{-3}) = 4.0\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 4.0\ \mathrm{mm}\).
    2. The central maximum extends one fringe width beyond the central maximum on either side, so its width is \(2\beta = 8.0\ \mathrm{mm}\).
    3. Within this width the bright fringes are those at \(x = 0, \pm\beta\), so there are three bright fringes.
    4. The dark fringes inside the central maximum lie at \(x = \pm\beta/2 = \pm 2.0\ \mathrm{mm}\), exactly halfway between the bright ones.

    Answer: Fringe width \(\beta = 4.0\ \mathrm{mm}\), central maximum width \(8.0\ \mathrm{mm}\), and three bright fringes inside the central maximum.

    Example 2.

    In a Young's double-slit experiment the fringe width is 0.5 mm when the screen is at 1 m with the original slit separation. Find the fringe width when (a) the screen is moved to 1.5 m, (b) the slit separation is increased 1.5 times, and (c) the whole apparatus is immersed in water of refractive index 4/3.

    1. (a) Since \(\beta \propto D\), \(\beta_1 = 0.5\times 1.5/1.0 = 0.75\ \mathrm{mm}\).
    2. (b) Since \(\beta \propto 1/d\), \(\beta_2 = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333\ \mathrm{mm}\).
    3. (c) In water the wavelength becomes \(\lambda/1.5\), so \(\beta_3 = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333\ \mathrm{mm}\).
    4. Note that cases (b) and (c) give the same numerical answer but for different physical reasons, which is a favourite trap in JEE questions.
    5. A quick check on (c) uses the fact that the speed in water is \(c/(4/3) = 0.75c\), so the wavelength falls by a factor of 1.5 while the frequency is unchanged.

    Answer: (a) \(0.75\ \mathrm{mm}\); (b) \(0.333\ \mathrm{mm}\); (c) \(0.333\ \mathrm{mm}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Claiming the fringe width changes with the order of the fringe
    • Forgetting that the wavelength changes when the apparatus is immersed, which multiplies \(\beta\) by \(1/n_m\)
    • Using the new screen distance with the original slit separation, or the reverse
    • Confusing the width of the central maximum (\(2\beta\)) with the fringe width (\(\beta\))

    Explanation

    Concept. Path difference is the algebraic difference of the two distances from the coherent sources to the observation point, and it is the only quantity needed to decide whether a point is bright, dark or partially illuminated. Converting it into a phase through \(\phi = 2\pi\Delta/\lambda\) and then into intensity through \(\cos\phi\) is the entire computational core of interference. The JEE insight is to compute the path difference first and only then decide the fringe, because the odd-half-wavelength form of the minimum condition is where most solutions slip.
    Key formula(s). \[\Delta = S_2P-S_1P = d\sin\theta \approx \frac{dx}{D}\]; \[\phi = \frac{2\pi\Delta}{\lambda}\]; \[\text{maximum: } \Delta = n\lambda\]; \[\text{minimum: } \Delta = \left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\lambda\]
    Key points.
    • In a double-slit arrangement \(\Delta = d\sin\theta\) exactly and \(\Delta = dx/D\) in the paraxial approximation.
    • Bright fringes satisfy \(\Delta = n\lambda\) and dark fringes \(\Delta = (2n+1)\lambda/2\), with \(n = 0,1,2,\ldots\).
    • A phase difference of one full cycle, \(2\pi\), corresponds to exactly one fringe, or a path difference of one wavelength.
    • A thin film, a glass plate, or a mirror all add a fixed extra optical path, and hence shift rather than blur the pattern.
    • A film of thickness \(t\) and index \(\mu\) adds \(2\mu t\) of optical path for near-normal reflection, and the \(\pi\) reversal at the top surface must still be included.
    • A prism placed in one path adds an optical path proportional to \((\mu-1)A\) over the angular width it subtends.
    Example 1.

    In a Young's double-slit experiment with slit separation 0.5 mm, screen distance 1 m and wavelength 500 nm, find the path difference at a point 1 mm from the central maximum and state the nature of that point.

    1. Using the paraxial form, \(\Delta = dx/D = 0.5\times 10^{-3}\times 1\times 10^{-3}/1 = 5\times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}\).
    2. In wavelengths, \(\Delta/\lambda = 5\times 10^{-7}/5\times 10^{-7} = 1\), so the path difference is exactly one wavelength.
    3. Since \(\Delta = n\lambda\) with \(n=1\), the point is a bright first-order maximum.
    4. Its position also satisfies \(x = n\beta\) with \(\beta = \lambda D/d = 1.0\ \mathrm{mm}\), so \(x = 1\ \mathrm{mm}\), confirming the result.

    Answer: \(\Delta = 5\times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m} = \lambda\), and the point is the first-order bright maximum.

    Example 2.

    A thin transparent film of thickness 1.2 micrometres and refractive index 1.5 is surrounded by air, and light of wavelength 600 nm is incident normally. Considering the two reflected beams, find whether the reflected light is constructive or destructive and the condition in general.

    1. The reflection at the upper surface, air to glass, is from a rarer to a denser medium and introduces a phase change of \(\pi\).
    2. The reflection at the lower surface, glass to air, is from a denser to a rarer medium and introduces no phase change, so there is exactly one reversal.
    3. The optical path difference is \(2\mu t = 2\times 1.5\times 1.2 = 3.6\ \mathrm{\mu m} = 6\lambda\).
    4. With one reversal, constructive reflection requires \(2\mu t = (2n+1)\lambda/2\), and destructive reflection requires \(2\mu t = n\lambda\).
    5. Here \(2\mu t = 6\lambda\) corresponds to \(n = 6\) in the destructive condition, so the reflected beams cancel completely and the film appears dark in reflection.

    Answer: The reflected light is completely destructive (dark), since \(2\mu t = 6\lambda = n\lambda\) with one phase reversal.

    Common mistakes.
    • Writing the minimum condition as \(n\lambda/2\) instead of \((2n+1)\lambda/2\)
    • Using the geometrical path \(2t\) in a film instead of the optical path \(2\mu t\)
    • Forgetting the \(\pi\) reversal at the air-glass surface, which swaps the constructive and destructive conditions
    • Using \(dx/D\) without checking that the paraxial approximation is valid

    Explanation

    Concept. Phase difference is the difference between the arguments of two oscillations evaluated at the same time, and it controls whether the waves reinforce or oppose one another. For coherent waves of equal frequency, this difference remains constant in time and may arise from a path difference, an initial phase offset, or both. Since phase is defined modulo \(2\pi\), it should always be reduced to the principal interval before applying interference conditions.
    Key formula(s). \[y_i=a\sin(\omega t+\phi_i),\qquad \Delta\phi=(\phi_2-\phi_1)_0\]; \[\Delta\phi=\mathbf{k}_2\cdot\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{k}_1\cdot\mathbf{r}+(\phi_{02}-\phi_{01})\]; for equal intensities \(I_0\), \[I=4I_0\cos^2\left(\frac{\Delta\phi}{2}\right)=2I_0[1+\cos(\Delta\phi)]\]
    Key points.
    • For co-propagating coherent waves, a path difference \(\Delta r\) produces \(\Delta\phi=2\pi\Delta r/\lambda\); a time delay \(\Delta t\) gives \(2\pi\Delta t/T\).
    • Constructive interference occurs when \(\Delta\phi=2m\pi\), while destructive interference occurs when \(\Delta\phi=(2m+1)\pi\), where \(m\in\mathbb Z\).
    • A path change of \(\lambda/2\) and \(3\lambda/2\) changes phase by \(\pi\) and \(3\pi\), respectively; a full \(\lambda\) changes it by \(2\pi\).
    • Coherence requires equal frequency and a time-independent phase relation; ordinary independent sources are not coherent.
    • Only the principal phase difference matters because \(\cos(\Delta\phi+2m\pi)=\cos\Delta\phi\).
    • For unequal intensities \(I_1\) and \(I_2\), the interference term is \(2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\Delta\phi\), not \(2(I_1+I_2)\cos\Delta\phi\).
    Example 1.

    Two coherent waves, each of amplitude \(5.0\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}\), have an initial phase difference of \(120^\circ\). Find their resultant amplitude and the resultant intensity relative to the intensity of either wave alone.

    1. The initial phase difference is \(\Delta\phi=120^\circ=2\pi/3\).
    2. Two equal-amplitude waves superpose to give \(A_R=2a\cos(\Delta\phi/2)\).
    3. Hence \(A_R=2(5.0\times10^{-7})\cos60^\circ=5.0\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so \(I_R/I_0=(A_R/a)^2=1\).

    Answer: The resultant amplitude is \(5.0\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}\), and the resultant intensity equals the intensity of either incident wave.

    Example 2.

    Two coherent sources are initially in phase and emit \(600\,\mathrm{nm}\) light. At point \(P\), one ray has travelled \(0.300\,\mathrm{mm}\) more than the other; at point \(Q\), the path difference is \(0.600\,\mathrm{mm}\). Find the phase lag of the longer-path wave at each point and its change from \(P\) to \(Q\), and classify both points.

    1. At \(P\), the additional path is \(\Delta r_P=0.300\,\mathrm{mm}=3.00\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}\).
    2. Its phase lag is \(\Delta\phi_P=2\pi\Delta r_P/\lambda=2\pi(3.00\times10^{-4})/(6.00\times10^{-7})=\pi\).
    3. At \(Q\), \(\Delta\phi_Q=2\pi(6.00\times10^{-4})/(6.00\times10^{-7})=2\pi\).
    4. The phase lag increases by \(2\pi-\pi=\pi\) when the path difference increases by \(300\,\mathrm{nm}=\lambda/2\).
    5. An odd multiple of \(\pi\) gives destructive interference at \(P\), while an even multiple gives constructive interference at \(Q\).

    Answer: The lags are \(\pi\) at \(P\) and \(2\pi\) at \(Q\); the change is \(+\pi\), so \(P\) is dark and \(Q\) is bright.

    Common mistakes.
    • Do not use a phase difference of \(5\pi\) as distinct from \(\pi\), since phases differing by \(2m\pi\) are equivalent.
    • Do not compare path differences directly; first convert them to phase using \(2\pi\Delta r/\lambda\).
    • Do not apply the equal-intensity formula \(4I_0\cos^2(\Delta\phi/2)\) when the two wave intensities are unequal.

    Chapter 21 · Topic 6

    Coherent sources

    Wave OpticsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsWavefront and InterferenceStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Two sources are coherent when they emit waves of the same frequency whose phase difference does not change with time, so that the interference pattern they produce is stationary. Ordinary independent emitters fail this test because their phase wanders randomly on a timescale of roughly \(10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s}\), far faster than the eye can follow, so any pattern is washed out. Every practical interference experiment therefore divides a single original source into two beams. The JEE insight is that equal frequency is necessary but not sufficient, and that the constancy of phase is the actual defining condition.
    Key formula(s). \[\Delta\phi = \phi_1-\phi_2 = (\omega t+\phi_{01})-(\omega t+\phi_{02}) = \phi_{01}-\phi_{02} = \text{constant}\]; \[\phi_1 = 2\pi f t + \phi_{01},\ \phi_2 = 2\pi f t + \phi_{02}\]; \[\Delta = d\sin\theta\]
    Key points.
    • Sustained interference needs same frequency, constant phase difference, and intensities that are not too unequal.
    • Independent sources are incoherent: their phase changes randomly in about \(10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s}\), while the eye's persistence is about \(1/16\ \mathrm{s}\), so only an average intensity is seen.
    • A single source plus a beam splitter, or a single source illuminating two slits, guarantees coherence because the two beams share a common origin.
    • Two speakers driven by the same oscillator are coherent, while two tuning forks of the same nominal pitch are not.
    • Even perfectly coherent beams show no visible fringes if one is far weaker, since the visibility then tends to zero.
    • Spatial coherence also requires the two beams to have travelled comparable paths, so an extended source limits the useful slit separation.
    Example 1.

    Two coherent sources emitting in phase waves of wavelength 1 m and of equal amplitudes are placed 2 m apart. Find the path difference and the intensity at a point \(P\) on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them, and then find the intensity at \(P\) if one source alone gives intensity \(I_0\) and the second source is shifted by a phase of \(\pi\).

    1. On the perpendicular bisector the two distances are equal, so the path difference is \(\Delta = 0\).
    2. Each source alone gives \(I_0\), so the amplitudes are \(\sqrt{I_0}\) and \(\sqrt{I_0}\) and they are initially in phase.
    3. Constructive interference gives \(I = I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2} = 2I_0+2I_0 = 4I_0\).
    4. Shifting the second source by \(\pi\) makes the two waves exactly out of phase, so the interference term is \(-2\sqrt{I_1I_2} = -2I_0\).
    5. The new intensity is \(I = 2I_0-2I_0 = 0\); since the amplitudes are equal the cancellation is complete.

    Answer: Initially the path difference is zero and the intensity is \(4I_0\); after a phase shift of \(\pi\) the intensity at \(P\) is zero.

    Example 2.

    Two coherent sources of equal amplitude, frequency 500 Hz and wavelength 1 m, are placed 3 m apart. Find the number of maxima and the number of minima on the line joining the two sources, and hence their ratio.

    1. On the line joining the sources, with light travelling from \(S_1\) to \(S_2\), the path difference varies from \(-d\) to \(+d\), i.e. from \(-3\ \mathrm{m}\) to \(+3\ \mathrm{m}\).
    2. Maxima occur where \(\Delta = n\lambda = n\) metres, so \(n = -3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\), giving seven maxima.
    3. Minima occur where \(\Delta = (2n+1)\lambda/2 = 0.5, 1.5, 2.5\) metres in magnitude, giving six minima.
    4. The end points \(\Delta = \pm 3\ \mathrm{m} = \pm 3\lambda\) are maxima, not minima, which is a common slip.
    5. The ratio is therefore \(7:6\), one more maximum than minima, as it must be on any line of odd integer length in wavelengths.

    Answer: Seven maxima and six minima, in the ratio \(7:6\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Treating two sources of equal frequency as automatically coherent
    • Ignoring the loss of visibility when the two intensities are very unequal
    • Counting the endpoints as minima in the line-joining-sources counting problem
    • Forgetting that spatial coherence also requires the two beams to have travelled comparable optical paths

    Chapter 21 · Topic 7

    Diffraction

    Wave OpticsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsDiffraction and PolarizationStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Diffraction is the spreading of a wavefront into the geometrical shadow region because every point of a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets. It becomes significant when the dimensions of an obstacle or aperture are comparable to the wavelength, as in optical diffraction. A sharp ray-optics shadow is therefore only an approximation, and the diffraction pattern depends on aperture size, wavelength, and distance from the screen.
    Key formula(s). \[\theta_1\simeq\frac{\lambda}{a}\quad\text{for a slit or obstacle of width }a\]; for a circular aperture of diameter \(D\), \[\sin\theta_1=1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}\]
    Key points.
    • Diffraction and interference are both wave phenomena, but diffraction concerns spreading from finite apertures or obstacles and interference concerns superposition of distinct coherent contributions.
    • For a fixed wavelength, a narrower obstacle or aperture produces a wider angular diffraction pattern.
    • The angular spread is inversely proportional to the characteristic aperture dimension, so optical diffraction is usually small but measurable.
    • Fresnel diffraction occurs when Fresnel number \(F=a^2/(\lambda D)\) is not negligible, whereas Fraunhofer diffraction requires \(F\ll1\).
    • A circular aperture gives an Airy pattern with central maximum of finite width and surrounding rings, not the sinc-squared pattern of a straight slit.
    • A smaller wavelength gives sharper diffraction and improved spatial resolution, a principle used in microscopes and telescopes.
    Example 1.

    A thin wire of diameter \(0.100\,\mathrm{mm}\) is placed in a path of \(500\,\mathrm{nm}\) light. Estimate the angular position of the first diffraction minimum and the width of the central maximum on a screen \(1.00\,\mathrm{m}\) away.

    1. For a thin wire, diffraction occurs by Babinet's principle with effective slit width \(a=1.00\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}\).
    2. The first minimum satisfies \(a\sin\theta_1=\lambda\).
    3. Since \(\lambda/a=5.00\times10^{-3}\ll1\), use \(\sin\theta_1\simeq\theta_1\), giving \(\theta_1=5.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}\).
    4. The first minima occur on opposite sides, so the central width is \(2D\theta_1=2(1.00)(5.00\times10^{-3})=1.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The first minimum is at \(5.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}\) from the axis, and the central maximum has width \(10.0\,\mathrm{mm}\).

    Example 2.

    Light of wavelength \(632.8\,\mathrm{nm}\) passes through a circular aperture of diameter \(1.00\,\mathrm{mm}\). Find the angular diameter of the central Airy maximum and its width on a screen \(2.00\,\mathrm{m}\) from the aperture.

    1. For a circular aperture, the first Airy minimum obeys \(\sin\theta_1=1.22\lambda/D\).
    2. Here \(1.22\lambda/D=1.22(6.328\times10^{-7})/(1.00\times10^{-3})=7.72\times10^{-4}\), so \(\theta_1\simeq7.72\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{rad}\).
    3. The angular diameter between the two first minima is \(2\theta_1=1.544\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}\).
    4. With the small-angle approximation, the diameter on the screen is \(W=2D\theta_1=2(2.00)(7.72\times10^{-4})=3.09\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The central Airy maximum has angular diameter \(1.54\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}\) and screen width \(3.09\,\mathrm{mm}\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Do not confuse the angular width between the first minima with the position of one first minimum.
    • Do not use the circular-aperture factor \(1.22\) for a slit or thin wire.
    • Do not use \(x=D\tan\theta\) without checking the small-angle approximation.

    Chapter 21 · Topic 8

    Single-slit diffraction

    Wave OpticsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsDiffraction and PolarizationStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. In Fraunhofer diffraction by a single slit, contributions from the width of the slit superpose to produce a broad central maximum and weaker secondary maxima. The relative phase changes across the aperture, so division of the slit into halves or other zones reveals the conditions for minima and maxima. In JEE problems, locating the zeros of this envelope and then locating interference maxima within it is the central technique.
    Key formula(s). \[I(\theta)=I_0\left(\frac{\sin\beta}{\beta}\right)^2,\qquad \beta=\frac{\pi a\sin\theta}{\lambda}\]; minima: \[a\sin\theta_m=m\lambda,\qquad m=\pm1,\pm2,\ldots\]; \[\Delta x_1=\frac{D\lambda}{a},\qquad W_{\mathrm{central}}=\frac{2D\lambda}{a}\]
    Key points.
    • The central maximum extends from the first minimum on one side to the first minimum on the other and is twice as wide as every other principal region.
    • The central intensity is approximately four times the first secondary maximum intensity for a single slit.
    • Secondary maxima are not exactly midway between adjacent minima; their exact condition is \(\tan\beta=\beta\).
    • The central solution \(\beta=0\) is a maximum by the limiting value; the other zeros satisfy \(\beta=m\pi\) and give minima.
    • In a double-slit experiment, interference maxima at \(d\sin\theta=n\lambda\) are missing when they coincide with single-slit minima \(a\sin\theta=m\lambda\).
    • If \(d/a\) is an integer \(p\), every \(p\)th interference maximum is missing.
    Example 1.

    Monochromatic light of wavelength \(500\,\mathrm{nm}\) is incident normally on a slit of width \(0.200\,\mathrm{mm}\). Find the angular position of the first minimum and the width of the central diffraction maximum on a screen \(2.00\,\mathrm{m}\) away.

    1. The first minimum obeys \(a\sin\theta_1=\lambda\).
    2. Thus \(\sin\theta_1=(5.00\times10^{-7})/(2.00\times10^{-4})=2.50\times10^{-3}\), giving \(\theta_1\simeq2.50\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}\).
    3. The first minimum on either side is at \(x_1=D\tan\theta_1\simeq D\theta_1=5.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\).
    4. Therefore the full central width is \(W=2x_1=1.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}\).

    Answer: The first minima are at \(2.50\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}\), and the central maximum is \(10.0\,\mathrm{mm}\) wide.

    Example 2.

    In a Fraunhofer double-slit experiment, each slit has width \(a=0.100\,\mathrm{mm}\) and the centre-to-centre separation is \(d=0.400\,\mathrm{mm}\). For \(\lambda=500\,\mathrm{nm}\) and screen distance \(D=1.00\,\mathrm{m}\), locate the first diffraction minimum, the first interference maximum on one side, and count the observable interference maxima inside the central diffraction maximum.

    1. The first single-slit minimum is at \(x_{\mathrm{diff}}=\lambda D/a=(5.00\times10^{-7})(1.00)/(1.00\times10^{-4})=5.00\,\mathrm{mm}\).
    2. The first double-slit interference maximum is at \(x_{\mathrm{int}}=\lambda D/d=(5.00\times10^{-7})(1.00)/(4.00\times10^{-4})=1.25\,\mathrm{mm}\).
    3. Interference maxima satisfy \(n=\lambda D/(dx)\), while being inside the central envelope requires \(|x|<5.00\,\mathrm{mm}\).
    4. Hence \(|n|<d/a=4\), giving integer orders \(n=-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\); orders \(n=\pm4\) coincide with the first minima and are missing.
    5. Thus the central envelope contains seven observable bright fringes, including the central one.

    Answer: \(x_{\mathrm{diff}}=5.00\,\mathrm{mm}\), \(x_{\mathrm{int}}=1.25\,\mathrm{mm}\), and the number of observable maxima inside the central maximum is \(7\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Do not include \(m=0\) among diffraction minima, because \(\beta=0\) gives the central maximum.
    • Do not confuse slit width \(a\) with slit separation \(d\) in a double-slit calculation.
    • Do not count interference orders that coincide with single-slit diffraction zeros.

    Chapter 21 · Topic 9

    Polarization

    Wave OpticsElectromagnetic Waves and OpticsDiffraction and PolarizationStep-by-step Topic

    Topic in Depth

    Explanation

    Concept. Polarization describes the transverse electric-field pattern of light and provides direct experimental evidence that light is transverse. Linearly polarized light has a fixed oscillation direction, while circularly and elliptically polarized light have rotating field vectors. Unpolarized light has no stable direction over an observation time, and partially polarized light lies between linear polarization and complete unpolarization.
    Key formula(s). \[I_{\mathrm{analyser}}=I_0\cos^2\theta\] for a linearly polarized incident wave; for orthogonal components with relative phase \(\delta\), \[I=I_x\cos^2\theta+I_y\sin^2\theta+2\sqrt{I_xI_y}\sin\theta\cos\theta\cos\delta\]; unpolarized light gives \[\langle I_{\mathrm{analyser}}\rangle=\frac{I_0}{2}\]
    Key points.
    • A polarizer transmits one electric-field component and absorbs or reflects the perpendicular component; an analyser is a polarizer used to measure existing polarization.
    • Rotating a linear analyser through \(360^\circ\) gives intensity period \(180^\circ\).
    • Two perpendicular equal-amplitude components in phase produce linear polarization at \(45^\circ\); a phase difference of \(\pi/2\) produces circular polarization, and other nonzero phase differences produce elliptical polarization.
    • In circular polarization the electric-field magnitude is constant, whereas in elliptical polarization it varies periodically.
    • An ideal analyser transmits half the intensity of unpolarized light for every orientation.
    • Superposition of coherent orthogonal components requires their relative phase, so their projected intensities can include an interference cross term.
    Example 1.

    A beam of intensity \(I_0\) is linearly polarized along a direction making \(30^\circ\) with the vertical. Find the fractions of incident intensity associated with its vertical and horizontal electric-field components.

    1. The vertical component is \(E_v=E_0\cos30^\circ\), so \(I_v=I_0\cos^230^\circ=3I_0/4\).
    2. The horizontal component is \(E_h=E_0\sin30^\circ\), so \(I_h=I_0\sin^230^\circ=I_0/4\).
    3. Their intensities add because the two components are orthogonal, and \(3I_0/4+I_0/4=I_0\).
    4. Thus the two projections account for the entire incident intensity, with no energy assigned to another transverse direction.

    Answer: The vertical and horizontal components carry \(3I_0/4\) and \(I_0/4\), respectively.

    Example 2.

    The principal perpendicular electric-field components of an elliptically polarized beam have intensities \(4I_0\) and \(I_0\) and are \(90^\circ\) out of phase. An ideal analyser is placed at \(30^\circ\) to the stronger component. Find the transmitted intensity and state whether the emerging light is linearly or elliptically polarized.

    1. Let the strong component be along \(x\) and the weak component along \(y\); the analyser is at \(\theta=30^\circ\) to \(x\).
    2. Since \(\cos\delta=\cos90^\circ=0\), the cross term vanishes and \(I=I_x\cos^230^\circ+I_y\sin^230^\circ\).
    3. Substitution gives \(I=4I_0(3/4)+I_0(1/4)=13I_0/4\).
    4. The emerging direction is a single fixed linear direction because an ideal linear analyser selects one field direction.
    5. The unequal principal-component intensities imply that the original beam was elliptically, not circularly, polarized.

    Answer: The analyser transmits \(13I_0/4\), and the emerging light is linearly polarized along the analyser axis.

    Common mistakes.
    • Do not use Malus' law directly for unpolarized light; an ideal analyser first reduces its intensity to \(I_0/2\).
    • Do not infer circular polarization unless the two orthogonal components have equal amplitudes and a phase difference of \(90^\circ\).
    • Do not reverse the roles of \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) without redefining the reference axis.

    Explanation

    Concept. Malus' law gives the intensity transmitted by an ideal linear analyser when incident light is already linearly polarized. It follows from projecting the electric-field amplitude onto the transmission axis, after which intensity is proportional to the square of that amplitude. In a sequence of polarizers, the law must be applied once for every analyser whose orientation changes the polarization.
    Key formula(s). \[I=I_0\cos^2\theta\]; for \(N\) ideal polaroids starting with unpolarized light, \[I_{\mathrm{final}}=\frac{I_0}{2}\prod_{k=2}^{N}\cos^2(\theta_k-\theta_{k-1})\]
    Key points.
    • The angle \(\theta\) is between the incident polarization direction and the analyser axis, not the angle between the analyser and the screen.
    • At \(\theta=0^\circ\), all polarized intensity is transmitted; at \(\theta=90^\circ\), an ideal crossed analyser gives zero intensity.
    • Rotating the analyser through \(180^\circ\) restores the same intensity.
    • Doubling the angle does not generally halve the intensity; for example, \(60^\circ\) transmits one quarter, while \(30^\circ\) transmits three quarters.
    • For unpolarized light, no orientation-dependent \(\cos^2\theta\) factor applies before the first ideal polarizer.
    • Inserting an additional polarizer at \(45^\circ\) between crossed polarizers produces light instead of extinction.
    Example 1.

    Unpolarized light of intensity \(8.00\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}\) passes through two ideal polarizers whose axes are at \(30^\circ\) and then \(45^\circ\) relative to the first. Find the final intensity.

    1. The first polarizer transmits half the unpolarized intensity: \(I_1=8.00/2=4.00\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}\).
    2. The relative angle for the second polarizer is \(45^\circ-30^\circ=15^\circ\).
    3. Apply Malus' law: \(I_2=I_1\cos^215^\circ\).
    4. Numerically, \(I_2=4.00(0.9330)=3.73\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}\).

    Answer: The final intensity is \(3.73\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}\).

    Example 2.

    Two ideal polarizers are crossed. A third ideal polarizer is inserted between them at an angle \(\theta\) to the first. Show the intensity as a fraction of the original unpolarized intensity and find its maximum.

    1. After the first polarizer, the incident intensity is \(I_0/2\).
    2. The third polarizer is at \(\theta\) to the first, giving \(I_a=(I_0/2)\cos^2\theta\).
    3. The final polarizer is at \(90^\circ\) to the first, hence at \(90^\circ-\theta\) to the third, giving \(I=(I_0/2)\cos^2\theta\cos^2(90^\circ-\theta)\).
    4. Since \(\cos(90^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta\), \(I/I_0=(1/2)\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta=(1/8)\sin^22\theta\).
    5. This is maximum for \(2\theta=90^\circ\), so \(\theta=45^\circ\), and the maximum fraction is \(1/8\).

    Answer: \(I=(I_0/8)\sin^22\theta\), with maximum \(I_{\max}=I_0/8\) when the inserted polarizer is at \(45^\circ\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Do not apply \(\cos^2\theta\) to unpolarized light before the first polarizer.
    • Do not use the original angle for every polarizer; use the angle between consecutive polarization directions.
    • Do not assume three polarizers always extinguish light; the middle one changes the polarization before the last one.

    Explanation

    Concept. A polaroid is a practical linear polarizer made from a sheet containing aligned dichroic molecules or aligned microscopic crystals. The long molecular axis preferentially absorbs one electric-field component, so the emerging light is polarized along the transmission axis. Real polaroids do not transmit one component perfectly and do not absorb the other perfectly, which explains residual light in nominally crossed polaroids.
    Key formula(s). for \(n\) ideal polaroids applied to unpolarized light, \[I_n=\frac{I_0}{2}\prod_{k=2}^{n}\cos^2(\theta_k-\theta_{k-1})\]; extinction ratio is \[\eta=\frac{I_{\mathrm{parallel}}}{I_{\mathrm{crossed}}}\]
    Key points.
    • The transmission axis, not the polaroid's geometrical long or short edge, defines its polarization direction.
    • For real crossed polaroids, \(I_{\mathrm{crossed}}>0\) because of imperfect extinction and imperfect optical quality.
    • A pair of ideal crossed polaroids transmits zero light; inserting any non-axis-aligned ideal polarizer between them restores some light.
    • For \(N\) ideal polaroids applied to an initial unpolarized beam, the total intensity is found by multiplying one initial factor \(1/2\) and all squared angular factors.
    • Rotating one polaroid through \(180^\circ\) repeats the same intensity sequence.
    • Polaroid sunglasses reduce glare because reflected light from many smooth surfaces is at least partially polarized.
    Example 1.

    Unpolarized light of intensity \(I_0\) passes through three ideal polaroids whose transmission axes are at \(0^\circ\), \(30^\circ\), and \(90^\circ\). Find the final intensity.

    1. The first polarizer transmits \(I_0/2\) and establishes linear polarization at \(0^\circ\).
    2. From \(0^\circ\) to \(30^\circ\), the second transmits the factor \(\cos^230^\circ=3/4\).
    3. From \(30^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\), the third transmits \(\cos^260^\circ=1/4\).
    4. Therefore \(I=(I_0/2)(3/4)(1/4)=3I_0/32\).

    Answer: The final intensity is \(3I_0/32\).

    Example 2.

    Two ideal polaroids are crossed, and a third is inserted at angle \(\theta\) to the first. Derive the transmitted intensity and find both the position and value of its maximum relative to the original unpolarized intensity.

    1. The first polarizer reduces the original intensity \(I_0\) to \(I_0/2\).
    2. The inserted polarizer transmits a factor \(\cos^2\theta\).
    3. The last polarizer, perpendicular to the first, is at \(90^\circ-\theta\) to the inserted one and transmits \(\cos^2(90^\circ-\theta)=\sin^2\theta\).
    4. Hence \(I=(I_0/2)\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta=(I_0/8)\sin^22\theta\).
    5. Since \(\sin^22\theta\) is maximum at \(2\theta=90^\circ\), the optimum angle is \(\theta=45^\circ\), where \(\sin^22\theta=1\).

    Answer: \(I=(I_0/8)\sin^22\theta\), and \(I_{\max}=I_0/8\) at \(\theta=45^\circ\).

    Common mistakes.
    • Do not identify a polaroid's transmission axis with its physical edge without given calibration.
    • Do not expect exact extinction with a poor-quality real polaroid.
    • Do not omit the factor \(1/2\) when the original light is unpolarized.
